News.title: Heinz makes major change to its iconic soup range after 116 years
News.content:
Heinz makes major change to its iconic soup range after 116 years

The food giant has announced a big change to its soup line-up that customers will notice almost immediately in Tesco and online at Ocado

View 2 Images Tins of Heinz soup have been a UK staple for 116 years

Heinz is making a major change to its soup range more than 100 years after it first introduced cans to British shelves.

‌



‌



After bringing tomato soup to Britain in 1910, Heinz’s cans of soup have been a ubiquitous sight on the shelves, in cupboards, and on office desks across the country. But that’s about to change.

‌



The company has now started to sell a range of soups in plastic pouches, marketing them as “ready-to-eat recipes”. Unlike metal tins, the plastic “bags” can be microwaved without first decanting the soup into a microwave-safe bowl.

‌



Making it easier to warm up soup was the motivation for shaking up the product, Alessandra de Dreuille, Heinz’s director of meals said. She told Metro: “Heinz has always been committed to making mealtimes easier without compromising on great flavours.

“We wanted to create something new that combines the comfort of a bowl of soup with natural ingredients and a convenient format for busy lifestyles. With four delicious recipes to choose from, our new range offers a simple way to enjoy a warming and nutritious meal, at home or on the go.”

‌



View 2 Images The new pouches are being marketed for people with busy lives

The four flavours sold in pouches are Butternut Squash & Spices, Chicken Broth & Garden Veg, Black Lentil Dhal, and Roasted Red Pepper & Tomato. The bags were introduced to Canada last month as the company made its “first entry into Canada’s ready-to-eat soup category”.

‌



In the UK, soup fans eager to try the new pouches can find them online at Ocado or on the shelves at Tesco. They retail for £2.25 per 350g pouch.

It does not appear to be the beginning of the end for Heinz metal cans as the company has not suggested they will be phased out.

Article continues below

Soup tins are typically made from steel, rather than the aluminium used for canned rinks. However, both metals can be recycled indefinitely without loss of quality, unlike plastic.

News.title: Donald Trump lashes out at Republican 'loser' in tantrum over Hegseth impeachment attempt
News.content:
Donald Trump lashes out at Republican 'loser' in tantrum over Hegseth impeachment attempt

The impeachment attempt comes after a major loss for the Republican Party last week, and although Pete Hegseth was saved from impeachment on Tuesday, attempts may be made again in January

View 2 Images Trump has backed Hegseth in social media post (Image: Getty Images)

US President Donald Trump has lashed out at Democrats, and a member of his own Republican Party, after an attempt to impeach his defence chief.

‌



‌



The impeachment attempt comes after a major loss for Mr Trump. Republicans lost both the House and the Senate to Democrats last week in the midterm elections as voters made their opposition Mr Trump - and effectively Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's - war known.

‌



Mr Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Tuesday: "The Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!

‌



"Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete."

View 2 Images Pete Hegseth has defended the Iran war (Image: AP Photo/Nathan Howard)

Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky on Monday moved to force a vote to impeach Mr Hegseth, largely over his execution of the war, but his motion proved unsuccessful the following day.

‌



Republicans in the House blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Mr Hegseth, but he is not yet safe. Democrats will take control of Congress next year and possibly try again.

Democrats sang support for impeachment articles. The articles accuse the defense secretary of the "high crimes and misdemeanors" of illegally ordering the military to wage war ⁠in Iran and Yemen, attack boats in the Caribbean Sea, and capture Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro at the start of the year, Reuters reports.

‌



The elections last week highlighted American dissatisfaction over the eight-month-old war, which has led to a surge in fuel prices and impacted the US economy as well as global markets.

Mr Hegseth has been one of the administration's most prominent defenders of the war. Critics have long said the war was launched without proper authorization, but now Mr Hegseth has come under renewed fire.

Article continues below

Mr Trump's rant continued: "Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.

"The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped! MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN. President DONALD J. TRUMP"

News.title: Mum smothered baby to death in Birmingham home, manslaughter trial told
News.content:
Mum smothered baby to death in Birmingham home, manslaughter trial told

Yunus Rezaie was only 14 months old when he died - his mother, Hafiza Safi, has been accused of his manslaughter but deemed unfit to stand trial at Birmingham Crown Court

View 2 Images Police at Laxey Road in Edgbaston in April 2022 (Image: BirminghamLive/Harry Leach)

A mum 'smothered' her baby son to death inside their Birmingham home, a court has been told. One-year-old Yunus Rezaie was tragically found dead on Laxey Road, in the suburb of Edgbaston, on April 16, 2022.

‌



‌



Paramedics and police had been called by dad Abdullah Rezaie when he got home from work. Yunus' mother, Hafiza Safi, had been with him all day.

‌



A court heard on Tuesday the infant's injuries were consistent with smothering, Birmingham Live reports. It's alleged Safi killed her baby while she was mentally unwell.

‌



The 29-year-old has been charged with manslaughter - but has been deemed unfit to stand trial. The jury at Birmingham Crown Court will not be asked to decide whether Safi is guilty or not, but instead whether she was 'responsible for doing the acts' which caused Yunus's death.

Opening the case prosecutor Richard Atkins KC said: "This is a tragic case. It concerns the death of a young child, Yunus Rezaie, who the prosecution say was killed by his mother, Hafiza Safi, on April 16, 2022, when he was 14 months old."

The prosecutor told the court that Yunus's father left the home for work shortly after 3am that day and returned at 7.46pm. He said the only other adults present at the address throughout the day apart from Safi were her brother-in-law and a gas engineer he let into the home at 3.30pm for a 20-minute inspection.

‌



It is believed Yunus was still alive at that time. Mr Atkins said after Yunus's father came home at 7.46pm he called 999 at 7.53pm and paramedics attended within minutes.

He continued: "When paramedics arrived, they found Abdullah holding Yunus in his arms in the downstairs room. Hafiza was changing the nappy of an older child in the same room. It struck the paramedics how normally she was acting. She was oblivious to what was going on around her."

‌



View 2 Images Birmingham Crown Court, where proceedings are taking place (Image: BPM Media)

‌



The prosecutor stated Yunus had a fresh 'large abrasion' above his right eye as well as bruising to his head and blood around his mouth. He added: "He asked Abdullah to put him on the floor. He immediately realised Yunus was dead and it appeared to him he had been so for some time."

Mr Atkins stated rigor mortis had already set in to the boy's body. He was taken to Birmingham Children's Hospital where he was formally pronounced deceased.

‌



Mr Atkins told the court that Yunus had an 'uncommon pattern' of bruising for a child which led to 'suspicions of having been caused by inflicted injuries, not accidental'. He also said there was bruising to his neck and little bleeding to his face, commonly associated with pressure being applied to the neck.

While the prosecutor added that the injuries inside and outside of Yunus's mouth were 'indicative of smothering' - his mouth being covered. Mr Atkins said a pathologist concluded that his cause of death was 'interference with the mechanics of respiration', which means his airways being blocked.

‌



The home at Laxey Road was searched and bloodstained items of clothing belonging to Yunus and Safi were found in a bin in an upstairs bedroom as well as a washing basket in a downstairs bathroom.

The prosecutor concluded: "It all points, I'm afraid, to Hafiza Safi having smothered or asphyxiated Yunus while alone with him during the day while mentally unwell. She was arrested and taken to a police station but wasn't mentally well enough to be interviewed.

Article continues below

"We submit, having heard the evidence, you will be left in no doubt it was Hafiza Safi who was responsible for whatever acts led to Yunus's death."

The trial continues.

News.title: Trump slams BBC as ‘terrible abuser of the truth’ after judge rules on defamation lawsuit
News.content:
Trump slams BBC as ‘terrible abuser of the truth’ after judge rules on defamation lawsuit

Both the US president and the BBC have issued statements as the Trump-appointed judge has allowed the $10bn (£7.5 billion) defamation lawsuit against BBC to proceed

View 3 Images The BBC filed a motion to dismiss Mr Trump’s 10 billion dollar (£7.5 billion) defamation lawsuit (Image: Nathan Howard, Getty Images)

President Donald Trump has issued a statement after a federal judge ruled that his lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, partially denying the British national broadcaster's motion to dmiss the case.

Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz made the ruling on Tuesday that the president's $10bn (£7.5 billion) defamation lawsuit can continue.

Trump is seeking substantial damages in a Florida court over the editing of a 2024 Panorama documentary about the US Capitol riots. The documentary faced criticism for giving the impression Trump had encouraged his supporters to storm the Capitol building on January 6 2021 after he lost the 2020 White House race to Joe Biden.

The BBC had been seeking to have the case thrown out, warning of the “chilling effect” it would have on “robust reporting on public figures and events”.

View 3 Images US President Donald Trump (Image: PA Wire)

In a statement made on Truth Social, the president took to social media to hail the decision, saying: "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth, just handed down by highly respected District Court Judge, Jeffrey T. Kuntz, of the Southern District of Florida.

"In his powerful ruling, Judge Kuntz wrote, “Here, the news entity created the story. BBC admitted as much by confirming it had edited a video to make it appear as though President Trump made a statement he never made.”

"We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP"

A BBC spokesperson said in a statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process. It would be inappropriate to comment further while proceedings are ongoing.”

The allegations against the documentary led the then-BBC director-general Tim Davie to announce his resignation.

BBC chairman Samir Shah apologised on behalf of the broadcaster over an “error of judgment” and accepted the editing of the programme gave “the impression of a direct call for violent action”.

The BBC has been ordered to file a response to the ruling by December 1.

View 3 Images Trump flags fly as rioters take over the steps of the Capitol on January 6, 2021 (Image: CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

The Trump-appointed Florida district court judge, Jeffrey T Kuntz, wrote in his ruling: “Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm.

‌



“It would be difficult for the Court to accept a different framing without completely negating the significance and fragility of political elections.”

The ruling did not decide whether Mr Trump’s claims were proven.

‌



The judge said that “Trump’s allegations regarding BBC’s departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence”.

While the judge determined that Trump had “sufficiently pleaded” that the BBC acted with actual malice, the legal standard for a public figure to win a defamation case, he will have to actually prove they did so at trial.

Article continues below

The judge also dismissed Trump’s claim that the BBC violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. Judge Kuntz decided that the president will have to prove that he suffered “actual damages” from the airing of the document, which was not broadcast in Florida.

In late October, a Florida magistrate judge ruled that Trump will have to sit for a deposition conducted by lawyers for the BBC by December 11, or be hit with sanctions.

News.title: Thomas Markle seen in mugshot for first time after ‘cutting off electronic tag’
News.content:
Thomas Markle seen in mugshot for first time after ‘cutting off electronic tag’

Thomas Markle Snr was released on bail over child sexual abuse material charges but, days later, he is back in custody after allegedly cutting off his electronic monitoring tag

View 3 Images Meghan Markle’s father Thomas Markle Senior (Image: Pinellas County Sheriff's Office / BACKGRID)

The mugshot of Thomas Markle Snr has been released by police after he was remanded in custody after allegedly cutting off his electronic monitoring tag.

‌



‌



Thomas Markle Sr, 82, was arrested by FBI agents on Friday following the seizure of suspected child sexual abuse material from two Los Angeles storage units he had rented for almost two decades. He was granted bail on Friday on condition that he remain under house arrest, wear a location monitoring device and comply with travel restrictions imposed by a court in Tampa, Florida.

‌



He faces one federal charge of possessing child pornography. The investigation began after his son, Thomas Markle Jr, allegedly discovered illegal images among his father's belongings in Cebu City in the Philippines and reported the matter to local police and the FBI last month.

‌



View 3 Images If convicted, he faces a minimum of 20 years in federal prison. (Image: Channel 5)

US prosecutors said he allegedly removed the electronic bracelet at 1.45am, prompting an urgent application to have his bail revoked. Writing on X, first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said: “Four days ago, a federal judge allowed Mr Markle to remain out of custody pending trial. He was ordered to wear a location monitoring device. He allegedly cut the bracelet off at 1.45am last night. Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions.”

Prosecutors asked the court to detain Markle pending trial, saying they would continue to pursue the case to the fullest extent of the law.

‌



US Magistrate Judge Lindsay Saxe Griffin subsequently ordered him back into custody.

Acting under search warrants, FBI agents examined the two units, which had been rented by Markle since 2008, and seized around 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books containing suspected child sexual abuse material.

‌



The allegations have not been proven. Markle has denied possessing child sexual abuse material, although he has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines. If convicted, he faces a minimum of 20 years in federal prison.

View 3 Images Meghan Markle will co-operate with police in any investigation into her father, a source said

‌



Meghan Markle has said she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations. She previously revealed that she received a letter through the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection in 2019 containing what she described as “troubling and disturbing allegations” about her father.

She was reportedly assured the claims were being investigated.

Article continues below

However, the Metropolitan Police has admitted it did not pass the details to other law enforcement agencies. The Independent Office for Police Conduct is now investigating the force's handling of the matter.

News.title: NATO fighter jets scrambled in Latvia and Lithuania over ‘unidentified drones’
News.content:
NATO fighter jets scrambled in Latvia and Lithuania over ‘unidentified drones’

It is believed that drones entered the countries' airspace from neighbouring Russia or Belarus and people across several regions were warned to take shelter

View 3 Images It is believed that the drones entered the countries' airspace from neighbouring Russia or Belarus [file image] (Image: Getty Images)

People living in Latvia and Lithuania have been told to seek safety after threats of unidentified drones entering their airspace. It is believed that the drones entered the countries' airspace from neighbouring Russia or Belarus.

‌



‌



People across several regions were warned to take shelter on Wednesday. There have been no reports of any injuries.

‌



NATO air defence fighter jets have been activated in response to the security incident.

‌



View 3 Images NATO fighter jets have been scrambled (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre said its warning included the ⁠country's second city Kaunas. The city is home to around 300,000 people. Kaunas Airport had suspended operations, according to reports.

Code yellow was broadcast around 11pm. People in the counties of Vilnius and Utena were urged to head for their nearest shelter.

‌



The alert said: "The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: POSSIBLE AIR RAID ALERT (YELLOW). Find a safe place.

"If you see a suspicious object, keep away, call 112. Wait for the all-clear."

‌



The alert from Latvian authorities warned of a possible threat in the airspace of Jēkabpils and Madona municipalities.

The warning posted to X reads: "We are informing you of a possible threat in Latvia’s airspace.

‌



"No further action is currently required.

"If the situation changes, you will receive a cell broadcast notification about the action you need to take."

‌



Latvian authorities subsequently said: "We inform you that the threat to airspace in Madona Municipality has ended."

View 3 Images Fighter jets were activated [file] (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Ukrainian military drones have been straying into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

This has raised concern that the war is teetering into NATO countries that border Russia and its ally Belarus.

‌



Moscow has blamed Kyiv of using NATO airspace as cover for attacks. Kyiv, on the other hand, ⁠says some of its drones have been steered off course due to Russian signal jamming.

The NATO ⁠countries blame Russia for the incidents, saying it ignited the war.

Article continues below

Ukrainian attacks on ⁠Russian Baltic Sea oil shipping ports has seen some of its drones miss their targets. This has led to security warnings in neighbouring countries.

In Latvia, it led to a government collapse earlier this year.

News.title: Dad, 44, charged with sexual abuse after 'making his 10-year-old daughter his second wife'
News.content:
Dad, 44, charged with sexual abuse after 'making his 10-year-old daughter his second wife'

The 44-year-old man, from Eagle Mountain in Utah, now faces 22 charges after investigations by the police and child protection services - he has been remanded in custody

View 2 Images Eagle Mountain in Utah, where the man lived with his family

A father has been charged after allegedly sexually abusing his 10-year-old daughter as a “second wife”. The 44-year-old is now in custody.

Court documents say the man, from Eagle Mountain in Utah, “used his juvenile daughter as a second wife because his first wife was not providing him with what he needed”, reports ABC4 News. It’s alleged he touched the girl and took abusive photos of her.

He has been charged with 22 crimes. They include four counts of sodomy on a child, seven counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child, one count of aggravated sexual exploitation of a minor, nine counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, and one count of rape.

It’s understood the police probe ran at the same time as a child protection services’ investigation. They started after an adult family member reportedly saw child abuse images on a device owned by the 44-year-old man.

View 2 Images File photo of a Utah prison

He reportedly confessed to touching his daughter as a child and taking child abuse photos before deleting them. The victim has reportedly confronted the man about the abuse.

He is said to have cried and “told the victim that she could not say anything to anyone about the abuse or he would go to jail”, ABC4 adds. Previously the child remained quiet about the abuse because the dad financially supported the family, the report also said.

He is now in custody without bail.

News.title: 'No one in charge' of social care as governments branded 'asleep at the wheel'
News.content:
'No one in charge' of social care as governments branded 'asleep at the wheel'

Baroness Louise Casey will sound the alarm over the state of the social care system in a speech on Wednesday as part of a major review into the crisis-hit sector

View 2 Images The social care system is 'fundamentally fragmented' - with no one in overall charge (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Successive governments have been “asleep at the wheel” on social care, leading to a “fundamentally fragmented system” with no one in charge, Baroness Casey will say today.

‌



‌



The Whitehall trouble-shooter has been tasked with a coming up with plans for a sweeping overhaul of the crisis-hit sector by next summer, which will shape Andy Burnham’s vision for a National Care Service. New research commissioned by her team laid bare the chaos in the system, which is dominated by private providers in a “largely uncontrolled and unintended way”.

‌



Two people with the same condition often have different experiences depending on where they live - including different assessment processes, waits, and levels of support. People paying for their own care are being charged, on average, 40 per cent more for the same service than people for whom care is arranged by their council, the report found.

‌



And while more than 1.5 million social care staff work across around 19,000 employers, England is the only one of the UK nations without a mandatory register of care workers.

Victory for care workers as Shabana Mahmood unveils biggest migration overhaul in a generation READ MORE :

View 2 Images Baroness Louise Casey is looking at how to fix the crisis-hit social care system (Image: Iain Buist/Newcastle Chronicle)

Baroness Casey has also written to the Covid Inquiry, branding its findings a cause of national shame. It comes after the official probe found Government failures allowed Covid to spread like wildfire in care homes and rejected the then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock's claim that a "protective ring" had been thrown around the sector.

‌



Speaking at the National Children and Adult Services Conference, she is expected to say: “The Covid-19 Inquiry took apart the argument that a “protective ring” had been thrown around care homes during the pandemic.

"Many old people died without their loved ones by their side. Many care workers left their jobs after what they had seen. It is a national shame that this was allowed to happen. It should never happen again.

‌



"Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel. In research we’re publishing today the lack of ‘stewardship’ of social care comes through clearly. No one is in charge.

"Together, we can build a new settlement for care. One based on values I still believe this country shares: decency, contribution, and a duty to care for our neighbours, our loved ones and ourselves.”

‌



The Prime Minister has said he will fight the next election on radical plans for a social care system that is free at the point of use. His determination has been fuelled by the experience his dad Roy, who died in a care home in September aged 86 after battling Alzheimer's disease.

Mr Burnham said he would scrap the pensions triple lock after the next election to fund a universal service. The PM has said he wants to shield people from personal care costs, and stop pensioners from being forced to sell their homes to fund their care.

Article continues below

Unlike NHS care, social care is not free at the point of use. People with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with the cost of care from their local council.

News.title: Jonathan Ross 'horrified' by Walliams allegations and Brand conviction
News.content:
TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is "horrified" by allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams and the rape conviction of Russell Brand.

In a statement, Ross said he was once "on friendly terms with both men", but that at the time he was "genuinely unaware of their conduct".

ITV News and the Guardian on Tuesday published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. Walliams denies all the allegations against him. Brand was sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape on Monday.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said that the allegations against Walliams were the "latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the media.

Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliams and Russell Brand.

He said he was "as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation".

He added: "My thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

News.title: Why Walliams' unprecedented legal battle to stay anonymous failed
News.content:
David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle not to be named in relation to allegations against him went downhill as he tried to secure a permanent injunction.

He was named by the Guardian and ITN because he had no sound legal reason to prevent the news organisations' investigation from being published. In response to the allegations included, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

The 55-year-old's bid for an injunction had been an open secret from the start after what would have normally been an anonymised application briefly appeared under his own name on a court cases register.

His exceptionally unusual attempt to gag the media - forever - became clear at the full trial last month - but that's when his bid to remain anonymous got worse.

In court, his lawyers did not claim that the investigation would be disclosing legally confidential or private information the journalists were not entitled to - two avenues often trod to silence reporters.

Instead lawyers for Walliams argued that such was the threat to his life from publication that the court itself would be breaching his human rights, were it to allow the story to go ahead.

This was, the court ultimately concluded, unheard of.

Under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the British state has a duty to take reasonable steps to try to protect life where they can do so and, importantly, where a particular body has an actual responsibility to do so.

There's no expectation that a state agency can save all lives in all circumstances - but it must show it has done its best if it is clear it had a responsibility to act.

The most obvious example of this law in practice is that the police must try to act on credible intelligence of a threat to life, even if the intended victim is a gangster.

But that duty, and how it should be applied in the real world, is also why Walliams lost: he was expecting the wrong public body to be doing the protecting.

The High Court's Mr Justice Nicklin said that the responsibility to try to protect the comedian and author's life was on clinicians and the hospital he had already been taken to. He had been detained for his own protection, meaning the state was already trying to meet its obligation to protect him from harm.

The court could not do that protecting because it had not taken responsibility for Walliams' psychiatric treatment or safety. Its role was to decide the legal dispute between Walliams and the news organisations.

Walliams' lawyers had suggested that there might be a right to private family life issue in the case but the judge said there had been no evidence to detail that, and he had to take into account the media's right to freedom of speech to publish what was described in court as a detailed investigation in the public interest.

If the media were wrong about their claims, Walliams could later sue for defamation - the way that any wrong party seeks redress against journalists.

News.title: Prince George's artwork featured in Country Life magazine
News.content:
Elsewhere in the edition, Catherine, who revealed two years ago that she was receiving cancer treatment, is said to have discussed the healing power of nature.

Prince William discusses walks with the family's dogs, Orla and Otto, and how his children love to go outside and explore. He also tells of his fondness for a pub visit and a pint of cider with ice.

Aston Villa manager Unai Emery is also featured in the magazine, and described the prince's support for the club as "fantastic" ahead of publication.

"If we can give him good news, good results or good moments in football, we are proud of it," he said in a video.

Another prominent part of the Country Life edition, published this week, is Prince William setting out his drive to ensure women in the British armed forces feel safe.

The Prince of Wales called for a military culture that is more inclusive and respectful of women, saying that more must be done to ensure women in the military are shown respect and protected from sexual harassment.

It follows the death of 19-year-old soldier Jaysley Beck in 2021. A coroner ruled the Army's failure to take action - after Gunner Beck was harassed by her line manager and sexually assaulted by another colleague - had contributed to her suicide.

Prince William is not the first senior royal to guest edit Country Life.

The King has guest edited the magazine on several occasions, including to mark his 65th and 70th birthdays. Queen Camilla and Anne, the Princess Royal, have also previously edited editions.

News.title: New photos are 'essential evidence' of possible SAS war crimes, inquiry told
News.content:
An inquiry into UK special forces operations in Afghanistan has released photos described as "essential evidence", showing soldiers could have executed unarmed people laying asleep.

For the first time, the inquiry has made public photos taken of the deceased, across two SAS operations, that show multiple individuals lying in bed with shots to the head.

The inquiry's lead barrister, Oliver Glasgow KC, said the photos may be evidence of possible war crimes and worthy of expert interrogation.

The public inquiry is examining allegations that the SAS murdered unarmed civilians and detainees on night raids between 2010 and 2013 and planted weapons to cover up the killings.

The graphic photographs show multiple unarmed people lying in bed.

One person was tucked under a floral blanket, others with their heads on pillows, blood pooling around their heads. Blood spatter is visible low on the wall in one of the images, consistent with someone being shot while lying down.

Glasgow described how many "look like they sustained head shots" and in a number of cases "there appears to be a dead body with his head on a pillow".

He said further analysis may be able to confirm if the people in the photographs were "shot when asleep".

Seventeen people were killed across the two operations which took place in Helmand province in 2011. The youngest of those killed in each of the operations were 15 and 14 years old respectively.

Glasgow said the photos appeared to contradict the accounts given by the SAS and would have raised serious questions for the military police officers investigating the operations as potential murders.

Lt Col John Harvey, who led the military police's murder probe, agreed they "didn't look right".

He told the inquiry his team were clear the photos could be vital evidence.

Despite the repeated requests of the police investigators to submit the photographs for further testing, this never took place.

One of the investigators, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the BBC "you can see why we were concerned", adding: "Bullet marks on the walls so low to the ground appeared to undermine the special forces' version of events."

The inquiry is subjecting the photographs to expert forensic analysis.

BBC Panorama has been investigating allegations the SAS executed unarmed civilians and children for more than eight years. The public inquiry was established in 2022 in the wake of Panorama's revelations.

The photos appear to support the findings of Panorama's 2022 investigation into raids in Helmand province which took place a decade before.

Panorama travelled to Afghanistan to gather evidence related to four raids on homes that killed 26 people.

The BBC visited the same guesthouses where the photographs released by the inquiry on Tuesday were taken. Panorama's team were the first British investigators to visit the sites of the shootings, despite a five-year-long military police investigation.

Official special forces accounts of the incidents claim Taliban insurgents opened fire on troops as they entered the compounds, forcing the SAS to return fire and kill those inside.

However weaponry experts told the BBC evidence collected by Panorama indicated multiple rounds appeared to have been fired from above.

This suggests those killed were either lying down or sitting against the wall and not in a firefight.

Family members also told Panorama those killed had been shot cleanly in the head or chest - a common characteristic of a deliberate SAS shooting at close range.

The photographs released by the inquiry show multiple "traumatic injuries to the head or face" of those killed by the SAS, according to its lead barrister.

The inquiry also heard evidence that calls into question whether alleged war crimes were thoroughly investigated.

It heard how investigators were still in Afghanistan in July 2019 gathering evidence as senior officers prepared to close their murder investigation and inform ministers.

The military police investigators were looking for eyewitnesses to unlawful killings and the planting of weapons.

One member of the Afghan partner unit that served on operations alongside the SAS told military police he had personally witnessed a British soldier planting a rifle on an unarmed person after they had been killed.

News.title: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds
News.content:
One drug comes out top in a large analysis, external of how effective antidepressants are at keeping patients free of symptoms of depression.

Escitalopram performed best at preventing patients from relapsing in a study involving nearly 10,000 people prescribed different medications for up to a year.

Two other pills - agomelatine and duloxetine - came next, while prozac (also known as fluoxetine) ranked just below them.

Experts stress the findings don't mean that everyone with severe depression should switch to escitalopram, or that other antidepressants aren't any good, because all the drugs can work and each has its pros and cons.

Depression is common, affecting around one in six people in the UK. With the right treatment and support, people can make a good recovery although for some their depression can return.

To prevent relapse, doctors already recommend people stay on antidepressants for at least six months after depression ends, and then taper off gradually.

The new analysis, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, looked at previous studies comparing the effectiveness of more than a dozen common antidepressants in total.

The differences found were modest and experts say longer studies are still needed to find out more.

There are many contributing causes to depression and a variety of ways to treat it, including drugs and talking therapies. Experts say patients should discuss what treatment options are best with their doctor.

News.title: Judge allows Trump's $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed
News.content:
A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it.

But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (Â£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state's unfair trade practices law.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."

The BBC spokesperson added: "We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process."

Judge Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case.

"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," he wrote in Tuesday's order.

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised and said that the broadcast had given "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

Along with defamation, Trump claimed in the lawsuit that the broadcaster had violated Florida law, specifically the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

Kuntz on Tuesday dismissed that part of the lawsuit, ruling that the documentary did not constitute commercial speech.

News.title: Students passing university assessments in minutes using AI, regulator warns
News.content:
Too many university students can use AI to complete assessments without staff finding out, the higher education regulator in England has said.

The Office for Students (OfS) said "a significant proportion" of assessments are unsupervised and many can be completed to a high standard with AI, sometimes in minutes.

It said this posed a "significant risk" to their credibility, and closed-book and practical exams were the most effective forms of assessments.

Universities UK said many institutions had "made substantial changes" to make assessments "AI-proof".

Universities that do not meet OfS quality standards could soon be banned from charging increased tuition fees or have caps imposed on their student numbers, under proposals that are now being consulted on.

The new research from the OfS and Advance HE, a charity that gives awards for teaching excellence, is based on the views of 244 higher education staff and 91 students from at least 127 universities.

It said "a significant proportion of assessments" were in "unsupervised, non-controlled formats where AI can be accessed by students completing them".

"Many of these can be completed to a high standard using AI tools with limited engagement from students," it added.

It also concluded it was "frequently possible" for students to use AI "in ways that cannot be reliably detected".

Unsupervised assessment can include coursework, but also remote online exams. They were rolled out widely during Covid, and research from Swansea University, external last year suggests 93 universities in the UK still use them in some form.

Josh Fleming, director of strategy and delivery at the OfS, said there were "fantastic" examples of universities seizing opportunities presented by AI, but there should be "far greater use of AI-free assessment".

"It also presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students' learning and institutions' ability to assess them," he said.

Kathryn Harrison-Graves, deputy chief executive at Advance HE, said students wanted "greater clarity about what is expected of them" but staff had "varying levels of confidence and support".

News.title: Stickers and building sets help drive toy sales ahead of Christmas rush
News.content:
Traditional games and stickers are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show.

The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK.

The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana.

The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between Â£5 and Â£10.

Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults".

The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves.

This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year.

But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far.

Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular.

"Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said.

News.title: Duchy tenants may have to buy farms or leave as Prince William plans sell-off
News.content:
"In the main, our mission is to sell to our farmers. We are keen that wherever possible we can achieve that continuity," Morris explained.

"For many of our farmers, it's a generational aspiration to own their farm. A few people have said it to me: 'My grandfather wanted to buy his farm. My father wanted to buy the farm. And now I've got the opportunity and it's an amazing outcome'.

"That's kind of what's driving me through what, at times, has been a little bit of turbulence."

The Duchy - which was established in 1337 - currently has around 700 agricultural lettings, with around 300 whole farm holdings made up of a farmhouse, land and buildings.

Farmers are on a mix of contracts ranging from time-limited to lifelong, with an option to pass the tenancy down through a family.

George Dunn, TFA chief executive, said the organisation was in "deep discussions" with the Duchy and that poor communication had led to tenants "facing prolonged uncertainty over valuations, timing and the options available to them".

"Once a family is told that its long-term relationship with the Duchy may change permanently, that uncertainty lives with them 24/7," he told the BBC.

He added that while he welcomed the Duchy's assurance that "nobody will be made homeless" not every tenant "will be able or want to buy the farms that they operate and fair alternatives must be explored for those for whom ownership is unaffordable".

A spokeswoman for the Duchy said: "We are engaging with people directly and supporting them through the process with care and respect.

"We recognise that each of our tenant's circumstances are different, and we are taking a careful, case-by-case approach."

News.title: Train attack driver's '10 seconds' to change line
News.content:
The driver of a high-speed train where a mass stabbing took place said he had "probably about 10 seconds" to decide to switch to the slow line before making an unscheduled stop.

Andrew Johnson was driving the London-bound LNER service on 1 November last year when the train stopped at Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire.

Giving evidence, Johnson told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court he heard someone on the intercom "screaming 'there's a knifeman stabbing people'".

Anthony Williams, 33, of Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder on the train.

He is also charged with four other attempted murders following earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

News.title: Poundland hopeful for last-minute rescue deal to stave off collapse
News.content:
Poundland and its 11,000 employees are hopeful that the retailer's impending collapse can be delayed to allow time for a last-minute rescue deal.

The discount chain has been edging towards administration after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation have told the BBC that they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of Â£10m in funding.

A committee of MPs is set to question Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just Â£1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm has denied the claims.

But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About Â£50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of Â£10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored.

News.title: Carrick's Man Utd future to be decided as Berrada and Wilcox retain support
News.content:
Looking back, the 48 hours before United's season-opening match at Hull were pivotal.

With Benjamin Sesko still trying to ease his way back from the shin issue that ended his previous campaign early, Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out for seven weeks. It meant Carrick was deprived of his first-choice striking alternative, with Bryan Mbeumo having to play on the right of the attack.

Carrick instead turned to Matheus Cunha, whose preference for dropping deep took him into the spaces captain Bruno Fernandes likes to occupy.

It neutralised United's attack on a day they seemed ill-prepared to meet the physical challenge of an opponent motivated by their long-awaited Premier League return.

In his role as interviewer for Nordic broadcaster Viaplay, former Norway and Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft later claimed United had lacked passion - something Carrick dismissed as "ridiculous".

"It's one game," Carrick told the media afterwards.

The following week, United were losing to Ipswich - another newly promoted side. Only a slip from Marcelino Nunez inside his own half allowed Cunha to tee up Fernandes for an undeserved equaliser.

The Portugal playmaker, who had just been crowned PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26, went on to complete a hat-trick in a 5-2 win.

He has scored just once - a penalty against Villa on Sunday - in the league since.

After the Ipswich win came a trip to Everton.

Twice United led, the second occasion when Sesko struck two minutes from full-time after coming on as a substitute. Deep into stoppage time, Ainsley Maitland-Niles drove home from long range to deny the visitors.

Asked how confident he was in his side's ability to react to a disappointing start to the season, Carrick snapped back: "It's not been that bad."

What happened next, however, was.

Time and again, United's fitness was called into question. They struggled badly against a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men in the first half before their rivals benefited from an Erling Haaland goal that referees' chief Howard Webb later admitted should not have stood.

Carrick's complaints were justified - but they masked a poor performance from his team.

After taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes against Brighton in the EFL Cup, United were outplayed and beaten, thanks to two goals in four second-half minutes.

The fine margins United benefited from during Carrick's interim spell were now going against them, and his coaching staff - lauded months earlier - could not find an answer.

Carrick called Cunha's injury-time equaliser against a Fulham side who started the game bottom of the table a positive to build on. But immediately after the international break, United were held to another draw - conceding in injury time to an out-of-form and 10-man Tottenham.

The whirlwind was starting to pick up strength.

Lisandro Martinez, who scored an own goal against Fulham, was at fault for Spurs' leveller, which made his post-match outburst after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid more amazing.

The Argentina defender criticised United's summer recruitment and placed the blame at the door of "the technical director" - Wilcox.

By the time of Martinez's outburst, Sesko and left-back Luke Shaw were injured. Marcus Rashford has not played since. The rotation at left-back that eventually led to Carrick starting five different players in that role was in full swing.

After conceding in the opening minute against Atletico, Como scored inside the first two in a 4-1 Champions League defeat for United. Fernandes came out afterwards and criticised Carrick's tactics.

He was dropped for the Bournemouth game, but returned as captain at Chelsea. United were beaten in both matches.

With just three wins in 15 matches in all competitions this season and United stuck in 18th in the Premier League, Carrick is set to pay the price.

News.title: Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them during the trial and following the conviction and sentencing of the disgraced comedian Russell Brand, "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".

A Met spokesperson said: "Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Det Supt Andy Furphy, who led the Brand investigation, said officers were "looking at exactly what we've got" and "whether they're information that points to behaviour or whether they could constitute a criminal offence".

Brand is already being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. He has been interviewed under caution in connection to those allegations.

News.title: Arrests made in Mohamed Al Fayed probe in France, police say
News.content:
Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC documentary and podcast in September 2024.

One of the women featured in the documentary said she was sexually assaulted by Al Fayed at the Ritz hotel in Paris, while another woman said she had been raped by him at the Villa Windsor residence.

Since those allegations, more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.

A woman has also told BBC Scotland she was trafficked, drugged, sexually assaulted and held prisoner on the Balnagown Estate by Al Fayed's brother, Salah Fayed, who died in 2010.

Both brothers died without facing legal charges in relation to these allegations.

Earlier this year, Police Scotland said it was carrying out further investigations into allegations connected to Balnagown Estate.

In a statement, a force spokesperson said: "Three people have been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims.

"Our inquiries are ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

The Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors group said it welcomed the "significant developments" and cooperation between the Met and French authorities.

"We believe that all properties owned by Fayed should be investigated with the same thoroughness as those already searched, wherever they are located, to ensure that no potentially relevant evidence is overlooked," the group said.

"We hope these developments represent meaningful progress towards identifying and holding to account all those who facilitated, concealed or assisted his offending, wherever they operated."

The survivor advocacy group No One Above said: "France is treating this as organised human trafficking, led by specialists, with properties searched and evidence seized. That is what a serious investigation into a network looks like.

"Two years on, survivors are still waiting for the same from the Met. It is time the National Crime Agency took this investigation over."

The management of the Ritz Paris told AFP news agency that it "does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour" and that it was ready "to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities".

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line.

News.title: More than 12 US military aircraft leave second UK base
News.content:
Retired Royal Air Force Air Marshal Greg Bagwell told BBC Verify "we need to keep an open mind" about the reasons behind the US aircraft movements.

He suggested they could be the result of an exercise, or because the weather forecast meant it was safer to move the aircraft to other bases ahead of planned deployments elsewhere.

Bagwell said the decision may also have been taken because of a hoax as part of "nuisance hybrid warfare" by countries like Iran - or it could be a genuine threat.

He said the aircraft being dispersed to several bases could indicate the US was spreading them around to keep them safe and the moves have been "triggered by something".

Bagwell added that the reason "we haven't seen an attack succeed or even happen" could be that "maybe our intelligence and our security is better than people might believe".

Monday's departures from Mildenhall follow a security incident at RAF Fairford, a US-operated airbase in Gloucestershire.

A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near that base in September. It later emerged that the US had pulled its bombers from there and returned them to America.

Two British nationals appeared in court in October in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot.

Seven men have been arrested as part of the investigation, Counter Terrorism Policing confirmed to the BBC on Tuesday, while an eighth has been interviewed under caution and since charged under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023.

Iran has previously said that it considered UK bases used by the US for military strikes to be "legitimate targets".

Additional reporting by Nick Johnson at RAF Mildenhall, and Rob Corp, BBC Verify.

News.title: Seven in hospital after car 'mounts pavement' in Glasgow
News.content:
Seven people have been taken to hospital after they were struck by a car in the west end of Glasgow.

Police Scotland said the driver was assessed by paramedics and treated at the scene of the incident, which happened at about 15:45 on Hyndland Road.

Unconfirmed reports suggest the vehicle mounted the pavement, hit a bus stop shelter and then struck scaffolding before coming to a halt.

A force spokesperson said: "Officers remain in attendance and inquiries are ongoing into the incident which is being treated as a road traffic collision."

News.title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Ukrainian oil refinery attacks ‘cut Russia’s processing capacity by 30%’ as talks underway
News.content:
