Florida prosecutors, working alongside the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), at the time granted him a lenient 18-month sentence alongside extensive work-release privileges, a period during which he continued to abuse women, according to the report.

The panel ascribed the outcomes to “poor judgment” and Epstein’s influence, while flagging potential conflicts of interest involving two former prosecutors, Matthew Menchel and Bruce Reinhart, then employed in the US Attorney’s Office (USAO) for the Southern District of Florida.

“Former US Attorney Alexander Acosta’s hands-off approach to the investigation and his failures to oversee the daily involvement of those at the USAO left the investigation in the hands of potential Epstein loyalists,” the report read.

Cell left unmonitored

Separately, the report blamed understaffing and institutional dysfunction at the New York federal jail where Epstein died by alleged suicide in August 2019, revealing that guards skipped 12 patrols and three inmate counts, failing to perform the required 30-minute safety checks.

Epstein was being housed in the Metropolitan Correctional Center’s (MCC) Special Housing Unit when his cell was left unmonitored for nearly eight hours the night he died.

According to testimony provided to the committee by Tova Noel, a former MCC correctional officer who performed Epstein’s final cell check, the critical lapse was simply “the MCC way”.

The committee’s report defined the jail’s institutional culture as one in which “departures from established policies and procedures had become routine”.

To deliver long-awaited accountability, the Republican-led committee urged the Department of Justice (DOJ) to interview or re-interview key witnesses and to investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity. The report includes testimony from a witness who accused two high-profile figures of abuse: former Miami Beach Mayor Philip Levine and French celebrity hairstylist Frederic Fekkai.



“The evidence we uncovered makes clear that the Department of Justice must interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records,” Comer said in a statement, adding that “Congress must also pass legislation protecting the ability of individuals with knowledge of sexual abuse and survivors to speak freely about these crimes, regardless of nondisclosure agreements”.

‘Witch hunt’

The report also dismissed the committee Democrats’ probe into Trump as an “unfounded witch hunt”, saying they were “obsessed with trying to implicate President Trump and insinuate that he was involved in the crimes of Epstein and Maxwell”.

Questions remain about whether the DOJ provided all required records under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, a measure passed by a near-unanimous Congress and signed into law by US President Donald Trump in November 2025.

The rushed nature of the disclosure led to “deficient redaction” that “exposed sensitive information” belonging to victims, the GOP-led report added.

The panel further recommended measures granting survivors access to unredacted personal files and urged passing the Survivor’s Voice Protection Act to prohibit using non-disclosure agreements to conceal sexual abuse.

World.title: Protesters throw milk at Joe Biden during Hunter event in Dublin
World.content:
Protesters throw milk at Joe Biden during Hunter event in Dublin

NewsFeed Protesters throw milk at Joe Biden during Hunter event in Dublin

Pro-Palestinian protesters hurled milk towards Joe Biden in Ireland over his support for Israel. The former president was making an unannounced visit to Dublin’s Trinity College to see his son Hunter receive an award for public discourse.

World.title: Former Iraqi lawmaker Ahmed al-Alwani found dead in Beirut
World.content:
Lebanese authorities launch ‘murder’ investigation after al-Alwani’s body is found in an apartment in Beirut.

Former Iraqi lawmaker Ahmed al-Alwani has been found dead in an apartment in the Lebanese capital, Beirut, according to a security source, with Lebanese authorities investigating his death as a killing.

The source, who spoke to Al Jazeera on Tuesday, did not disclose how al-Alwani had died.

His body was found on Tuesday evening in an apartment in the Tariq al-Jdideh neighbourhood of Beirut, according to Lebanese media.

The official National News Agency (NNA) said Lebanon’s top prosecutor, Judge Ahmed Rami al-Hajj, is personally overseeing the investigation into al-Alwani’s killing, which is being carried out by the Information Branch of Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces.

In a statement on X, al-Alwani’s office called the former lawmaker’s death an “assassination” and a “treacherous crime”.

It called for an investigation and accountability for the perpetrators.

“This is not a passing incident to be brushed aside with condolences and condemnation,” it said. “It is a crime that demands a firm official response and a transparent investigation that reveals who planned it, who carried it out and who else was involved. Whoever is behind it, no one is above accountability.”

A Lebanese judicial source, meanwhile, told the AFP news agency that preliminary findings indicate al-Alwani was strangled to death and that a Lebanese national suspected of involvement has been arrested.

The source said authorities are looking for two Syrian suspects still at large.

He added that the suspects had taken al-Alwani from the airport to his hotel when he arrived in Beirut last week.



Al-Alwani, a Sunni politician, formerly represented the western province of Anbar in Iraq’s parliament. He rose to prominence during the protests of 2012 and 2013, against the Shia-led government of then-Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, whom protesters accused of sectarian policies and of marginalising Sunnis.

He was also a vocal critic of Iran’s influence in Iraq and of Iranian-backed Shia armed groups in the country.

Al-Alwani was arrested in December 2013 during a security raid on his home in Ramadi, during which his brother and several others were killed.

He was sentenced to death in 2014 on “terrorism” charges, but released in April 2025 under Iraq’s General Amnesty Law after more than a decade in prison.

Iraq’s Ambassador to Lebanon Mohammed Reda al-Husseini said on Tuesday that the Iraqi embassy was following the case closely.

He said the embassy is awaiting the final report from the Lebanese security agencies to “disclose the circumstances of the crime”.

World.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
World.content:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the base. Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident.

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI).

"Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".

Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.

"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.

He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.

Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.

World.title: US Army soldier suspected of spying for Russia arrested in UK
World.content:
A soldier in the US Army has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British counter-terror police have said.

The 41-year-old senior serviceman was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday.

Counter Terrorism Policing London said the man had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023.

Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire.

The BBC understands the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC), a strategic operational base for the alliance.

Counter Terrorism Policing said it was not linked to any other ongoing investigations.

FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies."

He added: "While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message â this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

World.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
World.content:
An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.

A majority of the House of Representatives agreed to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky - for now.

In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".

The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.

Massie was the only Republican to vote against moving the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.

His effort failed in a 211-204 vote, with more than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missing the vote.

The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress before Democrats take control in January.

President Trump celebrated the vote in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED".

"Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.

After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS.

"My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."

Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

World.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
World.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.

The BBC has contacted his representatives.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.

FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".

Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

World.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
World.content:
"It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.

Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.

The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.

Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives.

"Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."

With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid â especially following warnings that the El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding.

"I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."

Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the frontline of preparations for the potential impact of El NiÃ±o.

Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.

In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.

Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.

This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El NiÃ±o.

World.title: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says
World.content:
The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salvador's military, the Salvadoran president has said.

The infamous 400 Mawozo gang, which is known for kidnappings and intimidation tactics, was targeted in a ground and air attack at a complex on the outskirts of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince.

It is El Salvador's first military action on a Haitian target since it deployed more than 2,000 soldiers there last month, as part of a mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran technicians.

Haiti has been plagued by gang violence for years, with heavily armed groups controlling large parts of the capital, and beyond.

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele announced the news on X, external, boasting that most of the gang members fled without trying to fight.

"We destroyed the house of [gang leader] LanmÃ² San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters," he wrote on Tuesday.

The post was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex, reportedly in the suburb of Croix-des-Bouquets, the gang's stronghold.

As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.

Several media outlets have reported that as many as 20 people were killed, however that has not been confirmed by authorities. There has also been no official confirmation of the extent of the damage at the property, with Haitians questioning whether it has been destroyed or just damaged.

The Miami Herald reports that the gang's leader, Wilson "LanmÃ² San Jou" Joseph, was not there at the time.

The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the gang's headquarters.

World.title: Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
World.content:
A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."

The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."

Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.

It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.

Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.

Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.

The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.

Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.

The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.

Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".

Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.

"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."

Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

World.title: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave
World.content:
The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.

Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.

The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery".

"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC.

"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.

World.title: 2027: Reps aspirant faults election panel constituted by APC chair
World.content:
Hassan Dangaladima, a House of Representatives aspirant for the Kaura Namoda/Birnin Magaji Federal Constituency of Zamfara State, has faulted the election panel constituted by the All Progressives Congress (APC) for the conduct of a fresh primary election in the constituency.

The panel was constituted by the APC National Chairman, Nentawe Yilwatda, after the Court of Appeal nullified the earlier outcome of the primary election and ordered a fresh exercise to select the party’s candidate for the constituency.

Mr Dangaladima alleged that the APC national chairman was unfair in selecting members of the panel, arguing that he failed to consult other organs of the party before constituting it.

He made the allegations in a petition addressed to the party’s National Executive Committee (NEC) and National Working Committee (NWC), urging them to urgently review the composition of the panel.

“The said nomination was made unilaterally by the national chairman: no meeting of the National Working Committee was convened for that purpose; no quorum of the NWC deliberated upon or resolved on the composition of the committee; the nomination was never presented to, ratified or approved by the NWC or the NEC as required by the party’s Constitution; and neither the aspirants nor the Zamfara State Chapter nor other relevant stakeholders were consulted,” he said.

The aspirant further alleged that members of the panel were loyalists and supporters of one of his opponents, Aminu Jaji, arguing that their alleged affiliations could compromise the credibility of the exercise.

“The composition of the committee as announced raises a real and reasonable apprehension of bias: members of the committee are known loyalists, supporters and/or agents of a particular aspirant in the contest, namely Hon. Aminu Sani Jaji, thereby placing them in a position of manifest conflict of interest,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Dangaladima also questioned Mr Jaji’s eligibility to contest the primary, alleging that his name was missing from the APC membership register for Birnin Magaji Ward submitted to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

“Further and on a related note, the very aspirant the impugned committee is designed to favour, Honourable Aminu Sani Jaji, is not a registered member of the Party: his name is not contained in the Register of Members of the All Progressives Congress for Birnin Magaji Ward submitted to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), as confirmed by the Certified True Copy of the said Register obtained from INEC (Exhibit A).

“A formal demand to that effect was made on the Party by letter dated 4th November, 2026 from Trinity Chambers (D.C. Enwelum, SAN), Solicitors in Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/1060/2026 — Hon. Hassan Umar v. Aminu Sani Jaji & 4 Ors. (Exhibit B). By Section 77(5) of the Electoral Act 2026, only members whose names are contained in the register of members shall be eligible to vote and be voted for in party primaries, congresses and conventions; the said aspirant is therefore ineligible to contest the court-ordered primary election.”

The aspirant also argued that the composition of the panel violated the party’s rules because other aspirants were neither consulted nor given an opportunity to raise objections to the selection of its members.

“The membership of the committee was never published in advance; aspirants were afforded no notice of its composition and no opportunity to object to members with conflicts of interest; and no screening or vetting mechanism whatsoever was applied to secure the impartiality and independence of the committee.

“The manner of the committee’s constitution violates the rules of natural justice (audi alteram partem and nemo judex in causa sua), the principle of internal democracy enshrined in the Party’s Constitution, the Party’s guidelines for the conduct of primaries, and the Electoral Act, particularly the requirement of transparent, credible and INEC-monitored primaries,” he said.

Mr Dangaladima consequently urged the APC NEC and NWC to suspend the fresh primary election and reconstitute the panel to ensure a fair and credible exercise.

It is not clear whether the date for the primary election for the constituency has been scheduled or not.

APC responds

Responding to the allegations, Mr Yilwatda, through his media aide, Abimbola Tooki, denied that the panel was constituted unilaterally, insisting that the selection of its members followed the party’s established decision-making procedures.

Mr Tooki said decisions concerning party affairs were not taken by the national chairman without consultation with the NWC.

“The allegation is completely unfounded and does not reflect the established decision-making process of the All Progressives Congress. The National Working Committee (NWC) has always operated as a collective decision-making body, with members working together, deliberating on issues and taking decisions in the overall interest of the party.

“It is therefore incorrect to suggest that the National Chairman, Professor Nentawe Yilwatda, takes unilateral decisions on matters concerning the activities and administration of the party, particularly on issues as important as the conduct of party primaries.

“The national chairman does not operate in isolation. He works in consultation and collaboration with other members of the NWC, and decisions are taken collectively in accordance with the party’s constitution, established procedures and internal mechanisms,” he said.

World.title: Anniversary: Many wrote us off when we started Dunamis Church 30 years ago – Enenche
World.content:
The Senior Pastor of the Dunamis International Centre (DIGC), Paul Enenche, has said many people did not give him and his wife any chances of survival when they founded the church 30 years ago.

He said this during a special healing and deliverance service at the church’s headquarters in Abuja on Tuesday to mark its 30th anniversary.

Mr Enenche and his wife, Becky, both medical doctors, began the church on Sunday, 10 November 1996. That first service was held in a restaurant at the Centre for Arts and Culture (now known as Cyprian Ekwensi Arts and Culture Centre), Garki District, Abuja, with 55 people in attendance.

In a sermon titled “The faithfulness of God,” to mark the anniversary, the pastor praised God for His faithfulness in the past 30 years.

Drawing from 1 Thes 5:24, he said God had been faithful to His calling, word, praise, promise, and covenant.

Mr Enenche said the church was founded based on the power of the Holy Spirit, as stated in Acts 1:8, adding that Dunamis is a Greek word for power.

“You cannot talk about Dunamis without talking about power, the power of the Holy Ghost,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The clergyman then narrated the early beginnings of the church, stating that some people they encountered along the line at that time wrote them off.

“When this ministry started, many people didn’t give us any chances of survival… of anything. Some wrote us off from scratch. And I don’t know why human beings think that they can predict a person’s future, how they think in their minds!

“At one point, they said it was only strugglers, the masses, not classes but masses that are members. ‘Oh, they are plenty, but they are just full of struggling people. Big men are not there, rich men are not there, and wealthy men are not there.’ They thought that was our focus.

“At a time, almost every church has a sponsor, identifiable. You can say, ‘This one is the person behind this church. For us, we have nothing but God and that God brought us to where we are.”

Likening the beginning of the church to a mustard seed, Mr Enenche said some of the people who looked down on the church at the beginning have approached him and the church for multiple helps, particularly in the area of finance.

He added that the church has impacted the world so much that he receives invitations from across the world to preach the gospel of Jesus Christ.

“Some people who looked down on us and said, ‘They are just a small church, strugglers, have looked for our help multiple times, help that bordered on finance. It was a small mustard seed that has impacted every inhabited continent on the earth. We have calls from literally all places around the earth that we cannot meet,” he said.

Turning to the congregation, the pastor prayed, “That is the God you are connected to. He will disappoint the voices of the wicked people. He will disappoint the expectations of negative people for your life, your family, and your destiny. He will prove wrong people who are waiting to see that it didn’t work. ‘You say you are a doctor, your wife is a doctor, you decided to become a pastor, you will soon return; we are waiting for you.’ Those who are waiting to say that it did not work, they will never see it.”

Recounting the construction of the church’s 100,000-capacity sanctuary called Glory Dome, Mr Enenche said, “When this construction was going on, we were spending more money every month than the offering of the whole year. So, resources were coming beyond what the offering would account for.”

He added, “One of those people of those days said, What is the source of your people’s money? How are you getting the things done? We said, ‘It is God.’ Do you know what he said – ‘only ’? It’s like saying God alone is not enough. It’s like saying there has to be something more. Is that all? Is there nothing else? Is there no business going on somewhere? It is God. God alone is enough for you, for your life, for your family.

“The faithfulness of God is the reliability of God. He is reliable, dependable, trustworthy, and constant. You can actually trust Him and go to sleep.”

Earlier, Mrs Enenche, while recounting how the church began, said the first service in November 1996 at the Arts and Culture Centre was attended by 55 people, adding, “See where God has brought us.”

She subsequently led the congregation in a brief prayer of thanksgiving to God,

Mr Enenche and his wife, who were medical practitioners in Jos, Plateau State, moved to Abuja to establish the church after an encounter with God. Although it began with 55 members, some of whom still worship there, the church now has thousands of branches and members worldwide.

READ ALSO: Wike praises Dunamis Church for building pedestrian bridge in Abuja

Although the church’s first service was held on 10 November 1996, it marks its anniversary in the last week of November every year with a conference known as the Kingdom Power Glory World Conference (KPGWC). This year’s edition, themed “Open Heavens,” is scheduled for 23 to 29 November.

With its 100,000-capacity sanctuary called Glory Dome, Dunamis Church had the biggest auditorium in Nigeria until last week, when the 120,000-seater “Five Fingers of God Cathedral” was dedicated by the Salvation Ministries in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, South-South Nigeria. David Ibiyeomie founded Salvation Ministries in April 1997.

Yet Glory Dome, dedicated on 24 November 2018, may soon become the third largest, as Living Faith Church, founded by David Oyedepo, a bishop, is currently constructing a sanctuary, “The Ark,” that will accommodate approximately 109,000 worshippers. Messrs. Enenche and Ibiyeomie are spiritual sons of Mr Oyedepo.

World.title: NAHCON, Saudi Arabia sign 2027 Hajj deal, to improve services
World.content:
The National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON) and the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Hajj and Umrah have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for the 2027 Hajj, establishing a framework for improved pilgrimage arrangements and better welfare services for Nigerian pilgrims.

The agreement, signed on Tuesday, 10 November, in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, covers key areas of Hajj operations, including pilgrims’ quota, accommodation, transportation, healthcare, compliance with Saudi regulations and adherence to operational deadlines.

NAHCON Chairman Ismail Yusuf signed the agreement on behalf of Nigeria, while Saudi Arabia was represented by its Vice Minister of Hajj and Umrah, Abdulfattah bin Sulaiman Mashat.

Shafii Mohammed, head of Information and Publications at NAHCON, said in a statement on Tuesday that the agreement would strengthen cooperation between the two countries, improve service delivery, and better protect Nigerian pilgrims’ welfare ahead of the 2027 pilgrimage.

Read the full statement:

NAHCON, SAUDI ARABIA SEAL 2027 HAJJ MoU, SET STAGE FOR IMPROVED PILGRIMAGE OPERATIONS

Jeddah, Saudi Arabia – 10th November 2026

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON) and the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia officially signed the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for the 2027 Hajj pilgrimage, laying the groundwork for improved pilgrimage operations.

The agreement was signed on Tuesday, 10th November 2026, in Jeddah at the prestigious Super Dome by NAHCON Chairman/CEO, Ambassador Ismail Abba Yusuf, on behalf of Nigeria, while the Saudi Vice Minister of Hajj and Umrah, Dr Abdulfattah bin Sulaiman Mashat, signed on behalf of Saudi Arabia.

The MoU establishes a framework for coordinating Nigeria’s participation in the pilgrimage, including country quota allocation, compliance with Saudi Hajj regulations, adherence to operational deadlines and cooperation on essential services such as accommodation, transportation and healthcare. It also provides a basis for closer engagement between the two countries to address logistical challenges, monitor service standards, and protect pilgrims’ welfare.

Speaking at the event, Mr Yusuf commended the Saudi Government and the Minister of Hajj and Umrah for their continued investment in pilgrims’ infrastructure, the significant improvements in pilgrimage arrangements, and sustained constructive engagement with Nigeria.

He reaffirmed NAHCON’s commitment to align with these achievements through stronger institutional collaboration and better services for Nigerian pilgrims.

In his remarks, Dr Mashat disclosed that the Kingdom recorded a 93 per cent pilgrim satisfaction rate during the 2026 Hajj and applauded Nigeria for contributing to the achievement. On arrangements for the 2027 Hajj, the minister commended Nigeria for meeting all established timelines while encouraging NAHCON to sustain the milestone.

READ ALSO: NAHCON pushes sustainable Hajj fund management digital transformation at global forum

The ceremony was attended by Nigeria’s Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Ambassador Yakubu Gambo, and members of the National Assembly led by Hon. Jafar Mohammed, Chairman of the House Committee on Hajj Pilgrimage, alongside other senior officials.

To give effect to the agreement, NAHCON will coordinate with State Muslim Pilgrims’ Welfare Boards, licensed tour operators and relevant Saudi institutions to align operational arrangements, strengthen service monitoring and address potential challenges before the commencement of the 2027 Hajj pilgrimage.

Signed

Shafii Sani Mohammed

Head, Information and Publications, NAHCON

World.title: NCDMB, NLNG commits US$9m to endowment of professorial research chairs in Six Nigerian universities
World.content:
The Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB) and the Nigeria LNG Limited (NLNG) have launched a US$9 million professorial chair endowment programme across six Nigerian universities to develop commercially viable solutions to industry challenges, strengthen local research capacity and advance technological innovation.

Under the Nigerian Content Research and Development (NC-R&D) Professorial Chair Endowment Programme, each university is to receive US$1.5 million to establish a specialised professorial chair focused on agreed industry research priorities. The initiative is being implemented in partnership with the NCDMB, under the supervision of its Planning, Research and Statistics Directorate.

The schools include the University of Ibadan, Oyo State, Rivers State University, Modibbo Adama University, Yola, Adamawa State, Aliko Dangote University of Science and Technology, Kano State, University of Nigeria, Nsukka, Enugu State, and Yakubu Gowon University, formerly the University of Abuja.

Speaking at the kick-off ceremony, NLNG’s Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Adeleye Falade, described the programme as an investment in Nigeria’s capacity to translate academic knowledge into practical solutions. His keynote address, titled “Reshaping Nigeria’s Future Through Innovation, Research and Capacity Development,” emphasised the importance of sustained collaboration between government, industry and academia.

“In the energy industry, we understand that technology and energy systems are evolving and the requirement for sustained research cannot be overemphasised,” Falade said.

He noted that the programme would support research into challenges central to the energy industry’s future, including improving operational efficiency, managing emissions, strengthening safety, maintaining critical infrastructure and making industrial processes more sustainable.

Beyond the research endowments, Falade outlined opportunities for a “triple helix” approach that brings government, industry and academia together through specialised programmes, sabbaticals, exchange opportunities, practical testing of research assumptions and the joint development of postgraduate curricula.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The six beneficiary universities will undertake research in distinct areas and the NLNG Research and Innovation Centre for Computer and Electrical Engineering (RICCEE) at Rivers State University is envisaged as the coordinating point for these collaborations among the universities. Falade said discussions were already under way with the university on implementation arrangements and commended its Vice-Chancellor, Professor Isaac Zeb-Obipi, for his role in advancing the proposed collaboration. We have already gotten indications of other partners like Google, Cisco and MTN who showing interest to support this initiative, he said.

Falade also highlighted the opportunities for younger researchers to deepen their expertise, investigate industry problems and learn from experienced academics and practitioners. He urged the beneficiary institutions to build on the endowments by strengthening research partnerships, attracting additional funding and pursuing the commercialisation of intellectual property.

“Expand the scope, reach for more grants and funding which can push the frontiers of knowledge and commercialisation of intellectual property,” he said.

Acknowledging NCDMB’s role in bringing the initiative to fruition, Falade called for sustained commitment to technology transfer and the development of home-grown solutions without compromising quality assurance or safety. He emphasised that the programme’s lasting value would lie in stronger institutions, research outcomes deployed in the field and the development of the next generation of Nigerian researchers and industry professionals.

In his remarks, the Executive Secretary of the NCDMB, Felix Omatsola Ogbe said the US$9 million endowment programme represents a strategic investment in the future of Nigeria’s research and innovation ecosystem.

The initiative, he said, complements the Board’s ongoing investments in research infrastructure, including the establishment of specialized R&D Centres of Excellence across six universities in the country.

He added that “taken together, these interventions demonstrate the Nigerian oil and gas industry’s commitment to creating an integrated research ecosystem that connects academic expertise, modern research infrastructure, industry requirements, and commercialization opportunities.”

Represented by the Senior Technical Adviser, Austin Uzoka, the Executive Secretary underscored that by supporting specialized professorial chairs in critical areas of the industry operations, NLNG and NCDMB is creating opportunities to bridge the longstanding gap between academic research and industrial application.

He further charged the universities to deliberately transition from research for publication to research for application, and from innovation as an academic pursuit to innovation as a driver of industrial transformation. According to him “the beneficiary universities must see this endowment as both an opportunity and a responsibility and they would be expected to deliver clearly defined research objectives, measurable outcomes, prudent resource utilization, effective stakeholder engagement, and sustained collaboration with industry partners.”

He further demanded that “these professorial chairs will generate commercially viable solutions, strengthen local technological capabilities, support industrial competitiveness, and contribute meaningfully to the long-term sustainability of Nigeria’s oil and gas industry.”

Details of the endowment indicates that the University of Ibadan will focus on natural gas processing, pollution control and environmental management, while Rivers State University will concentrate on digital engineering, intelligent energy systems, automation and asset integrity.

Modibbo Adama University will undertake research in energy transition and the environment. Aliko Dangote University of Science and Technology will focus on sustainable energy innovation and climate-resilient food systems.

The University of Nigeria, Nsukka, will specialise in green energy production and geoenvironmental engineering, while Yakubu Gowon University, formerly the University of Abuja, will focus on geoscience and satellite intelligence for resilient gas infrastructure.

Each university will work towards agreed research targets and commercialisation pathways, providing a framework for measuring progress and translating findings into practical applications. The institutions will also jointly host an information management hub to support knowledge sharing and exchange programmes.

The funding includes provision for minor civil works and infrastructure upgrades to transform identified spaces into fit-for-purpose research centres.

Proposed arrangements would enable industry professionals to contribute practical expertise in technical and non-technical disciplines while pursuing master’s and doctoral degrees. This would give students greater exposure to industry experience while strengthening the connection between postgraduate study and practical problem-solving.

The programme reinforces NLNG’s commitment to developing Nigerian capability and creating opportunities for local expertise to address industry needs, guided by its recently approved ‘NextGen Nigerian Content Strategy’ where NLNG plans to Sustain the gains through focused delivery of previous commitments in alignment with NCDMB; Enable its business by facilitating deeper adoption Nigerian Content Development as a business principle and Accelerate growth by showing up and support the Nigerian Content transformation for posterity, in line with its vision of inspiring a sustainable future.

World.title: NHRC records 384,196 human rights violation complaints in October, cases up 13.4%
World.content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) on Tuesday said it recorded 384,196 reports of human rights violations in October across Nigeria, up by 13.4 per cent from the previous month.

The number of cases stood at 338,810 in September.

In October, complaints on the violation of the freedom from discrimination were the highest at 217, 243.

Giving the report at the NHRC’s headquarters in Abuja on Tuesday, the Executive Secretary, Tony Ojukwu, said 180,000 of the 217,243 discrimination cases were from the camps of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs).

He said, “Every complaint is a person, a family, or a community whose rights and dignity need protection.

“Our responsibility is not simply to document these complaints, but to ensure that the information gathered informs appropriate intervention as well as effective remedy.”

He stressed the importance of ensuring that “displacement does not deprive individuals and families of their dignity, security, and access to basic rights.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Across many states, many Nigerians live under poor conditions of the camps of Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) after fleeing their homes over terrorists’ attacks, banditry and other threats of violence.

The complaints by IDPs reflect a systemic rights issue, social marginalisation, institutional neglect, and discriminatory barriers affecting displaced communities in Nigeria.

Complaints due to insecurity

Other issues of concern highlighted in Tuesday’s dashboard include insecurity, reports of killings, armed attacks, and abductions.

The commission’s Human Rights Observatory documented incidents involving attacks on farming communities, travellers, women, traditional leaders, and security personnel, particularly concerning their reports of mass killings and abductions in parts of Taraba, Borno, Zamfara, Niger, and Plateau State, among other locations.

Mr Ojukwu stressed that the reported incidents are not merely security concerns but also concern issues with “direct humanitarian implications.”

He said, “They affect the right to life, liberty, and dignity, and security of the person. They disrupt livelihoods, restrict freedom of movement, and expose children and mothers.

“The commission reiterates that the protection of lives and property is an environmental responsibility of the state.”

Mr Ojukwu also encouraged political actors to exercise restraint and conduct themselves within the ambit of electoral laws and human rights.

As the 2027 elections draw near, “we should not lose focus on the fact that elections, voting process and outcomes reflect the interplay of various human rights.”

Dashboard details

Senior Human Rights Adviser to the NHRC, Hilary Ogbonna, noted that the human rights complaints recorded by the commission in 2026 have crossed the 2.5 million mark.

The commission recorded 116,739 complaints from the North Central, 65,309 from the South West, 63,120 from the North West, 50,902 from the South South, 49,618 from the North East, and 38,508 from the South East.

The FCT, Lagos, Benue, Kaduna, Borno, Plateau, Kano, Rivers, Imo and Niger were among the top ten states with the highest violation complaints. This is the first time Lagos and Rivers are among the top ten states in 2026.

Mr Ogbonna attributed this to the tension with the upcoming elections, particularly in Rivers State.

The 10 states accounted for 52 per cent of the entire complaints recorded in October.

Women’s right violations

The commission recorded 632 complaints of women denied access to children, 591 abandonment, 339 trafficking and 376 forced marriages.

Mr Ogbonna noted an upsurge in men abandoning their wives.

“Month after month, we try to ask ourselves, even in the commission, what could be the reason for this. It’s not our mandate to go and look for white men abandoning their marriages, but when it becomes a human rights issue, it gives us cause for worry,” he said.

Six rapes, 18 sexual violence incidents, and 1,873 domestic violence incidents were recorded in the month under focus. According to Mr Ogbonna, they each represent a woman who has been given a permanent scar.

Child rights violations

Similarly, child abandonment in October rose by over 250 per cent to 2,479, with Mr Ogbonna describing the trend as a human rights breach.

Also, 2,093 children were forced into marriage, 2,141 cases of sexual abuse, 2,581 were denied their rights to education, and 1,681 were trafficked.

Cases resolved

Among the entire figures recorded in October, the NHRC resolved 1,455 cases.

The commission also visited 108 places of detention, five military formations and summoned the police 45 times.

World.title: Court orders forfeiture of two Mercedes-Benz cars, phones linked to convicted fraudster
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Lagos has ordered the final forfeiture of two luxury Mercedes-Benz vehicles, four electronic devices and other properties linked to a convicted internet fraudster, Ifeanyi Arinze.

Judge Yellim Bogoro made the order on Monday after considering an application by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC).

“The vehicles include a white Mercedes-Benz GLE 53 AMG and a grey Mercedes-Benz GLC 300 AMG, while the electronic devices comprise an orange iPhone 17 Pro Max, a silver Samsung Fold 7, a blue iPhone 13 and a silver iPad,” according to a statement issued on Tuesday by the EFCC Head of Media and Publicity, Dele Oyewale.

According to the statement, the court had earlier granted an interim forfeiture order on 17 July. It directed the EFCC to publish the order in a national newspaper.

The publication was intended to give any interested person or organisation an opportunity to explain why the properties should not be permanently forfeited.

When the commission’s lawyer, C. C. Okezie, moved the application for final forfeiture on Monday, she told the court that the EFCC had complied with the directive.

She ordered the commission to publish the interim forfeiture order in The Guardian newspaper on 16 September 2026.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ms Okezie also informed the court that no interested person or organisation had come forward to challenge the forfeiture.

After considering the application and affidavit evidence, Judge Bogoro granted the application and ordered the final forfeiture of the properties to the Federal Government.

Proceeds of fraudulent activities

The commission alleged in the statement that the properties “were reasonably suspected to have been acquired with proceeds of unlawful activities.”

EFCC to file the application through its lawyer, Ms Okezie.

In a supporting affidavit accompanying EFCC’s forfeiture application, an EFCC operative, Buluebiere Karamo, stated that the commission received intelligence alleging that Mr Arinze led a syndicate of fraudsters operating in Lagos.

The EFCC alleged that he used the identity “Tonya” on iMessage to contact several victims in the United States. He allegedly instructed them to create foreign financial accounts, including Zelle, Apple Pay, PayPal, Cash App and Venmo.

The victims were then allegedly directed to transfer funds received through those accounts to a Chinese national identified as “Chinko Applepay”.

The Chinese national allegedly credited Mr Arinze’s Kuda Bank account with the naira equivalent of the funds. He then transferred the money to other members of the syndicate and retained 10 per cent as commission, according to the EFCC.

The commission maintained that an analysis of his Kuda Bank account allegedly revealed total inflows of N2,149,495,381.42 between August 2022 and February 2026.

“Further investigation revealed that Arinze operated 49 Gmail accounts, alongside several Facebook and Instagram accounts, which were allegedly used for his fraudulent activities.” the EFCC wrote.

it said arrested Mr Arinze on 20 April 2024 during a sting operation on Remi Olowude Street, Lekki, Lagos. Several other individuals were also arrested.

He was subsequently charged before the Federal High Court on two counts of computer-related fraud.

The EFCC said he pleaded guilty and was convicted on 5 June 2024 by Judge Aneke. The judge ordered him to be of good behaviour and desist from further involvement in cyber-related offences.

However, the commission alleged that he breached the terms of the judgement by continuing to engage in money laundering and computer-related fraud after his conviction and payment of the option of a fine.

The EFCC said it later received fresh intelligence indicating that Mr Arinze had continued his alleged fraudulent activities. This prompted another investigation.

During the investigation, the commission said it traced the properties listed in the forfeiture application to proceeds of fraudulent activities committed after his earlier conviction.

Asset forfeiture

Nigeria’s Proceeds of Crime (Recovery and Management) Act 2022 provides for the recovery and forfeiture of assets reasonably suspected to have come from unlawful activities. The law allows courts to order forfeiture through civil proceedings, separately from criminal prosecutions. This means that an asset can be forfeited even without a criminal conviction against its owner.

The Act provides for a two-stage process. A court first issues an order to preserve the property while interested persons are notified and given an opportunity to challenge the forfeiture.

The court may then grant a final forfeiture order if the evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that the property is linked to unlawful activity.

World.title: Stop following Tinubu to rallies, Uzor Kalu tells APC leaders
World.content:
Abia North Senator Orji Uzor Kalu has advised All Progressives Congress (APC) leaders to prioritise grassroots mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections instead of accompanying President Bola Tinubu to campaign rallies across the country.

Mr Kalu, a former governor of Abia State, said party leaders should remain in their respective political constituencies to engage voters, strengthen party structures and build support at the ward and local government levels.

The senator, who coordinates parliamentary mobilisation for the South-east, made the recommendation in a statement titled, “The APC Presidential Campaign Council and the Need for a Leaner Campaign Train,” Vanguard newspaper reported on Monday.

He argued that the president should be accompanied by a smaller campaign entourage, while other influential party members concentrate on mobilising support in their political strongholds.

APC adopts grassroots mobilisation strategy

Mr Kalu’s position comes days after the APC Presidential Campaign Council directed ministers, political appointees and members of its campaign council to attend only rallies organised in their respective home states.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the council issued the directive in a circular dated 3 November and signed by its Director-General, Abdulaziz Yari.

The directive was addressed to directors and heads of directorates within the campaign council and was intended to improve coordination and strengthen grassroots mobilisation ahead of the elections.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The council also adopted a pyramid-style mobilisation strategy that emphasises building political support from polling units through wards and local government areas to the state level.

Under the arrangement, party officials are expected to mobilise voters within their respective jurisdictions rather than concentrate their activities around the president during campaign events.

Kalu cites political mobilisation in Abia

Citing his political activities in Abia, Mr Kalu said effective mobilisation must begin at the ward level, where party leaders have direct access to voters.

He recalled leading more than 4,000 APC members from Igbere Wards A and B in Bende Local Government Area during the party’s presidential primary in May.

According to him, the experience showed the importance of building political structures and consolidating grassroots support.

Mr Kalu maintained that the party’s chances in the 2027 elections would depend largely on its ability to sustain direct engagement with voters across communities.

He stressed that a campaign’s effectiveness should not be measured by the number of political leaders accompanying the president to rallies, but by the strength of the party’s structures and its connection with voters at the grassroots.

Mr Kalu’s comments reinforce the campaign council’s recent directive restricting political appointees and campaign officials to rallies in their home states as the APC begins preparations for the 2027 general elections.

World.title: NNPC, Oando join global push to end gas flaring as Nigeria’s emissions rise
World.content:
The Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited and Oando are among oil and gas companies committed to ending routine gas flaring by 2030 under a global decarbonisation initiative, even as Nigeria continues to record rising gas-flaring volumes.

The companies are signatories to the Oil and Gas Decarbonisation Charter (OGDC), which on Tuesday released its 2026 Status Report at the ongoing United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

The report, released three years after the initiative was launched at COP28 in Dubai, shows that 41 signatory companies now have action plans to eliminate routine gas flaring, representing a 78 per cent increase from the 2024 baseline.

The initiative is particularly noteworthy for Nigeria, one of the world’s largest gas-flaring countries, where regulatory weaknesses and inadequate infrastructure have continued to undermine efforts to reduce emissions from oil and gas operations.

According to the World Bank’s Global Gas Flaring Tracker, Nigeria flared 6.6 billion cubic metres of gas in 2025, compared with 6.1 billion cubic metres in 2024 and 5.1 billion cubic metres in 2023.

The figures indicate that gas flaring in Nigeria has increased for three consecutive years, despite the country’s commitments to eliminate routine flaring by 2030.

The OGDC brings together 57 oil and gas companies operating in more than 100 countries and representing one-third of global oil and gas production.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Its signatories have committed to achieving net-zero operational emissions by or before 2050, near-zero upstream methane emissions and zero routine flaring by 2030.

Beyond NNPC and Oando, other companies with Nigerian operations identified among the charter’s signatories include ExxonMobil, which has its subsidiaries in Nigeria as Esso Exploration and Production Nigeria Limited and Esso Exploration and Production Nigeria (Deepwater) Limited; Shell, through its subsidiary Shell Nigeria Exploration and Production Company (SNEPCo), and TotalEnergies.

Shell also holds a 25.6 per cent interest in Nigeria LNG Limited.

More companies develop emission-reduction plans

The 2026 report indicates increasing participation by companies in emissions monitoring, planning and investment, although progress remains mostly measured through corporate disclosures and commitments.

Of the 56 companies that were members during the reporting period, 52 submitted emissions data, covering 97 per cent of the charter’s operated production.

Four companies reported their operational emissions for the first time, while another national oil company established its emissions baseline and shared data with the initiative for the first time.

The number of companies that have set interim 2030 targets to reduce Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions also rose to 46, up from 42 in the previous reporting year.

Of these, 42 have developed action plans to achieve their emissions-reduction ambitions, representing a 40 per cent increase from the 2024 baseline.

Scope 1 emissions are those generated directly by a company’s operations, including emissions from burning fuel and gas flaring, while Scope 2 emissions arise indirectly from purchased electricity, heating and cooling.

The report also found that 39 companies had developed methane action plans, representing a 63 per cent increase from the 2024 baseline.

Methane is the principal component of natural gas and a potent greenhouse gas. It escapes into the atmosphere through leaks, venting and incomplete combustion during gas flaring.

Billions of dollars committed to decarbonisation

The report also highlighted growing financial commitments to reducing operational emissions.

Thirty-five signatory companies, accounting for 84 per cent of the initiative’s operated production, have allocated capital towards achieving their interim emissions-reduction targets.

Half of these companies said their allocated budgets now cover their entire decarbonisation roadmaps.

In addition, 34 companies reported $28 billion in lower-carbon investments and acquisitions in 2025.

The report also identified improvements in emissions verification, with 39 companies, representing 92 per cent of the initiative’s operated production, having individual third-party verification procedures for their emissions data.

Twenty-one companies now use direct measurement technologies for most of their reported methane emissions, while another 18 use the technologies for some of their reported emissions.

The report said 30 companies also provided the OGDC secretariat with information not currently publicly disclosed, allowing the initiative to assess progress and identify areas needing further support.

Nigeria’s persistent gas-flaring problem

The commitments come against the backdrop of Nigeria’s persistent difficulties in enforcing regulations intended to curb gas flaring and methane emissions.

A PREMIUM TIMES report published on 24 September, titled Inside Nigeria’s methane problem, found that Nigeria’s gas-flaring volumes increased from 5.1 billion cubic metres in 2023 to 6.6 billion cubic metres in 2025.

The investigation attributed the persistent problem to weak regulatory enforcement, inadequate infrastructure and the transfer of environmental liabilities following the divestment of assets by international oil companies to indigenous operators.

It also found that only 15 of the 62 companies covered by the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative‘s (NEITI) first upstream greenhouse gas audit submitted emissions data, while 47 companies did not.

NEITI warned that the poor disclosure rate posed a significant risk to Nigeria’s ability to meet its climate commitments.

A separate PREMIUM TIMES investigation published on 1 September found that oil companies continued to violate gas-flaring regulations without facing corresponding sanctions.

Another investigation published on 12 October examined TotalEnergies’ declaration that it had ended routine gas flaring in Nigeria. PREMIUM TIMES’ analysis of satellite data and observations around the company’s assets identified persistent flare activity despite the company’s claims.

The investigation also showed that TotalEnergies failed to report its methane emissions in Nigeria.

Nigeria’s Petroleum Industry Act and subsequent regulations have established obligations for oil and gas operators to reduce flaring, monitor methane emissions and implement measures to eliminate routine flaring.

However, flaring persists, raising questions about the effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and how well companies are translating climate commitments into measurable reductions.

Bjørn Otto Sverdrup, head of the OGDC secretariat and chair of the Executive Committee of the Oil and Gas Climate Initiative, said the report showed increasing participation in emissions reporting, the development of action plans and the allocation of capital towards decarbonisation.

“Our focus now is to build on that momentum towards delivery,” he said.

He said improved data, practical support, collaboration and technology were helping companies identify emissions sources, prioritise interventions and accelerate decarbonisation.

“With four years to go until 2030, the priority is to get more complete data, scale proven solutions and turn plans into more projects,” he added.

The OGDC said more than 4,000 professionals from signatory companies had participated in its technical workshops and training programmes since the initiative began.

World.title: I was soaked for hours before help came — 74-year-old blind man whose home was wrecked by wind storms
World.content:
Flooded and submerged canal at Oluwaseyi Street, Isashi, Iba LCDA, Lagos

…Good-spirited man begins rebuilding the house

By Chinedu Adonu

ENUGU – For 74-year-old Mr. Stephen Ogbo, the rainstorm that ripped through his residence at Ugbo Ezeji, D-Line, Abakpa Nike, Enugu metropolis, was a terrifying, unforgettable experience. The ugly incident left him soaked in water for hours, trapped in a shattered building and unable to find his way to safety because of his blindness.



As the storm raged, Ogbo could neither see the destruction around him nor find his way out. He remained helpless until an unidentified female tenant eventually came to his rescue.



Recounting his ordeal, Ogbo said the woman approached him after he had spent several hours soaked in water, unable to escape from the disaster.



“The female tenant came to me after several hours but couldn’t find any way to escape as a blind man. She said: “Daddy, we have been trapped by the windstorm,” he recalled.



According to him, the woman held him, led him out of the destroyed building, and searched for shelter where he could find safety. Although he could not identify his rescuer, he remembered that the voice belonged to a woman.



“I do not know the name of the woman who came to my rescue, but the voice was a woman’s voice,” he said.



A native of Nomeh Unateze in Nkanu East Local Government Area of Enugu State, Ogbo said he had lived in the compound for about eight years before the incident.



The rainstorm damaged the residential building housing 23 families, ripping off its roof and destroying property belonging to tenants. The incident left the occupants struggling to find shelter and salvage their belongings.



For the affected families, what began as an ordinary evening quickly turned into a nightmare, with the destruction leaving them with the difficult task of restoring their homes and livelihoods.

A cry for help



However, days after the incident, help has begun to come following an appeal by the victims for help.



Chief Kingsley Chizoba Nweke, the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) senatorial candidate for Enugu East Senatorial District, where the blind man hails from, has commenced the reconstruction of the damaged home after watching a video in which the victims appealed for assistance.



Nweke visited the affected residents at Ugbo Ezeji and said their plight moved him to intervene, and announced that building materials had been purchased and contractors mobilised to commence the reconstruction.



“It’s a pity, actually. If you look at the roof, it is damaged, and the place is messed up. I saw them interviewed two days ago and they cried out that they needed help.



“That touched me so much, so I said it was important that I come to their rescue. We have bought the materials, mobilized the contractors, and the work has already commenced,” he said.



He explained that the exercise would involve reinforcing the affected structures and replacing damaged roofs to enable the residents to return to their homes.



“My priority is to make sure they get back to their houses and keep living again,” he said.



Nweke said the intervention was humanitarian and not politically motivated, insisting that he would have assisted the victims irrespective of their political affiliations.



“This is not politically motivated. If they were wearing the caps of a different party and they said they needed help, I would still come. They just need help, not because of party,” he said.



He described the intervention as part of his broader humanitarian activities, which he said included supporting people who had lost their jobs and means of livelihood.



“I will do more than this. We have been doing more than this already. This is just a minor thing from what we have been doing,” he said.



He answered my cry.



Another resident and woman leader in the area, Mrs. Promise Ugochukwu, described the incident as devastating. She said the storm occurred between 9pm and 10pm, when strong winds ripped off the roof, and rainwater damaged household belongings.



Ugochukwu thanked Nweke for responding to the residents’ appeal, describing his intervention as an answer to their call for help.

“When I cried out to my father, Odaa Opuo (Nweke), the man whom I trusted, he answered me,” she said.



Ogbo also expressed gratitude to Nweke for the intervention and prayed for God’s guidance in his political career.



For the 23 families affected by the disaster, the immediate challenge is to restore their homes, replace damaged belongings, and regain the sense of security they lost when the storm struck.



But for Ogbo, the memory of that night will remain tied to the kindness of a woman whose name he may not know, but whose helping hands guided him out of danger.



In the aftermath of the destruction, her intervention stands as a reminder that even in moments of helplessness, an unexpected act of kindness can make the difference between despair and hope.

World.title: FG coming with major agric reforms to boost food production, cut inflation — ADENLE
World.content:
File image

The Federal Government (FG) has proposed sweeping reforms in the agricultural sector, including digitalisation, mechanisation and improved coordination among government agencies in the sector, to boost food production, reduce food inflation and strengthen food security.



Senior Special Adviser on Agricultural Innovation to the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, Professor Ademola Adenle, disclosed this in an interview where he outlined plans to resolve long-standing challenges in the sector.



Adenle said digitalisation will help government identify genuine farmers, monitor production, ensure transparent distribution of inputs and expand farmers’ access to markets.



He said the National Agricultural Growth initiative had introduced a system where agro-dealers distribute inputs to verified farmers while monitoring their output. According to him, the intervention has increased production by 30%, with wheat output rising from 420,000 tonnes to 480,000 tonnes annually.



He, however, admitted that higher production alone would not bring down food prices unless institutional weaknesses and structural inefficiencies were addressed.



“Previous programmes focused mainly on production and input distribution without addressing institutional capacity, food security and agro-industrialisation,” he said.



Adenle called for an overhaul of the ministry’s administrative and legal structures, noting that bureaucratic bottlenecks had limited the impact of interventions.



He identified poor coordination among federal, state and local governments as a major challenge, and advocated harmonised agricultural policies across the three tiers.



He also proposed performance-based financing, annual key performance indicators, stronger monitoring and evaluation, data-driven decision-making, and legislation to promote accountability and transparency.



On rising food prices, Adenle blamed illegal movement of produce across Nigeria’s borders and hoarding of food commodities for creating artificial scarcity.



He said the Nigeria Customs Service and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission are working with security agencies to address the problem.

World.title: Climate plans: CAPPA warns against fossil fuel expansion, corporate capture
World.content:
… Says Nigeria’s 2060 net-zero ambition contradicts 3m barrels-per-day oil target

… Demands phase-down of fossil fuels, grants, protection of community land rights



By Chioma Obinna

Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) on Tuesday warned that African governments risk turning their climate commitments into instruments for expanding fossil fuel production and advancing corporate interests at the expense of vulnerable communities.



The organisation, alongside the Africa Make Big Polluters Pay Coalition (MBPP Africa), said Africa’s climate transition would amount to little more than rhetoric unless governments confronted the contradictions between their renewable energy commitments, continued investments in oil and gas, and growing dependence on foreign climate financing.



The warning came as the organisations unveiled two reports examining Nigeria’s Energy Transition Plan and the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) of five African countries at a media presentation in Lagos.



The reports, titled Four Years On: Examining Nigeria’s Just Transition Plan and Nationally Determined Contributions in Africa: A Five-Country Policy Analysis, assessed the climate commitments of Nigeria, Cameroon, South Africa, Togo and Uganda.



They identified fossil fuel expansion, uncertain climate financing, carbon markets and the growing influence of private corporations in climate policy development as major threats to achieving a genuinely just transition across the continent.



Speaking, the Executive Director of CAPPA, Akinbode Oluwafemi, said the central question was whether African climate policies were genuinely transforming economies and protecting people or creating fresh opportunities for corporate interests to profit while communities bear the consequences.

He said: “These reports emerge from a fundamental concern: Are Africa’s climate policies genuinely transforming our economies and protecting our people, or are they creating new opportunities for corporate interests to profit while communities bear the consequences?”



Oluwafemi said governments could not claim to be pursuing decarbonisation while simultaneously approving projects and infrastructure that entrenched dependence on fossil fuels.



He cited the contradictions in Uganda, where French multinational TotalEnergies promotes investments in renewable energy, including solar, while remaining a leading developer of the East African Crude Oil Pipeline, EACOP, and the Tilenga oil project.

He also referenced Cameroon’s award of five of nine oil blocks offered to fossil fuel operators, including Murphy Oil and Octavia Energy, despite its stated decarbonisation commitments.



In Nigeria, the report identified a major contradiction between the country’s ambition to achieve net-zero emissions by 2060 and its official target of producing three million barrels of crude oil daily by 2030.



It acknowledged progress in renewable energy deployment and policy development but argued that the country’s energy transition was being layered onto an economy still heavily dependent on oil and gas.



The report also questioned the promotion of natural gas as a clean transition fuel, warning that methane, its principal component, is a powerful greenhouse gas responsible, alongside methane emissions from other sources, for nearly 30 per cent of global warming since the Industrial Revolution.



According to the organisations, the challenge is not merely setting climate targets but establishing institutions, financing arrangements and enforceable social protections capable of delivering them.



They noted that Nigeria’s Energy Transition Plan lacked sufficiently enforceable guarantees for workers and communities affected by the transition, particularly in areas where livelihoods depend on oil and gas activities.



The report further highlighted the scale of Nigeria’s energy access challenge, citing World Bank figures showing that more than 80 million Nigerians lacked access to electricity as of March 2025.



It argued that a successful transition must deliver affordable and reliable electricity, secure livelihoods, environmental restoration and viable economic alternatives for communities in the Niger Delta and other extraction zones.



On climate financing, the reports raised concerns about the growing dependence of African countries on international funding, particularly loans that could deepen their debt burden.



Nigeria estimates that it requires $337 billion between 2026 and 2035 to implement its climate commitments, with 80 per cent expected from international funding.

Similarly, Togo has made 69.9 per cent of its financing requirements conditional on international support, while South Africa’s NDC indicates that approximately 80 per cent of international financial support recorded for 2021 and 2022 came in the form of loans.

Oluwafemi, in his opening remarks, warned against financing arrangements that could further impoverish countries already bearing the consequences of a climate crisis they contributed relatively little to creating.

He said: “Even worse, climate finance delivered as loans risks pushing African nations deeper into debt as they respond to a crisis they have contributed little to creating.”



He also criticised the outsourcing of climate policy development to foreign private companies, citing Togo’s engagement of Paris-based Cibola Partners to prepare key technical deliverables for its climate mitigation, adaptation and investment planning.

He said such arrangements raised questions about whose interests ultimately shaped national climate policies.
