World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 10, 2026
World.content:
Nine Zimbabweans Arrested Over Alleged Russia-Ukraine War Recruitment

Nine Zimbabwean nationals have been arrested in South Africa on suspicion of attempting to travel abroad to fight in the Russia-Ukraine war. The suspects, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in Johannesburg. Five were detained at OR Tambo International Airport and four at a hotel in Bruma. They face charges under South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which prohibits unauthorised mercenary activities. Authorities have not disclosed whether the group intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine, or which organisations allegedly facilitated their recruitment. The arrests come amid growing concern over the recruitment of African nationals into the conflict. Zimbabwe previously reported that several of its citizens had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia. South Africa has also helped repatriate citizens allegedly tricked into joining the war.

Kenya Seizes $27 Million Methamphetamine Haul in Major Drug Bust

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kenyan authorities have seized 454 kilograms of methamphetamine worth an estimated 27 million dollars in an operation targeting international drug trafficking networks. Three suspects, two Tanzanians and a Ugandan, were arrested in the coastal region following a joint intelligence-led operation involving Kenyan and Tanzanian anti-narcotics officers. Investigations suggest the network operates across several African countries, including Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa and Mozambique, as well as Afghanistan and the United Arab Emirates. Authorities believe some of the drugs seized in Tanzania may have entered through Kenya's port of Mombasa. The latest seizure is among the largest in Kenya's history and comes amid growing concerns about East Africa's role as both a transit route and destination for illegal drugs. Police said that investigations are continuing, with further arrests possible.

U.S. Deports Rwandan Genocide Suspect Jean Léonard Teganya

The United States has deported Rwandan genocide suspect Jean Léonard Teganya, who was handed over to authorities in Kigali and arrested. The 55-year-old is accused of participating in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, including alleged killings at a hospital and student dormitory in Butare. Teganya was previously convicted in the US in 2019 of immigration fraud and perjury after concealing his alleged involvement in the genocide. Rwanda's National Public Prosecution Authority said that he is the eighth genocide fugitive to be deported to the country from the US since 2007. His American trial focused on immigration offences. However, prosecutors presented evidence linking him to the Interahamwe militia and alleged involvement in the killings. Rwandan authorities say his deportation forms part of ongoing international efforts to ensure accountability for genocide crimes.

21 Killed in Bus and Truck Collision in Tanzania

At least 21 people, including two young boys, have been killed and five others injured in a road crash in Tanzania's Iringa Region. The collision involved a passenger minibus and a cargo truck at Kiponzero Junction along the Iringa-Njombe Highway. Police said that preliminary investigations suggest the minibus driver entered the main highway from a feeder road without ensuring it was safe, resulting in the crash. President Samia Suluhu Hassan has sent condolences to the bereaved families, while the injured are receiving medical treatment. The fatalities comprised 10 men, nine women and two boys aged between three and five. Two of the injured have been transferred to Iringa Regional Referral Hospital for further treatment, while the others remain at a local dispensary.

Ethiopian Families Fleeing to Kenya Face Food, Water and Shelter Shortages

Around 50,000 people have fled violent clashes in Ethiopia and crossed into Kenya's northern Moyale region since late October, prompting calls for urgent humanitarian assistance. The displaced are facing severe shortages of food, clean water, shelter and healthcare, according to an assessment by Kenyan authorities and humanitarian partners. An assessment found that 80 percent of households said their most urgent need was food and 44% did not have adequate access to drinking water. More than half of the displaced are children, adding pressure to already stretched host communities. Most of the arrivals have fled Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regions, with nine in ten households reporting that their entire villages had been displaced. Humanitarian agencies warn that urgent funding is needed to support both the displaced families and the communities hosting them.

Close 

Malawi Unveils Strategy to Tackle Transnational Organised Crime

Malawi is developing a new national strategy to combat organised crime, including human trafficking, cybercrime and cross-border criminal networks. Homeland Security Minister Peter Mukhito says the government will strengthen cooperation between law enforcement agencies and international partners to tackle increasingly sophisticated criminal operations. The proposed strategy includes establishing a National Task Force and developing a clear implementation plan. Police Chief Richard Luhanga says authorities are also investing in specialised training to equip officers to tackle emerging threats, particularly cybercrime. Malawi is among only six countries to develop a dedicated national strategy against transnational organised crime. The government says the framework will provide a coordinated, long-term response to criminal networks that threaten national security, economic stability and public safety.

World.title: South Africa: Matlala Blames Medication for R500K Bribery Claims - South African News Briefs - November 10, 2026
World.content:
press review

Matlala Claims Medication Affected R500K Bribery Statement

Alleged crime kingpin Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala has told the Madlanga Commission that he was heavily medicated and not mentally well when he made statements alleging he paid former police deputy commissioner Shadrack Sibiya R500,000, reports EWN. Matlala has denied making the payments, claiming he gave Sibiya only R50,000 during the SAPS Excellence Awards in KwaZulu-Natal. The statements were part of a failed plea agreement in a R360 million tender fraud case involving his company, Medicare24. Matlala is set to return to the witness stand.

Senzo Meyiwa Trial Continues

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Defence witness Thabiso Buthelezi is set to continue testifying in the Senzo Meyiwa murder trial at the Pretoria High Court, reports SABC News. Buthelezi has told the court that his late uncle, Simphiwe Buthelezi, was seriously ill and mentally incapacitated when police allegedly obtained a statement from him in June 2020. He claimed his uncle could barely speak, feed himself, or hold a conversation and therefore was not in a condition to make or sign a statement. The defence is challenging the circumstances surrounding the alleged statement.

UK Triple-Murder Suspect Seeks to Withdraw Guilty Plea

UK fugitive Ndodana Tshuma is set to appear in the Johannesburg Magistrates Court as his extradition to Britain remains delayed, reports EWN. Tshuma, who is wanted over the alleged murders of his wife and two daughters at their London home in July, is seeking to withdraw his guilty plea to charges of possessing an unlicensed firearm and contravening immigration laws. He previously told his lawyer he could not remember signing the plea and sentence agreement, despite weeks of negotiations. The proceedings are expected to determine whether the court will allow him to retract his plea, further affecting the extradition process.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: 66 Soldiers Sentenced to Death for Cowardice
World.content:
Dozens of defendants were put on trial over accusations that they abandoned their posts and refused to follow direct orders.

Some 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in DR Congo on charged of cowardice, mutiny, and failure to obey orders. The sentence was handed down by the Goma Garrison Military Court.

At least 71 members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were arrested in several separate incidents related to the fierce fighting between the military and rebel groups near the country's borders with Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi.

They were arrested on allegations of abandoning their posts or running away from clashes with FRN rebels. Prosecutors had sought capital punishment for 70 of the defendants, while asking for a 10-year jail term for an intelligence officer. The court, however, acquitted four defendants,



Major Dieudonné Kasereka, head of communications for FARDC in the affected region, said that the charges were necessary to reinforce discipline in the country's embattled North Kivu and South Kivu regions.

What is the FRN?

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation is an umbrella group of rebels that also includes the March 23 Movement (M23) and Alliance River Congo (AFC).

The group's origins can be traced back to the Rwandan genocide in 1994 and the ensuing ethnic conflict, as it emerged from the Congolese Tutsi militias of the time.

It is led by former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila. When current President Felix Tshisekedi came into power in 2019, Kabila found himself increasingly ostracized politically and went into self-imposed exile in an area occupied my what was then M23. Further complicating the conflict is the involvement of the FDLR rebel group, an ethnic Rwandan Hutu militia also active in South Kivu.

Although Rwanda's strongman president Paul Kagame denied involvement in the conflict, both DR Congo and many in the international community held that evidence of Rwandan involvement was clear. Indeed, Rwanda was involved in the 2025 US-brokered peace deal — which was seen as mostly serving US economic interests and doing little to resolve the long-running conflict.

Earlier this year, the United Nations condemned FRN and Rwandan soldiers for "murder, torture and other ill-treatment, corporal punishment, forced unlawful recruitment and abusive labor, and use of child soldiers."

Edited by Kieran Burke

World.title: Africa: Africa Seeks Terms For Backing COP31's Global Electrification Push
World.content:
The COP31 presidency wants electricity to make up 35% of global energy use by 2035, but African countries question how it will be financed and whether it can support industrial growth.

A proposal to accelerate global electrification has emerged as one of the major energy initiatives at COP31, placing Africa's electricity needs and the cost of expanding power infrastructure firmly in the climate debate.

The Turkish presidency is seeking support for a target that would increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, from around 23% today.

The initiative, known as the 35 by 35 pledge, is intended to encourage governments to expand electricity use across transport, industry, buildings and other sectors.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

COP31 President Murat Kurum has described the target as an attempt to establish a clear international goal for electrification, linking the initiative to energy security, economic growth and the need to reduce dependence on imported fuels.

"We need the 35-by-35 target because until now electrification has not been underpinned by a clear global goal," Kurum said.

Chris Bowen, Australia's climate minister and COP31 President of Negotiations, has placed particular emphasis on the investment needed to make the target achievable.

"Ambition matters, but it must be backed by investment, infrastructure and implementation," Bowen said.

For African countries, the proposal comes at a time when expanding electricity access has become central to economic planning. Governments are investing in generation, transmission networks and regional power markets to support manufacturing, mineral processing, agriculture and rapidly growing urban populations.

Yet the scale of the investment required remains considerable. Roughly 600 million people in sub-Saharan Africa were living without electricity in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency. Many more households and businesses contend with unreliable supply, expensive backup generators and power systems unable to meet rising demand.

The proposed target has therefore opened a discussion about the financing arrangements, energy choices and national priorities that would determine how African countries participate in a global electrification drive.

Kapwani Kavenuke, lawyer and an energy campaigner at Power Shift Africa, said the initiative needed to reflect the circumstances of African countries, where access to electricity remains a major development challenge.

"Electrification is a good way to go because we are trying to transition away from fossil fuels," Kavenuke told bird story agency on the sidelines of COP31.

She said the continent's priorities should include expanding access to renewable electricity in communities still outside existing power networks, alongside efforts to improve electricity efficiency.

African negotiators are expected to examine how the initiative accommodates different levels of development and the substantial investment required to expand electricity supply across the continent.

Their position could influence whether the target is incorporated into the final COP31 outcome, and under what terms.

The financing question

The scale of Africa's electricity deficit provides a measure of what is at stake.

The IEA estimates that annual financial commitments for new electricity connections in sub-Saharan Africa remain below $2.5 billion, with concessional finance needing to increase roughly sixfold to support universal access goals.

The African Development Bank and World Bank have already placed electricity access at the centre of their development programmes through Mission 300, an initiative intended to connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030.

The programme is expected to mobilise public and private investment, expand national grids, support decentralised renewable energy systems and encourage regulatory reforms that make electricity projects commercially viable.

Its progress will offer an important test of whether international financing can translate into connections at the pace required.

The financing discussion gained fresh momentum on Tuesday with the launch of the Electrify Now Finance Coalition, bringing together governments, development banks and private financial institutions to support electrification in emerging and developing economies.

The World Bank and African Development Bank will become the coalition's inaugural co-chairs in 2027, placing two institutions already involved in Africa's electricity expansion efforts at the centre of the new initiative.

The COP31 presidency is also working with the International Renewable Energy Agency on a programme to help developing countries identify distribution grid investment needs, prepare projects and access finance.

For African governments, financing also extends to the terms on which money is available. High borrowing costs, currency risks and the financial condition of national utilities can make otherwise viable power projects difficult to finance.

Transmission networks require large amounts of capital upfront and often generate returns over several decades. Distribution companies must also recover enough revenue to maintain equipment and invest in new connections, while keeping electricity affordable for consumers.

These challenges are particularly acute in countries where public debt already consumes a significant share of government revenue.

Kavenuke said Power Shift Africa was pressing for grants to play a larger role in financing electrification, particularly for communities with limited access to existing electricity networks.

"What we are pushing for is instead of having loans in order to finance electrification, it needs to come in terms of grants," she said.

She also called for greater involvement of civil society organisations in directing financing towards community-level projects, drawing on her experience working with communities in Uganda and Zanzibar.

The financing demands have also gained support from a coalition of civil society organisations pressing the COP31 presidency to strengthen the proposed electrification framework.

In an open letter updated ahead of the summit, more than 120 organisations called for significantly increased public climate finance, with grants and concessional funding directed towards developing economies.

The signatories also want financing to reach smaller enterprises, community energy providers and local organisations, arguing that the expansion of electricity networks must be accompanied by measures to improve affordability and access.

The proposed COP31 pledge could provide a framework for increasing international investment in electrification. Its value for African economies will depend in part on how financing is mobilised, the instruments available and the extent to which support reaches countries facing the greatest electricity deficits.

Electrification and industrial growth

Africa's electricity needs extend well beyond household connections.

Reliable power is increasingly important to the continent's efforts to process more of its agricultural produce, manufacture consumer goods and capture greater value from its mineral resources.

Countries including Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo are seeking to expand mineral processing and related industries, while South Africa, Morocco and Egypt are pursuing investments in manufacturing, renewable energy and cleaner industrial production.

These ambitions depend on electricity systems capable of supplying large industrial customers at competitive prices.

The challenge is particularly important for Africa's position in global supply chains. As international markets introduce stricter environmental requirements, the cost and carbon intensity of electricity could increasingly influence where manufacturers choose to invest.

For countries seeking to develop battery materials, green steel, fertiliser production and other energy-intensive industries, electricity policy has become closely linked to trade and industrial strategy.

Damilola Ogunbiyi, chief executive of Sustainable Energy for All and the UN Secretary-General's Special Representative for Sustainable Energy for All, has identified industrial development as one of the major opportunities associated with the proposed target.

"Electrification presents an opportunity to industrialize, create jobs, improve livelihoods and strengthen energy independence," Ogunbiyi said.

Sustainable Energy for All has worked with the COP31 presidency on a new report, The Electrification Opportunity, examining the challenges and opportunities facing emerging markets and developing economies.

Kavenuke expressed a similar view, arguing that renewable-powered electrification could create economic opportunities for communities and support the development of African industries.

"It's not just about household lighting. It's not just about having e-mobility or e-cars. It's about economic transformation and what opportunities then does it bring?" she said.

The 35 by 35 initiative could provide additional momentum for investment in these sectors, particularly if international financing supports generation capacity, transmission infrastructure and regional electricity trade.

It also raises questions about how the benefits of electrification will be distributed. Large industrial projects may attract financing more readily than rural distribution networks or smaller enterprises, even as both contribute to economic development.

The terms of international support could therefore shape which parts of African economies gain access to new electricity supplies and at what cost.

The debate over energy sources

The COP31 initiative is also attracting scrutiny over the sources of electricity that would support the proposed expansion.

In an analysis published ahead of the summit, the Heinrich Böll Foundation argued that the pledge leaves considerable room for governments to increase electricity consumption using fossil fuel generation.

The foundation pointed to language referring to diverse and sustainable energy sources, arguing that the proposal needs stronger provisions linking electrification to renewable energy and the transition away from fossil fuels.

The concern has also surfaced in the wider international debate. Portugal has advocated cleaner electrification, while climate-vulnerable Pacific countries are seeking clearer progress on reducing fossil fuel dependence, according to Reuters.

The COP31 pledge already recognises renewable energy, energy efficiency, nationally determined policies and the need for affordable finance. It also calls for investment in grids, storage and decentralised generation, including through grants and concessional instruments for developing economies.

Power Shift Africa is among the organisations calling for a stronger emphasis on renewable energy within the proposed electrification framework.

"Our position is it must push forward for renewables," Kavenuke said.

She argued that renewable energy investment could help countries expand electricity access while developing local industries and creating employment.

The distinction between expanding electricity consumption and increasing renewable generation matters for African countries, where national energy systems differ considerably.

South Africa continues to depend heavily on coal, while countries including Kenya and Ethiopia generate substantial shares of their electricity from renewable sources. Natural gas also features in the electricity development plans of several African economies.

These differences will influence how governments approach an international electrification target and the financial and technological support they seek.

Africa also has significant renewable energy resources, including solar, wind, hydropower and geothermal potential. Developing these resources at scale requires investment in transmission, storage, regional interconnections and electricity markets capable of attracting long-term capital.

Close 

The COP31 presidency is seeking to address some of these infrastructure challenges through an international programme on distribution grids, supported by IRENA, and a tracking mechanism led by the IEA to monitor electrification progress.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said electric technologies were increasingly competitive and could improve energy security for countries dependent on imported fuels. The agency will support the COP31 initiative by monitoring global and regional electrification trends.

"Electric technologies are often cost-competitive and can improve energy security for fuel importers," Birol said.

Utilities participating in the Utilities for Net Zero Alliance have also increased their annual investment commitment for grids, renewable energy and storage from $148 billion to $156 billion.

A global target, different national realities

The proposed 35% target measures electricity's share of final energy consumption globally. It does not prescribe an identical target for every country.

This is an important consideration for African economies, where electricity consumption remains low, and access gaps are substantial.

An increase in the global share could be driven largely by electric vehicles, industrial equipment and heating systems in economies that already have extensive electricity networks.

For many African countries, the immediate priorities include building those networks, connecting households, expanding generation capacity and providing sufficient electricity for economic activity.

Kavenuke said the proposed timetable needed to be considered alongside the practical challenges facing communities that have yet to gain electricity access.

Drawing on her work in Uganda and Zanzibar, she said some communities still rely heavily on charcoal and other traditional fuels for cooking and have limited access to electricity infrastructure.

"So when you go present this idea to people in those grassroots communities about we want to do this by 2035, which by the way is just around the corner, they are saying how?" she posed.

The pace of electrification will therefore depend on national circumstances, available technology, investment conditions and the structure of domestic energy demand.

The pledge acknowledges these differences through its emphasis on nationally determined policies and development priorities.

African negotiators will have an opportunity to establish how those provisions should be reflected in any wider COP31 outcome and whether additional language is needed on finance, access and implementation.

The COP31 presidency has presented electrification as a central part of its effort to accelerate implementation of existing climate goals.

Its progress in Antalya will provide an early indication of how governments intend to translate those goals into investment and national energy policies.

For Africa, the discussion comes as governments and development lenders seek to accelerate electricity connections through Mission 300 and attract investment in generation, transmission and industrial power supply.

World.title: Gambia: Electoral Commission Says 12 Presidential Aspirants Submit Papers As Six Withdraw
World.content:
Twelve of 18 presidential aspirants submitted nomination papers by Monday, November 9, while six withdrew from the process, the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) says.

IEC chairperson Joseph Colley said the nomination period began on November 3 and will close on November 14.

The six who withdrew after collecting nomination papers were the All Inclusive Party, Gambia Action Party, National Unity Party, Musa Jallow, Ismaila Joof and Alkali Cham.

Four of the 12 submissions had not been processed because the required D1 million deposit had not been paid. They were the Democratic Party, Salifu Jallow, Yusupha Dumbuya and Joseph Henry Joof. The latter three are standing as independent candidates.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The IEC said it had also not processed the submission by the Gambia Labour Party, which is sponsoring Bamusa Dukureh. The Commission said Dukureh had publicly acknowledged holding dual citizenship, and his senior secondary school certificate had been sent to the relevant authorities for verification.

The IEC provided updates on seven other aspirants whose papers had been processed or reviewed. Some still need to provide signatures or documents, and the Commission has not yet announced the final list of candidates.

Modou Lamin Sima of the Alliance of Progressive Citizens must submit 1,040 more registered-voter signatures to reach the national requirement of 5,000.

Independent aspirant Isatou Touray needs 12 more signatures from the Kerewan Administrative Area to meet the regional threshold of 200.

Ansu Sanneh of the National Builders Party must provide 144 additional signatures from Banjul, 23 from Basse and 379 nationally. The Commission is also carrying out further checks on his citizenship.

Kebba Bojang of the National Democratic Party needs five more signatures from Banjul, 21 from Kanifing and 1,914 nationally. The IEC is also verifying his senior secondary school certificate.

Independent aspirant Bakary K. Badjie needs 125 more signatures from Banjul, 36 from Kanifing, 110 from Kerewan, 127 from Mansakonko, 44 from Janjanbureh and 91 from Basse. He needs another 2,310 signatures nationally.

Ebrima Tabora Manneh of the People's Alliance Party must provide 57 more signatures from Kanifing, eight from Mansakonko and three from Janjanbureh. He also needs 1,507 additional signatures nationally.

The IEC said Talib Ahmed Bensouda of the Unite Party did not need to submit further documents or signatures.

The Commission said the nomination process remained open and more aspirants could submit papers before the November 14 deadline. It said it would continue updating the public on submissions and corrections, and announce the approved candidates later.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian Airline Removes Passenger After Threat to 'Burn Down' Aircraft
World.content:
"The anger I am feeling can burn down this plane," a passenger allegedly told cabin crew before Air Peace returned its aircraft to the airport ramp and removed him.

A Nigerian airline has removed a passenger from one of its aircraft after he allegedly threatened that his anger could "burn down" the plane during a confrontation with the cabin crew before take-off.

The incident occurred aboard an Air Peace flight P47866, scheduled to fly to Asaba, Delta State, after the passenger, identified as Celestine Ezeudu, allegedly refused repeated instructions from the cabin crew to stop taking pictures and put away his device.

The Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection at the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), Michael Achimugu, disclosed the incident in a post on X on Monday.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to Mr Achimugu, the situation escalated when another crew member approached Mr Ezeudu, leading to a wrangle during which he allegedly made the threat.

"The passenger ignored the instructions and when a second member of the crew approached, an altercation broke out, and the passenger made a statement: 'The anger I am feeling can burn down this plane,"' Mr Achimugu said.

He said the crew immediately alerted the captain, who initiated a ramp return at 15:57, allowing the passenger to be removed from the aircraft.

Mr Ezeudu reportedly complied with instructions to disembark without further resistance, while his travelling companion also left the aircraft voluntarily.

Mr Achimugu said the passenger later explained that his anger stemmed from missing an earlier flight, but he had not anticipated that his conduct would lead to the aircraft returning to the ramp.

The incident comes amid recurring confrontations between passengers and aviation personnel in Nigeria, some of which have triggered flight disruptions, arrests and sanctions.

In August 2025, Ibom Air reported a confrontation involving passenger Comfort Emmanson on its Uyo-Lagos flight.

The airline said the incident began before a take-off in Uyo when Ms Emmanson refused to switch off her mobile phone after being instructed to do so in line with aviation safety procedures.

Although the situation was initially resolved and the flight departed, the airline said Ms Emmanson later confronted the cabin crew member who had given the instruction after the aircraft arrived in Lagos.

Ibom Air alleged that she assaulted the crew member, another cabin crew member and security personnel, and attempted to remove a fire extinguisher from the aircraft.

She was subsequently restrained, removed from the aircraft and handed over to the police for investigation. The incident generated widespread public debate after videos of the confrontation circulated online.

Close 

Another aviation disruption occurred in August 2025 involving Fuji musician Wasiu Ayinde, popularly known as KWAM 1, at the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport, Abuja.

The incident followed a disagreement over a flask containing liquid he was attempting to take aboard a ValueJet aircraft bound for Lagos.

The Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria said Mr Ayinde allegedly obstructed the aircraft from taxiing after boarding had been completed, prompting airport security personnel to intervene.

The NCAA subsequently initiated action over the incident, while the aviation minister announced sanctions that were later reviewed following the musician's apology.

It has repeatedly warned against unruly behaviour on aircraft, including verbal abuse, physical assault, refusal to comply with crew instructions and conduct that threatens aviation safety.

Passengers who have complaints about airline services are expected to use appropriate channels rather than confront crew members or interfere with flight operations.

World.title: Somalia: U.S. Airstrikes Target Islamic State Positions in Somalia's Puntland Region
World.content:
Bosaso — A series of airstrikes targeted suspected Islamic State positions in Somalia's northeastern Puntland region overnight, with the strikes hitting areas in Qandala district, security sources said.

The bombardments mainly struck the areas of Dabablayaal and Hal Baalade, east of Dhaadaar, near key positions held by Puntland's regional security forces around the Togga Jaceel Sare area, according to local security information.

The strikes were reportedly carried out by US forces supporting operations against Islamic State fighters in the Cal Miskaad mountains, where Puntland forces have been conducting a prolonged campaign against the group. There was no immediate official confirmation from US Africa Command or Puntland authorities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Security information gathered over the past four weeks indicated that Islamic State operatives, particularly members involved in operational activities and planting landmines, had been gathering in Hal Baalade and Dabablayaal, according to local sources.

The fighters were also reportedly active near the Wangable well and the settlements of Goob and Gardaadin, all within Qandala district. Some of the militants had previously operated east of the Togga Jaceel area, where Islamic State maintained bases and strategic positions.

The latest reported strikes come amid continued efforts by Puntland forces, backed by US air support, to weaken the group's presence in the rugged Cal Miskaad mountain range. The area has served as a major stronghold for Islamic State's Somalia branch.

The group last carried out direct attacks in the Dasaan area on September 27, using explosive-laden drones, according to security information. The incident highlighted its continued ability to deploy improvised aerial weapons despite sustained military pressure.

On September 5, a landmine explosion that was reportedly unsuccessful occurred between Sheebaab and Dhaadaar, killing one Islamic State member, according to the same sources.

Islamic State maintains a smaller presence in Somalia than Al-Shabaab but has established networks in the mountainous areas of Puntland, where it has faced repeated military operations by regional forces and US support.

The number of casualties and the extent of damage from the latest airstrikes were not immediately known.

World.title: Kenya: Millions Spent, No Flights - Ruto Makes Fresh Promise On Kisii Airport
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has renewed his promise to transform Suneka Airstrip into a fully operational airport, years after millions of shillings were spent on the facility without delivering the commercial flights residents have been waiting for.

Ruto said his government would partner with Kisii Governor Simba Arati to expand the runway and upgrade the facility to accommodate bigger aircraft.

The President made the announcement on Tuesday while addressing residents during the third day of his Gusii region tour in Bonchari Constituency, where the airstrip is located.

"I want to tell the people of Bonchari as well, and Simba, that we are going to build that new airport," Ruto said.



He acknowledged that the facility had experienced numerous challenges but said he had reached an agreement with Arati to address them and ensure the project is completed.

"That airport had many challenges, but I have agreed with this Simba that we are going to build that new airport," he said.

Ruto said the two leaders would work on extending the runway to allow bigger aircraft to land in Kisii, reducing residents' dependence on airports in neighboring counties.

"He will plan with me how we will extend that runway so that the big aircraft can land here for the people of Kisii," he added.

The latest promise comes after years of uncertainty, stalled construction and changing government plans that have left Suneka Airstrip struggling to achieve its ambition of becoming a commercial aviation hub.

Millions spent but airport remains unfinished

Suneka Airstrip first received major rehabilitation in 2015, when a Sh52 million project was launched to improve its facilities.

The first phase included a passenger lounge designed to accommodate 200 people, toilets, a car park, an administration block, a perimeter fence and runway markings.

The Kisii County Government announced the works in February 2015, saying the improvements would boost tourism and business in the region.

However, the bigger ambition of accommodating commercial passenger and cargo aircraft required further investment and runway expansion.

In 2020, the national government allocated an additional Sh300 million towards expanding the facility to accommodate larger aircraft.

The Kenya Airports Authority subsequently undertook Phase II runway rehabilitation works under a contract initially valued at Sh134 million before being revised to approximately Sh129.2 million.

But the project stalled after the contractor abandoned the site.

According to the authority's 2021/2022 audited accounts, construction had reached only 58 per cent before the contractor demobilized equipment in April 2022.

Ruto previously announced plans to close the airstrip

Close 

In August 2023, Ruto announced plans to decommission Suneka Airstrip, citing insufficient land for the Kenya Airports Authority to undertake the required expansion.

The announcement dealt a major blow to residents and local leaders who had pushed for years to have the facility upgraded.

However, the government later changed direction.

In August 2025, Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba announced that the government was moving to recommission the airstrip following consultations between Ruto and Gusii leaders.

Ogamba said the President had directed leaders to review the facility's status and facilitate the resumption of construction.

The revival efforts received another boost in July 2026 when Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo announced that a new contractor had taken over the stalled project.

Omollo said the previous contractor had encountered challenges and that the necessary documentation had been completed to allow construction to resume.

World.title: Former West Point cadet sued over alleged drugging, forced abortion of ex-girlfriend: 'Horrifying'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A former West Point cadet who pleaded guilty to drugging his then-girlfriend and administering abortion pills without her consent, causing a miscarriage, is facing a civil lawsuit that seeks unspecified damages.

Caleb Suh pleaded guilty in June to assault resulting in substantial bodily injury to a dating partner in connection with the March 2022 incident involving the woman, who was also a cadet at the U.S. Military Academy at the time.

Suh studied at two Ivy League universities since the incident, including one where he began attending classes after his guilty plea. He graduated from Cornell University this year and was enrolled as a graduate student at Columbia University when the woman filed a lawsuit Oct. 28.

The woman wanted to have the baby, but Suh did not want her to keep the child. Suh told the judge that he used the woman's identity to set up an online pharmacy account, ordered abortion drugs through the mail, obtained Xanax from a friend to use as a sedative and tricked his girlfriend into drinking what he claimed was a prenatal protein shake. When she fell asleep, Suh inserted the abortion pills into her mouth and vagina.

PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND

Erin Hawley, a lawyer with the pro-life legal group Alliance Defending Freedom who played a key role in helping overturn Roe v. Wade, said the woman was put in an "absolutely horrific situation."

"She was expecting a child she very much wanted, was drugged and assaulted," Hawley, who is not representing the woman, told Fox News Digital. "The horrifying assault ended up causing the death of her very much wanted child — something no woman should ever have to endure. It has obviously caused a lot of harm and trauma, in addition to the loss of the baby she very much wanted."

"She was drugged and assaulted with abortion pills, even though Mr. Suh knew she very much wanted that child. I expect that he will be prosecuted to the full extent of the law," she added.

Suh is still awaiting sentencing.

Suh left the woman alone and incapacitated and ignored her attempts to reach him once she woke up and noticed that she was bleeding, according to the lawsuit. She was then hospitalized.

As the woman was receiving medical attention, Suh returned to the online pharmacy's website and posted questions about whether doctors could detect the medication he administered, according to the lawsuit.

"She’s suffered a life-changing event that she is still dealing with and will be dealing with for the rest of her life," her lawyer, Russell Kornblith, told The Associated Press last week.

"We hope that by our client coming forward with this lawsuit, it will, at least, ensure that this never happens to anyone else," Kornblith said.

INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Fox News Digital reached out to Suh's attorney for comment.

During a court hearing in June, Suh said that he was "deeply and immeasurably sorry for my actions and the pain that I have caused."

Suh's sentencing has been postponed until Jan. 21, 2027, at his attorney's request, allowing him to finish the semester at Columbia. Prosecutors did not oppose the delay for Suh's sentencing.

He has also been taking a three-month life skills course for people facing federal charges, his attorney said in a letter to the court.

Suh transferred to Cornell during the 2023-2024 school year. The university said in a statement last week that he answered "no" on an application when asked if he had been found responsible for a disciplinary violation at any previous institution.

The university said West Point noted that he was in good academic standing and was eligible to return. He had been involved in health and medicine at Cornell and wanted to become a physician, according to the university's website.

In September, Suh started a master's program at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health, his lawyer wrote to the judge in his federal case. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that Mailman applicants are not asked about their criminal records but are questioned about whether they have ever been disciplined for student conduct violations or poor academic performance.

Suh’s application never made any mention of past disciplinary proceedings, the person told the outlet.

"Regardless of one’s position on abortion, it is not good medicine to allow an abortion drug to be shipped across the country to a dorm room or a home without a woman ever having talked to a doctor," Hawley said.

"The defendant in this case impersonated his girlfriend, had those drugs shipped and then assaulted her with them. That would never have happened if the FDA had done its job in 2023. Hopefully, when the courts do their job and reinstate that safeguard, it won’t continue to happen," she continued, referring to Alliance Defending Freedom's lawsuit challenging the Food and Drug Administration's 2023 decision to remove the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, after the agency had already stopped enforcing the requirement in 2021.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

However, the assault occurred in March 2022, before the FDA's 2023 decision. The agency had already announced in April 2021 that it would temporarily stop enforcing the in-person dispensing requirement during the COVID-19 public health emergency. In December 2021, the FDA announced plans to permanently remove the requirement, a change formally implemented in January 2023.

The FDA has said its decision to remove the requirement followed a review of available evidence. Other restrictions, including prescriber certification requirements, remained in place.

Hawley added that the case at West Point would never have happened if that requirement had been in place.

"Horrific incidents like that throughout the country would never have happened if that basic safeguard had been in place," she said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Stacy Keach dead at 85 as ‘Mike Hammer’ star’s wife shares emotional tribute

Stacy Keach, the legendary actor whose unmistakable voice and powerful performances captivated generations of Americans, is being remembered by his beloved wife as a devoted husband, loving father and courageous fighter after his death at 85.

Keach, best known for portraying the hard-boiled private detective Mike Hammer and for his celebrated work on stage and screen, died Tuesday, Nov. 10, at his family home in Magdalenka, Poland.

His wife, Małgosia Tomassi Keach, shared an emotional statement announcing his passing following a lengthy battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure.

PATRICK STEWART, LEGENDARY 'STAR TREK' AND 'X-MEN' ACTOR, DIES AT 86

"It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach," she said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

"After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength."

She remembered her husband as a man whose remarkable resilience extended far beyond the characters he brought to life on-screen.

"He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life," she continued.

'TOP GUN' STAR TOM SKERRITT DEAD AT 93

"Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family."

For millions of television viewers, Keach will forever be remembered as Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer, the tough-talking private investigator he portrayed with grit, charisma and an unmistakable screen presence.

EVA MARIE SAINT, OSCAR-WINNING ‘ON THE WATERFRONT’ AND ‘NORTH BY NORTHWEST’ STAR, DEAD AT 102

But his extraordinary career stretched far beyond the detective series. A gifted Shakespearean actor, Keach tackled some of theater's most demanding roles, including Hamlet, Richard III and King Lear. He also earned a Golden Globe for his portrayal of Ernest Hemingway.

His television appearances included "Blue Bloods," "Titus" and "Prison Break," while his film credits ranged from "The Long Riders" to "Nebraska" and "The Bourne Legacy."

Keach also appeared in the Biblical miniseries "Jesus of Nazareth," portraying the criminal Barabbas.

In 2017, Keach suffered a heart attack while performing in a one-man production about Ernest Hemingway at Chicago's Goodman Theatre, an ordeal that forced the cancellation of the show's run.

Throughout a career spanning more than six decades, Keach earned admiration not only for his versatility but also for the unmistakable voice and commanding presence that made him one of Hollywood's most recognizable performers.

Yet for those closest to him, his greatest legacy was the love he shared with his family.

"His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives," his wife said. "But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever."

Host Jon Stewart and Maddow discussed the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) decision to cancel plans to build a 10,000-detainee immigration center in a commercial warehouse in Social Circle, Georgia, after the proposal faced local opposition.

"Social circle stood up for itself," Maddow said. "You know, people all over the country where Trump wanted to put these mega prisons, these were huge warehouses to hold people by the thousands. Places that would hold five, six, seven, ten, 14,000 people, all without trial, held indefinitely."

"No, I'm sorry, with a president like this, if you give him seven to ten prisons around the country that hold 10,000 people each, where he can hold people without trial, without access to lawyers, indefinitely, you think he's only going to leave immigrants in there?" she asked.

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT
