World.title: What are childhood vaccination rates in your community and schools?
World.content:
This is part of The Vaccine Divide, an updated data investigation into America potentially losing its measles-free status as the deadly virus roars back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble.

As vaccination rates among children go down, the risk of getting sick from a vaccine-preventable illness such as measles goes up.

Use these maps to see the childhood vaccination rates for your community.

World.title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
World.content:
Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.

Methodology

How NBC News collected the data

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.

The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.

After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:

Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful. Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions. MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates. Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.

How the data was processed

With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.

Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.

All data was checked for accuracy.

Analyzing the data

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Variations in the data

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.

World.title: Bernie Sanders says he won’t support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., announced Tuesday he won’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to be majority leader for the next two years after Democrats’ big 2026 victories.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. [There’s] nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said at a news conference.

Sanders, who is in line to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, becomes a high-profile opponent with inside power and grassroots clout when it comes to Schumer’s staying on as leader.

Schumer has spent a decade as caucus leader and is vying for another two years after having led his party to a net pickup of at least seven Senate seats in the midterm elections, with Mississippi and Alaska still counting votes as two more prospects. Senate Democrats won’t elect their new leadership until next month.

The progressive wing of the party has been calling for Schumer to step aside, while some new Democratic senators haven’t committed to support him. He’ll need a majority of the caucus to win another term as leader.

Standing next to Sanders at Tuesday’s news conference was Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who has similarly called for a change of leadership without backing an alternative candidate.

“I am not actively seeking this job. I am seeking change,” she said. “I’ve been very consistent for a very long time that we need a new generation of leadership. ... It’s important to demonstrate that we’ve heard what people want from this last election.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., whom grassroots progressive advocates are drafting to challenge Schumer, said Tuesday he’s still “actively listening” to colleagues about a potential run.

But he wouldn’t say whether he’ll jump in the race.

“We should not have a coronation,” Van Hollen told reporters in the Capitol. “We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan, and as you know, there are many people who think change is required.”

Until a challenger jumps in and gains traction, Schumer is the clear favorite to win and become majority leader. Despite grumbling in his own caucus, Senate Republican leader John Thune of South Dakota was re-elected by his colleagues Tuesday after detractors failed to recruit an opponent.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., faces some opposition in his bid for another term as leader. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty

“Our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday afternoon. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it as majority leader.”

Some Democrats credit his role in the election victories and believe he deserves the post.

“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give them another contract,” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters. “Chuck and I have had our differences, but at the end of the day, it’s time to unify.”

Asked whether he’s supporting Schumer for majority leader, former and returning Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio replied simply: “Yes.”

Sanders wouldn’t say when he was asked by NBC News whether he favors abolishing the filibuster for the upcoming two-year session, a cause that some on the left are pushing for. It would allow Democrats to pass most legislation without any Republican support, but the same power could be used against them the next time the GOP takes the majority.

“That’s a very important question, and I haven’t reached an answer on it. I think there are a lot of reasons to support it, and that is the majority — we believe the majority rule, not necessarily having 40 people be able to deny what the majority wants,” Sanders said. “I am worried about protecting minority rights, as well.”

Sanders pointed to the “reconciliation” process, which allows the majority party to pass some legislation on its own, as long as it’s related to spending and taxes; Republicans used the process to pass President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”

“What I do believe, absolutely,” Sanders continued, “is that we can, with a major budget reconciliation bill, do a whole lot.”

World.title: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar wins re-election in Florida after clashing with Trump
World.content:
GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has won re-election in her Miami-based congressional district, NBC News projects, after having clashed with President Donald Trump over his immigration agenda.

A recount that was completed Tuesday, one week after Election Day, showed that Salazar was narrowly ahead of her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, by roughly 1,000 votes. In 2024, Salazar won re-election by nearly 20 percentage points.

Salazar drew national attention in September when she released an ad criticizing Trump’s aggressive deportation policy. She said that many Hispanics felt “betrayed” by the crackdown and that the administration’s tactics had “gone too far,” with many deportations targeting individuals without criminal records.

Trump carried Salazar’s district, which is heavily Hispanic, by 15 points in the 2024 presidential election. He responded to the ad by amplifying social media posts that labeled Salazar a “backstabber” and called for her to be replaced as the district’s GOP candidate.

Rodriguez, a former local news anchor, tried to capitalize on the rift. He said Salazar had become “so politically toxic that now even Daddy Trump appears to be distancing himself from his problem child.”

But Trump never officially rescinded his initial endorsement of Salazar.

Democrat Eliott Rodriguez. Marta Lavandier / AP

The close election spurred a legal battle after Rodriguez sued Miami-Dade’s election supervisor, Alina García, last week, alleging that she was biased in favor of Salazar and should recuse herself from the recount. Rodriguez claimed that García’s son-in-law was representing Salazar in the recount, which he said raised concerns about impartiality. Rodriguez also cited an interview in which García told The Miami Herald, “Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount.”

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit Monday, saying the allegations Rodriguez laid out were not adequate grounds to remove García from carrying out her duties, while adding that García’s remarks had been “perhaps unwise.”

With one of the largest concentrations of immigrants in the U.S., Miami has been on the front lines of Trump’s deportation campaign, with more than 130,000 pending removal cases — the most of any county in the country. Salazar’s district has been heavily affected, as it spans multiple working-class, largely Hispanic enclaves, though it also encompasses some of the wealthiest ZIP codes in the nation.

Notably, the district is also home to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who previously represented Florida as a U.S. senator.

In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to carry Miami-Dade County in 36 years. Florida’s 27th District is now set to be home to Trump’s presidential library.

Salazar was first elected to the seat in 2020, when she defeated former Health Secretary and former University of Miami President Donna Shalala in a major upset. The victory foreshadowed the Miami area’s rightward shift in the years that followed.

World.title: U.S. charges 3 men with plotting multiple terror attacks, including planned attack against U.K. airbase
World.content:
Three men, including one already jailed in the U.S., were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in federal court in New York City.

Only Al-Saadi — an alleged pro-Iranian terrorist who is believed to have plotted attacks across Europe, Canada and the U.S., as first reported by NBC News — is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that Al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said McDonald, whose office is handling the case.

“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real,” he added in the statement.

A USAF Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber takes off on a sortie from RAF Fairford over the Cotswold village of Kempsford and the village church of St. Mary the Virgin, in Fairford, England, on March 21, 2026. Christopher Furlong / Getty

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight Sept. 27 on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

The Justice Department indictment alleges that Al-Hassani paid associates to carry out surveillance of RAF Fairford in August and paid several people to move forward with the plot in September “by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel.”

The group even made custom decals to give the vans the appearance that they were used by a fuel company and a swimming pool supply business, authorities say.

Al-Hassani is alleged to have then tasked the people to go to the base with the fuel when U.K. law enforcement took the men into custody.

Al-Saadi was helping direct the RAF Fairford plot while he was in a U.S. prison, according to the indictment. He made video and phone calls to his family members in Iraq, who are alleged to have passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri.

In a July call with his sister, Al-Saadi asked, “What are we doing about all our old work?” — a reference to terrorist activity — according to investigators.

His sister replied, “It isn’t cancelled,” investigators said.

The indictment alleges that the three men conspired to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.

In June, Al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.

The U.S. government has designated Kata’ib Hizballah and the Revolutionary Guards as foreign terrorist organizations.

World.title: Senior U.S. Army soldier arrested in U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence
World.content:
LONDON — A senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said Tuesday.

The 41-year-old man was arrested “as part of an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing” near the ⁠city of Gloucester, ​in the west ⁠of England, London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement, adding that he remained in custody at a police station in London.

He was ​arrested ⁠on suspicion of ‌offenses under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, ‌the statement said. They relate to obtaining ‌or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“The country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” the statement added.

Three people familiar with the matter told NBC News that the soldier was based at NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters at Imjin Barracks on the outskirts of Gloucester.

A senior NATO military official also confirmed the location of the soldier’s assignment.

“We can confirm that the American service member arrested by British police was assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC),” the official said in a statement.

FBI Director Kash Patel was quoted in the statement as saying that the arrest was “important” and that it “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”

The FBI, he added, “has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, was quoted in the police statement as saying, “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”said.

“This case demonstrates the strength of our partnerships and the resolve of the counterintelligence community,” he added. “I am grateful to the U.K. and the FBI for their professionalism and teamwork throughout this investigation.”

Calling the allegations “very serious,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Britain’s senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said the “investigation is very much ongoing.”

The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counterterrorism operations, the statement said.

The arrest comes at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil.

Officials in the U.K. have said proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson fires and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.

The U.S. has moved military aircraft from an air base in the U.K. amid threats from Iran.

A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.

At least eight air refueling tankers and three Osprey tilt-rotor military transports left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.

World.title: Matthew Farwell convicted of killing Sandra Birchmore, unborn child
World.content:
A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child. The verdict was read in federal court in South Boston Tuesday afternoon.

Farwell was charged with killing a witness or victim and causing the death of an unborn child. He pleaded not guilty. The jury had previously said in a note on Monday that it was "in a deadlock."

There were gasps from Birchmore's family as the verdict was read aloud in court.

Farwell faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. Sentencing is scheduled for Feb. 3, 2027. The Department of Justice could have pursued the death penalty against Farwell, but decided last year it would not.

Jurors heard from 50 witnesses over four weeks of testimony. To convict Farwell on the charge of killing a witness or victim, jurors had to find find that he not only killed Birchmore, but that he did so to prevent her from reporting his crimes to federal authorities.

"Today, justice was served for Ms. Sandra Birchmore and her unborn son, both of whom died at the hands of Matthew Farwell. The evidence presented at trial was both shocking and clear," U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts Leah Foley said during a news conference, calling Farwell's actions "absolutely diabolical behavior."

Farwell and Birchmore met when she was a 13-year-old cadet in the Stoughton Police Department's youth explorers program. Prosecutors say Farwell began a sexual relationship with her when she was just 15.

Sandra Birchmore and Matthew Farwell. Department of Justice

"We finally got justice," family says

The 23-year-old Birchmore was found dead in her Canton apartment with a strap hanging around her neck in February 2021. Her death was initially ruled a suicide. But more than three years later, Farwell was arrested and the medical examiner changed Birchmore's manner of death to "undetermined."

Prosecutors made the case that Farwell strangled Birchmore, who was pregnant with what she believed was his child, and then staged her death to look like a suicide in order to cover up their years-long affair. The defense said Birchmore had a history of mental health problems and committed suicide because Farwell told her he was not the father and the relationship was over.

Barbara Wright, Birchmore's cousin, said she was feeling a mixture of sadness, happiness and relief.

"It's been almost six years since we lost Sandra and let's not forget her baby boy," she said outside court. "We finally got justice. We've been fighting long and hard for her. And she deserves it. She's waited a long time."

Norfolk DA responds to verdict

Norfolk District Attorney Michael Morrissey said in a statement that he hopes the verdict brings closure to Birchmore's family and friends.

Morrissey's office has faced criticism from Birchmore's loved ones for choosing not to prosecute Farwell on state charges.

"The Norfolk District Attorney's Office (NDAO) recognizes the criticism it has received for its handling of this case. However, its ability to prosecute was constrained by the finding of the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) that the manner of death was suicide," the DA said. "The NDAO referred the case to the Attorney General's Office for further review, and at all times worked collaboratively with the federal prosecution, including funding the development of additional evidence. Beginning as early as October of 2022, in an effort to be transparent, the NDAO made public its case file and investigative materials in its possession. We respect the jury's verdict and will have no further comments."

Stoughton Police Department reaction

James O'Connor, acting police chief of the Stoughton Police Department, released a statement following the verdict.

"I am grateful for this verdict. It is the outcome Sandra, her unborn child, and her family have deserved for more than five years. The jury heard the evidence and reached a decision, and I fully support it," O'Connor said. "What happened to Sandra is a profound betrayal of the trust every police officer is sworn to uphold. Matthew Farwell used his position to harm someone the community had put in the care of this department. He no longer wears this badge, and he does not represent the men and women of the Stoughton Police Department, who serve this town with honor every day."

Chief Donna McNamara is currently on paid leave from the Stoughton Police Department as part of an investigation not related to the Farwell case. McNamara said in a statement that the verdict is not about Farwell, but instead honoring Birchmore.

"That's what today is about. Today is not just about a verdict. Today is about Sandra. Today a federal jury has confirmed what became apparent to me some time ago, that Sandra was murdered and that her murderer was a police officer who took advantage of her trust and faith in the badge and uniform," McNamara said. "There are those who wanted to forget Sandra Birchmore. But enough people would not remain silent. Enough people spoke up. Enough people asked questions. And rest assured that there are still more questions unanswered than are answered, even after today."

World.title: At least 3 killed when SUV crashes into North Hollywood food stand
World.content:
At least three people are dead after an SUV crashed into a food stand near a North Hollywood bus stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday night.

The collision occurred at around 5:55 p.m. local time near the Metro bus stop at the corner of Lankershim and Chandler boulevards, according to the L.A. Fire Department.

Firefighters said three people were pronounced dead at the scene, while three others were taken to a nearby hospital, two of whom were in critical condition. Crews extricated one person from the wreckage, according to LAFD.

"I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," Mayor Karen Bass wrote in a statement on X. "We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."

The scene of a crash in North Hollywood that left three people dead and several others hospitalized on Nov. 10, 2026. CBS LA

L.A. Police Department officers said the driver of the white SUV, a man in his 60s, was one of the three people taken to an area hospital. He was said to be in serious condition and was being analyzed by LAPD drug recognition experts to determine if he was under the influence at the time of the crash.

The circumstances surrounding the collision remain under investigation, and police said they were looking for security camera footage from the Metro bus station to determine what led up to the incident. Investigators do not at this time believe a second vehicle was involved in the crash, despite witness accounts, police said.

"It'll be a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here," LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said. "Our hearts go out to the families of the victims that were struck here tonight."

Aerial footage showed the white SUV stopped on the sidewalk underneath a canopy, where the food stand was set up. Witnesses told CBS LA the three deceased victims were street vendors in the area.

This is a developing story. Check back for details.

World.title: Meghan Markle's father jailed after cutting off monitoring device
World.content:
Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was jailed in Florida on Tuesday after federal prosecutors alleged that he cut off his location monitoring device earlier in the day.

The 82-year-old Markle, who is facing charges for possessing child sex abuse material, was previously permitted to remain out of custody pending trial as long as he abided by certain conditions.

"He allegedly cut the bracelet off at 1:45 a.m. last night," Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a post on X earlier Tuesday.

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Essayli said. "We are asking the court to revoke his release and detain him pending trial, and we will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law."

According to The Associated Press, Markle was taken into custody and appeared in federal court in Tampa after authorities learned he had cut off the device.

Essayli told The AP he didn't know why the ankle device was removed. It also wasn't clear where it occurred.

Markle was previously released on personal recognizance and was ordered to submit to home detention and electronic monitoring. Markle is also not permitted to travel outside the Middle District of Florida and the Central District of California.

Psychiatric exam ordered

Thomas Markle Pinellas County Sheriff's Office

Separately, a U.S. judge ordered a psychiatric examination for Markle after his arrest for alleged possession of images of child sexual abuse.

Markle is charged with one count of "possession of child pornography" and made an initial court appearance in Tampa, Florida, on Friday.

Judge Lindsay Griffin cited his "health condition," "advanced age" and "lack of recall" in the order issued on Friday, without providing further details.

Markle was taken into custody by FBI agents earlier that day at the retirement home where he lives in Lakeland, Florida.

The Justice Department said he allegedly "kept child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades."

"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.

Pictures of child sex abuse have also allegedly been found at Markle's former home in the Philippines and at a storage unit he rented in Mexico.

The judge said she found "reasonable cause to believe" that Markle was suffering from a condition "rendering him mentally incompetent to the extent that he is unable to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him or to assist properly in his defense."

She instructed a psychiatrist to provide a report on Markle's mental state by Nov. 20.

Markle had been living in Cebu in the Philippines until reportedly returning to the United States this year.

Meghan Markle said last month that she was "deeply distressed" by accusations that her father possessed images of child sexual abuse.

He could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

Investigations in the Philippines, U.S. and Mexico

Last month, it was reported that Markle was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse material. Markle has denied the claims against him, calling them "sick lies."

"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the Daily Mail.

A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.

Markle Jr. told the Sun tabloid last month that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.

"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."

The Daily Mail reported that it alerted the FBI of a cache of child porn found inside a storage unit Markle Sr. had rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico.

The Baja California State Attorney General's Office in Mexico confirmed to CBS News that a search was conducted on Oct. 29 after a report via the 911 emergency line.

"During the operation, three old magazines and VHS tapes containing child pornography were discovered," the office said in its statement. "The evidence and the associated case files were referred to the Attorney General's Office (FGR), which will handle the follow-up to the case."

World.title: Mississippi Senate race leans Democratic; Colom holds narrow lead
World.content:
Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi leans toward Democrat Scott Colom, who has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge against incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

As of Tuesday evening, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by just under 3,000 votes, with 98% of the vote in, according to CBS News projections. At one point on the morning after the election, a mere few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State.

The state's top election official, Secretary of State Michael Watson, said in a post on X Monday that seven more counties of the state's 82 counties still needed to upload their unofficial results, with certified results due from all the counties by Friday. He also said 2,732 absentee mail ballots were still out, and the deadline for election officials to receive them would be Tuesday, Nov. 10.

Hyde-Smith, asked by CBS News' Caitlin Huey-Burns what she could have done differently during the campaign to make it less competitive, responded, "I think we worked very hard and had a very good campaign."

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races in the midterms, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.

Speaking to supporters in the wee hours after election night, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."

"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said Friday there are approximately 3,300 outstanding mail ballots. The state is also processing an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Mail ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov. 13.

Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.

Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.

"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colom told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt." His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will win reelection, posting on X: "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.

Colom and Hyde-Smith have faced off before.

Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination in April 2023, citing questions about Colom's stance on transgender issues and other concerns. Colom won the support of Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker.

Under the Senate's "blue slip" tradition, the Senate Judiciary Committee generally does not move forward with federal district court nominees unless the senators who represent the judicial district sign off — preventing Colom from being confirmed to a lifetime judicial appointment. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.

Colom told CNN that "not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all" in his Senate campaign, saying he forgives Hyde-Smith.

The Mississippi contest is one of two still-unresolved Senate races. Alaska's Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

World.title: Kennedy family members join lawsuit to block Trump's arch
World.content:
Several members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal battle to prevent President Trump from building a large triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

In court filings Tuesday, nine members of the famous family — including several children and grandchildren of Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy and Sen. Ted Kennedy — argued the 250-foot-tall arch would block the sightlines of the Kennedy family's gravesites and the "Eternal Flame" commemorating President John F. Kennedy. The three brothers — Robert F. Kennedy, Ted Kennedy and John F. Kennedy — are buried at Arlington.

The family members wrote that the project will "permanently cast a shadow over the graves of servicemen and women who made the ultimate sacrifice for this country, including the Kennedy Gravesites."

The family members are seeking to intervene as plaintiffs in a lawsuit opposing the arch from the city of Washington, D.C., and the Commonwealth of Virginia. Several Vietnam War veterans are also suing the Trump administration over the arch.

"Americans from every corner of the country visit Arlington to honor those who served and sacrificed for our nation," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement on the lawsuit. "A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come."

The Justice Department had no comment on the filing when reached by CBS News.

The proposed arch — slated for a traffic circle across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial in D.C. — is part of a slew of construction projects in and around the nation's capital that Mr. Trump has personally pushed for. His administration says the arch would commemorate 250 years of American independence. It sought to break ground as early as this month.

But the project has drawn stiff pushback from local officials, congressional Democrats and some veterans and others with an interest in Arlington National Cemetery. Opponents argue the Trump administration did not follow the proper legal processes to build the arch, and warn it would block the sightlines between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

The National Capital Planning Commission, which is stacked with Trump allies, voted to approve plans for the arch last week. But U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan quickly blocked the government from starting any "construction-related activity" for 14 days, finding the plan is likely illegal. The plaintiffs have asked the court for a longer-term injunction.

The government has argued the proposed arch does not violate the law, and says the plaintiffs don't have standing to sue over the project.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement last week: "We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch — a tribute to 250 years of American greatness."

It isn't the first time that members of the Kennedy family have criticized Mr. Trump's architectural overhaul of the D.C. area. Several family members have also spoken out against Mr. Trump's attempts to add his name to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, including the niece and grandnephew of the center's namesake, Kerry Kennedy and Joe Kennedy III, both of whom are seeking to join the triumphal arch lawsuit as plaintiffs.

Kerry Kennedy's brother, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., told CBS News earlier this year he was not involved in the proposed name change for the performing arts center and did not recommend against the move.

"Of course, I understand it, but I have bigger fish to fry," he said when asked about the pushback from some of his relatives.

World.title: Top lawyer in DOJ's Civil Division is latest in string of resignations
World.content:
The top lawyer in the Justice Department's Civil Division resigned on Monday, marking the latest in a wave of departures since Democrats won back control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Brett Shumate, the assistant attorney general of the Civil Division, tendered his resignation on Monday, leaving behind a division that has been struggling to keep pace as it defends the federal government in a flurry of lawsuits since President Trump took office.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, praised Shumate for pursuing "important affirmative litigation to challenge sanctuary policies" and for "delivering key wins in lawsuits against local policies that endangered federal law enforcement."

Last week, the assistant attorneys general for the Justice Department's national security and civil rights divisions also departed, leaving those key offices without Senate-confirmed leadership as well. The U.S. Attorney in the Southern District of Florida who was overseeing the so-called "grand conspiracy" investigation into Obama and Biden-era intelligence officials also departed last week.

Blanche said Tuesday that Craig Trainor will serve as acting assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division. He currently serves in a Senate-confirmed leadership role at the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

T. Elliot Gaiser, the assistant attorney general for the DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel, meanwhile, is being considered by Mr. Trump to be nominated to serve as a judge for the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, according to a Senate aide, who confirmed that the Justice Department had submitted his nomination paperwork. The Office of Legal Counsel offers legal advice to the executive branch, issuing opinions on thorny legal questions.

Gaiser has authored controversial legal opinions such as the classified legal justification for the U.S. military's boat strikes targeting suspected drug traffickers. He does not appear to have any direct ties to Texas, apart from a one-year clerkship in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

Shumate, a former partner at the law firm Jones Day, was widely seen by attorneys in the Civil Division as a reasonable and "decent" leader at a time when chaos has descended on the Justice Department, forcing it to adopt often novel or controversial legal positions to defend the government from hundreds of lawsuits.

He also served in the Civil Division during Mr. Trump's first term in office.

Under Shumate's leadership, the department has fought to defend countless firings of career civil servants, many of whom received no explanation other than a letter citing Article II of the U.S. Constitution.

It has also defended controversial and aggressive mass deportation policies, as well as a number of controversial renovation projects that Mr. Trump has personally directed, including efforts to tear down the White House's East Wing and replace it with a ballroom, and overhauls of the Kennedy Center and the East Potomac Golf Course.

The Civil Division has also had to contend with a flood of habeas corpus petitions this year from detained immigrants, after a Justice Department-run immigration court made a sweeping determination that the government could essentially detain a large swath of immigrants indefinitely while their removal proceedings are pending.

Lawyers in the Civil Division were taken by surprise by the abrupt and unexpected nature of Shumate's resignation, which was effective immediately, sources told CBS News.

His departure comes after Stephen Miller late last week was named as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

One source familiar with the matter told CBS News that Miller has been critical of Shumate in the past and believes he is not aggressive enough, and this was a factor in Shumate's decision to step down.

World.title: Federal government failed to hold Epstein accountable, Republican committee says
World.content:
Federal government failed to hold Epstein accountable, Republican committee says

toggle caption i Jose Luis Magana/FR159526 AP

The Republican-controlled House Oversight Committee released a report Tuesday on its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associates, concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal investigations into the disgraced financier and failed survivors.

"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said committee Chair James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky.

The scathing report comes after 15 months of interviews with 19 people, including former President Bill Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton , Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick . Many of the interviews were conducted behind closed doors, with transcripts released days later.

Sponsor Message

Appearing in the Department of Justice's Epstein files or before the committee is not necessarily an indication of criminal wrongdoing.

The report found that the facts revealed by the investigation do not suggest President Donald Trump was implicated in any of Epstein's crimes . The report also accuses Democrats of launching an "unfounded witch hunt" by attempting to insinuate that Trump was involved in Epstein's crimes.

Epstein was arrested on federal sex-trafficking charges in 2019 and later died in prison. Authorities determined his death was a suicide.

Changing of the guard

In January, Democrats will take control of the House, with Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA) expected to be at the helm of the committee. In a statement Tuesday, Garcia criticized the report as "partisan."

"Oversight Republicans have released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein," Garcia said. "We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started."

Trump has long maintained he had a falling out with the disgraced financier before Epstein was indicted for soliciting prostitution in 2006. In February, White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson told NPR in a statement that "just as President Trump has said, he's been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein."

Sponsor Message

The report puts the next steps in the Epstein investigation into the hands of the DOJ, saying that the agency needs to interview or re-interview witnesses and investigate crimes committed by Epstein's associates. Maxwell is the only associate of Epstein to be charged with a crime and sentenced to prison.

In June , the committee interviewed Sarah Kellen, a longtime assistant of Epstein, who says she is also a survivor of his abuse. According to the committee's report, Kellen revealed the names of two men in her transcribed testimony that the committee sent to the DOJ for further investigation. The DOJ has not announced any investigations into the men.

The report concludes that if not for the "failures" of federal prosecutors in South Florida and Washington, Epstein's crimes after 2005 could have been prevented. Epstein's conviction in 2008 for soliciting sex from girls as young as 14 has long been criticized as a "sweetheart deal." Epstein served 13 months in Palm Beach County Jail with a 12-hour work release during the day . In addition, he had to register as a sex offender.

toggle caption i Jacquelyn Martin/AP

The report also says that "Epstein's pervasive influence and far-reaching connections" shielded him from further investigation. After Gates appeared before the committee in June , Rep. Tim Burchett, a Republican from Tennessee, called Epstein a "friend collector."

"He just liked to have people around him that were a big deal," Burchett said.

The report also says Trump's DOJ did not adequately communicate about the release of the Epstein files or protect survivors' personal information. The release was after the passage of the Epstein Transparency Act in 2025 and the release of millions of pages of documents. Large portions of the files were redacted, but the identities of many survivors were exposed.

Finally, the report concludes that some financial institutions failed to act on indicators of human trafficking and immigration fraud, enabling Epstein's activities. It said that the Treasury Department and its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network should review whether financial institutions are meeting their reporting responsibilities.

Sponsor Message

In a statement released Tuesday, the DOJ said Attorney General Todd Blanche has repeatedly said "the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking."

"With all due respect, the Chairman's recommendations have already been addressed," the DOJ statement said of committee chair, James Comer. "The Department will continue following all additional investigative leads in matters relating to Jeffrey Epstein. Any victims with evidence and information are encouraged to reach out to the FBI."

The Treasury Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

toggle caption i New York State Sex Offender Registry/via AP

What's next?

Garcia has promised that when the committee is under Democratic control that it will continue the investigation into Epstein with hearings open to the public.

Other Democrats, as well as some Republicans, have continued to push to hold Epstein associates accountable.

World.title: House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
World.content:
House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

The House has voted 211 to 204 to refer the articles of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively killing the impeachment effort spearheaded by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

Tuesday's vote short-circuits any potential floor vote on the articles of impeachment, and virtually guarantees the measure will not be taken up before the current session of Congress expires.

The vote provided a surprise reprieve for President Trump's embattled Defense Secretary, who was facing an impeachment vote by the full House as early as Wednesday.

Massie reintroduced the articles of impeachment on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors in connection to the war with Iran and U.S. strikes against Iran and on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean.

Sponsor Message

Massie's impeachment resolution sought to oust Hegseth over the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization, and the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for a video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders.

Hegseth defended himself against the impeachment effort during a rare press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday, criticizing Massie as a "disgruntled and defeated congressman."

"I stand behind every one of these operations," Hegseth said. "I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow."

On Monday, Trump expressed support for Hegseth during a wide-ranging, impromptu press briefing at the White House.

"I'll stand by him," Trump said. "He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won."

The impeachment measure was Massie's second attempt against Hegseth. He first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections, prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution again this week.

While the impeachment push may be quelled for now, Hegseth's troubles on Capitol Hill are not over. Democrats have promised vigorous investigations into Hegseth's Pentagon once they assume the majority in January.

Sponsor Message

Whether they will mount another impeachment effort remains unclear, but in an interview with NPR last week, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next Speaker of the House, said simply of Hegseth, "He's got to go."

World.title: Supreme Court seems split over federal agencies' ability to fine for law violations
World.content:
Supreme Court seems split over federal agencies' ability to fine for law violations

toggle caption i Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

At the Supreme Court, the justices seemed divided on Tuesday in a case that could undermine the ability of many federal regulatory agencies to fine businesses that violate federal laws.

For decades, farmers have relied on a federal immigration program that allows them to temporarily employ migrant workers to pick crops.

In addition to wages, farm owners must provide basic necessities, such as housing, access to meals and water. The whole system is essentially policed by the Department of Labor to ensure that foreign workers don't undercut domestic laborers.

Sponsor Message

In that role, the department fined Sun Valley Orchards, based in New Jersey, a half-million dollars for unsanitary conditions, including providing unsafe drinking water, housing people in 20-bunk rooms, broken sinks and other violations, including failure to pay promised wages.

Sun Valley is disputing the charges and contends that the Department of Labor imposing monetary fines based on its administrative proceedings is unconstitutional. Sun Valley also says the process denies them the right to a jury trial when and if they appeal to a federal court.

At the high court Tuesday, Chief Justice John Roberts strongly suggested that the Trump administration, and many administrations before it, have exceeded the power of the executive branch. In this case, potentially wading into the judicial branch's territory.

Addressing Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who represented the Labor Department, Roberts said, "It seems to me you're just trying to leverage … the broad authority [of the executive branch] beyond the justification for its application."

Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked how disruptive it would be for the federal courts to enforce the law instead of the designated agency (in this case the Department of Labor).

Harris responded succinctly, "If the court were to say civil penalties always have to be in Article III courts, that's kind of the nuclear option."

Harris added that such a ruling would disrupt programs as diverse as Medicare, Medicaid, the federal student loan program and more.

That prompted this question from Justice Elena Kagan: "Why not just go to court always?" Harris quickly responded, "I think it would be catastrophic." She went on to explain that a system like that would inevitably result in massive under-enforcement of the law, given limited resources.

Sponsor Message

Lawyer Robert Johnson represented Sun Valley Orchards. "To be sure," he said, "the statute contemplates penalties, but it says nothing about where those penalties should be adjudicated."

Johnson further contended that penalties should be imposed by the federal courts, not the administrative agencies that do most of that work under current law.

To that Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson replied, "It seems like you're just sort of fighting the reality of … what Congress was trying to do … in ensuring that we don't have farm workers coming in and undercutting domestic workers."

A more skeptical observation came from Justice Brett Kavanaugh: "What you're proposing is really at war with clarity," he said, adding, "I think that's not great systematically going forward."

Justice Samuel Alito pointedly added, "What you're outlining is sort of a hodge-podge opinion, and maybe sometimes courts write that sort of thing," to which Justice Kagan quickly chimed in with a chuckling crowd in the court, "Not ever us!"

In rebuttal, Deputy Solicitor General Harris was unusually candid. "It would be a big deal for the government to lose, but an even bigger deal would be to have a mess," she said. She later added, "A lot of other statutory regimes also would be on the cutting-room floor."

And if that's the case, she said, the administration will have to go to Congress. Her voice rising, she added, "Please tell us now ... if we need to get Legislative Affairs on it right now, because this will snowball."

World.title: Should you trust new AI agents with your money and data?
World.content:
Should you trust new AI agents with your money and data?

Tech companies want agentic AI to be the new way you shop. But should you trust AI when your money's involved?

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

About that new tech that Sacha mentioned, yes, it's AI, but not just another chatbot. We are talking about more powerful AI agents that can actually manage your shopping, your inbox, your subscriptions and so on. But should you trust AI when your money is on the line? Let's bring in NPR tech reporter John Ruwitch and our personal finance reporter Stephan Bisaha. I'm glad to be talking to both of you about all of this 'cause I've been curious about this myself and kind of confused. So, John, let me start with you.

JOHN RUWITCH, BYLINE: Sure.

DETROW: Let's rewind a little bit for people who are getting confused by all these terms. What makes these new AI agents different from the chatbots that have been around for a while now?

RUWITCH: Yeah, AI agents are designed to actually do real world tasks for you, not just fetch data or answer questions. So you could ask an agent to manage your email, fill out forms online or maybe monitor websites for promotions on a specific product and then give you options for buying it when the price is right. These agents are based in the same AI as chatbots, but they're just way more capable. So one way of thinking of it is that chatbots are like GPS, right? They tell you where to drive, they give you directions, but you're doing the driving. These newer consumer-facing AI agents are kind of like a self driving car, right? You tell an agent where you want to go, what you want to do, and the car does the driving. You supervise, right?

There are a few on the market now. Dots is one from OpenAI. There's a thing called Grok Bot made by xAI. One that's really taken off is from Meta. It's called Muse. It's been one of the fastest-growing apps ever, actually, according to the data analytics company Sensor Tower.

DETROW: Stephan, then, walk us through whether and how using an AI agent could save people money.

STEPHAN BISAH, BYLINE: Yeah, so what these bots are really useful for when it comes to money is finding the low-hanging fruit options, the kind of stuff that's really easy to forget about or just really time consuming. Think, like, canceling subscriptions. That's how Scott Burka saved a lot of money. He's a Muse user in Nashville.

SCOTT BURKA: They were, like, things my kids had subscribed to on their iPads or, like, a chess account and things of that nature. And I said, no, I have not been using those. And it actually helped me cancel approximately $100 worth of expenses a month that were completely just under the radar.

BISAH: Another good example is car insurance. AI agents can be really helpful with that tedious and confusing work of comparing rates and doing it proactively every time your renewal is up, just letting you know without even asking you first.

DETROW: How much do they cost though?

BISAH: Dots from OpenAI comes in about $100 a month for a subscription. Grok Bot starts at 30. Meta's Muse, which again, seems to be the most popular one right now, has both a paid and free version. And the Muse users I spoke with said free seemed to be doing more than what they needed.

RUWITCH: Yeah, Scott, one of the currencies that you pay with for these things, though, is personal data. I mean, these apps only really work for you if you give them access to your accounts, email, calendars, Google Drive or contacts, so they can make a date with somebody, for instance. As with human assistants - right? - you're going to want - you know, if you want them to, like, go shopping for you, it's hard to do that if they don't know, first of all, where you are, what your brands are, where you like to shop. So the more data you give these things, the more useful they are as a tool, and, in turn, the more data the companies have on you.

DETROW: And that's where I've struggled because a lot of these, you know, personal finance, keeping-up-with-it stuff is stuff that I personally really struggle with, but I'm very hesitant...

RUWITCH: Right.

DETROW: ...To turn over my passwords to AI. So I'm curious, John, what is Meta, which makes Muse, told you about how they are handling user privacy?

RUWITCH: Yeah, Meta says Muse is highly secure. Each Muse agent is designed to not be linked to other agents. It's also limited in how and when it can go on the internet. Meta says people are always in control of how much access Muse has to their accounts, what permissions you give the app or whether it can access your passwords. And also, if a user wants Muse to check every time before doing something sensitive, like sending an email or buying something, it will. Critics say agents - you know, these agents can do tasks that humans can do, but they can also fail at them. Jiaxin Pei is an assistant professor of information science at the University of Texas, Austin, and he studies AI agents.

JIAXIN PEI: They're not as reliable as human beings. They make stupid mistakes all the time. They are now trained to interact with third parties very well.

RUWITCH: Yeah, so he says caution is warranted. At this point, users should be careful what tasks they delegate to agents.

DETROW: A lot of AI agents in the news this year - and the headlines have not always been positive, often not - a lot about them going rogue in one way or another. Is that a concern here?

BISAH: No, not really so much in these cases. These are not these souped-up AI agents companies were experimenting with, the ones that really push the edge of cybersecurity. These ones, like, are supposed to be much more limited.

DETROW: OK.

BISAH: Instead, many of the mistakes that we just heard about, these are just dumb shopping mistakes in many cases. For example, like, I recently got a new gas grill. I wanted to buy some inserts to make it act like a griddle, and Muse confidently gave me this recommendation that looked good, but it would have been a waste of money 'cause they're just the wrong size. So these agents, they can find you deals you'd otherwise miss, but it pays to double check their work.

DETROW: Look, a griddle on a grill is great, but let's talk about higher-level purchases. I mean, like, you're connecting your credit card and your bank account through Muse, right? Like, that could go wrong very quickly.

RUWITCH: Yeah, these transactions though are usually going through third party apps just like regular e-commerce, right? So it's not holding onto your credit card info. Muse, for instance, can peek into your bank account if you give it that permission, but it can't move money. It can just look inside, maybe give you some budgeting tips.

BISAH: But a lot of banks are coming out and warning that without proper guidelines, AI agents could raise risk of fraud and scam. They all say it is not clear who is liable when something goes wrong - the bank, the AI company or you.

DETROW: That is NPR personal finance reporter Stephan Bisaha and tech reporter John Ruwitch. Thanks so much.

RUWITCH: You bet.

BISAH: Thank you.
