World.title: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
World.content:
Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones

toggle caption i Halle Zander

On a rare overcast day in late summer, red-and-white fire trucks pepper a grassy strip of land in the mountains of western Colorado.

A persistent buzzing rises and falls as several uniformed staff from the Aspen Fire Protection District huddle around an iPad, watching one of their volunteer firefighters control a massive drone.

This first-of-its-kind machine looks like a giant bug. Black and white with propellers attached to four large arms, it's about 10 by 12 feet wide — roughly the size of a small U-Haul trailer.

While firefighters have used drones to monitor wildfires for decades, this new product could use AI to help extinguish fires.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Halle Zander

Eye of the swarm

Developed by the California-based company Seneca, the drones are designed to work in a swarm. Similar to a small fire engine, five of them can carry 500 to 1,000 gallons of finished fire foam, and firefighters in Aspen reported they were easy to operate.

"We were just joking that my 12-year-old could fly these things," said Andy Fisher, deputy chief of Aspen Fire.

When Aspen Fire officially launches its new drone program, as early as next year, it'll be the first fire department in the world to operate the drones independently. So far, they've only been used on prescribed burns in California with support from Seneca's staff.

toggle caption i Halle Zander

Fisher wants to send these drones to hard-to-reach fires, like remote lightning strikes, before firefighters arrive. The city of Aspen, famously home to billions of dollars in real estate, is surrounded by dense forests — like an expensive tinderbox with few evacuation routes for residents and visitors.

"If we could get it quick, keep them small and attack them while they're smoldering instead of waiting for the wind to pick them up, I feel like that's the most ideal use case," Fisher said.

According to Seneca's founder Stuart Landesberg, the drones can bypass steep or otherwise treacherous terrain quickly and have a range of 5 to ten miles — double that if they're empty.

Sponsor Message

Hovering over a fire, they use an AI-supported "sensor suite," that can calculate distance and wind speed, then release water or retardant at a specific angle and velocity to tamp down flames.

"You can think about it almost like a flying Waymo," he said.

But will they make a difference?

Landesberg said the drones won't replace air tankers on big fires, but they can carry tools, monitor ongoing fires and help extinguish lingering hot spots. Compared to helicopters, they could also make aerial firefighting more affordable.

"We can be the next best thing at two orders of magnitude less cost," he said.

Aspen Fire says it'll pay about $2.5 million over the next five years with private donors footing the bill.

Before other fire departments around the country invest in this experimental technology, many are keeping an eye on Aspen to see how effective the drones can be.

Joe Stutler is a firefighter with nearly 60 years experience, including decades as an incident commander on wildfires. He's not affiliated with Aspen Fire or Seneca, and said he's a "big proponent of technology."

He's excited that the drones could help fight fires overnight when manned aircraft are often grounded, and he hopes they'll reduce risk for firefighters on the ground and in the air.

"You look at how many wildland firefighters that have died this year — some aviation accidents," Stutler said. "We say, 'Gosh, we really want a retardant or water drop here.' … We transfer risk to those people that are flying those helicopters and those air tankers."

But Stutler remains skeptical. Seneca has tested the drones on prescribed burns, not real wildfires yet.

"I haven't seen any results," he said. "It's one thing to make a claim. It's something else to back it up with data."

If he had access, Stutler said he'd definitely try the new drones, but no matter how effective they prove to be, he still has to put firefighters on the ground.

Sponsor Message

"I've seen very few times that a 3,000-gallon water drop or a 5,000-gallon retardant drop actually put anything out," he said.

The FAA granted Aspen Fire a waiver in late October, and once training is complete, Fisher said the department could start flying the drones up to 200 feet in Pitkin County.

They can't fly the drones over populated areas, and someone has to have eyes on them at all times. Firefighters can't blindly send a drone over a ridgeline without someone perched on top of a mountain or on the other side to watch them and communicate with the pilots.

But if the drones are useful, Aspen Fire hopes to expand the waiver and help fight fires around the state.

World.title: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running
World.content:
U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running

toggle caption i Lian Yi/Xinhua via Getty Images

GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.

As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Sponsor Message

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Sponsor Message

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."

World.title: Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says
World.content:
Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says

toggle caption i LM Otero/AP

How much money would it take for you to feel financially secure? Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Mona Chalabi spent five years following 10 Americans, from those living paycheck to paycheck to those earning hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, in an effort to answer that question. Her new book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are, explores why financial security can feel so elusive.

"It's called 10 Lives because I specifically didn't just want to focus on the 1%," Chalabi says. "Instead I wanted to talk about how the 99% of us aren't all in it together, and the kind of power differentials between us."

Sponsor Message

Chalabi says almost everyone she profiled in the book was deeply worried about their financial future, even those who earn plenty of money.

"Across the board, everyone just seemed to be expressing this feeling of panic that I think is really, really particular to U.S. capitalism, which is an incredibly precarious and cruel system where you are one crisis away from experiencing a real economic shock," she says.

Chalabi also noticed that many of the people she profiled considered themselves middle class, regardless of what their actual income was. She says that disconnect between actual wealth and a sense of class has consequences — not just for how we see ourselves, but also in how we judge everybody else.

"To be poor in this country is to encounter an enormous, enormous array of obstacles, including assumptions about your intelligence [and] your educational level," she says. "And so it's actually quite rational sometimes for people to try to present themselves as middle class, maybe even to try and signal wealth with the clothes that they buy or the cars that they drive. I don't think it's simply aspirational. I also think it is them trying to avoid the discrimination that they might face if their real income level were disclosed."

Sponsor Message

Interview highlights

Penguin Random House

On the importance of parents when it comes to financial security

If you really want to understand somebody's economic security, you need to understand who they can turn to when times get hard, and obviously a household is an imperfect measure of that. People sometimes even live with spouses that they can't necessarily lean on. ... But one of the things that came out time and time and time again from the book is how much money your parents have is so profound in shaping your economic security. …

Class is about more than the number that is printed on your pay slip or the number that's in your bank balance. Our class identities are very often tied to our households that we were in growing up. They're tied to the professions that our parents had. ... Most people who are born in poverty in this country do not make it out.

On younger generations choosing partners for economic compatibility

Who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.





There was this TikTok trend that I saw a while ago with people talking about how they were looking for a partner who was 6'5", blue eyes and working in finance, which has never been any partner of mine. I grew up with a particular model of feminism that was about being able to support yourself, not relying on a man. But I also think that for my generation, there was this ... understanding of romance that it's somehow supposed to be post-materialist, that you're not really supposed to talk about wanting a partner from a particular set of economic circumstances. …

[There] was a study that was published by the National Bureau for Economic Research. And they compared 1960 to 2005 and what they found was that it's not necessarily that people are seeking out partners in the same income bracket, but people very often seek out partners with a similar educational background, and education has a huge impact on income. So they actually found that over that period from 1960 to 2005, the trend has gotten even stronger. So we are much more likely now to date someone with a similar educational backgrounds to ours. And the reason why this is important to scrutinize is because I would say who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.

Sponsor Message

On being transparent about her own finances, including her large book advance

I felt the people that I was speaking to had a right to understand my economic privilege, my vantage point as I'm asking them these deeply personal questions. And as you know, as journalists, we typically do not pay people for their time for interviewing them. … But that's a very different kind of equation when you are asking people to share these vulnerable parts of their lives, and especially when I am profiting from those stories.

At the start of every interview with everybody that I spoke to, I told them a number of things. I said, one, I will be paying you $40 per hour for your time. If that feels uncomfortable for you, let's talk about it. I said that anything that I asked them as a journalist, they had the right to ask me back. So if I asked them how much money they made, they had the right to ask me that exact same question.

On making judgments about her class from her accent

The accent thing is huge. ... When I'm back in the U.K., people can get a pretty good read, honestly, on my class by my voice. And what's fascinating is that as an immigrant, Americans don't really understand these nuances in the British accent. And so I'm just read as posh here. And I think that has conferred me, actually, these huge class benefits. I think that my accent in the U.S. has been really powerful in counterbalancing some of the obstacles I might have faced because of my race and gender. Because with this voice, it is assumed that I am educated, that I'm cultured. Not sure how true any of these things are, but there's just this assumption that I think is very beneficial in a corporate environment.

Sponsor Message

Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

World.title: Gas prices dip below $4 but inflation remains stubbornly high
World.content:
Gas prices dip below $4 but inflation remains stubbornly high

toggle caption i Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

Inflation-scarred consumers are finding a bit of relief these days at an unlikely place: the gas pump.

The average price of gasoline dipped below $4 a gallon Tuesday for the first time in three months, according to AAA. The price of regular gas has fallen by 38 cents in the last month to a national average of $3.98.

The overall cost of living, however, remains stubbornly high. Consumer prices in October were up 0.4% from the previous month, according to a report Tuesday from the Labor Department. That's a bigger monthly increase than forecasters had expected.

Rising housing costs accounted for about a third of the monthly increase. Grocery prices were also up sharply during the month.

Sponsor Message

Why gas prices are falling

The drop in gasoline prices in recent weeks is thanks to a combination of falling crude oil prices, refineries' switch to a cheaper blend of winter fuel, and the typical seasonal drop in demand for gas.

"Temperatures are getting colder," says Patrick De Haan, petroleum analyst for GasBuddy. "People who have boats and RVs are probably done for the year. I would say, by Thanksgiving, so long as we don't get any wild cards geopolitically, the national average could be $3.75 a gallon."

Gas prices are still at a record high for this time of year, however — about a dollar a gallon higher than when the U.S. went to war with Iran. Even with the recent drop in prices, this year's drive to grandma's for Thanksgiving could be the most expensive ever.

Diesel prices have also fallen, but more slowly than gas prices. AAA says the average price of diesel fuel is $6.15 a gallon, down about 13 cents from a month ago.

The high cost of diesel fuel is another byproduct of the war — not only the U.S. war with Iran but also Russia's war with Ukraine. Russia is ordinarily a big exporter of diesel fuel, but that supply has largely dried up because of damage to Russia's refineries.

Sponsor Message

"When a country like Russia isn't exporting diesel, that is very impactful for the global market. So diesel prices – they will come down but they will still remain very elevated," De Haan says.

Heating oil prices are also high

Rising diesel prices are also driving up the cost of heating oil in the northeast, because heating oil is a close cousin of diesel.

Mild fall weather has kept heating costs in check so far, but De Haan says a blast of cold air could push heating oil prices even higher.

Higher diesel prices also affect the cost of other goods that have to be moved by truck or train or cargo ship.

"You're starting to see higher freight costs get passed through," says economist Mike Reid of RBC Capital Markets. "We've seen it show up notably in goods that are heavily imported — apparel, recreation goods, IT equipment."

In a speech Tuesday before the inflation release, Federal Reserve Chris Waller suggested that energy shocks could have more lasting effects on inflation that previously though. Waller suggested the central bank may need to raise interest rates more aggressively to curb price hikes than markets had previously expected.

No annual comparison for inflation this time

While Tuesday's inflation report shows how much prices rose in the last month, it does not include the typical reading on how prices have changed over the last year. That's a casualty of last year's government shutdown, which idled hundreds of government price-checkers so prices from October 2025 were never recorded for comparison.

The Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank estimated before Tuesday's release that consumer prices in October were up 3.7% from a year ago. That would outstrip average wage gains of just 3.1% during the year, so the typical worker is losing buying power. That's a big reason for the heavy turnout in last week's mid-term elections. 49.1% of eligible voters took part in the election, the second highest total for any midterm in more than a century.

World.title: Republicans block impeachment push against Pete Hegseth
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called the articles of impeachment introduced against him a farce and a stunt at a news conference Tuesday morning. Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment against him on Monday, largely focusing on the war in Iran.

Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives closed ranks on Tuesday to block an effort to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.

The impeachment attempt was spearheaded by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, who was seeking to oust Hegseth largely over his handling of the U.S. war with Iran.

Members of the House voted 211 to 204 to refer Massie's impeachment resolution to a committee, effectively killing it for the remainder of this session of Congress.

The result preserves Hegseth's job, at least for now.

The new Congress, with Democrats in the majority in both House and Senate following their sweeping midterm wins, could resume a new impeachment push against Hegseth after its swearing in takes place on Jan. 3.

However, it's unclear whether the Democrats will want to make going after Hegseth a top priority.

WATCH | Hegseth survives impeachment vote as House Republicans close ranks: Republicans block impeachment effort against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 3:36 Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives blocked an effort to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth Tuesday. The impeachment attempt was spearheaded by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, who was seeking to oust Hegseth largely over his handling of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran. The result preserves Hegseth's job, at least for now.

"This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning," Democrat House Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters on Capitol Hill after the impeachment vote. Democrats will hold a sizable majority in the House come January, with at least 256 seats.

Massie, who won't be in Congress when the new session begins in January, was the only Republican member of the House to break ranks on the vote.

Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans did not vote on the resolution, according to the tally posted by the House clerk.

Trump calls vote an exoneration of Hegseth

The articles of impeachment drawn up by Massie alleged that Hegseth committed "high crimes and misdemeanors," including launching the war in Iran with neither congressional authorization nor an imminent threat, as well as ignoring laws about minimizing civilian casualties.

U.S. President Donald Trump celebrated the vote result in a post on social media, calling it the exoneration of a great American patriot.

"The Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!" Trump wrote in the post on his Truth Social platform. "The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!"

Trump has at least publicly shown nothing but firm support for Hegseth, giving the former Fox News personality a grade of "A PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" in a social media post earlier Tuesday before the vote.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky speaks Monday outside the Capitol about articles of impeachment against Hegseth. (Allison Robbert/The Associated Press)

Jesse Richman, an associate political science professor at Old Dominion University in Norfolk, Va., says Trump has a history of saying he supports someone on his team right up until the moment he pushes them out.

"There's no guarantee that even with positive things, supportive things [Trump] is saying now, he might not change his mind [about Hegseth] at some point," Richman told CBC News.

Richman said Trump may however want to keep Hegseth on because of how difficult it would be to get a replacement confirmed by the Senate once the Democrats form the majority in January.

Tuesday's vote came after Hegseth forcefully defended himself in a morning news conference at the Pentagon.

He said impeachment proceedings would be a "show trial against the president and the secretary of war" and he characterized the articles of impeachment as "policy disagreements" that don't meet the impeachment standard of high crimes and misdemeanours.

"The proper remedy for a policy disagreement, it's legislation, it's debate, it's the next presidential election," said Hegseth, holding his first press briefing from the Pentagon since May.

WATCH | Trump gives full-throated support to Hegseth amid push to impeach him: Trump backs Hegseth over 'stone cold loser' Republican rep's impeachment effort | Duration closed caption 2:44 U.S. President Donald Trump again backed his Secretary of War Pete Hegseth after outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie launched impeachment efforts over Hegseth's handling of the Iran war and extrajudicial strikes against alleged drug boat operators.

The articles of impeachment in Massie's motion begin with the lack of congressional authorization for the war in Iran. The articles also reference Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela, and the deadly strikes on boats allegedly transporting drugs in waters near South America.

Massie had introduced a similar measure in September, but the House legislators were sent home before a vote could occur.

Hegseth denies Maduro was kidnapped

"I stand behind every one of these operations," Hegseth said on Tuesday. He said "thousands of American lives" were saved with every boat strike — even as human rights organizations and international bodies have said they possibly constitute crimes against humanity.

Hegseth also said that former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro was "not kidnapped, he was brought to justice by America's best."

The articles also refer to attempts to prosecute Congress members Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin after they recorded a video advising service members they were not obliged to follow illegal orders.

Massie, who was defeated earlier this year by a Trump-backed Republican opponent in a primary, pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership, with outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson saying it would be "a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see."

The last House impeachment was of former Homeland Security chief Alejandro Mayorkas in Joe Biden's administration in 2024, for breach of public trust and willful refusal to comply with the law. The Republican-led House cited the surge of migrants at the southern border in just the second ever impeachment of a cabinet secretary, but the Democratic-led Senate then never took up the measure.

Trump was twice impeached in the House, in 2019 and 2021, but acquitted at Senate trials. In the second impeachment, many Republicans argued that Trump's actions leading up to the 2021 Capitol riot were best dealt with in the courts, but Trump completed a remarkable political comeback before criminal indictments he faced were resolved legally.

Hegseth called those Trump impeachments failures and predicted that the current efforts "will fail again."

What constitutes "high crimes and misdemeanours" is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide.

Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska has highlighted other concerns not contained in the articles, including Hegseth's firing of dozens of senior military leaders, but he also questioned Massie's motives.

"If we were allowed to amend it, I'd maybe feel a lot of differently," said Bacon.

Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of Hegseth, told reporters on Tuesday he wasn't a fan of the impeachment articles in their present form. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

Republican Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio said, "blaming Hegseth for a duty Congress shirked and the president made is wrong."

"This isn't about Iran, this about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon," said Vice-President JD Vance.

Vance broke a tie in the Senate to enable Hegseth's confirmation in early 2025. Republicans Susan Collins and Mitch McConnell — each set to leave Congress — voted against his confirmation, as did Republican Lisa Murkowski and all of the Senate Democrats.

Thom Tillis, a Republican also leaving the Senate, has expressed regret for his vote to confirm Hegseth, saying in part in September that the secretary "retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defence."

LISTEN | David Smith, Washington reporter for the Guardian, on Hegseth's influence (March 16): Front Burner 30:05 Pete Hegseth: the Iran war’s chief promoter

Democrats and a handful of Republicans questioned Hegseth's fitness for the job nearly two years ago. Hegseth admitted paying a settlement to a woman who alleged he sexually assaulted her, in order to prevent a costly and drawn-out process.

His confirmation hearings also included allegations of excessive drinking and financial mismanagement at two veterans' organizations he previously led.

During Trump's first term, Hegseth was an on-air Fox News contributor who lobbied the president on behalf of three service members who faced accusations of war crimes in military tribunals, arguing they were being treated unfairly.

Trump ultimately granted clemency to two of the men, and elevated a third in rank.

Hegseth's tenure at the Pentagon has been unconventional, and that was on display on Tuesday. Defence secretaries typically stay away from partisan political statements, but Hegseth laid out criticisms of predecessor Lloyd Austin and disparaged the military recruitment and retention efforts of Biden's administration.

He also told the U.S. troops to "stay the course" while evoking his Christianity, even as he has been sued for imposing his religion on federal workers.

World.title: U.S. comedian Josh Johnson surprised by CBC journalist in viral video
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday.

American Josh Johnson, a standup comedian and occasional host of The Daily Show, was cracking jokes about CBC's coverage of a bodega cat getting evicted due to health concerns, during his show at the Vogue Theatre in Vancouver last month.

"I want so badly to meet the editor," Johnson quipped.

A voice from the audience shouted out: "He's here!"

A befuddled Johnson replied: "The cat's here?"

Nope.

"The editor's here!" shouted the crowd.

Enter Jon Azpiri.

Wearing a dark grey hoodie, coincidentally mirroring Johnson's signature light grey hoodie, Azpiri walked onstage for a 10-minute back-and-forth filled with jokes about cats, disappearing islands and journalism.

Johnson started to ask Azpiri about the bodega cat situation before Azpiri interrupted.

"We do a lot of stories about cats. So I need to know the specific cat."

WATCH | The cat in question:

Azpiri, a copy editor and reporter, answered Johnson's various questions about how a newsroom chooses what to cover.

"We're a public broadcaster," Azpiri said. "So we have a thing called Journalistic Standards and Practices."

"There's really no need to brag," Johnson replied.

As of 2 p.m. PT, Johnson's video has more than 2.4 million v iews on Instagram, and it's been seen more than 860,000 times on TikTok.

Johnson ended the exchange, and the two shook hands.

As Azpiri left, he reminded Johnson the province was set to have an election the next day.

"That's a real editor right there, too," Johnson said. "Even as he's leaving, [he's like] 'We do have an election tomorrow.'"

WATCH | Exchange with CBC journalist goes viral: U.S. comedian Josh Johnson’s CBC surprise goes viral | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 14:19

Johnson told CBC's Hanomansing Live that he had a whole routine prepared about the cat story, about how the coverage was so local and quaint, and he decided instead to ask Azpiri about it since he was involved.

"The whole thing just felt like serendipity," he said, describing asking the copy editor about various CBC stories as a gift.

"When you're very open to the possibility of, like, spontaneous moments being gifts, it happens more often," he said. "And we get more of the things that we look for."

When asked what stands out to him about Canada, as an American comedian, Johnson says that there's a general understanding that people are more neighbourly to each other.

'My eyes kind of bugged out'

Azpiri said he didn't expect Johnson's video to be posted — let alone go viral. He didn't even know the show had been recorded.

He told CBC's BC Today he had just come off his copy editing shift before heading to the show.

As he was walking to the theatre with his wife, he told her he hoped they weren't sitting too close to the stage.

"Sometimes comedians do that thing where they talk to people in the audience," Azpiri said. "And I said 'I don't want to be one of those people.' "

Their tickets were for the lower deck, his wife said.

The show started, and when Johnson said he wanted to talk to a CBC editor, Azpiri reacted.

"My eyes kind of bugged out," Azpiri said.

"My wife couldn't help herself and shouted, 'Oh, he's here.' "

LISTEN | Azpiri on his viral Josh Johnson interaction: As It Happens 6:00 When Josh Johnson invited this CBC editor on stage, he just 'rolled with it'

Azpiri said everything happened so quickly, there was no time for stage fright.

"As I walked toward the stage, I did kind of realize, 'What have I gotten myself into?' "

He estimated 1,000 or so people were in the theatre, but he didn't realize there were cameras rolling.

"That seemed crazy to me … I thought that was a very pleasant thing I could tell my kids about. And then this happened this morning."

While he's been a hit in the comment section on social media, Azpiri has no plans to try one-upping Johnson on the comedy circuit.

"[I'm] very much second-billing to Josh."

World.title: Tensions between PM, Quebec premier continue to flare in new tiff over U.S. relations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The relationship between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has gotten off to a rocky start over the past couple of weeks.

The most recent incident happened on Tuesday. Carney was at a news conference in Montreal — highlighting his government's commitment in last week's federal budget to invest in culture — when he was asked about the Quebec government's intention to negotiate directly with American states.

The question came following news that Paul St. Pierre Plamondon had sent letters to 59 newly elected U.S. officials, including Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and re-elected governor Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire .

In the letters, the premier wrote about Quebec's trade relationship with each state, and invited the state representatives to work directly with a Quebec delegate on "new projects and initiatives for the benefit of our respective populations."

That gestured appeared to irk the prime minister. When he was asked about the Quebec premier's efforts, Carney pointed out that "the executive branch, the president, and the American courts," are still the decision-makers for agreements and trade initiatives.

WATCH | Parti Québécois sends letters to 59 new American senators and governors: Quebec premier courts newly elected U.S. officials | Duration closed caption 2:25 The Parti Québécois sent 59 letters to new American governors and senators to open channels of communication. After the U.S. midterms, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon promised a "diplomatic offensive" in the United States now that the political context has changed.

"Secondly," he said, "in a negotiation, it's always a good idea to have a single negotiator."

He then stated that this responsibility lies with the federal government.

'Mr. Carney is not my boss,' says Quebec premier

St-Pierre Plamondon responded to Carney's comments by doubling down.

“Mr. Carney dreams of us not putting on our skates and never setting foot on the ice because he wants the rink all to himself," he said.

"Welcome to Quebec. We have always asserted our place."

He said the letters are something other governments have done before, and that he's doing what he believes is in the best interest of the province.

"And Mr. Carney is not my boss, and he will not prevent Quebec from doing what it has always done, which is to have an international presence that allows us to represent our interests."

St-Pierre Plamondon made his comments to reporters on Tuesday, following a meeting he had at his office with Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-Francois Blanchet (pictured on his right) in Quebec City. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

St-Pierre Plamondon added that Quebec will continue to assert its place on the world stage over the coming months.

Not the first public spat for Carney and Quebec premier

Earlier this month, the Quebec premier accused the federal government of attempting to muzzle him, when Carney denied him speaking time at the 21st Canada-EU summit that was held in Montreal.

St-Pierre Plamondon opted to withdraw from the summit and sent Quebec's chief diplomat, Pascal Paradis, to represent him during the summit's activities.

Paradis has also been tasked with being the province's chief negotiator, including taking over the trade file with the United States.

Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard said it never would have crossed his mind to boycott the event if he were premier.

"Sulking isn't an option," said the Leader of the Opposition. "I don't think this is the best start to relations between Quebec and Ottawa."

Carney said at the time that it was St-Pierre Plamondon's choice to leave his seat at the table empty.

The prime minister has not yet had an in-person meeting with Quebec's new leader, who was sworn in on Oct. 21.

St-Pierre Plamondon has insisted that their first meeting take place in Quebec City, which the prime minister's schedule has reportedly not been able to accommodate so far.

On Tuesday, however, the prime minister was campaigning in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton ahead of a byelection scheduled there for Dec. 7. The Quebec electoral district is about a two-and-a-half-hour drive from the provincial capital.

Carney and St-Pierre Plamondon are set to meet in meet in Cambodia during the Francophonie Summit later this month.

World.title: Stacy Keach, stage actor and Mike Hammer star, dead at 85
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.

Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure," his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.

Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favourite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.

Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating World's Most Amazing Videos on TV. He played a deranged colonel in The Ninth Configuration (also known as Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane), led the TV show Titus, had a role in Alexander Payne's Oscar-nominated drama Nebraska and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama Blue Bloods. Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father in Jay Kelly.

"My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career," he told New York magazine in 2012. "My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I've gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything."

'One of the greats'

Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach's son in the 2008 TV movie Lone Rider, said in a post on X that Keach was a "consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him."

Keach played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries Mistral's Daughter, a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz's novel Princess Daisy, Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli's Jesus of Nazareth and Maj. Jonas Steele in The Blue and the Gray. He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds.

Keach, seen in April 1984, was one of America's finest stage actors. (Daily Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play Indians, played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in King Lear on Broadway and had other onstage roles there, including in 1993's The Kentucky Cycle, The Country Wife in 1965 and Other Desert Cities in 2011.

He also headed the national touring company cast of Frost/Nixon, portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with Sleuth with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of King Lear at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for Pamplona, a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run's cancellation.

'Lowest moment' was prison

While he was still doing Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer (later titled The New Mike Hammer), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London's Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.

Keach and his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, pose for a photo at a premiere in 2006. (Lucas Jackson/The Associated Press)

"As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats," he wrote in his 2013 book, All in All: An Actor's Life On and Off the Stage. He added: "It was the lowest moment of my life."

He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book The Blue and the Gray.

The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.

In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, The Long Riders. He said the experience was "very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity."

After prison, he narrated the TV documentary High on the Job, and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. "There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one's existence," he testified.

Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centres. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the Hammer series. He said he treasured the photos and letters she sent while he was behind bars.

Married 4 times

Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.

His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, Intimate Strangers with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, The Return of Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer, also played well, and then the Mike Hammer series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS's 1986-87 schedule.

Many years later, in the TV series Prison Break that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.

Born in Savannah, Ga., Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.

World.title: 4 grizzly bears responsible for killing mother and daughter in B.C., officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with an attack near Bella Coola that left a mother and daughter dead.

Forensic testing confirmed an adult sow and three cubs were involved in the attack that killed Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.

In an update Tuesday, BCCOS Insp. Jeff Tyre said the attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which is considered "very rare."

"We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, as well as these findings, bring some measure of closure," he said.

"Our thoughts remain with everyone affected."

WATCH | Officials give update on Bella Coola grizzly attack: WATCH IN FULL: Officials give update on 4 grizzly bears destroyed following deadly attack | Duration closed caption 8:57



All trapping equipment used in the response has been removed, and the investigation into the attack has concluded, the Conservation Officer Service said in a news release. It said further analysis will examine the response and the circumstances that led to the fatal event.

"They all had to be [killed], because bears that are involved in fatal attacks on people cannot be rehabilitated or relocated," explained Tyre.

"This type of behaviour presents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future."

The four bears captured over the weekend were not involved in the 2025 attack on a group of students and teachers in Bella Coola, Tyre said.

The bear responsible for that attack was never found.

Tyre said more than a dozen conservation officers worked to track down the bears involved in this month's attack, often in difficult terrain and weather conditions.

"We remain committed to working with the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community to help prevent future bear conflicts," he said.

Elected Chief Councillor Samuel Schooner called the event "deeply, deeply unsettling," and said they're still recovering from the attack from last year.

"Our community is rightfully still deeply affected, and will be for generations."

He said they will continue to provide supports for residents for as long as is needed, including night patrols, escorts for children going to school and offering rides to anyone who needs to get around.

The nation is asking community members to continue to take all necessary precautions outdoors, stay close to young children, ensure spaces are free of any bear attractants and stay away from the Snooka West Trail area.

WATCH | 2 grizzly attacks in same part of B.C.: Grizzly attacks again in same area of B.C. This time 2 are dead | Duration closed caption 7:05

Nuxalk cultural leaders will decide on how the bear remains are used, the nation said in a community update on social media.

"We continue to pray for Jenny and Selah’s family. Your loss is felt with each of us and Nuxalk stands ready to support you during this tragic time," the update read.

"Over the coming months, there will be ongoing discussion about bear coexistence. Nuxalk [leadership] is committed to hearing all perspectives and finding a good path forward."

'Two peas in a pod'

According to family members, Balcarras and Reed were out for a hike on the Snooka West Trail on Oct. 31 but never returned home. They were reported missing the following day.

Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter Selah Reed in this undated photo provided by their family. (Submitted by Matthew Balcarras)

Balcarras's remains were found on Nov. 2, and Reed's were discovered 150 metres away from her mother on Nov. 3.

Balcarras worked as an art therapist in the community, and loved painting, playing guitar and the outdoors. Reed was an education assistant, described as a gentle soul who loved ballet, art and hiking.

The two liked a lot of the same things, according to Josh Balcarras, Jennifer's brother.

"I think they got along really, really well," he said, speaking following their deaths. "They were two peas in a pod. When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her."

World.title: Who is Alice Huang? Alleged Chinese spy, businesswoman involved with Nvidia CEO
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang has been thrust into the spotlight for being involved with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

But little public information is available about the woman accused by U.S. officials of being a spy for Beijing by collecting intelligence from one of the world’s most valuable tech giants.

The two, who are not related, have been photographed at multiple events together.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, believed to be targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

Reuters could not independently verify the intelligence allegation, which China has denied. Reuters could not determine Alice Huang's whereabouts to seek comment.

Here’s what we know about the Chinese businesswoman accused of espionage.

From TV journalist to finance to AI chips

Alice Huang built a career in Chinese finance before emerging in a very different arena: the global race for artificial intelligence chips.

Known also as Huang Le, the Chinese businesswoman held senior roles at a Shanghai investment firm before becoming the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed International, according to more than 30 publicly available financial records, corporate filings and company materials reviewed by Reuters.

Nvidia lists Megaspeed as an official cloud partner on its directory. Megaspeed attracted public attention in October 2025, when the New York Times reported the company was under U.S. investigation over whether it was helping Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington's export controls.

Alice Huang, reported by Chinese financial publication Caixin to be about 42 years old, previously worked in banking and investment management, according to Chinese fund-industry records and an indexed profile on private-fund database Simuwang, which also listed an earlier career in television journalism.

Before her involvement with Megaspeed, she held senior positions at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, a Chinese investment firm.

Several posts on Hexi's official WeChat account between 2016 and 2017 identified her as the firm's deputy general manager, executive director and a member of its investment decision committee and said she had previously worked at HSBC's private bank in Hong Kong and at CITIC Securities. HSBC and CITIC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

A Hexi business card reviewed by Reuters identified Alice Huang as a partner and general manager, with an office in Shanghai's Lujiazui financial district. At the Aurora Plaza address listed on the card, Reuters found offices undergoing extensive renovation, with no Hexi signage or staff present. Calls to a number on the card went unanswered, and an email address could not receive messages.

WATCH | FBI investigating CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy: Trump says FBI 'looking into' Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 4:45 U.S. President Donald Trump said that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang should not worry about the FBI looking into his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese government agent.

Huang became Megaspeed's controlling shareholder in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS, which reviewed corporate records. Incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, Megaspeed provides cloud-computing services and describes itself on its company website as an Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region.

Huang also served as a director and managing director of Megaspeed's Indonesian subsidiary from March to November 2023, C4ADS said. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment.

At a party hosted by Taiwanese server manufacturer Gigabyte during the 2024 Computex technology trade show, Alice Huang and Jensen Huang were both present, according to a person who attended. A photograph posted on LinkedIn showed them seated next to each other.

Gigabyte, which makes AI servers using Nvidia chips, did not respond to a request for comment.

Business ties under scrutiny

Megaspeed has drawn scrutiny from U.S. authorities over suspicions that it helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington's export restrictions, but there has been no public finding that it violated the rules.

Shipping records from trade-data provider ImportGenius reviewed by Reuters show Megaspeed's Indonesian subsidiary imported Nvidia hardware between 2024 and 2026, including H100 processors and related components, in shipments from suppliers including Gigabyte subsidiary Giga Computing.

The H100 is among the advanced Nvidia processors restricted from export to China, although the shipments to Indonesia do not themselves establish any violation of U.S. export controls.

LISTEN | What this could mean for the AI industry: The Current 8:36 Sex, lies and AI chips: Why the Nvidia spy scandal matters Jensen Huang, the head of Nvidia, has admitted to an affair with a woman accused of spying for China. Washington Post reporter Ian Duncan breaks down who's involved, why it's causing such a stir, and what it could mean for the AI industry.

Megaspeed's shares were transferred in late 2023 to Singapore-based SwiftData, which holds all 10 million of its ordinary shares, according to C4ADS. Reuters could not immediately contact SwiftData.

C4ADS said it could not determine who ultimately controls SwiftData, but assessed that Alice Huang may have continued to exercise influence over Megaspeed after the transfer, citing appearances in which she was identified as its chair.

Allegations of Chinese espionage

The reports of ties between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang have prompted U.S. lawmakers to seek answers from the Nvidia CEO.

Central questions include whether he knew of any alleged intelligence activity and whether sensitive information was compromised, said George Chen, a partner at consultancy The Asia Group.

"In many respects, Jensen may also be viewed as a potential victim if he was deliberately targeted or manipulated without knowledge of the individual's true identity or intentions," Chen said.

The U.S. chipmaker has said its CEO meets with thousands of customer executives each year, and that its cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information rather than trade secrets or information related to U.S. national security.

Trump said on Monday he "was amazed" by allegations involving Jensen Huang, among the president's closest allies in Silicon Valley. Trump said he had spoken to the CEO, who told him that he had no idea that the woman was a spy.
