It’s not easy, but I have been through many fights, because I’m a breast cancer survivor, and during the time I was fighting for my job I was also fighting for my life. I believe that, even though it’s not the same thing, it’s still a fight,” she said then.

With the dispute simmering a meeting was organised last month with administrators at the institution and the education ministry’s Regional Educational Services, which mobilised an estimated 100 Merl Grove stakeholders and interested parties to the dispute.

According to Observer sources, the meeting was being spearheaded by the ministry not as a formal hearing, but to allow internal stakeholders to express their concerns and work towards achieving a more harmonious and conducive environment.

The ministry later indicated that it would be reviewing the outcome of the discussions for a follow-up meeting to be decided.

Some stakeholders said they were hopeful that the meeting would achieve a resolution but suggested that some of the issues were controversial and would require patience and a willingness to end the dispute.

When the Observer visited the institution on Monday, teachers were observed bearing placards calling for the resignation of Fullerton, but remained tight-lipped about what prompted the morning’s protest.

Efforts to speak with Fullerton were unsuccessful.

World.title: Resilience takes centre stage
World.content:
Protoje delivers a masterful set at the Treasure Beach Food, Rum and Reggae Festival at Breds Sports Park last weekend. (Photo: Brian Pitter)

If Friday night’s Dubwise session at Jack Sprat was the spark that ignited the 2026 Treasure Beach Food, Rum & Reggae Festival, then Saturday’s main stage concert at Breds Sports Park was a full-on fire.

Riding high on a wave of resilience, the Treasure Beach community pulled off a seamless post-Hurricane Melissa event, proving that a parish twice ravaged by back-to-back natural disasters simply refuses to lose its spark.

Through powerhouse performances from Lila Iké and Protoje the event transcended expectations. Song after song the concert became more than just another item on the annual entertainment calendar; it was a profound celebration of resilience, musical lineage, and cultural preservation.

Sporting her signature Afro, Lila Iké stepped into the spotlight, and the atmosphere inside the venue shifted instantly. Known for her remarkable ability to cater to a diverse cross section of fans, Lila Iké delivered a beautifully balanced set list that bridged the gap between sweet, vulnerable love songs and hard-hitting social commentary.

Opening her set with a soulful rendition of her powerful hit single Scatter, the artiste immediately captivated the crowd and established the tone for the rest of her performance. Building on that momentum with each successive track, the reggae songstress stamped her class on the evening. Songs such as Thy Will Be Done, Forget Me, Solitude, and Second Chance were well received by patrons, but it was her spirited performance of Where I’m Coming From that proved the highlight of her set.

As she introduced the track, she was met with screams of approval from the crowd. The single took on an added layer of purpose, resonating deeply with the St Elizabeth audience.

“Weh di people dem deh weh glad weh dem a come from dung a St Bess tonight? No disaster cyaan mash dis dung,” she said, sending the crowd into a frenzy.

“Yeah, St Bess, a we say resilience,” she continued before launching into the track.

Its lyrics, which speak to struggle, identity, resilience, and divine timing, struck a chord with the audience. The response was unmistakable, as Lila Iké’s set was punctuated by massive forwards and gun-fingers in the air from patrons who had connected deeply with her message.

By the time she brought her performance to a close the singer had further cemented her place among the leading voices of the modern reggae movement.

But the night’s musical treats didn’t end there. St Elizabeth was in for more, this time from one of its own, as Protoje took to the stage. As the headlining general of the In.Digg.Nation Collective, Protoje’s arrival was greeted by a thunderous roar that echoed across the sports park. With his signature effortless command, he delivered a structurally brilliant set, drawing heavily from his catalogue of “message music” and urgent social commentary, while seamlessly weaving in the relaxed, party-centric sounds that keep a festival crowd moving.

Protoje commanded the stage with precision, launching into conscious anthems such as Blood Money and Kingston Be Wise. The tracks, which highlight the socio-political issues affecting Jamaica, made quite an impact on the crowd. Chanting lyrics of resistance word for word, patrons transformed Breds Sports Park into a unified space of collective consciousness.

Recognising the assignment of a weekend festival fuelled by premium Jamaican rum, Protoje masterfully shifted gears into his lighter, feel-good catalogue. The weight of the socio-political commentary gave way to pure relaxation when the band struck up the infectious party anthem Big 45. The smooth, celebratory rhythms of Switch It Up and Who Knows continued to transform the atmosphere into one massive skanking party, allowing patrons to lose themselves in the sweet sounds of reggae.

But the true climax of Saturday night came when the catalogues of both main acts collided. The synergy between Protoje and Lila Iké was undeniable as the pair shared the stage. Bringing an entirely different level of artistic chemistry, the duo performed their collaboration All Over The World. Energy levels peaked as the two artistes traded verses with a seamless, almost familial rapport that spoke to their mutual artistic respect and the strength of their musical connection.

What’s more, patrons were treated to a little ‘brawta’ when Jesse Royal made a surprise appearance. The Small Axe artiste delivered a short but spicy set, joining Protoje for a performance of Sudden Flight, a collaboration the two entertainers recorded alongside Sevana more than a decade ago.

As the curtains closed on a successful staging of the St Elizabeth music festival, it became clear that the event was never just about entertainment. It was a declaration that the culture of the south coast cannot be washed away.

According to Gregory Wright, festival director, through the power of reggae’s finest contemporary voices, Treasure Beach didn’t just celebrate its recovery; it danced its way into a new chapter.

“Returning the festival to its home in St Elizabeth this year was especially meaningful for us, particularly after the parish was impacted by Hurricane Melissa last year. We are incredibly grateful for the opportunity to return and for the tremendous support and turnout we received, which exceeded our expectations,” he said. “The atmosphere throughout the festival was truly special, with the DJs delivering strong sets and the artistes putting on great performances, engaging with the audience and creating an experience that felt both celebratory and meaningful.

“We were also grateful for the artistes’ support beyond the stage, including our headliners, Lila Iké and Protoje, who took the time to interact with patrons and experience different aspects of the festival weekend,” he continued. “We are excited about what this means for the parish and look forward to building on this momentum in the years ahead.”

World.title: Chase credits Warrican for series win
World.content:
West Indies’ Jomel Warrican (centre) has been named Player of the Series after taking 16 wickets in the Caribbean side’s 1-0 series victory over Bangladesh. (Photo: AFP)

SYLHET, Bangladesh (CMC) — West Indies Test Captain Roston Chase has credited his deputy, Jomel Warrican, as one of the main reasons behind his side’s success in their just concluded two-match Test series against Bangladesh.

The West Indies won the series 1-0 after the second Test at the Sylhet International Cricket Stadium ended in a tame draw on Monday.

Left-arm spinner Warrican was named Player-of-the-Series after finishing with 16 wickets, the most of any player in the series.

He snared nine wickets and took home the Player-of-the-Match award in the opening Test in Dhaka, which the West Indies won by eight wickets, before returning to claim seven wickets in the final match.

Speaking in a post-match interview, Chase said Warrican’s variations were too much for the home side’s batters to handle.

“I thought Warrican bowled well in both games. He controlled his economy rate very well and I thought that he built a lot of pressure and put the balls in front of the batsmen for a long period of time, so I thought that was the hallmark of his bowling throughout the series along with straightening and spinning as well.

“I thought that he really kept us in this series and really won the series for us,” Chase said.

Speaking on the Windies’ victory, Chase said while they would have liked to win both matches, he was pleased with the team’s performance.

With the win, the regional team moved up to sixth in the ICC’s updated Test rankings, achieving a goal they set out to do from the start of the Test Championship cycle.

“I’m very happy obviously. Coming to Bangladesh is always a tough place to come and play cricket, so to beat them in their own back yard is always a pleasure.

“We wanted to win both games, but it didn’t happen. This game was a bit slower than the first one, especially with all the bad light taking time out of the game, but we still played well and kudos to the guys for winning the series,” Chase said.

“We had a tough year in the first year of the cycle and we sat down and we spoke about coming to dominate the second year in the cycle playing against Pakistan, Sri Lanka and also Bangladesh. We thought these were teams that were obviously closer to our skill level and closer to us in the rankings, so we wanted to challenge ourselves in terms of winning all three series.

“We won two out of three so I thought that it was a good year and also we went unbeaten in any series, which is something that hasn’t been done for a number of years. So, it just goes to show that when you sit down and plan and put in the hard work anything is achievable, so I think we’re going in the right direction as a unit,” the skipper added.

World.title: DIFFERENT BALL GAME!
World.content:
Demario Phillips (right) of Mount Pleasant moves in to close down LA Galaxy player Harbor Miller during both teams’ Concacaf Champions Cup match at the National Stadium on March 19, 2026. LA Galaxy won both legs by a 3-0 margin for a 6-0 aggregate score. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FORMER Reggae Boy Tyrone Marshall has noticed a challenge facing Jamaican clubs in continental football that goes beyond a lack of money and facilities. He said the way players are trained, prepared and taught to understand the game must also improve if local teams are to compete with clubs from Major League Soccer (MLS) and Liga MX.

Marshall, who has played more than 80 times for Jamaica, spent much of his playing career in MLS before moving into coaching in North America. His coaching experience includes roles as an assistant coach at Real Salt Lake and head coach of FC Cincinnati 2. He has also completed coaching certification at France’s Clairefontaine training centre.

His experience has given him an understanding of the differences between the professional environments in North America and Jamaica’s Legend Jamaica Premier League (JPL).

Marshall identifies the lack of an integrated sports science and recovery system as one of the biggest gaps affecting local players’ ability to maintain their performance over 90 minutes.

“In my experience in the professional game at the MLS level, it’s a different game compared to playing in the Jamaica Premier League,” Marshall told the Jamaica Observer.

“All the MLS and Liga MX teams have invested heavily in sports science — strengthening, conditioning, nutrition, physiotherapy, recovery technology, so on and so forth, to monitor the performance of their players so that they can maximise their efficiency when they get on the field.”

He said Jamaica has the talent and athletic ability, but players need consistent support with training, recovery and workload management. Without those systems, fatigue can affect more than their ability to run.

“When you have games and fatigue becomes a factor, the decision-making slows down, movement becomes less sharp, and the ability to maintain intensity begins to decline,” Marshall said.

His comments support concerns raised by Professional Football Jamaica Limited (PFJL) Chief Executive Officer Owen Hill, who has identified gyms, recovery facilities and technical analysis as areas that need improvement across the 14 JPL clubs.

Hill, in a recent interview with the Observer, also mentioned what he sees as a shortage of specialised technical support.

“We don’t have super technical analysts that can scout a team, can tell you how the formation works, can give you all of that information to guide your own preparation,” Hill said in an Observer article on Sunday.

Marshall’s assessment shows why those resources matter on the field. Players need to recover properly and maintain their physical condition, particularly when they face demanding schedules and opponents who can sustain a high tempo.

However, Marshall said the problem is not only physical. He pointed to tactical awareness and decision-making under pressure as other areas where Jamaican players need to improve.

“Jamaican players have excellent athletic ability,” he said. “The creative technical abilities are there in the individual flair, which is God-given. However, when they step up and play international competition, the game does become much more demanding tactically. The opponents are better organised, the space gets closed down quicker, the players have much less time to make decisions.”

One area he identifies for particular attention is playing without the ball. Players must understand how to create space and passing options, when to press, how to maintain their defensive shape and how to anticipate what opponents will do next.

“It is not just about being talented when you have possession. You must understand how to influence the game when you don’t have the ball,” Marshall said.

Marshall also said players sometimes try to force passes or solve problems individually when better decisions could help their teams retain possession and control the game.

Hill identified a related issue in the way Jamaican football approaches matches.

“Tactically, we’re getting better, but in terms of our strategic approach to games, which, I think, goes deeper than the talent we have, it’s probably the resource gaps, ” he said.

Marshall’s comments provide a closer look at what that gap means for players and coaches, especially the need to improve how teams prepare for opponents and respond to different situations during matches.

Marshall said the standard of competition in the JPL must also improve to prepare players for the demands of international football.

“When you compete against teams regionally, in particular MLS and Liga MX, or other established professional leagues, the tempo is different,” he said. “The level is higher. Speed is faster. Players are stronger. When they press, they press with more coordination. The transitions happen much quicker.”

Marshall said players cannot be expected to maintain a high press and defensive shape against stronger opponents if those habits are not developed during regular training and league matches.

“You cannot expect a team to suddenly execute in a high press and maintain defensive shape if they don’t practise it — develop the habit where they can do this on a day-to-day basis — during training and during the league,” he said.

Squad depth and finances are also important, particularly when clubs have to manage injuries, travel and congested schedules. However, Marshall cautions against treating money as the only explanation for the gap.

He mentions coaching methods, tactical education, player recruitment and the overall training culture as equally important.

For clubs working with limited resources, Marshall recommends making youth development a priority. He wants clubs to establish a consistent playing philosophy from their academies through to their senior teams so young players understand the style of football expected of them as they progress.

He also calls for greater attention to coaching education and the use of performance analysts.

Marshall recalls his experience at Clairefontaine, where young players aged 14 and 15 studied match footage in the classroom as part of their development. They learned about different defensive systems, pressing, and how to analyse their own performances before putting those lessons into practice on the field.

He said Jamaican clubs must place greater emphasis on teaching players to understand the game from an early age.

“Ultimately I would not put all our resources into the physical conditioning alone because ultimately you don’t want to have a fit player and he can’t think for himself and don’t know how to pass the ball and all of that,” Marshall said.

“When you invest, you want to ensure you develop a fitter, smarter and more tactically adept player in a sustainable system.”

Marshall said clubs can improve their coaching standards and training environments without having the financial resources of MLS and Liga MX teams. But he warns against looking for quick solutions.

“We need to stop looking for quick fixes and start building environments that will produce better players year after year after year,” he said.

While there is agreement that a solution can be found, Hill did say that building a league capable of competing consistently at the highest regional level will take at least 10 to 15 years.

Cavalier were eliminated by Inter Miami by a 4-0 aggregate scoreline in 2025 after suffering 2-0 defeats in both legs while Mount Pleasant suffered a 6-0 aggregate defeat to LA Galaxy in this year after losing both legs 3-0 in the most recent clashes between JPL and MLS clubs in the Concacaf Champions Cup round of 16.

World.title: How Health Systems Can Spot Risk Before a Crisis
World.content:
Cancer claims 10 million lives each year, the global shortage of health workers runs into the millions, and in some parts of the world, a single mosquito bite can be fatal.

These challenges may seem very different. Yet they share a common element in how many health systems operate: risk is often recognised only after it has become illness, outbreak or crisis. By then, a disease may have advanced, transmission of disease may be under way, or an already stretched workforce may be managing consequences that earlier action could have reduced.

The opportunity is to move that point of intervention earlier. This is what anticipatory health means in practice: using signals that already exist, at the bedside, in communities, and in routine health data, to help people and health systems act sooner. It is not prediction for its own sake. The value lies in connecting early and everyday signals to a timely, practical response.

Finding practical routes to earlier action

That principle sits at the heart of the Future Health Impact Challenge: Building Anticipatory Health Systems through Population Sensing, launched by Future Health – A Global Initiative by Abu Dhabi in collaboration with MIT Solve. The Challenge received 393 submissions from 68 countries. ThinkMD, VectorCam and Huna emerged as its three award-winning solutions: ThinkMD received the grand prize, with VectorCam and Huna recognised as distinguished finalists.

Future Health Impact Challenge: Trailer

The Challenge was designed to identify practical solutions with evidence of impact and potential to scale. Each of the three selected teams demonstrated their approach to using technology to turn an early signal into decisions that support anticipatory actions a health system can take.

Frontline care as a population signal

ThinkMD starts with the interaction between a frontline health worker and a patient. Its offline mobile platform guides structured assessments aligned with clinical protocols, supporting providers where doctors, connectivity, and diagnostic tools may be scarce. Almost 10,000 frontline health workers across 885 facilities are now using it.

Each consultation also creates structured data. Across facilities, that information can reveal changes in symptoms and service demand. In Zambia, analysis of around one million encounters identified symptom patterns several months before a confirmed cholera outbreak. In Kenya, deployment data showed improvements in identifying danger signs in infants and prescribing antibiotics correctly for childhood pneumonia.

It is not prediction for its own sake.

“The utilisation of AI in healthcare is an absolute game changer. Not only can we increase access for patients, but we can also increase access to information to make correct and appropriate diagnoses and give the right treatment to the right patient at the right time. Future Health has been a really critical platform to be able to accelerate our mission of moving from reactionary to anticipatory care,” said Dr Jackie Rabec of ThinkMD.

The award has given ThinkMD support and visibility as it works to expand into new health systems and strengthen how frontline data becomes timely intelligence for decision-makers. That is one measure of the Challenge’s impact: helping proven solutions move towards sustained, wider adoption.

Earlier signals from the environment and routine data

VectorCam begins with the environment around a community. Using a low-cost smartphone imaging device and offline AI, community health workers can photograph and identify mosquitoes in the field. Each observation generates time- and location-based data that can help authorities see changing vector risk as the first signal of disease patterns, before a spread in local communities and populations.

The value lies in connecting early and everyday signals to a timely, practical response.

Field evaluations show data completeness rising from approximately 60% to more than 90%. With support from the Future Health Impact Challenge, VectorCam aims to strengthen its early-warning capability, integrate additional data sources and expand into national surveillance programmes.

Huna looks for earlier cancer-risk signals in information that health systems already generate. Its platform analyses routine complete blood count data to identify people with an elevated risk and prioritises them for screening. It does not diagnose cancer from a blood test; it helps direct limited screening capacity, and supports patients and healthcare professionals through the next steps.

In Brazil, Huna’s deployments have screened more than 500,000 people and detected hundreds of cancer cases. Its experience also highlights a critical ‘last mile’: identifying risk is not enough if a person does not complete the diagnostic pathway. Recognition and funding from the Challenge could help support further validation across new populations and facilitate new international partnerships.

Innovation is only the starting point

Together, these solutions show that useful signals can come from a variety of sources – including clinical encounters, environmental surveillance, and routine diagnostics. They also show that anticipatory approaches can be built where connectivity, specialist capacity, or access to screening is limited, and that innovation developed in those settings can share insights that can be localised and adopted globally.

But a successful technology or pilot is not the same as system-wide impact. Scaling requires local validation, integrated into existing workflows, responsible data governance, sustainable financing, workforce training, and evidence that earlier insight changes decisions and outcomes.

A successful technology or pilot is not the same as system-wide impact.

“The solutions emerging from this Challenge reflect both the urgency and the opportunity facing health systems globally. By bringing innovators together with policymakers, funders and implementers through platforms such as Future Health, we can help accelerate solutions that are locally grounded and capable of delivering impact at scale,” said Hala Hanna, Executive Director of MIT Solve.

From recognition to system-level impact

The Future Health Impact Challenge is part of Future Health’s wider role as a year-round platform for action. Together with our partners and colleagues across diverse sectors and geographies, Future Health identifies promising solutions, supports their development, builds international connections and brings together the policy, clinical, research and investment expertise needed to move from proof to concept to measurable impact.

The Future Health impact documentary film is now available to watch, and shares personal commentary from the founders of the three companies, local stories of the solutions in action, and commentary from the Challenge owners and collaborator.

Watch the full Future Health Impact Challenge Film here.

World.title: Spanish election: How bad is the housing crisis?
World.content:
“We must look upwards at those in the penthouses and those who run vulture funds and put an end to their speculative practices and abuses,” he added, calling for voters to unite to protect “small property owners and tenants.”

It is no wonder Sánchez has attempted to seize on the topic of housing in a bid to be reelected. The high price of homes is at the forefront of voters’ minds: the most recent data shows house prices are double what they were at the same time in 2015; the average Spaniard doesn’t leave their parental home until after their 30th birthday; and in some historic centers tourist accommodation accounts for 45% of the rental market.

His big challenge, however, is that he could end up blamed for the problem exploding during his more than eight years in office. Between 2015 and 2025, average home prices in Spain rose by 80%, while salaries increased by only 30%. A pledge to use “all state resources” to provide 184,000 public and affordable rental homes has been difficult to realize.

And yet, on many metrics, Spain’s housing struggles are not even the worst in Europe. Rising rents and home prices across the bloc are fueling discontent and setting the stage for affordability to become a key issue in a string of elections set for the coming year.

Here’s everything you need to know:

Between 2015 and 2025, house prices in Spain rose 80%, according to Eurostat’s house price index. The first half of 2026 made this figure even starker: by the second quarter of this year, prices were around double what they were at the same time in 2015.

World.title: Turkey-Greece maritime spat threatens to spill into EU summit
World.content:
“Greece has explicitly stated ... that in the event of any escalation, it will request sanctions and support from the European Union,” Greece’s Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis said last week in an interview with local TV.

Despite being NATO allies, Greece and Turkey have quarreled over maritime boundaries and overlapping claims to their continental shelves. Athens fears Ankara could invoke the Libya deal to challenge offshore exploration south of Crete and the EU-funded undersea electricity cable linking Greece and Cyprus, turning both projects into flashpoints.

Turkey signed the agreement in 2019 with Libya’s U.N.-backed government in Tripoli, and it was unanimously ratified by rival authorities in eastern Libya on Oct. 20.

The EU immediately responded.

"This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states, it does not comply with the Law of the Sea, and is null and void," said a joint statement on Oct. 20 from the heads of the European Commission and Council.

Egypt also rejected the border pact, as did Bahrain, Cyprus (which has its own separate disputes with Turkey over Ankara's occupation of the northern part of the island since the 1970s), Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

World.title: Farage cries foul after Reform slips to a tie with the Tories
World.content:
It’s a major test of Reform’s claim to be the best-placed right-wing vessel to stop another Labour victory.

So what’s Farage’s answer? He is increasingly trying to remind voters how the Conservatives operated in government — and claiming the polls themselves are bogus.

POLITICO spoke to half a dozen figures on Reform’s frontline to try and understand their gripes with the polling. All were granted anonymity, like others in this piece, because of the generally held convention in Westminster that parties don’t discuss polling.

Farage goes after the number-crunchers

“The jiggery-pokery that is going on with polling is utterly astonishing,” Farage told journalists after a speech last week. “What you’ve seen from the polling industry is nonsense, and I mean that.”

The Reform UK leader claimed that the “raw data” shows his party is really eight points clear of the Tories — and berated a “desperate push from the establishment” to get back to the “Tweedledum and Tweedledee” state of two-party politics.

Two senior Reform Party insiders challenged the methodology used by Britain’s pollsters. They argued that Reform’s polling is suppressed because of the way undecided voters are partially stacked with the party they voted for at the last election. Both insiders argued this would harm the party because it was a much more nascent outfit back in 2024.

World.title: Zelenskyy tells Europe to hurry up and pick a rep for peace talks with Russia
World.content:
With Europe set to take on a more important role in talks with Russia and the United States, Zelenskyy’s comments join a growing chorus of demands for the EU and others to unite behind one top negotiator or a small team at the highest level.

Speaking to reporters during his trip to Denmark on Tuesday, the Ukrainian leader said he wanted a “dialogue” with the EU and other European powers over who will represent them. He said it would be “better” this way, rather than just presenting their answer to Ukraine, which is “not good, really.”

“I hope that not later than the end of November — better in Germany on 19th [at a Coalition of the Willing meeting] — fix it. We will see.”

Europe has been struggling to work out a plan for how to engage in top-level dialogue with Moscow and Washington over ending the war in Ukraine. Despite providing most of the foreign financing for Ukraine’s war effort, EU countries have been split over who should represent them, or whether they should be talking to Russian leader Vladimir Putin at all.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni last week blasted the European Union’s engagement with the peace talks as “all over the place.”

Leaders are due to grapple with these questions at a summit in Dublin later this week.

As talks with Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. resumed in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, American officials made clear they wanted Europe fully at the table next time the negotiations take place. That is partly because the U.S. wants to bring a review of wider European security arrangements for Europe into the negotiations over peace in Ukraine — a longstanding Russian demand.

World.title: Nvidia hires Wachtell Lipton for Jensen Huang investigation
World.content:
Co-founder, President and CEO of US technology company Nvidia, Jensen Huang, looks on during a press briefing in Paris on Oct. 13, 2026 | Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images

The independent investigation follows reports that the CEO had a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead an investigation into reports that CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation.

Law firm partner Joon H. Kim will lead the probe. Kim, a former acting attorney of the Southern District of New York, was appointed in 2021 as an independent investigator by New York Attorney General Letitia James to probe allegations of sexual harassment by former Gov. Andrew Cuomo.

The company’s board of directors on Sunday launched an independent investigation into Jensen Huang following reports of his romantic relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy. The board said that Jensen Huang supports the review.

Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang was first brought to light in an October New York Times report, which alleged the businesswoman had ties to Chinese intelligence. Officials suspected Alice Huang helped funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China, according to the report.

Jensen Huang in a message to the company Sunday admitted to an affair and pledged to cooperate with the investigation. He did not mention Alice Huang by name.

World.title: Poland says Pentagon backs permanent US base, with Trump decision due in December
World.content:
The Pentagon’s own account stopped short of endorsing the base or confirming the December timetable, but acknowledged ongoing talks about strengthening the permanent U.S. military presence in Poland.

Hegseth praised Poland’s military buildup, calling its army “one of the most formidable” in Europe. He also pushed for European NATO allies to take greater responsibility for their own defense, potentially allowing Washington to reduce its troop presence on the continent.

Poland already hosts thousands of American troops, largely on rotating deployments. But Warsaw is pushing for a permanent base as the Pentagon reviews its military presence across Europe, with other NATO allies fearing Trump could withdraw thousands more troops. The review is expected to conclude by December.

The project is also a rare point of agreement between Poland's feuding leaders. Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki — a Trump ally whom the U.S. president backed in last year's election — agreed last week to cooperate on securing the base, despite their bitter confrontation over control of Poland's top court.

Nawrocki has embraced the proposed name “Fort Trump,” first floated by his predecessor, Andrzej Duda, in 2018.

The U.S. Department of Defense didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

This article has been updated.

World.title: Brussels takes on the evils of online commerce
World.content:
According to a draft of the DFA obtained by POLITICO, the Commission will address several aspects of the design, service and terms under which businesses interact with consumers online.

“Europe should not accept a digital economy where profits depend on exploiting people’s vulnerabilities,” Spanish socialist lawmaker Laura Ballarín Cereza, a key European lawmaker on tech legislation, said in a statement.

Industry leaders have pushed back on this potential new rulebook ever since the EU executive began considering a revision of consumer law in 2022. They say current consumer protection and digital services laws already cover these practices. “Where existing rules already cover a practice, it should not be regulated or enforced a second time,” said Ben Brake, director general of tech lobby DOT Europe.

Consumer groups say existing rules, some dating back to 2005, are not clear enough and that many unfair design practices are still rampant.

The Commission would have the power to impose fines of up to 6% of global annual revenue for companies that violate the new law. Those penalties are similar to fines levied under the Digital Services Act, the EU’s platform rules meant to stop Big Tech platforms from provoking systemic, society-wide harms through everything from election interference to keeping minors away from violent content. The new law instead would apply to any business offering services to EU consumers online.

Dark patterns

The DFA would ban deceptive design known as “dark patterns,” which manipulate consumers through the use of such tactics as bright-colored buttons placed prominently to get customers to buy something. It also aims to ban personalized pricing that targets vulnerable consumers, including minors.

World.title: US Republicans block efforts to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over Iran war
World.content:
US Democrats suffered a blow on Tuesday as Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's impeachment over the war waged on Iran.

 

The House failed to secure the votes needed to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, with a vote of 211 to 204, handing President Donald Trump a victory just days after his party's disastrous midterm election defeat. Democrats and some Republicans had been hoping to hold a vote on Wednesday, which would have seen Hegseth face formal charges.

The resolution was formally proposed by Trump critic, Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, who was the only member of his party to oppose the procedural manoeuvre, according to US media.

Republicans currently hold a majority in the House, but this will end in January, when Democrats are expected to take control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump's party's midterm defeat comes amid widespread discontent among the US public over the country's war on Iran, as well as soaring gas prices and the rising cost of living.

Trump took to his social media platform, TRUTH Social, to express his strong support for Hegseth, describing him as a "Great American Patriot" who had been exonerated.

Meanwhile, earlier on Tuesday, Hegseth called the attempt to impeach him a "farce" while defending the military operations he has carried out under Trump, as well as the war on Iran.

During a Pentagon press conference, he said, "It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," branding the accusations as "slander" and "sabotage".

Following Hegseth's television appearance, Trump once again showed his support through a TRUTH Social post, writing, "Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS."

Vice President JD Vance also commented, saying that Hegseth had "obviously not" committed impeachable offences.

Massie's eight articles of impeachment

The eight articles of impeachment brought against Hegseth by Massie include several allegations concerning the handling of the Iran war, including waging war without congressional authorisation and abuse of power as Pentagon chief.

They also include allegations surrounding strikes carried out against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie described as "extrajudicial killings", as well as the 2025 conflict with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.

Massie also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech after he attempted to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video in which Kelly urged military and intelligence personnel to stand up against illegal orders.

Democrats will be able to revive impeachment efforts once they take control of Congress in January. At the same time, Massie will be leaving Congress after losing his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger.

World.title: Spain: 69 candles lit at Toledo Cathedral for train crash victims
World.content:
The royal couple joined victims' relatives for a solemn funeral Mass in Toledo's 13th-century cathedral, held nearly two weeks after one of Europe's deadliest rail disasters this century.

 

Residents of Urda placed 69 candles near the altar, one for each person who died, and a 16th-century sculpture of Christ was brought from the town especially for the ceremony. Mourners gathered inside, where candles were burning in tribute to the dead.

Spain's second fatal high-speed rail accident this year has left 69 people dead after a Renfe train collided with a stationary Iryo service near Urda on 28 October. The disaster prompted the resignations of the transport minister and the head of the railway operator, while European prosecutors have launched a fraud investigation into EU safety funds.

Citing his refusal to attend religious ceremonies, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez did not attend the funeral Mass, drawing criticism from opponents who accused him of dodging an angry public during an election campaign.

With a general election scheduled for 29 November, the tragedy has intensified pressure on the government, while rail services were further disrupted by a train drivers' strike.

World.title: Argentina: Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass before 650,000 in Córdoba
World.content:
The ceremony took place at the Military Aviation School, on the grounds of the Argentine Aircraft Factory (FAdeA), where vast crowds gathered to welcome the pontiff. Arriving in his popemobile, he travelled past the faithful, waving and greeting those who had come to see him, before making his way to the altar.

 

Footage shows thousands of worshippers filling the grounds, nuns and priests praying, and people holding rosaries, singing and embracing. During the ceremony, the pope kissed the altar and offered incense before a statue of the Virgin Mary. In his homily, he encouraged Catholics to live out their faith in everyday life: “Open your hearts and, with God’s grace, go and be saints!”

The Mass is a major moment in Leo XIV’s first visit to Latin America since becoming head of the Catholic Church. His 12-day tour takes in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he spent nearly two decades as a missionary and bishop before his election as pope.

Argentina is also the homeland of his predecessor, the late Pope Francis, and had not hosted a reigning pontiff since John Paul II in 1987. Many worshippers sheltered from the sun under umbrellas, while others followed the ceremony from a distance, using binoculars or phones.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV draws huge crowds in Córdoba after record Buenos Aires mass
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV urged Argentines on Tuesday to follow the holy example of the country’s best-known saints, as an estimated 650,000 people gathered in the central city of Córdoba for Mass.

 

The crowd came a day after an estimated 2.5 million people turned out to see the Pope in the Argentine capital, Buenos Aires, on Monday.

Faithful from all over Argentina drove for hours to attend the service, arriving from the far north of the country, from Patagonia in the south and from points in between.

Córdoba was chosen to host the Pope because of its central location. The city had gone nearly 40 years without a papal visit.

They include St. José Gabriel del Rosario Brochero, known as the “ Gaucho priest,” and “Mama Antula,” who in 2024 became Argentina’s first female saint. They were both canonised by the Argentine Pope Francis.

Members of the Catholic clergy attend a mass led by Pope Leo XIV at the Military Aviation School in Córdoba, Argentina, 10 November 2026 Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. (Foto AP/Andrew Medichini)

“We are all called to holiness,” he said. “These saints and blessed have already fulfilled their mission on Earth. Today, it is our turn to follow the radiant example of holiness they have left with us.”

After Mass, Leo surprised the crowds with a brief appearance on the balcony of the archbishop’s residence in downtown Córdoba, the same balcony from which St. John Paul II greeted Córdoba in 1987. Thousands of people chanting “León, León” packed the street below. “United, we can do anything,” the pope told them.

Erika Viñales, 39, and Elena Llanquenao, 54, religious education teachers from Santa Cruz province in Argentina’s Patagonia region, said they travelled 2,000 kilometres (more than 1,200 miles) to be on hand. “It was quite a journey,” Viñales said.

The mass in the city of Córdoba came ahead of a final mass in the town of Luján scheduled for Wednesday, the day on which the pope, also known as Robert Francis Prevost, will leave Argentina to travel to Peru.

Leo XIV posted on his X account: "My arrival in Argentina has, for me, a particular meaning: for twelve years, the universal Church listened to the voice of Pope Francis, who carried with him, in his memory and in his heart, the places, the people and the faith he received here."

"The truth is that to almost touch heaven with your hands is to be very close to it, to feel it in your own flesh," said Romeo Armando, a university student.

Meanwhile, Rosa Acevedo, a retired Argentine woman, could barely contain her emotion: "It is a very great feeling, something that fills me. I am going with all my heart full of blessings".

'Putting the person before the algorithm'

In Uruguay, a few days ago, the Pope warned at the Catholic University of Uruguay in Montevideo about the "dehumanisation" caused by AI: "It is urgent, then, that our school and university education contribute to the wise use of technologies and AI, putting the person before the algorithm and harmonising technical, emotional, social, spiritual and ecological intelligences".

Meanwhile, in Peru, the papal plane and its crew were blessed by Monsignor Paolo Rocco Gualtieri at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima on the eve of the pontiff's arrival.

A giant statue of Pope Leo XIV has been unveiled before his upcoming visit to the country in the port city of Callao, about 15 km from Lima. The Pope, who was born in the United States, holds Peruvian nationality and is returning to the country where he spent many years as a missionary and bishop.

World.title: Paraguay's new president vows to recover pension funds at risk in Ueno Bank crisis
World.content:
The president of Paraguay, Pedro Alliana, announced on Tuesday that the recovery of pension funds deposited in Ueno Bank will be a priority for his government. The intervention in the financial institution has put at risk around 800 million dollars (about 716 million euros) belonging to public bodies, including resources from five retirement funds, and has triggered a political crisis that ended with the removal of Santiago Peña from office.

 

Among the institutions affected is the Social Security Institute (IPS), which is responsible for managing pensions and part of the country's health services. Uncertainty over the recovery of these funds has caused growing concern among workers and retirees.

Alliana, who took over the presidency last Friday, has pledged to protect citizens' savings and to speed up compensation after the banking collapse.

Almost 95% of savers have already received compensation

The president has said that around 1.74 million depositors have received payments totalling 330 million dollars through the Deposit Guarantee Fund. The government plans to complete on Wednesday 11 November the outstanding reimbursements provided for in the emergency legislation approved by Congress.

However, the payments do not guarantee that all customers will recover the whole of their savings. The guarantee scheme covers up to about 38,600 dollars (about 34,575 euros) per depositor, while the initial advances are limited to approximately 20,000 dollars.

For many of those affected, the return of the money represents a first relief after several days of uncertainty. "At last they transferred the money I was missing," Rosario, a 45-year-old customer who preferred not to give her surname, told AFP.

A banking crisis that brought down the president

The intervention in Ueno Bank sparked mass demonstrations demanding both the return of deposits and the departure of then president Santiago Peña, who was linked to the financial institution.

Political and social pressure culminated in his removal through an impeachment trial in the Senate. His vice president at the time, Pedro Alliana, took over the government and accelerated compensation payments through the guarantee fund.

The crisis has also hit the labour market. According to Paraguayan labour minister Mónica Recalde, up to 7,000 people have lost their jobs in companies linked to the bank in Paraguay, Mexico, Nicaragua, Argentina and Panama.

World.title: Web Summit Lisbon day 2 cancelled due to Storm Charles
World.content:
The technology conference Web Summit in Lisbon will close its doors on Wednesday due to bad storms affecting Portugal.

 

It comes after a state of emergency was declared by the Portuguese government due to Storm Charles, which will close schools and non-essential public services.

"The Government of Portugal has formally advised Web Summit that, due to the risks posed by Storm Charles, including tidal flooding, severe disruption to public transport and the impact of high winds on external structures, Day 2 of Web Summit should not take place," an email to attendees read.

This follows discussions with the Portuguese Government, the National Emergency and Civil Protection Authority (ANEPC), and the Public Security Police (PSP).

"Web Summit will of course respect the Government's direction, and accordingly, Day 2 (Wednesday, November 11th) will not take place.The safety and security of our attendees, staff and contractors is always our absolute priority," the email added.

The summit plans to continue on Thursday, Web Summit said.

The concerns relate to high risks associated with coastal flooding, strong winds affecting external structures, and severe disruptions to public transport, according to the organisers of the technology fair taking place at FIL, in Parque das Nações

Lisbon Mayor, Carlos Moedas, suggested earlier on Tuesday that the tech summit should be cancelled, but left the decision up to the central government (MAI) and the organisation.

Schools and non-essential public services will therefore be closed tomorrow throughout the country, the Minister of Internal Administration announced in a briefing to the media this morning at the headquarters of the National Emergency and Civil Protection Authority (ANEPC) in Carnaxide.

Access to the coastline, riverside areas and other flood-prone locations will also remain prohibited, "particularly in areas historically identified as being most vulnerable," reads the statement from the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

Web Summit expects to receive close to 70,000 attendees, including 900 speakers, and more than two thousand startups.

World.title: Energy boss Birol urges governments to accelerate global electrification at COP31
World.content:
The world should increase electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol has told Euronews in an exclusive interview, as he urged governments to reduce their reliance fossil ahead of COP31.

 

Speaking on On the Record with Maria Tadeo, Birol urged leaders at the climate summit in Turkey this week to accelerate electrification to strengthen energy sovereignty, particularly in the EU, which remains exposed to global energy market volatility despite efforts to diversify away from Russian supplies.

The European Commission estimates that disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz have added €127 billion to the EU's energy import bill since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, while industrial production across the bloc continues to fall.

Birol also warned that a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz could have serious consequences for Europe and the global economy, urging governments to prepare for a difficult winter.

"If the Strait of Hormuz is closed for a very long time, it would have major implications for the global economy and that of Europe," he said.

Birol also played down hopes that a possible US decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports would provide significant relief to European markets.

Europe has lost supplies of refined products, including diesel and jet fuel, from the Middle East, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have further tightened global supplies. Winter is approaching, adding to pressure as demand for both fuels rises.

"The amount of diesel which could come from Russia will not be a solution to this problem," Birol said.

He acknowledged that additional Russian supplies could offer "some relief" but argued they would not address the structural shortage, particularly given the EU's declining refining capacity.

"We lost the Middle East's refined product delivery to Europe. It is not coming," he said.

Birol warned that refined product markets could remain tight in the coming months, raising the prospect of fuel shortages if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.

"If the current situation continues, there may be a question of availability in that case," he said.

Electrification en route to sovereignty

Birol argued that the answer to the EU's recurring exposure to energy shocks lies in accelerating the shift towards domestically generated electricity.

"Europe's energy future is electrification," he said, urging the bloc to generate more of its own power from solar, wind, nuclear and hydropower rather than rely on imported fossil fuels.

"If Europe wants to remain a sovereign part of the world, if Europe wants to be competitive and clean, the energy future is electrification," he added.

Birol criticised Europe's retreat from nuclear power, echoing European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's description of the shift as a "strategic mistake".

Nuclear power accounted for around one-third of EU electricity generation in the 1990s, compared with approximately 15% today, according to Birol.

His call for a faster rollout of electric vehicles and heat pumps comes as world leaders gather in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, where they are expected to agree on a target to raise electrification to 35% by 2035.

The European Commission for its part has proposed raising the EU's electrification rate to 46% by 2040, roughly double the 23% level at which it has stagnated over the past decade.

Although the 46% figure remains indicative, negotiations on the EU's post-2030 energy framework could turn it into a legally binding target.

EU countries broadly support a global electrification target but softened their position in the final COP31 conclusions, agreed on 12 October.

A September draft had welcomed the COP31 presidency's proposal to raise electrification to 35% by 2035. However, the final text merely states that the "EU looks forward to discussing" the initiative.

The Czech Republic is among the countries sceptical of the proposal, according to a senior Commission official, suggesting that the bloc's own 46% ambition could also face resistance.

Speaking to On The Record, Birol argued that the cost of transforming Europe's energy system must be weighed against the economic price of continued dependence on imported fuels.

"Energy security is a cost as well," he said, as he urged leaders to aim for consensus on electrification.

World.title: Democrats took the House, Senate and a good deal of Republican pride: So who are the real winners and losers?
World.content:
Start with the obvious: Democrats won and Republicans lost. The House was always expected to flip. The Senate was meant to be the nail-biter, and Democrats took it anyway, much of it on Republican turf. They won Senate races in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and South Carolina, a map only the most optimistic Democrats could have drawn, while Alaska and Mississippi may yet join them. Some Republicans are shrugging it off: presidents always lose midterms. They usually do. They lose battleground states and the swing suburbs. They do not usually lose their own strongholds.

 

Winner: Hakeem Jeffries

Two years ago, Hakeem Jeffries was a minority leader watching Republicans run the table in Washington. He is now the presumptive Speaker of the House, the most powerful member of Congress, and is expected to take the gavel in January. By Tuesday, the Associated Press had called 254 seats for Democrats to the Republicans' 165, with 16 still undecided. NBC News projects they will finish with 259, which would be the party's biggest majority in more than three decades. A narrow one would have handed a dozen or so left-wing members a veto over his speakership and his agenda, and several incoming Democrats are still withholding their support. He can now afford at least three dozen defections.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks at a news conference in Washington, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) AP Photo

The same arithmetic works on legislation: he can lose his party's fringe on a bill and still pass it. Jeffries is set to become the first black Speaker in American history, and he inherits the two things this White House fears most from a Democratic House: control of spending and the power to subpoena.

Loser: Donald Trump

For two months, Donald Trump told voters to “pretend I'm on the ballot.” He took that message to Texas, Iowa and Kansas, states where his party should never have needed the help. Voters did as they were asked. Trump won Texas by 13.6 points in 2024. Democrat James Talarico won it by 12 last week. Kansas swung 21 points towards the Democrats, and South Carolina swung 22.

Mississippi, a state Trump won by 23 points, is still too close to call. About 24 hours after his last plea, the president posted that he “wasn't on the ballot, and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

The exit polls disagree. His approval among midterm voters stood at 37%. Many of his voters also appear to have stayed home: Trump voters made up 44% of last week's electorate, well short of the 49.8% of the vote he won in 2024. Trump has blamed weak candidates.

The trouble is most of them were his. He endorsed Ken Paxton over a sitting senator, handpicked Darline Graham and backed Michael Whatley. “It wasn't me” is a hard sell when your name is on every endorsement.

Winner: Moderate Democrats

If Democrats had a strategy, it was to be boring in all the right places. In Kansas, they ran Adam Hamilton, a first-time candidate who leads the largest United Methodist church in the US. In South Carolina, a paediatrician.

In North Carolina, a former two-term governor. In Iowa, a state lawmaker and four-time Paralympian who promised to work with Trump on border security. Independents were ready to punish Trump, and boring gave them a safe place to land.

Supporters cheer during an election night event for Iowa Democrats Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt) Supporters cheer during an election night event for Iowa Democrats Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt)

Kamala Harris won independents by just three points in 2024. Last week, Democrats won them 58% to 38%, a 20-point margin. Roughly two-thirds of moderates backed Democrats for the House, up from about six in 10 for Harris.

Even Talarico, more liberal than most of the other seat-flippers, won Texas with a friendly, centrist pitch, taking about two-thirds of moderates, most independents and roughly one in 10 Republicans.

In Mississippi, District Attorney Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes, and that race is likely headed for a legal fight.

Losers: Ken Paxton and the MAGA picks

Trump's own advisers warned him that Ken Paxton carried too much baggage. He endorsed him anyway, calling the scandal-plagued attorney general “a true MAGA Warrior” and helping him push Senator John Cornyn out in the May runoff.

In October, Trump said he had no regrets because “Cornyn would have lost.” We will never know. We do know Paxton lost by 12 points in once-red Texas.

The pattern repeated across the map. Majorities of voters in Iowa and Ohio said their Republican candidates were “too supportive” of Trump, and most North Carolina voters said the same of Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman. Nationally, 6% of Republicans voted for Democrats.

That sounds small until you get to Texas, where about one in 10 crossed over. When your own voters walk across the aisle at that rate, the problem is not the ground game. It is the candidate and the message.

Winner: Progressive Democrats

The moderates won the map, but the progressive left won the primaries and a fair number of general elections too. Abdul El-Sayed, a Bernie Sanders ally, beat Mike Rogers in Michigan to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., center, poses for a photograph in his office with Sen.-elects Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., Josh Turek, D-Iowa, Roy Cooper, D-N.C. AP Photo

Peggy Flanagan held Minnesota and Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins in Maine, both from the party's progressive wing. In 2010, a Tea Party wave swept into Washington, and its heirs went on to form the Freedom Caucus and make life miserable for Republican speakers.

The new progressive class could build the same kind of bloc and do the same to Jeffries. Majorities are easier to win than to manage.

Loser: The Graham name in South Carolina

For 23 years, Graham meant South Carolina's Senate seat. After Lindsey Graham unexpectedly died in July, his sister Darline took over as interim senator and became Trump's handpicked candidate to keep the seat in the family.

It did not go to plan. She flubbed a foreign policy question on the debate stage, and about two-thirds of voters said she lacked the right experience.

Even some Republicans hesitated. Others split their tickets, backing Republican Alan Wilson for governor but not Graham. Annie Andrews, a paediatrician, became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since Fritz Hollings in 1998.

The family name carried a seat for two decades. It could not carry this campaign.

Winners: Kyiv and Brussels

The Kyiv Independent's headline said it plainly: “Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine.” A Democratic Congress holds the purse strings, and a Democratic Senate will be in no mood to wave through a deal that leaves Ukraine short.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he was optimistic both parties would now engage more with each other to boost backing for Ukraine.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, hands over the Ukraine state award to European Council President Antonio Costa during a commemorative ceremony in Kyiv, AP Photo

Brussels will also note that tariffs proved a liability at the ballot box, with 66% of voters saying they hurt the US economy. Ukraine is one of the few places Trump could throw Democrats a bone, claim a bipartisan win and look like a dealmaker in the process. Whether he prioritises it over Israel and Iran is another matter.

Loser: JD Vance

JD Vance went into election day as a Republican front-runner for 2028. He comes out of it as vice president during a historic defeat. The morning after, he offered his own verdict: “The reason we lost is the war.”

It is a rare thing for a vice president to say about his own president's war in Iran, and Republican primary voters will read it either as courage or as a man reaching for the exit.

Some on the right have already chosen the second reading. A Washington Examiner op-ed called him “fundamentally unfit to lead the Republican Party".

It did not help that, asked a week before the election by a young Republican how her generation could afford to start a family, Vance opened with a joke about Jon Husted's backside. Husted lost Ohio. The seat he was defending was Vance's old one.

Vice President JD Vance starts to say a prayer for a person who required medical attention while he was speaking during a campaign rally at the D&N Event Center in North Platt AP Photo

Winners: James Talarico and Jon Ossoff

Every wave produces its stars, and this one produced two. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker, ended a Democratic drought of more than 30 years in Texas statewide races and summed it up in five words: “We just took back Texas.”

Jon Ossoff, 39, did the harder thing in a wave year and made Georgia look easy. He beat Mike Collins by 18 points in a state Trump won two years ago, after raising $126 million more than his opponent.

Ossoff insists he has “zero interest in running for president.”

Washington has heard that before. Both men will spend the next two years fielding questions about 2028, and both will enjoy it more than they let on.

Loser: Trump's inner circle

Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee, summed up his plans in two words on election night: “Lawyer up.” His first target, he says, is “the Trump Crime Family.”

World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto company, tops that list, along with the Emirati royal nicknamed the “Spy Sheikh", who bought a $500 million stake in it.

Donald Trump Jr.'s venture firm, 1789 Capital, is next in the queue. Jamie Raskin, set to chair the Judiciary Committee, says Don Jr. “seems to have a clairvoyant sensibility of exactly who is going to get government contracts.”

Jared Kushner, Raskin says, “is a corporate executive that we absolutely will need to talk to.” Aides are on the list too.

Jared Kushner, center, and Steve Witkoff, right, U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, meet with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Mariinsky palace in Kyiv, Ukraine AP Photo

Garcia says Attorney General Todd Blanche could face a subpoena on “day one” and has promised quick action on alleged pay-to-play involving Kristi Noem and Corey Lewandowski. The White House can lean on executive privilege. The family businesses and their backers cannot.

Winners: Ad-makers, TV stations and, finally, viewers

OpenSecrets projects this will be the most expensive midterm in American history, at $11.9 billion, about a third more than in 2022. Ohio's Senate race topped $500 million on its own, more than $100 for every vote cast.

For the ad-makers, consultants and local TV stations of Ohio, Texas and Georgia, Christmas came in October.

The real winners, though, are viewers, who can now watch the evening news or a football game without being told someone's opponent wants to destroy America. Enjoy the quiet. The 2028 primaries start sooner than anyone would like.

Loser: Americans who want Washington to get something done

Voters sent Washington a to-do list last week. Washington is about to lose it. About eight in 10 registered voters told an AP-NORC poll last month that lowering the cost of living should be one of Congress' highest priorities, and roughly seven in 10 said the same of ending the war with Iran.

About half said the same about finding common ground between the parties. What they will get is a stand-off.

Trump has already told Fox News what happens next: “They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them.” Democrats are well short of the two-thirds needed to override him, and Senate Republicans still have the numbers to filibuster.

That leaves the executive order, even though 71% of voters told exit pollsters they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president. Add the investigations, and expect a lot of hearings and very few laws.

Three-quarters of voters already disapprove of Congress, according to the NBC News Exit Poll, and two years of gridlock will not change that. Prices, the war, the deficit and immigration will mostly be kicked down the road to 2028, by which point everyone will be campaigning again.

World.title: ‘Monstrous injustice’: King Charles condemns slavery as UK agrees to talks
World.content:
In this episode of Spotlight on Africa, we talked to scholars from the continent and the Caribbean about slavery reparations – a key topic discussed at this year’s Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

Advertising

The Commonwealth is a 56-nation group of mostly former British colonies, 21 of them in Africa. King Charles III remains head of state in 15 of them, including the UK.

Its biennial Heads of Government Meeting took place from 1 to 4 November 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda.

In a final communiqué issued on Wednesday, the group said the time had come for “meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation towards forging a common future based on equity”.

Timetable of talks

While no timetable for talks was announced, the group welcomed the United Kingdom’s willingness to engage “in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms”.

In his opening speech, King Charles III, who is politically neutral, called the slave trade “a monstrous injustice” that filled him with “profound personal sorrow”, but stopped short of a formal apology.

UN backs resolution calling slave trade ‘gravest crime against humanity’

For his part, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to saying sorry but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also said it was “not feasible” for the country to pay reparations for slavery, but that “there are things we can work on co-operatively”.

According to reports, Britain could issue a formal apology next year, during its G20 presidency.

Britain played a pivotal role in the slave trade, which saw between 10 and 15 million enslaved Africans taken to the Americas over four centuries.

The country abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833. It paid financial compensation, but to plantation owners rather than to the enslaved people themselves.

UN resolution

In March this year, the United Nations adopted a resolution recognising the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity”, in a motion spearheaded by Ghana.

Ghana backs Jamaica’s petition to push UK for slavery reparations

For many countries, the time has come for formal apologies and concrete plans for slavery reparations.

To find out how these issues are being tackled on the African continent and in the Caribbean, RFI spoke to a panel of four guests:

Edem Adotey: professor at the Institute of African Studies in Accra, Ghana,

Joel Kibazo: Commonwealth spokesperson,

Matiangai Sirleaf: professor at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law in the United States,

Verene A. Shepherd: Jamaican historian and one of three vice-chairs of the Caricom Reparations Commission.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.

World.title: Turkey courts Egypt to tip the scales in eastern Mediterranean power game
World.content:
This week’s joint naval exercises between Turkey and Egypt in the eastern Mediterranean are the latest move in a burgeoning partnership, as Ankara intensifies its efforts to draw Cairo closer and loosen its bonds with Turkish rivals Greece, Cyprus and Israel.

Advertising

The "Sea of Friendship 2026" naval drills, held from 4-9 November off the coast of Alexandria, follow five years of rapprochement after nearly a decade of mistrust sparked by the 2013 ouster of Mohamed Morsi, a close ally of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, by Egypt's President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

It is the second year in a row that Turkey and Egypt have held the joint drills, after a 13-year break.

“I think it's already a sign that the two countries are getting closer,” said Africa expert Elem Tepecikoglu of Ankara’s Social Sciences University. In her view, the naval exercises are part of an evolving partnership.

“This normalisation process started five years ago in the diplomatic realm,” she explained. “And then we see cooperation in the security domain as well. So this is why I say I'm optimistic that Egypt might come closer to the Turkish side.”

The strengthening alliance between Turkey and Egypt is stirring unease in Israel, at a time when Israeli-Turkish relations are already frayed by the war in Gaza and Ankara’s support for Hamas.

“Obviously, Israel does not see this as necessarily positive, because of the heightened tensions between Israel and Turkey,” warned Turkey analyst Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

She noted that Israel is growing ever more wary of Turkey’s expanding reach in the eastern Mediterranean. “There is concern that Turkey and Egypt can cooperate in ways that will squeeze Israel’s room to manoeuver, politically but also militarily.”

Lindenstrauss said she does not see this as a likely scenario, affirming that the 1979 peace agreement between Israel and Egypt is “still very much in place, despite many geopolitical turnovers”.

“But there was always a fear that the other countries surrounding it would unite and act against Israel,” the analyst added.

Lindenstrauss believes Egypt’s strong ties with Turkey’s rivals, Greece and Cyprus, allay fears of Israeli encirclement. “It is very important that this relationship keeps going ahead because it is a source of stability in the eastern Mediterranean,” she said.

Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff

Turkish leverage

Egypt, Greece, Cyprus and Israel are bound by a tightly knit strategic energy alliance centred on the Eastern Mediterranean Gas Forum, a regional organisation formed in 2020 that has its headquarters in Cairo.

Just last month, they stood united in condemning the Libyan parliament's ratification of a maritime deal with Turkey that encroached on Greek and Egyptian waters.

Still, Jalel Harchaoui, a regional expert at the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank, observes that Turkey and Egypt are forging ever-closer collaboration on issues ranging from Libya to the Sudanese civil war to the Horn of Africa. Harchaoui suggests this growing cooperation is steadily boosting Ankara’s leverage over Cairo.

“I think observers should ask, can Egypt afford to do without Turkey? And the answer is probably no, and Turkey probably is aware of it,” he said.

Even so, Harchaoui doubts Cairo is ready to pivot fully toward Ankara. “If [Egypt] switches 180 degrees, it would be a disaster for the other side. I'm talking about Greece and Cyprus and Israel. So you could also ask yourself, can Egypt afford to anger its traditional friends?”

Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean

Egypt's balancing act

Ankara is stepping up its diplomatic courtship of Cairo, hoping to lure Egypt away from its longstanding partners.

But Turkish ambitions stumbled when Egypt declined to join the Mecca Defence Alliance with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. Analyst Lindenstrauss sees this as a clear sign of the boundaries in Turkish-Egyptian ties.

“Egypt has already moved closer to Turkey than was imaginable a few years ago,” she said. “However, at the end of the day, there are limits to how much it can accept greater Turkish influence. I think Turkey pretty much reached where Egypt is willing to agree to, and it will not give Turkey concessions in the eastern Mediterranean that will endanger its relationship with Greece and Cyprus, or its peace agreement with Israel.”

Lindenstrauss believes that despite diplomatic tensions with Israel over the war in Gaza, it still remains in Egypt’s interests to maintain ties with all sides. “Because of Egypt's importance in the region, I think it can definitely go ahead with this balancing act. It gives it all the gains and the risk is relatively low compared to having Egypt choose sides,” she added.

Ankara stands ready to ramp up its campaign to win over Cairo as the battle for influence in the eastern Mediterranean intensifies. In the unfolding rivalry between between Turkey on one hand and Greece, Cyprus and Israel on the other, Egypt is emerging as the pivotal player.
