World.title: Serbia Prosecution Accused of Mishandling Cases of Anti-Govt Protesters
World.content:
A commission established by Serbia’s Supreme Public Prosecution Office said in a report published on Tuesday that the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade had committed irregularities in handling several high-profile cases.

These cases relate to an alleged sonic weapon used during a huge anti-government protest in March 2025, as well as attacks on students and a police raid on the university rectorate building.

“There are grounds to suspect that criminal offences falling under the jurisdiction of the Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime have been committed,” the commission said, adding that the report had been forwarded to the Prosecutor’s Office for the start of criminal proceedings.

The commission was formed on October 27, two days after parliamentary elections in which the opposition Student List beat the Serbian Progressive Party, which had held power for 14 years.

The report focused on seven cases at the Higher Prosecutor’s Office, and is likely just the first report.

The report claims the head of the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade, Nenad Stefanovic, “instrumentalised certain public prosecutors in pursuit of illegitimate objectives, and effectively established a parallel prosecutorial system”.

It says the commission had identified bias in the prosecution’s handling of cases, violations of the law through unlawful searches and seizures, and the collection of data unrelated to the subject matter of the proceedings.

The commission also pointed to the alleged abuse of organisational and hierarchical powers, the use of prosecutorial authority against citizens and witnesses and restrictions on the exercise of the rights of injured parties.

The ‘sonic weapon’ claims were made after around 300,000 people gathered at an anti-government protest in Belgrade in March 2025. During a 15-minute silence held in memory of the victims of the Novi Sad railway station disaster in 2024, protesters were suddenly startled by an unexpected noise and began running and screaming, triggering a brief stampede.

A case was opened by the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office following complaints from protesters who suspected that a long-range acoustic weapon had been used. However, in September 2025, the prosecution decided that there were no grounds for criminal proceedings.

The commission’s report said that numerous irregularities had occurred in the handling of the case, and the office had done less to investigate the incident and more to “formalise a decision, made in advance, that no sound cannon had been used”.

According to the report, the prosecution treated claims by authorities that no acoustic weapon had been deployed as an indisputable fact, disregarding material evidence that directly contradicted them.

“In several instances, the political affiliations of the authors of video recordings or critics were used as an argument against the credibility of their claims”, the report noted, referring to footage of the incident itself.

The report also stated that, in June 2026, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office asked Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA, to conduct checks on 154 citizens who had given statements about the alleged use of a sound cannon.

Following publication of the report, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office said that it “rejects as unfounded the allegations contained in the report of the Supreme Public Prosecutor’s Office”.

It questioned “whether the report was intended to examine the legality, effectiveness and consistency of the prosecution’s conduct, or whether it was in fact used as a means for the Supreme Public Prosecutor and certain prosecutors … to settle scores with the Chief Public Prosecutor and certain prosecutors of the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade”.

On Tuesday, Stefanovic said he was filing a criminal complaint against Goran Ilic, a public prosecutor at the Supreme Public Prosecutor’s Office who chairs the commission.

Stefanovic filed the complaint with the Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime, accusing Ilic of abuse of office and obstruction of justice, He alleges that Ilic interfered with the performance of his prosecutorial duties and advised him to resign.

World.title: UN Court Rejects Bosnian Serb War Criminal’s Early Release Plea Again
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Mico Stanisic in court in The Hague in March 2005. Photo: EPA/Fred Ernst/Pool.



The UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals in The Hague announced on Tuesday that it has denied early release to convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mico Stanisic for a second time.

Stanisic was the interior minister of Bosnia’s Serb-dominated entity, Republika Srpska, during Bosnia’s 1992-95 war. The Hague Tribunal sentenced him to 22 years in prison for persecution, murder and torture under a final verdict in 2016.

Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, the president of the court, said that while Stanisic is eligible to be considered for early release after serving two-thirds of his sentence, there are “significant factors” militating against it.

These include “the high gravity of his crimes and his failure to sufficiently demonstrate rehabilitation. Further, there is no evidence establishing the existence of compelling humanitarian grounds that would otherwise warrant overriding this negative assessment,” Gatti Santana added.

He previously requested early release in November 2024, but was turned down.

His renewed request to the court in September this year stated that Stanisic served his sentence in a multi-ethnic prison and has had friendly relations with inmates of different ethnic backgrounds. It also noted that during his time in prison no disciplinary proceedings were brought against him.

“The petitioner claims that, especially given the length of his sentence, his behaviour manifests a great level of re-socialisation,” the submission said.

Responding to the submission, Gatti Santana said: “While Stanisic continues to exhibit good behaviour in detention and has maintained family relationships that would support his reintegration into society, the new evidence does not sufficiently address the concerns regarding his lack of acceptance of responsibility and critical reflection identified in the previous decision [in 2024].”

Stanisic voluntarily surrendered to the Hague Tribunal in March 2005 and his trial began in September 2009, alongside his co-defandant, Stojan Zupljanin, the wartime head of the regional police centre in Banja Luka. Zupljanin was convicted of persecution, murder, torture and extermination.

World.title: Bulgaria Declares Mourning Over Deadly Motorway Pile-Up
World.content:
The accident scene near Trakia,. Photo: Bulgarian Ministry of Internal Affairs.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Tuesday declared November 11 a national day of mourning following one of the deadliest road accidents in the country’s history.

Radev described Tuesday as “a dark day for the whole of Bulgaria”, Bulgarian National Radio reported.

Just after 7 a.m., a chain-reaction crash on the Trakia motorway caused a massive pile-up in which at least 86 vehicles were involved, leaving 12 dead and 51 injured, according to reports.

“A truck [carrying grain] blocked the path of a bus carrying passengers, triggering the first chain crash,” said Chief Secretary of the Interior Ministry Lyubomir Nikolov, adding that poor visibility amid dense fog was likely a factor.

Traffic on the motorway is halted in both directions for the day as rescue missions continue. The injured who have been rescued have been transferred to hospitals in Yambol, Sliven and Burgas.

Calls for blood donations to hospitals in Sofia and Sliven have been widely shared on social media.

“I would like to express my deepest condolences and I would like to pay respects to the rescue teams,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in Varna, where she gave a joint briefing with Prime Minister Radev.

Their talks were cancelled as Radev headed to the crash scene. Von der Leyen’s visit is part of her round of talks in Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey designed to boost security in the Black Sea region following increased drone attacks.

Parliament in Bulgaria cancelled its sessions, delaying the vote on several draft laws. President Iliana Iotova also halted her participation in the Paris Peace Forum and announced that she would return to Bulgaria.

The accident has renewed debate about poor road safety in Bulgaria. According to the National Statistical Institute, in 2025 alone, 6,665 serious traffic accidents occurred, which left 465 dead and 8,295 injured.

World.title: Turkey Bans Media Reporting on Deadly Factory Blast in Izmir
World.content:
Turkey’s broadcasting regulator, the Radio and Television Supreme Council, RTUK, on Monday announced a ban on reporting an explosion at an iron and steel factory in Aliaga, Izmir that has cost 17 lives.

“A ban has been imposed on all news reports, interviews and commentary concerning the incident in print, visual and social media, as well as online, until the investigation is completed,” RTUK said.

Authorities said the ban was intended to prevent disinformation and public unrest, protect public order and ensure the investigation could proceed properly. Turkey has previously introduced reporting bans when there have been terror attacks, natural disasters, fatal accidents and major police operations targeting critics.

In 2025, for example, the RTUK issued a broadcasting ban about a fire in a ski resort that killed 66 holidaymakers. Critics say that the practice undermines the public’s right to access information.

The death toll from Monday’s blast rose to 17, while 14 workers were injured.

“The explosion occurred after falling material severed natural gas and oxygen pipes during ongoing maintenance work,” Labour and Social Security Minister Vedat Isikhan said while visiting the blast site on Tuesday.

Prosecutors have launched an investigation into the explosion, while six people have been detained in connection with the incident.

It was not the first deadly incident at the site. Previous accidents have claimed workers’ lives, but the factory continued to operate.

Fatal accidents have been reported repeatedly since 2018, including workers killed in explosions, falls from height and accidents involving steel blocks and loading operations; in a compensation case over the 2020 death of worker Kadir Ozdemir, a court found the Habas plant 70 per cent primarily at fault.

Recently, a subcontracted worker, Hakan Dogan, died after falling around eight metres on October 21. Another subcontracted worker, Eyup Eginli, was killed in an explosion while inflating a heavy machinery tyre on November 5, days before Monday’s disaster.

World.title: ‘Obligations Are Equal, Rights Rarely Are’: The Citizens Bosnia Still Treats as ‘Others’
World.content:
Othered

I walk through Sarajevo, looking at all the faces staring back at me, and think of one person who is not on those posters: Dervo Sejdic.

The Bosnian constitution was drawn up as part of the Dayton Agreement, which in 1995 brought an end to the brutal wars in the Balkans. Peace had to be forged between the three warring parties, so the state was built around three ‘constituent peoples’: Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats.

The system was designed to end a war, not to create an ideal democracy. But what helped secure peace in 1995 has, over the decades, also helped entrench the very ethnic divisions it was meant to contain. Thirty-one years later, those divisions still shape the political life of this small country.

To put it simply: at the highest levels of government, the chairs are labelled with the names of the nations. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina has three seats: one for a Bosniak, one for a Croat and one for a Serb. The 15 seats in the state’s House of Peoples are also divided between these three groups: 3 times 5 equals 15. If you are a Romani person, a Jew or do not wish to identify as any of the three nations, you cannot stand for election to these positions. You can vote, you can become a councillor, you can work in the civil service, you can pay taxes. But you will never become president. Never. By design.

In 2006, Dervo Sejdic, Romani, and Jakob Finci, Jewish, lodged complaints with the European Court of Human Rights, or ECHR. Three years later, they won their case. The Grand Chamber of the court ruled that such exclusion constituted blatant discrimination and should be rectified.

That was in December 2009. Since then, Bosnia has held another election. And another. And another. Yet the constitutional seats still bear the same labels.

The year after he won his case against his own country in Strasbourg, Sejdic wrote to Bosnia’s Central Electoral Commission. He knew the judgement had not yet been implemented, but he thought he would ask anyway: could he, in the spirit of that judgement, stand as a candidate for the Presidency?

The reply, as he recalls it today, went something like this: “You may come; you may submit your documents. The Constitution and the Electoral Code will give you the answer.” In short: no.

Seventeen years later, I ask him: “If the ruling had been carried out back then, perhaps your face would be on those posters today. Do you ever think about that?”

“All the time,” he says. “Why should I be any worse than other presidential candidates?”

Sejdic’s case shows you can succeed before the ECHR yet, 17 years later, still be unable to exercise the right you fought for and won. The court cannot walk into the Bosnian parliament and amend the constitution. Bosnia and Herzegovina is obliged to implement its judgment, and implementation is overseen by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. The Sejdic-Finci case has therefore been returning to the Committee of Ministers for years.

I asked the Council of Europe what exactly 17 years of waiting means. The reply leaves little room for diplomatic interpretation: “The continued retention of the present discriminatory electoral system constitutes a clear violation of the requirements of the European Convention on Human Rights, going to the heart of the democratic process.”

The Committee of Ministers, which supervises the implementation of the ECHR’s judgments, has set June 2027 for its next examination of the case. If there is no tangible progress by then, it will consider further action.

The European Commission also insists that the issue remains on its agenda. “The EU has underlined the importance of implementing the Sejdic-Finci case law since the 2009 judgement of the European Court of Human Rights,” a Commission spokesperson tells BIRN. Brussels expects reforms ensuring that state institutions function without discrimination as part of Bosnia’s EU accession negotiations, it says. The constitutional changes, however, remain Bosnia’s responsibility.

In the meantime, I’m trying to understand who, exactly, can become a European here? Not in a geographical sense, because the geography is simple: Bosnia and Herzegovina lies in Europe. In 2016, it applied for EU membership; in 2022, it was granted candidate status; and in March 2024, the European Council decided to open accession negotiations. Though by the end of September, just before the latest round of elections, the negotiating framework had still not been adopted and the actual negotiations had not yet begun.

What interests me, however, is a Europe smaller than the continent and larger than the Union: Europe as the promise that a citizen is a citizen. And this is where the Bosnian problem begins. Because here, one can be a citizen whilst at the same time belong to a category which the constitution refers to as ‘others’, who include, as well as Roma and Jews, 15 other ethnic groups, such as Hungarians, Austrians or Poles.

World.title: Kosovo’s PDK Urged to Embrace Change After Ex-Leaders’ Hague Convictions
World.content:
When Bedri Hamza took to the floor at the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK’s headquarters on October 21 to announce he was quitting as leader of the country’s biggest opposition party, the move caught many – though not all – by surprise.

“Time has come to take the responsibility to another level through an internal election process from which I am convinced the PDK will come out stronger and more consolidated,” 62-year-old economist Hamza told the media.

Hamza, a former mayor of South Mitrovica and former minister of finance, had only spent 11 months at the head of the party. The PDK has been embroiled in a prolonged transitional period since November 2020, when its then leader, Kadri Veseli, was put into detention after an indictment accusing him of war crimes was filed by the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

World.title: Albanian Talk Show Hosts Slam TV Regulator’s ‘Orwellian’ Fines
World.content:
Journalist Blendi Fevziu opened his TV programme “Opinion” last Thursday evening with a symbolic protest.

Wearing a uniform bearing the inscription “AMA Police”, Fevziu mocked the imposition of a fine for “content containing inappropriate language” imposed by the Audiovisual Media Authority, AMA – the body regulating television broadcasts in Albania.

“I am not complaining about the fine but about the fact that, after 30 years in this studio ... they want to turn my normal attire into the uniform of an AMA police officer,” Fevziu said.

“I am no longer supposed to be a journalist moderating a debate between two balanced sides or discussing a topic with different perspectives. Instead, I am supposed to be a police officer standing here to check and certify every word spoken by every guest, reprimanding them if it is deemed inappropriate,” he added.

World.title: EU Offers Black Sea Countries Support to Counter Security Threats
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Romanian President Nicusor Dan at Cotroceni Presidential Palace in Bucharest, 9 November 2026. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday announced a new support package worth around 60 million euros for EU countries bordering the Black Sea, as the region faces growing security challenges linked to Russia’s war against Ukraine, including drone incursions and attacks on commercial shipping.

Around 10 million euros will be allocated to maritime surveillance and search-and-rescue operations, while a further 50 million euros will go towards establishing a planned Security Hub, von der Leyen said in Bucharest, where she met Romanian President Nicusor Dan.

The proposed hub – including Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey – is intended to strengthen regional cooperation and improve the ability of countries in the area to monitor and respond to security threats, including incidents affecting maritime infrastructure and commercial navigation.

The Commission president said the EU needed to step up its response to escalating threats and ensure the safety of shipping routes across the Black Sea, which have become increasingly vulnerable since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Von der Leyen wrote on X before the visit that “security threats are escalating, attacks are increasing, and innocent lives have been lost” in the Black Sea region.

Von der Leyen reiterated the EU’s support for a ceasefire in Ukraine covering attacks on energy and food infrastructure, stressing the importance of protecting civilian facilities and ensuring the continued flow of essential goods.

Drone attacks reportedly damaged at least seven commercial vessels in the Black Sea last month, claiming the lives of two sailors and leaving at least 25 others unaccounted for. The incidents have heightened concerns over the spread of the conflict beyond Ukraine’s borders and its growing proximity to NATO territory.

While Romanian authorities have pointed the finger at Russia, Bulgaria has avoided naming the suspected perpetrator, saying only that the drones came from “an eastern direction”.

On Tuesday, von der Leyen is due to travel to Bulgaria, where she will meet Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Varna and visit the Naval Academy, before attending the COP 31 climate summit in Turkey.

World.title: Death toll in 86-vehicle chain crashes on Bulgaria’s Trakia Motorway is 12, with final figure pending
World.content:
The known death toll in the November 10 double chain crashes near Yambol on Bulgaria’s Trakia Motorway is 12, with 48 people seriously injured, according to Prime Minister Roumen Radev, while the Health Ministry cautioned that this may not be the final figure for the death toll.

The chain crash involved a succession of two accidents, according to the Interior Ministry, which said that on a section of the motorway in the direction of Bourgas, a lorry blocked the path of a bus carrying a group of people.

Subsequently, there was a collision involving a lorry carrying wheat, and a passenger car crashed into it, the Interior Ministry said.

The ministry said that 86 vehicles were involved in the incident in both directions of the motorway – 63 that had been travelling towards Bourgas and 23 towards Sofia.

Acting Interior Ministry chief secretary Lyubomir Nikolov said that all those who died had been travelling in the lane towards Bourgas.

A probable cause for the serious accident was sharp and dense fog, the ministry said.

According to witnesses, visibility was initially about 70–80 metres, but at a certain point it sharply decreased to about 10 metres.

The ministry said that it is assumed that the accident in the lane for Sofia occurred in a similar way, and it is possible that the drivers’ attention was diverted by the serious accident in the opposite lane.

Two pre-trial proceedings have been initiated, as the traffic accidents occurred in both directions of the highway.

The Health Ministry said that a total of 46 people had been admitted to hospitals in Sliven, Yambol and Bourgas.

Among the injured in Bourgas is a patient in serious condition who is in the operating room, as well as a patient with severe chest trauma.

Hospitals in Stara Zagora, Plovdiv, Haskovo and Sofia remain ready to accept injured people if necessary, the Health Ministry said.

It is possible that the death toll will rise after the cleanup is complete, the ministry said.

A medical helicopter took off from Sliven but was unable to land due to thick fog. The air ambulance teams were transported to the scene in police cars and joined the rescue operation. They remain on standby, the statement said.

It said that half of the area has been cleared so far. The most difficult stage of the operation is ahead – cutting up and clearing the cars that are piled up on top of each other, it said.

Sufficient quantities of blood have been provided in all medical facilities where injured people are being treated. Additional quantities will be provided if necessary.

The Bulgarian government information service said that Radev had cancelled events on his programme in Varna following his meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The November 10 meeting of the Cabinet also was cancelled. The agenda for the Cabinet meeting had included amendments to the Road Traffic Act.

Radev said that news of the crash had reached him while he was on the government aircraft on the way to Varna.

“Immediately after landing, I ordered the Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev to leave on the government plane for Bourgas so that it could transport the wounded to hospitals in Sofia,” Radev said.

Two Spartan military transport planes immediately landed at Bourgas airport with stretchers and medical teams, he said.

At the moment, the information from the incident is about 12 dead and 48 injured, Radev said.

Since the concentration of the injured is in the hospitals in Sliven and Yambol, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov ordered the military transport planes to be re-based from Bourgas to the Bezmer airport in Yambol.

“We remain fully prepared for the evacuation of the injured from Sliven, Yambol and Bourgas to the hospitals in Sofia,” Radev said.

He said that the government would declare November 11 a day of national mourning.

President Ilana Yotova cancelled a trip to Paris that had been scheduled for November 10.

(Photo: Interior Ministry)

World.title: VDL: EC proposes dedicated funding of 50 million euro for Black Sea maritime security hub
World.content:
The European Commission (EC) is proposing dedicated funding of 50 million euro for the Black Sea maritime security hub, which is to be brought into operation by Bulgaria and Romania, EC President Ursula von der Leyen said in Varna on November 10.

The EC also is to provide an additional 10 million euro for the search and rescue authorities in Bulgaria.

Von der Leyen visited Romania on November 9 and Bulgaria on November 10, against the background of the attacks – generally blamed on Russia – on merchant shipping in the Black Sea.

The EC president visited the Nikola Vaptsarov Naval Academy and held talks with Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev.

Speaking at a joint news conference with Radev, Von der Leyen said: “Europe stands with Bulgaria, in these testing times. Because Black Sea security is European security”.

“We have witnessed together this year and specifically in the last month an increase in the number of threats, attacks and incursions into Bulgaria, which is EU territory,” Von der Leyen said.

“Now, drones are sinking commercial ships, setting vessels ablaze and killing civilians. Lives are lost at sea, navigation is disrupted, and the cost of insurance is skyrocketing,” she said.

“And the intention of these attacks is clear: Russia wants to spread fear and uncertainty in Europe. We know the playbook. And we are building resilience against it. So you can count on a strong and united European response.”

“In a wider context, we need to operationalise the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, conducted by Bulgaria and Romania. In this context I welcome the closer maritime cooperation between Bulgaria, Romania and Türkiye,” Von der Leyen said.

“It is important to have it now up and running, and therefore we want to have clear timelines for its completion, and we want to offer a dedicated funding of 50 million euro to this Black Sea maritime security hub. We need it now.”

Radev, who along with his government opposes military equipment assistance for Ukraine, said that Bulgaria’s efforts to support Ukraine “have never ceased”.

“Especially here in Varna people know very well that we have been providing support for thousands of Ukrainian citizens free of charge and this is significant,” Radev said.

“You see that we are putting we are investing and putting in not only the material but also the human efforts and support for the protection of Ukrainian citizens at sea and you know that the Chelsea 3 vessel a significant part of the crew was Ukrainian citizens,” he said.

“We continue our support for Ukraine also with the export of electricity and power and energy towards Ukraine. We continue also with our efforts at bringing back into use the energy and electricity plants and also in the maintenance and re-establishment of the railway infrastructure.”

Radev said that in terms of financial support, Bulgaria was in an excessive deficit procedure, “so we do experience we are supporting in the financial capabilities that we have and respective to our financial capabilities but I would like to say that Bulgaria is in no way blocking the decisions at the council level that are being taken in unity for everyone to support as they can”.

Asked about the origin of the attacks on merchant shipping in the Black Sea, Radev said: “The attacks are a result of the escalation of the war between Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea. This is the reason for the attacks. As far as the details are concerned, we are continuing to work”.

“The international teams that we have announced are still in Bulgaria. They are working hard. We are keeping in touch with them but they still have not been able to identify the perpetrator,” Radev said.

“We base our claims against the third country on facts and not on preliminary conclusions. They clearly stated that these attacks are the result of an escalation of the military aggression of the war that Russia initiated against Ukraine. This is the origin, this is the reason.”

Radev said: “We would like to receive further data and specific facts as to who was the perpetrator in terms of the work that is still ongoing from the international teams. We are still continuing and working hard in order to be able to clearly state supported by the facts what the origin is”.

“Unfortunately, I would like to say that we would prefer to stick to the facts and not to any preliminary presuppositions and expectations,” Radev said.

(Photo via Von der Leyen’s page on X)

World.title: Bulgaria’s Foreign Ministry warns of public sector strike in Ireland planned for November 12
World.content:
A strike by public sector trade unions is planned for Ireland on November 12, Bulgaria’s Foreign Ministry said.

Local authorities are warning of protest marches and rallies in the time range of noon to 2pm, which will cover the entire country.

Marches and rallies are reportedly planned for the capital Dublin, they will pass through O’Connell Street and are expected to head towards government buildings; and the cities of Cork, Limerick, Galway, Waterford, Sligo, Tullamore and Letterkenny will also be affected by the protest marches.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs recommends that Bulgarian citizens located or residing in Ireland inform themselves and monitor current developments, including possible restrictions on certain public services, the ministry said.

(Photo: Gareth Jones, via Wikimedia Commons)

World.title: EU extends EU Military Assistance Mission supporting Ukraine for further two years
World.content:
European Union ministers adopted a decision on November 9 extending the mandate of the European Union Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine) for a further two years, until November 15 2028, with a budget allocation of nearly 300 million euro for this period, a statement by the Council of the EU said.

The decision follows the recent strategic review of EUMAM.

In this context, the Council also decided to establish a presence in Ukraine to ensure direct and effective coordination with the Ukrainian military authorities, the UAF and like-minded international partners, thus ensuring that the EU training continues to evolve in line with the UAF’s needs.

The mission’s mandate is also enriched so as to focus on lessons learned from the battlefield and on strengthening military training in support of Ukraine’s defence agenda.

EUMAM Ukraine will continue to coordinate closely with other like-minded international partners such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Norway.

It will also cooperate with the Coalition of the Willing, as well as with Nato within the framework of the Nato Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine (NSATU) command.

EUMAM Ukraine is a key tool for the EU’s military support to Ukraine, with its core objective of contributing to enhancing the military capacity of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, the statement said.

The mission has trained more than 100 000 soldiers since it was established in October 2022 at Ukraine’s request.

World.title: German Christmas Market in Sofia’s City Garden to open on November 14
World.content:
Sofia’s now-traditional German Christmas Market in the City Garden opens in 2026 on November 14 and continues until December 21.

Bulgaria’s capital city’s oldest German Christmas Market (Deutscher Weihnachtsmarkt ) was first held in 2011, in its location in Alexander Battenberg Square near the Ivan Vazov National Theatre.

It features food and drink including mulled wine, crafts on sale, and fun for the children.

(Photo via the event’s Facebook page)

World.title: Anglican Church in Sofia holding Christmas Carol service on December 15
World.content:
The Anglican Church in Sofia is starting off its Christmas celebrations with a carol service on December 15 at 10am, the church said on its Facebook page.

“We will welcome our guest choir to support us as we join together to sing some familiar carols. Afterwards we will have seasonal refreshments including cakes and mulled wine,” the church said.

The doors are usually open by 9.30am, and you can enjoy some refreshments before the service, it said.

The church’s services are held in the chapel at 5 Oborishte Street, Sofia.

More information via Facebook.

World.title: Bulgaria’s consumer watchdog fines retailer Kaufland 75.7 M euro
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Consumer Protection Commission (CPC) said on November 9 that it fined supermarket chain Kaufland Bulgaria 75.7 million euro, citing “unfair trade practices towards Bulgarian food producers.”

CPC said that it launched an investigation against Kaufland Bulgaria in May, following an analysis of competition in the retail trade of agricultural and fast-moving food products.

The regulator said that it found Kaufland breached competition rules by seeking discounts from suppliers, taking advantage of its stronger negotiating position; applying further supplier price reductions by subtracting the cost of services rendered to suppliers; and by creating “unjustified barriers” for suppliers who sought a price increase for their goods.

CPC said that it imposed separate fines for those violations, which combined for 75.7 million euro. This is one of the largest amounts imposed as a fine by the regulator on a single entity.

In a statement, Kaufland Bulgaria said that it rejected in full both the accusations and the fines imposed on the company. It questioned the size of the fines, arguing that CPC’s decision disregarded European proportionality standards.

The company said that it intended to fight the fines in court (the fines can be appealed within 14 days of being handed down) and said that it would be “forced to review in full future investment in the country, including 200 million euro planned for the next three years ago.”

The statement further said that Kaufland would recommend that its parent, Schwarz Group, review its planned investments in Bulgaria. The group owns retailer Lidl, which also operates in the country.

(Photo: kaufland.bg)

World.title: Von der Leyen to pledge new support for Romania and Bulgaria
World.content:
European Commission (EC) President Ursula von der Leyen is visiting Romania and Bulgaria on November 9 and 10, the EC said.

This year, Europe has faced an alarming rise in hybrid threats, attacks, and incursions into EU territory, the statement said.

Around half of these incidents have affected Romania, Bulgaria and the Black Sea region.

During her visit, Von der Leyen will reaffirm Europe’s solidarity with both countries and determination to restore and preserve freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, the EC said.

Discussions will focus on strengthening maritime surveillance, accelerating defence investments and improving our capacity to respond to crises.

Von der Leyen will also announce new EU support for both countries to strengthen their security and resilience in these uncertain times.

In Bucharest on November 9,Von der Leyen is meeting Nicușor Dan, President of Romania, and Luca-Alexandru Niculescu, Prime Minister of Romania.

On November 10, Von der Leyen will be in Varna, Bulgaria. She will meet Prime Minister Roumen Radev and visit the Nikola Vaptsarov Naval Academy.

World.title: Croatian Unemployment Rate Continued to Fall in October 2026
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – The Croatian unemployment rate is continuing to drop, with the figure having fallen by 15% in October this year compared to October 2025.

In October this year, 20,075 persons or 30.2 percent of the total number of unemployed used state monetary benefits. Poslovni reports that back at the end of October this year 66,425 unemployed individuals were recorded at the Croatian Employment Service (HZZ), which is 11,400 persons or 14.6 percent less than in October 2025, HZZ data published this week revealed.

a mixed bag

Compared to September the number of unemployed increased by 6.1 percent or 3,830 persons. According to HZZ daily data, currently 67,308 unemployed are registered at the service, and 13,099 free job positions have been advertised. During the month of October, a total of 16,792 new persons were registered in the unemployment register, which is 7.1 percent less than back in October last year. In this sum, the majority came from an employment relationship, that is 12,476 of them or 74.3 percent.

1,746 people from regular education (10.4 percent of the total number) and 2,570 persons from inactivity (15.3 percent) also entered into the unemployment register in the past month. The latest HZZ data shows that 12,962 persons left the unemployment register, which is 12.5 percent less than in October 2025. Of that 7,554 persons were employed, namely 7,029 persons or 93.1 percent on the basis of establishing an employment relationship and 525 persons or 6.9 percent on the basis of other business activities.

manufacturing reigns strong

The most frequent employment was established in the manufacturing industry. This October, 1,128 persons or 16 percent were employed in this sector. Wholesale and retail trade followed relatively closely with 983 individuals or 14 percent. This was followed by people coming directly from education, with the number totalling 903, or 12.8 percent. In October, 5,408 persons were removed from the unemployment register due to other reasons, e.g. leaving the force corps (retirement, inclusion in regular education), non-compliance with legal provisions (not actively seeking a job, unavailable for work), personal de-registration from the register and others.

Looking at the situation on a county by county basis, employment was led by Split-Dalmatia County (986 persons or 14 percent of the total number of those employed by establishing an employment relationship), the City of Zagreb (984 persons or 14 percent) and Osijek-Baranja County (736 persons or 10.5 percent). Split-Dalmatia County is also currently the home of the largest number of registered unemployed persons – 10,657 or 16 percent of the total number in all of Croatia. Looking at the situation based on the number of registered unemployed persons, the City of Zagreb (9,013 or 13.6 percent) and Osijek-Baranja County (7,757 or 11.7 percent) follow next.

In October this year, 20,075 persons or 30.2 percent of the total number of unemployed used the monetary benefit. The number of monetary benefit users decreased compared to the same month last year by 1.8 percent or by 374 persons. In October, 13,886 job positions were advertised through HZZ, through which the requirement for 21,519 employees was expressed. The number of sought workers decreased by 6.1 percent compared to the same month last year, the latest HZZ data shows.

World.title: Pantheon Data Centre Boss Refuses to Say How Much Water it Will Consume
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – The Pantheon data centre boss has refused to reveal just how much water the giant, guzzling centre will actually consume in Topusko. Criticism of the planned centre in Topusko is growing louder and louder.

The project manager of the data centre in Topusko has openly rejected claims that the enormous consumption of electricity and water would endanger the public or raise their bills. Poslovni reports that Pantheon project manager Mario Gudelj appeared on HRT’s Dnevnik, stating that the data centre’s investors plan to invest more than 500 million euros in new electricity infrastructure, including around 300 kilometres of brand new transmission lines and a new substation.

“If we were to connect to the existing system, then that would be an overload. We’re building new infrastructure, 300 kilometres of new transmission lines and a new substation, and we’re handing all of that over into the ownership of HOPS,” Gudelj said. HOPS had earlier confirmed that the project requires the construction of four new 400-kilovolt transmission lines with a total length of around 300 kilometres and that the investor would bear the connection costs.

one gigawatt – a massive consumer

Pantheon has been conceived as a data and AI campus of one gigawatt power, or 1,000 megawatts. This is an exceptionally large new consumer. HOPS representative Igor Šumonja at the end of October said that the current load of the Croatian electricity system ranges between 2,000 and 3,000 megawatts and that connecting Pantheon by itself would increase the load by approximately a third. Back in July, HOPS initially accepted the study of the optimal technical connection solution, and the investor and the network operator expect the conclusion of the connection contract. The start of construction is planned for 2027, and the investors want to put the first computing capacities into operation in 2029.

“electricity won’t be more expensive” gudelj claims, but topusko locals aren’t having it

One of the main criticisms of the project relates to the question of whether such a large new consumer can increase electricity prices. Gudelj just keeps on claiming that this will not happen. According to his words, the construction of the new network infrastructure will enable the connection of approximately five gigawatts of new renewable energy sources, whose production should be greater than the needs of the data centre itself.

“I don’t know on the basis of what someone made calculations that the price of electricity will rise because of us. I think that those calculations were impossibly made in the way they are presented to the public,” he said. In doing so he also reacted to an earlier statement by a HOPS representative that the operator cannot predict how the project will affect electricity prices. Gudelj emphasised that HOPS manages the transmission network and does not determine market electricity prices.

“we won’t take water from the public water supply” – but refuses to reveal what the water consumption will actually be

The second major question relates to the amount of water needed for cooling the data centre. Gudelj said that Pantheon will not connect to the public water supply system of Topusko or Sisak-Moslavina County. The investors, according to his words, are researching their own wells from which they would draw water, and the final quantity will depend on the results of the research. He did not, however, specify what the total water consumption of the data centre will be. That is quite telling.

criticism and protest against harmful data centres are growing louder and louder…

In more recent weeks, the contested Pantheon project has been encountering increasingly strong opposition from part of the political parties, local initiatives and environmental organisations. Green Action (Zelena akcija) has warned of the possible consumption of large quantities of energy and water, noise, electronic waste and the impact on the local environment. From that organisation they consider that Croatia before approving a project of such proportions needs to determine a national strategy for the development of large data centres. Criticisms have also been expressed by individual SDP deputies and local initiatives from Topusko, who are seeking additional information on the impact of the project on water, the energy network and the local population.

Gudelj, of course, rejects such claims. None are in his interest.

“Those are well-placed untruths that have no basis in anything. Our project will in no way affect things the way it is being pushed through public opinion,” he claimed for HRT. It will be interesting to see how those claims hold up when we take the likes of what happened in Ireland and Finland into account.

Despite Gudelj’s assurances, the project has not yet passed all the procedures necessary for construction. Sisak-Moslavina County has launched amendments to the spatial plan and the procedure of strategic environmental impact assessment. A main assessment of the acceptability of the intervention for the ecological network is also planned. Gudelj himself earlier said that the project cannot start construction before the completion of the spatial planning procedures and the acceptance of the necessary environmental studies. Therefore the final impact of Pantheon on water, the environment and energy infrastructure cannot for now be considered established.

Gudelj also commented on the accusations due to his earlier function in HOPS. He said that he left the executive function of president of the HOPS Management Board in 2019, after which until 2023 he remained an adviser, when he left the company at his own request. He rejected claims that due to his previous work in the transmission system operator he finds himself in a conflict of interest. Gudelj also considers that the current resistance to large data centres in Europe and the USA will not in the long term stop their development, but he expects that future projects will have to invest significantly more in their own energy infrastructure.

World.title: Zagreb Airport Attraction Wins Yet Another Prestigious Award
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – Zagreb Airport has an attraction that has won yet another prestigious award. The Museum Zone took home silver and has done very well in attracting passengers.

The Museum Zone at Franjo Tuđman Airport, a commendable project realised in cooperation between the Croatian History Museum and Zagreb International Airport, has won the silver the! Award in the multi-stakeholder and multi-sectoral cooperation category at the KoMference of the Croatian Public Relations Association. Poslovni reports that this is otherwise the second professional recognition for that particular project, which in the spring of this year took home the Grand PRix.

The Croatian History Museum, located in Zagreb’s Upper Town (Gornji grad) palaces, was severely damaged in the March 2020 earthquake, because of which it could no longer use its space for exhibiting its museum holdings. On the initiative of the Val Group, cooperation between the Croatian History Museum and Zagreb International Airport began. It was then that the Museum Zone was formally established, within which the exhibition “Stars of Croatian History – The Sky Is Their Limit. Get to Know Them!” was officially opened.

The exhibition presents 24 important figures from throughout Croatian history who, with their work spanning four areas – science, culture, politics and society, and sport – contributed to the development of Croatia and left a mark on the European and global level. “We’re pleased that a project that connected a heritage institution with Zagreb International Airport has been awarded and that this has been recognised as a very good model of communication,” said Minister of Culture and Media Nina Obuljen Koržinek at the KoMference.

Director of the Croatian History Museum Matea Brstilo Rešetar emphasised that when they entered that project they wanted to prove that heritage can meet the public even outside museum walls. According to her words, the Museum Zone has become the second most visited exhibition space in all of Croatia. President of the Management Board of Zagreb International Airport Huseyin Bahadir Bedir said that passengers have been given the opportunity to get to know Croatian history and cultural heritage in an interesting and accessible way, turning the time spent at the airport into an educational experience.

World.title: Crafted in the Capital: Meet the Last Masters of Zagreb’s Old Trades
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – The last masters of Zagreb’s old trades keep the door to simpler times open, all while exposing the soul of the Croatian capital in an increasingly fast-paced world.

If you happen to take a stroll down Zagreb’s old main artery, Ilica, or into one of the (many) historic courtyards of Lower Town (Donji grad), you’ll notice a distinct shift in the bustling city’s rhythm. Beyond the hum of modern life, endless coffee shops and modern boutiques, lies a quieter Zagreb. I’d say the real Zagreb. Situated behind modest, easily overlooked and century-old wooden storefronts, a dedicated group of local master artisans is keeping the Croatian capital’s medieval guild traditions alive and well. In the face of modernity, which is frankly becoming more and more concerning in many ways, these artisans do far more than just preserve tradition.

For many centuries, Zagreb’s economy and civic identity were built and constantly maintained by its obrtnici the master craftsmen. Today, in an era of mass production, fast fashion and people insisting on robots doing absolutely everything for them, these last surviving workshops are grounding for very many people. They’re living, working museums of intangible cultural heritage, offering visitors a rare chance to witness authentic, slow-crafted artistry firsthand. If this is up your street, let’s take a peel inside the workshops of Zagreb’s fascinating master umbrella makers, hatters, and cobblers, as all of them shape the capital’s true artisanal soul.

the crimson canopy of the Šestine umbrella

TZGZ/Ernest Mazarekic

No visit to Zagreb is complete without seeing the iconic Šestine umbrella (Šestinski kišobran, if you want to go local). Towering in vibrant crimson over the stalls of the busy Dolac Market, this striking parasol with its multicoloured horizontal stripes and natural chestnut handle is the city’s most recognisable visual symbol. What many travellers fail to realise is that every single authentic Šestine umbrella is still handcrafted in one single location – the Cerovečki Umbrella Workshop. You’ll find it on Ilica. Founded back in 1912 and now led by the fourth generation of the Cerovečki family, this is the last remaining umbrella-making workshop out of the eight that once operated across the capital. Recognising its profound historical value, the Croatian Ministry of Culture inscribed the traditional craft of making the Šestine umbrella on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of the Republic of Croatia. Stepping inside the shop, you’ll immediately be struck by the aroma of steamed chestnut wood and fine cotton. It’s an instant sensory reminder that a true souvenir isn’t always a magnet or a keyring that will fall to bits quickly, it can still be something built to weather decades of rain.

zagreb’s hatters – crowning the capital

Sandra Simunovic/PIXSELL

The word “hatter” is often associated with the term “mad hatter” and little else anymore, and while we can’t 100% guarantee you won’t run into a mad hatter in Zagreb, we can guarantee you’ll be impressed by what they do. If you turn the clock back to the early 20th century, however, a refined gentleman or lady living in Zagreb would never dream of stepping out onto Ban Jelačić Square without donning a proper hat. Today, that bygone Central European elegance survives in the workshops of the city’s historic milliners and hatters (known as klobučari).

Tucked into the historic Octagon passage (Oktogon) and along Ilica, old institutions like Kobali Hat Shop and Salon Šešira Cahun continue to block, steam, and stitch headwear using century-old wooden molds. Whether crafting traditional wool felt fedoras, bespoke bridal fascinators, or the classic caps worn by very many regional folk ensembles, Zagreb’s hatters bridge the gap of time, linking historical preservation and contemporary high fashion. Visitors are welcomed directly into spaces lined floor-to-ceiling with what seems like endless hatboxes, where a master artisan will measure your head and fit a piece tailored specifically to your silhouette. You don’t get that in Primark.

the bespoke cobblers who aid life spent walking the city’s cobbles

Goran Stanzl/PIXSELL

Before industrial footwear flooded the market, Zagreb’s shoemakers (postolari) and bootmakers (čizmari) were among the most respected tradespeople in the entire city. While many have since transitioned into repair shops, a handful of master cobblers still practice the careful, painstaking art of bespoke shoemaking from scratch.

Along Ilica, workshops like Postolar Bočak continue to maintain the rigorous standards of traditional Central European leatherwork. Creating a single pair of handmade shoes requires dozens of individual steps, from carving custom wooden lasts (kalupi) to hand-stitching supple calfskin uppers and natural leather soles. For those seeking sustainable, buy-it-for-life luxury, commissioning a pair of shoes or leather goods in Zagreb connects you directly to generations of ergonomic mastery. These people know that wandering the cobbled streets of the much older parts of the city, such as Upper Town, can take quite the toll on the ankle without the right footwear. So, if you plan to get your steps in while wandering all over Zagreb, this might be the best place to start!

preserving zagreb’s soul in a world full of confusion

TZGZ/Julien Duval

We currently live in a world dominated by rapidly evolving tech, uncertainty and a lot of worries we wouldn’t have had a clue about even a decade ago. Most of us feel that insecurity and desire something to ground us to the good old days. That’s exactly why these workshops matter so deeply to modern Zagreb. They take us back to simpler times, all while anchoring the city’s identity. Through dedicated cultural preservation initiatives championed by the Zagreb Tourist Board and the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts, these fantastic traditional businesses are actively protected as vital cultural assets. Many carry the prestigious “Tradicijski obrt” (Traditional craft) designation. This is a mark of authenticity guaranteeing that the techniques used inside have been passed down through many generations.

For visitors looking to trade mass-produced trinkets (and especially umbrellas and shoes that fall to bits after a few weeks) for genuine stories and something made to go the distance, exploring Zagreb’s old trades is an unforgettable way to spend an afternoon. In an uncertain world moving faster than we can keep up with every single day, Zagreb’s last master craftsmen remind us that the finest things in life, much like the many hidden gems dotted around the Croatian capital itself, are best appreciated slowly.

World.title: How to Claim Croatian Citizenship If Your Ancestral Records Were Destroyed in the War
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – Claiming Croatian citizenship is no easy feat without professional assistance, but it becomes even more of a quagmire when your ancestral records were destroyed during the war. Luckily, there’s help available to guide you through what’s often a difficult, lengthy process.

America is a melting pot and there’s a lot of Croatian “ingredients” within it. There are countless Americans who have Croatian descendants scattered across North America, and many have a desire to not only reconnect with their family histories, but cement that connection with a Croatian passport of their own. For all of them, the journey toward claiming a Croatian and as such EU passport begins with a simple request, and that’s obtaining an ancestor’s birth certificate (rodni list) from that usually long gone relative’s home village somewhere in Croatia. For many such would-be applicants, that’s where the journey typically ends.

the dead end… or is it?

There’s a reason why what sounds like such a simple procedure comes unstuck so often – the war. For families whose roots trace back to areas of the country which were particularly heavily impacted by the Homeland War, including Slavonia, Banovina, Kordun, or the Dalmatian hinterland, the first step is also the last.

When DIY applicants reach out to local municipal registry offices or consular officials, they’re frequently met with the response that the old local archives were burned, shelled, or simply became completely lost during the war, and the primary civil records simply no longer exist. For most diaspora applicants, this feels like the end of the road. They assume that without an original birth certificate of a relative who actually came from Croatia, proving their lineage under the Croatian Citizenship Act is impossible. Fortunately, a destroyed municipal archive doesn’t erase your legal right to Croatian citizenship, even if those who destroyed it during the 1990s had hoped that would be the case. It just means your application requires administrative (and often legal) reconstruction rather than standard document retrieval.

a missing birth certificate doesn’t have to mean the end of the croatian citizenship road…

Under current Croatian administrative law, the Interior Ministry requires an unbroken chain of evidence proving your ancestor’s identity, birthplace, and connection to Croatia. When primary civil registries end up being destroyed, the law does allow applicants to rebuild that proof using secondary historical records. However, you can’t simply submit a family story or a letter stating the records were burned or lost during the war. To satisfy Croatia’s somewhat strict legal thresholds, you need obtain an official certificate confirming the destruction of the primary registry, and then pair it with alternative, state-recognised proof of your ancestor’s birth and residency.

duplicate histories, and why croatia’s love of recording everything more than once leans in your favour…

Back during the 19th and early 20th centuries, vital events in Croatia (and there were very many) were rarely recorded in just one single book. This era was a very turbulent time for what is now Croatia, with regimes and empires coming and going fairly often. That means that even if a local town hall was destroyed in the 1990s, parallel records often survived in completely different institutions across the country. It’s finding them that can be tricky. Reconstructing a lost Croatian lineage often involves hunting down secondary evidence across four main repositories.

First, you usually need to begin with the Diocesan church archives. Catholic parishes usually held meticulous baptismal, marriage, and death registers. Parishes were, at least historically speaking, required to send duplicate copies of these books to regional bishoprics or archdiocesan archives in bigger cities like Zagreb, Split, or even (again, historically speaking) Đakovo. This largely kept them safe from localised village destruction.

Then comes the regional state archives. These often contain much older civil records. Usually older than 100, these records were frequently transferred out of local municipal offices and into regional state vaults long before the final fall of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.

Another particularly important area to explore are the property registries. These are historical court records detailing land ownership, agricultural plots, and inheritance deeds. Logically, they tend to list exact family lineages, birth years, and familial relationships.

Then comes the historical Census and conscription lists. Austro-Hungarian or early 20th-century regional tax rolls, school registries, and military draft lists can serve as vital corroborating evidence to establish an ancestor’s presence in a specific village. The interesting thing here is that you shouldn’t necessarily be put off if you don’t find your ancestor listed as even being Croatian. Given the period we’re talking about here, they very likely wouldn’t be.

why taking the diy approach often falls flat

While secondary reconstruction is completely legal, executing it from thousands of miles away is nearly impossible for a DIY applicant. Local municipal clerks in Croatia are rarely equipped (or obligated) to act as historical detectives on behalf of overseas applicants. Frankly, they’ll likely ignore a single rogue applicant from somewhere in America until you go away. If a record is missing from their immediate database, their job ends at telling you it isn’t there. Hunting down duplicate baptismal books in a diocesan vault or pulling 19th-century inheritance deeds from a regional court requires physical presence, archival knowledge, and proper knowledge of administrative Croatian – and that’s not something you can muster up overnight (trust me on that).

how croatian by descent‘s services can be your guide

All is not lost. There are services which aid would-be Croatian citizenship applicants in exactly this, and Croatian By Descent is one of them. Their guidance and knowledge of the process, particularly for US applicants, can turn what seems like an administrative dead end into a genuine, flowing path towards that Croatian and EU passport. Instead of accepting a “records not found” notice at face value, their team, comprised of diaspora Croats themselves, utilises local archival experts who not only understand how to trace where surviving duplicates are housed, but have the skills to grasp what that undertaking looks like. They navigate the regional state archives, coordinate with authorities, and help you to compile the combination of documents required by the Interior Ministry. They also work with lawyer partners who are on hand to help push through anything that ends up being trickier than expected.

By pairing this investigative archival work with document formatting, they give you the best chance possible of your application meeting the requirements, even if your ancestral village’s town hall didn’t survive the war.

World.title: Landlords in Top Croatian Tourist Spots Could Pay More Tax – Breakdown by City
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – Landlords located in the top Croatian tourist spots could find themselves paying much more out in tax next year – here’s a breakdown of what that looks like on a city by city basis.

As of 2027, private landlords who rent out their properties to tourists could face new rules for calculating their lump-sum tax. Lukrecija Zderic reports for Index that with the proposed amendments to the law, the minimum annual tax amounts per bed would increase, and how much landlords will pay will also depend on the decisions of cities and municipalities, should parliament adopt these amendments. The increase won’t hit all landlords equally. Here’s a full breakdown of exactly which Croatian tourist spots could see the future lump sum change and how much more apartment owners could pay annually depending on the number of beds they have.

four beds could mean 200 euros higher annual tax

According to the current proposal of legal amendments, the minimum annual lump-sum tax in the first category of tourist development would rise from 100 to 150 euros per bed, and in the second from 70 to 100 euros. Cities and municipalities that have so far prescribed lower amounts would have to align them with the new minima. That would mean at least 50 euros more annually per bed in the first, or 30 euros in the second category, but not an automatic tax increase for all landlords. In those categories, there are a total of 105 cities and municipalities, including the best-known tourist destinations. Below we bring an overview of the existing amounts and possible changes from 2027.

The largest increase in the first category would be felt by landlords who currently pay 100 euros per bed. If local authorities align that amount with the new minimum of 150 euros, the owner of an apartment with four beds would see the annual tax rise by 200 euros.

Ston, Kaštela, Senj, Vir and Trogir…

In the second category, the largest change would affect Ston, Kaštela, Senj, Vir and Trogir. There landlords with four beds, with the application of the new minimum, would pay 120 euros more annually. Changes will not be equal in all parts of individual cities. Where the lump sum differs according to zones, the increase would apply only to zones in which the current amount is lower than the new minimum. For example, in Split the lump sum could increase in zones where it is now lower than 150 euros per bed, while in others it would remain unchanged. On the other hand, in Zagreb, Makarska and Rijeka, the existing lump sum is already higher than the proposed minimum, so it would not have to rise solely because of the legal amendments. The final amounts will nevertheless depend on the decisions of cities and municipalities, which can prescribe even higher lump sums than the legal minimum.

a higher lump sum even if the cities themselves fail to make a decision

The draft law also provides for an increase in the amounts that are applied if city or municipal councils do not make a decision on the amount of their lump-sum tax. In the first category of tourist development, that amount would increase from the previous 200 to 225 euros per bed or accommodation unit, while in the second category it would rise from 135 to 150 euros. For example, a landlord with six beds in the first category, to whom that legal amount would apply, would instead of the previous 1,200 euros pay 1,350 euros annually, or 150 euros more. These are legal amounts provided for in the proposal, and not the final tax obligations of all landlords.

Since 2025, the lump-sum tax for private landlords has been determined according to the tourist development of the city or municipality in which the accommodation is located. Four groups were introduced, and for each a special range of amounts per bed was prescribed, within which cities and municipalities themselves determine the amount of tax. Before that, all units of local self-government had the same legal range, from 150 to 1,500 kuna, (or from approximately 19.91 to 199.08 euros per bed). Local authorities even then independently determined the final amount, but regardless of the tourist development of their specific area.

as expected, the smallest landlords will actually be hit hardest…

Vedran Tomić, representative of the association Save Small Family Landlords, considers that with the proposed amendments the state is forcing cities and municipalities to increase the lump-sum tax. He emphasises that in the association they are not against lump-sum taxation, but warns that the increase in the legal minimum would hit precisely the landlords who offer the cheapest accommodation the most.

“More than 90 percent of beds are in the first and second category. Thereby, the lower limit of the lump-sum tax is practically shifted for all landlords. We consider the shifting of the lower limit absurd because units of local self-government already had the possibility to increase the amounts, and they did not. Now the minimum is increased by 50 percent, that is to 150 euros. I’ll give a concrete example. I’m from Crikvenica and I know the situation there very well. The lump-sum tax per bed there first amounted to 45 euros, then it was increased to 100, and then to 150 euros. Such an increase is contrary to the interests of the residents of Crikvenica and all political options in the city.

Regardless of whether it is the government or the opposition, no one considers that the tax on rental, which is one of the main economic activities of Crikvenica, should be additionally increased. One should look at that more broadly. Units of local self-government should find it important that people understand that in smaller places on the Adriatic that tax is not such a significant source of revenue for the local budget. The goal should be to encourage people to work and earn, and then spend that money precisely in their community. These are people who live in those communities and spend their money there. We consider that the state should not force cities and municipalities to increase tax on their own population,” Tomić believes.

will this result in the loss of the local guest?

When asked about how the proposed increase in the lump-sum tax will be reflected in the business of landlords and whether the additional cost will spill over into accommodation prices, he believes Croatian guests will be among the first affected.

“First of all, the tax increase will at least partially spill over into accommodation prices, which will additionally encourage inflation. It is a pro-inflationary, and not an anti-inflationary measure because every additional tax cost someone has to pay. The second important problem is the social effect of such an increase. It will hit landlords with lower incomes harder, as well as guests who use the most favourable private accommodation. It’s precisely in these most favourably priced apartments where Croatian guests like to spend their summer holidays. Due to the possible increase in prices the affordability of summer holidays will also be endangered because part of Croats could remain without the possibility of being able to afford the accommodation they have been used to so far and will choose other locations,” Tomić stated.

He also added that he fears that the increase in the lump-sum tax could encourage part of the landlords to move into the grey zone, that is unregistered rental of accommodation. “If the tax rises so much that landlords with the lowest incomes can no longer bear it, part of them could move into the grey zone, because of which the state, that is cities and municipalities, would ultimately collect nothing. In doing so all those costs are added up. For some the additional amount may not represent a great burden, but for many it will. Everything depends on the incomes they achieve. Ultimately, I consider that the system of lump-sum taxation according to the number of beds itself is quite unfair.”

Whether the announced increases will indeed be reflected in accommodation prices and supply will be known after the adoption of the law and the decisions of cities and municipalities, while a clearer picture of their real consequences will be given only by the next summer tourist season.

World.title: Should Pula Airport Follow Zadar’s Model?
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – Pula Airport is notoriously empty during the winter season, and some are saying over-reliance on just Ryanair might be more of an issue than we realise – should it therefore follow Zadar’s model?

Much has been said recently about the business model employed by Pula Airport, and the debate even reached the Croatian Parliament recently. Boris Bilas reports for Glas Istre/Voice of Istria reports that SDP MP Sanja Radolović proposed an initiative to establish a route between Pula and nearby Venice. Given the previous management’s neglect of the airport, Pula Airport is still far from reaching the passenger numbers it recorded just under a decade ago. It’s therefore hardly surprising that Istrian politicians, as well as the general public in Istria, are becoming quite concerned.

The new airport director, Marko Ražem, has quickly demonstrated that he is the complete opposite of his predecessor, and it seems that Pula Airport finally has a chance to recover under his leadership. At the same time, many people in Pula are calling for the Zadar model to be adopted, wondering why Pula cannot have an airport just as successful as Zadar’s, especially given that Istria is a much stronger tourist region than the Zadar area.

However, Marko Ražem himself has already stated publicly that he doesn’t consider Zadar’s airport management model particularly appealing and would rather develop Pula Airport in a completely different direction. Indeed, the two airports have completely different business strategies, and a comparison of passenger traffic at Zadar and Pula airports reveals a fundamental divide in their approaches to route development. Zadar’s rapid rise, which saw passenger numbers exceed 1.6 million in 2025 and 2026, has been built on the back of one dominant partner, the ultra-popular Irish low-cost giant Ryanair.

Pula, on the other hand, records stable but more modest passenger traffic of around 554,000, approximately 200,000 fewer than its record year of 2019. However, its strength lies in spreading risk and maintaining a network of traditional and diverse airlines.

the two different strategies employed by zadar and pula

Zadar Airport has become one of Ryanair’s key hubs in this part of the Adriatic coastline. According to estimates, Ryanair accounts for between 75 and 80 percent of Zadar Airport’s total annual passenger traffic. The Irish airline group connects Zadar with more than 70 destinations, bringing record passenger numbers to the airport during the summer season, but also leaving it completely exposed to the business decisions of a single board of directors in Dublin.

Pula Airport, on the other hand, has historically maintained a more balanced portfolio. Although Ryanair first entered the Croatian market through Pula in 2006, Pula does not allow its future to be determined exclusively by the low-cost model. Germany and the United Kingdom account for more than half of all arrivals, while, alongside Ryanair, a significantly larger proportion of passengers travelling to Istria are brought in by other airlines and numerous charter operators.

In the aviation industry, having 80 percent of your traffic dependent on a single airline is considered an extremely high-risk gamble. Ryanair operates according to a highly aggressive business model: it has no particular loyalty to destinations. Its bases are established wherever subsidies from local tourism boards are highest and airport fees are lowest. When an airport refuses to reduce its charges or a government raises taxes, Ryanair does not hesitate to withdraw aircraft and shut down routes overnight. Zadar is currently undergoing a massive infrastructure expansion of its passenger terminal. Investments in increased capacity are justified by the current overcrowding. However, if Ryanair were to decide to drastically cut its operations or relocate its base, as it recently announced reductions and withdrawals from cities such as Berlin, Bremen and Thessaloniki due to disagreements over airport charges, Zadar Airport could be left with an enormous empty terminal, high fixed costs for maintaining unused facilities and a dramatic drop in revenue.

a broader airline range

This is precisely what the new director of Pula Airport, Marko Ražem, wants to avoid. He has announced that the airport will attempt to further expand its range of airlines in the future, even if this might mean slightly fewer passengers in the short term compared with Zadar.

In the long run, however, this would mean a much more stable and secure business model that does not depend on the whims of a single person in Dublin. All things considered, Zadar is currently enjoying the fruits of its tourism boom and making headlines with record-breaking passenger numbers. However, its Ryanair “monoculture” is unsustainable in the long run without a strong Plan B. Pula, despite having fewer passengers, can sleep much more peacefully because losing any individual airline would not automatically mean the end of the airport’s operations. The lesson for Croatian tourism and aviation authorities is clear: low-cost airline partners are an excellent engine for growth, but turning an airport into the private runway of a single airline creates a vulnerability that could bring an entire region’s air connectivity to a standstill in an instant.

ryanair’s cautionary tale…

The risks of depending on a single airline are not merely theoretical. Several smaller European airports have experienced complete collapse after becoming dependent on Ryanair and subsequently attempting to make the airline pay market-rate prices. It’s no secret that Ryanair offers the best prices for the vast majority of its routes, and that making sure it is present at your airport has become paramount across Europe, but it shouldn’t imply total reliance. There are a few cautionary tales to keep in mind…

Frankfurt-Hahn Airport (Germany): Once a textbook example of Ryanair’s success outside Frankfurt. When the Irish airline began transferring flights to Frankfurt’s main airport and cutting routes at Hahn, the airport sank into debts amounting to millions of euros and eventually declared bankruptcy.

Altenburg-Nobitz Airport (Germany): A regional airport that invested millions in modernisation to meet Ryanair’s requirements. Following disagreements over marketing funding, Ryanair completely abandoned the airport in 2011. The airport was left without commercial flights, and the project ended in business failure.

Ciudad Real Airport (Spain): Although it also suffered from other structural problems, this so-called “ghost airport” attracted Ryanair with millions in subsidies. When the subsidies dried up and Ryanair left, the airport closed and ended up in insolvency proceedings. The recent wave of base closures and capacity cuts across Germany and Belgium clearly demonstrates that O’Leary’s management is not afraid to make radical cuts.
