His lawyer, Sara Mansoori, told London's High Court that he had attempted suicide when he received letters from the Guardian and ITV News seeking his response to the allegations.

He later made another attempt, she said, and he was recently admitted to the hospital for psychiatric care.

On November 3, London's High Court rejected his application for an injunction.

Overnight, a deadline for Walliams to appeal passed, meaning the news outlets were able to publish their investigation.

Attorney Gavin Millar, who represented the outlets, said the allegations were gathered after "a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation" and that there was a strong public interest in publishing them.

Queen Elizabeth met David Walliams at the Royal Albert Hall in 2012. (Reuters: Andrew Winning)

Has Walliams been charged?

No police charges have been laid against Walliams and there is no suggestion he is under police investigation.

After the reports were published overnight, London's Metropolitan Police said it had contacted the Guardian and ITV News "to ensure that any potential victims" were "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".

What has the reaction been so far?

HarperCollins UK dropped Walliams in December 2025 after Britain's Daily Telegraph reported the publisher had investigated allegations of harassment involving junior female employees.

One employee agreed to a financial settlement and the publisher advised staff not to visit Walliams at his home and to work in pairs, the Telegraph wrote.

Walliams's spokesperson told the BBC at the time he strongly denied behaving inappropriately and that HarperCollins had never informed him of the allegations.

The latest accusations have prompted more organisations to distance themselves from Walliams.

The BBC said it was removing some programs, including Little Britain, while it reviewed "all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms".

A spokesperson for his literary agents, Independent Talent Group, said it was "no longer representing him in any capacity".

Producers of Fing! — an upcoming film based on Walliams's book — said they had removed his cameo appearance and that Walliams would "have no involvement in the film's release or promotion".

World.title: Nurse treated for broken wrist after alleged assault in Sydney hospital
World.content:
A nurse and a doctor at Concord Hospital in Sydney's inner west have been treated for injuries after allegedly being attacked by a patient.

Police said a 44-year-old female patient was restrained and sedated, after allegedly assaulting the two women, aged 34 and 57, on Tuesday morning.

Health Minister Ryan Park said both women required medical treatment, one for a broken wrist.

The attack came a day before the NSW government announced a boost in security staff at 27 hospitals across the state.

One hospital staff member, who began their shift shortly after the alleged assault, said colleagues told them the woman shoved a nurse manager in the chest, causing her to fall backwards and sustain multiple wrist fractures.

They said the second woman, a junior doctor, suffered a cut to her head after being pushed over and hitting the edge of a table.

Staff at Concord Hospital were injured. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The staff member said assaults against hospital staff by acute mental health patients were an "almost daily" occurrence at Concord, and had created a "mutinous feeling" among some emergency department staff.

In an email sent to staff, hospital management described it as a "serious incident" and said the staff members had been "injured by a mental health consumer".

The email said one of the staff members requires some time off work to recover from their injuries.

Management said a "number of violence prevention initiatives" were in place at the hospital.

"It is deeply disappointing that these measures were not yet able to protect our team," the email read.

Guard backs boost to security

Mr Rowling says he's been injured at work many times. (ABC News)

Bruce Rowling is a security guard at Sydney's Royal North Shore Hospital and says he has been injured on the job "many a time".

The worst of those injuries was his thumb pulled out of its socket, ripping his tendons.

Mr Rowling says his thumb was pulled out of its socket. (ABC News)

He said he was restraining a male patient who had been told by a doctor he was moving to another hospital.

"He didn't like that, he just went a bit crazy, started swinging and punching the doctor," Mr Rowling said.

Before the patient could be sedated, Mr Rowling held him down.

"In the process of me holding him, my thumb was pulled out of its socket," he said.

Mr Rowling says usually four security staff worked in a hospital of hundreds. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

Mr Rowling said in a big hospital with about 650 beds, there were usually four security staff working at a time.

He said a general rule was one security guard for every 100 people, but that number was not achievable once visitors and hospital staff were taken into account.

At a media conference with the health minister, he backed government plans to boost security staff at hospitals.

The state government has committed to recruiting 129 extra full-time security staff to reduce gaps in security ratios in New South Wales hospitals.

Bigger hospitals with high-volume emergency departments see the most violent incidents, including Westmead Hospital, Prince of Wales Hospital and Royal North Shore Hospital.

Extra security staff will be hired across 27 hospitals. (ABC News)

Mr Park said the additional security staff would be deployed at 27 hospitals across the state.

"The ability for them to handle challenging patients, challenging visitors, challenging people who are coming into our hospitals is far easier when they feel supporter by additional staff," he said.

Health Services Union secretary Gerard Hayes said the additional staff would help prevent violent incidents before they happened.

"We will now be in a position to prevent issues occurring as opposed to responding to them, which is the most important thing," he said.

Mr Hayes described a hospital as a "microcosm of the community".

"And we're seeing the community now under pressure, we're seeing the community also becoming more anxious," he said.

'Drug of choice' increasing violence

Mr Park said changes in drug use had contributed to an increase in violence in emergency departments.

"Back 20 years ago, the drug of choice, heroin at the time, had a different effect on the body than what the types of drugs that we see now, particularly methamphetamine," he said.

Ryan Park says a nurse suffered a serious enough injury they required care. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

Mr Park said people using methamphetamines presenting at hospitals could bring some "pretty frightening issues" for staff and security officers, requiring extra resources.

"We're working very closely with police about the way in which we interact with those patients when they come into our hospital settings," he said.

Calls for extra powers

Mr Rowling said ongoing underworld crime in Sydney had also been a concern for hospital security.

"They end up in hospital, you have their friends and relatives turning up and they don't always like each other," he said.

He said when police do not have capacity to watch patients in hospital, security guards "take up that slack".

"Everything you see out on the street happens in hospitals as well, but you have a thousand people in a big building," he said.

While security guards receive training, they do not have any "extra powers than the average citizen", Mr Rowling said.

"We can ask someone to leave if they're misbehaving problem is you can't do that to everyone who's a patient because they might be a critical patient," he said.

Mr Park said the government had "not made a decision" about increasing powers available to hospital security guards.

"Additional powers comes with other challenges, but we are working through those," he said.

World.title: Tribute to former Adelaide Hills passenger rail in backyard model
World.content:
Calls may be continuing for a reinstated passenger railway service to the Adelaide Hills, but a world away from public transport lobbying, Peter Michalak is building his own version in a backyard shed.

Harking back to the late 1980s and early 90s, Mr Michalak's HO scale (1:87) Hills Line railway layout represents the 315-kilometre stretch between Adelaide and Serviceton, just over the Victorian border.

Featuring the Murray Mallee town of Pinnaroo and Tailem Bend railway station with buildings modelled to scale, its centrepiece is Bridgewater railway station in the Adelaide Hills, complete with the old mill and tree-covered hillside.

Peter Michalak's layout includes the historic Bridgewater Mill in the Adelaide Hills. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"Bridgewater, in this reality, still has passenger train services to it," Mr Michalak said.

"I grew up catching SteamRanger [heritage] trains to Bridgewater as a kid in the school holidays, so I had a lot of memories of going up there, and I had to create it."

Bridgewater was the first railway station he created, and was designed to be portable and taken on exhibit.

The railway line goes through Pinnaroo, a town in SA's Murray Mallee. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

The layout, which Mr Michalak started in 2013, has since grown too big and too complicated to be exhibited.

It now gives a "selectively compressed" version of the much longer railway, and includes Mount Lofty Railway Station, while his brother, Nick, is currently building Blackwood Railway Station.

Peter Michalak has been working on his Hills Line HO scale since 2013. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Mr Michalak has built about 50 metres of mainline rail, which loops around his shed over three levels, and hosts some very familiar trains built to scale.

"The only difference being, instead of running a 70-wagon container train, I'm running a 10-wagon container train because you obviously don't have the real estate to play with," Mr Michalak said.

"The platforms are also shortened, along with some other bits and pieces that have been selectively compressed to fit the space we've got."

An intricate model of Tailem Bend Railway Station in the Murray Mallee. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

A freight train engine even makes realistic sounds as it trundles past Bridgewater, with trees fashioned from the sedum "autumn joy" plant.

The engine whines through the hills and at one point lets loose a blast from its horn that could have come from the gullies of Belair.

A tunnel along the Adelaide Hills railway line replicated by Peter Michalak's model. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Mr Michalak is focused on building part of the once sprawling Adelaide Railway Station at the end of the line, which is being modelled on its appearance before the convention centre was built over part of the station in 1987.

His layout even includes the "international orange chairs" on the platform.

The model even includes the orange seating on the station platform. (Facebook: The Hills Line in HO scale)

He said his model of Serviceton Railway Station, with its heritage-listed two-storey brick complex, when finished "will probably be the key piece".

"Particularly given the size of the building that has to be built for that, it's going to be the real showpiece for the whole layout, but that's still a long way down the track," Mr Michalak said.

"It has a cardboard mock-up stuck to the back wall at the moment."

Not quite finished, the model station currently has a cardboard exterior background. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

The layout also includes a different branch line to Port Adelaide where a mill, based on the heritage Hart's Mill building, is modelled.

Mr Michalak estimates it will be another 10 years until the project is fully completed.

The scene includes a model of the Hart's Mill building in Port Adelaide. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Nick Michalak undertakes the computer-aided design drawings (CAD) and Mr Michalak 3D-prints the train engine and carriage components.

Some trains can be sourced, such as freight trains with a national profile, but many of those unique to South Australia have to be constructed by hand.

A model engine that had to be made for his collection. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

This includes the classic SA-built Redhen passenger series, which was in service across the metropolitan area from the 1950s to 1996.

They even took passengers into the Adelaide Hills, a service that was progressively wound back by the state government in the 1980s before it stopped altogether at Belair in 1987.

Far from reality

There has been growing pressure on the government to reinstate passenger rail transport to the hills due to its increasing population and rising congestion on the South Eastern Freeway.

SA voters' transport wishlist As more houses are being built in Adelaide's outer suburbs, more public transport is something on the minds of South Australian voters, in both the regions and the city.

Mr Michalak, who is also the SteamRanger Heritage Railway vice-president, would love to see it reinstated into the hills from Adelaide.

"Unfortunately, I think we've got a better chance of aliens being located and wanting to come and talk to us than getting our state government to commit to doing rail in the hills," he said.

"It's a shame because it's not that hard. It's just there's a lack of willpower to do it."

Peter Michalak with a passenger train his brother made for the set. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Helping to run a number of real-life steam- and diesel-hauled passenger trains between Mount Barker and Victor Harbor for tourists, Mr Michalak continues to work on his own layout at home, finding the occasional hour or two in the shed between full-time work, volunteering and family life.

Taking the creation as seriously as any number of similar enthusiasts across the city, Mr Michalak's friend, a former South Australian Railways and national train controller, has even drawn up train control graphs that replicate the real railway's timetable.

Bridgewater was the first setting Peter Michalak created and has been exhibited. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

The timetable, however, will compress a 12-hour shift into about a two-and-a-half-hour window.

"The idea is that we crack a few beers and we have someone here controlling the train movements," Mr Michalak said.

"It's a very social part of it all.

"It's built to use."

World.title: How a small scrap of sandpaper shed light on cricket's so-called dark arts
World.content:
Eight years after then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull felt the need to weigh in on Australia's ball tampering in the Cape Town Test, sandpaper and cricket are back in the headlines together.

Usman Khawaja's book, featuring revelations, allusions and confirmations of what most everyone already believed, has reignited conversations about the Australian team's conduct during that 2018 tour of South Africa.

But whatever the team did, who did it and who knew about it, one thing is for sure: they weren't the first to fiddle with the ball.

So why did they do it and why was the reaction so extreme?

'A beautiful art'

Reverse swing can make even the best batters look silly. (Getty Images: Tom Shaw)

In the wake of Khawaja's exclusive interview with Nine Newspapers on the weekend, outspoken former Australia fast bowler Geoff Lawson added to the conversation with a brilliantly headlined article.

" I don't know a bowler who hasn't licked, flicked, scratched or slobbered on a cricket ball. "

Thanks for those mental images, Geoff.

Evocative wording or not, the 46-Test veteran is right. But why?

Explaining the mysteries of swing bowling It is one of the most devastating weapons a fast bowler can own — but the art of swing is steeped in mystery and myths that only science can explain.

The science of conventionally swinging a cricket ball through the air is relatively simple and adheres to some basic rules of drag, air pressure and laminar flow (a lot of the same stuff that keeps an aeroplane in the air).

When a cricket ball is new, its stitched seam is standing at its tallest, allowing a bowler to angle that seam towards or away from the batter and the air will get caught on the seam, dragging the ball in that direction.

But the proud seam on a dark red ball is clearly visible to a batter, and the best ones can see what's happening and account for it.

Reverse swing is a little more complicated and prized due to it being more difficult to deliver, predict and face.

Conventional swing (left) vs reverse swing (right). (ABC News: Gabrielle Flood and Nina Maile Gordon)

"As a batter it's the hardest thing to face. It's a beautiful art," former Proteas captain Faf du Plessis told The Grade Cricketer podcast on the eve of Australia's return to Cape Town last month.

The ball swings towards the side of the ball that looks smoother due to small abrasions on that "shiny" side of the ball, more of which is facing the batter and therefore offering more surface area and turbulent airflow, this time dragging the ball in the opposite direction to the way the seam is facing.

It also happens later in the ball's flight, often too late for the batter to react.

It only comes after the ball has been bowled for a few dozen overs and whacked around the field a bit; once the seam has flattened out, and the leather has been, crucially, roughed up and dried out.

Weather conditions have to be perfect, the bowlers have to be incredibly skilled and the care for the ball has to be spot-on, to the point that former England captain Alastair Cook was prized as a ball shiner because he barely sweats.

Of course, there are other ways to help this along.

Spit, sunscreen and swing

There are plenty of legal ways to shine the ball. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Once a cricket pitch has flattened out from the start of a game, the new ball has lost its shine and proud seam, and before it becomes a spinner's paradise on days four and five (although this is becoming more and more rare), reverse swing is one of the few tools in fast bowler's arsenal.

For decades, cricket teams have worked on the ball feverishly to try to work on conventional and reverse swing.

Often players will shine the ball on their groin or hip, or some sweat from their forehead (or spit in pre-COVID times).

In those processes, there are some grey areas.

Any sensible cricketer will be wearing sunscreen, some will be wearing hair products, many will be chewing gum or chomping on a lolly.

Sweat can be used to shine the ball but keeping it dry is key to reverse swing. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

All of that gives a little extra viscosity to the sweat or saliva used on the ball, but match referees couldn't very well force players to spit their gum into a hanky on the boundary line or force them to have a shower before entering the field of play, so there is not much they can do.

Then there's the flip side, where players try to create a rougher surface to generate that turbulent airflow, which can include simple things like picking at the seam of a ball or fielders intentionally throwing the ball in short to ensure it bounces on the coarse pitch block.

Ironically enough, du Plessis, South Africa's captain on that fateful 2018 tour, twice stumbled from lightish grey into gun-metal territory earlier in his career.

In 2013, after a failed attempt with his fingernails, du Plessis was caught on camera blatantly scratching the ball on the zip of his pants pocket, mere centimetres from legal territory.

Teams work hard on the ball to create the conditions for conventional and reverse swing bowling. (Getty Images: Santanu Banik/MB Media)

A few years later, as he skippered the team during a 2016 tour of Australia, he was again seen on the field opening his mouth, touching his fingers to a massive white mint on the middle of his tongue, then applying that sugary saliva directly to the ball.

Had he simply sucked the mint, popped it into his cheek and then touched his tongue, he could have avoided his own chase through the airport and a hefty fine.

Du Plessis described the fallout from his 2013 zipper incident as "a week of hell", so it's no wonder he expressed so much sympathy for Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith (curiously no mention of David Warner) as the world closed in on them.

After massive bans and public disgrace, you would think the world would have moved on, but between the long-awaited Test return to South Africa and now Khawaja's book, the controversy seems never-ending.

Why the sandpaper saga?

One part absolutely boils to down to Australian cricket's sense of exceptionalism and perception of itself as arbiter of what is and isn't acceptable on a cricket field.

But the brazen nature of the ball tampering is perhaps the biggest reason that this was and remains such a big story.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

England skipper Michael Atherton was caught rubbing dirt into the ball and his reputation remains pristine but, like the various fructose or lotion-enhanced bodily fluids, that's the sort of thing one could use on the ball opportunistically or even inadvertently.

Perhaps that's why Bancroft's first feeble attempt at deflection was claiming he "saw an opportunity to potentially use some tape [and] get some granules from the rough patches on the wicket", rather than bringing some 300 grit onto the field where its only purpose could be ball tampering.

There are legendary tales of bottle caps being used to help out reverse swing kings like Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis in Test matches way back when, and Khawaja wrote about some of the methods he had seen or heard of in Sheffield Shield cricket.

But in a high-profile Test series, to be so obvious when the team knew they already had heat on them betrayed a sense that they thought they were untouchable or that winning was worth the risk.

Alas, the SuperSport cameras caught him in high definition and super slow-mo and put the so-called dark arts very much under a spotlight.

After du Plessis's minty moment, Dirk Nannes said in commentary at the time for ABC Sport: "It's an art and some of the art is doing it and not getting caught."

If that is the case, consider Cameron Bancroft less Gauguin and more Gallagher.

World.title: Orbit kicks off partner-funded NSW copper-gold drilling
World.content:

Orbit Resources has fired up the drill rig for a second stage of partner-funded diamond campaign at its Goodrich Porphyry prospect, 70 kilometres south-west of Orange, within the highly prospective Lachlan Fold Belt in New South Wales. The four-hole, 1000-metre program follows July’s stage-one discovery of the aptly named “Pencil Porphyry” - a narrow, vertically extensive mineralised structure - which delivered a solid hit of 136.55m grading 0.32 per cent copper, 0.16 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 43g/t molybdenum from 81.45m. That intercept also contained a richer 3.55-metre core running at an impressive 2.8 per cent copper. Orbit Resources has begun a new diamond drilling program at its Goodrich copper-gold project in New South Wales. Geologically, the company’s initial discovery was a textbook hit, intersecting a chalcopyrite-bearing monzonite porphyry. The intrusion also exhibited mineralised “unidirectional solidification textures”, key pathfinders for large ore systems, suggesting the ground may hold further treasures lurking below. The new drilling will test the lateral and down-dip extent of the interpreted porphyry system and investigate its continuity with historical copper-gold intercepts associated with the project’s nearby Goodrich open pit.



‘Stage two drilling is now underway and is designed to test how far the existing porphyry extends.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens Orbit’s joint venture partner, Canadian-listed Great Plains Metals Corp, is fully funding the program and is now providing an additional $1 million of work, including a minimum of 500m of drilling under the joint venture agreement as it works towards earning a 70 per cent stake. The deal will leave Orbit holding a 30 per cent interest, giving it cost-effective exposure to further exploration success without having to foot the bill during the earn-in period. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “Stage-one drilling at Goodrich returned a broad interval of copper-gold-molybdenum mineralisation from relatively shallow depth. Stage-two drilling is now underway and is designed to test how far the existing porphyry extends, and whether it connects with the shallower historical copper-gold intercepts around the Goodrich open pit.” While the JV drilling at Goodrich provides a free kick at goal, Orbit’s main game remains its flagship Lewis Ponds gold-silver-zinc project, also in the Lachlan Fold Belt. The project already hosts a hefty mineral resource of 17.52 million tonnes (Mt) containing 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent. A scoping study on Lewis Ponds outlined a robust base-case pre-tax net present value (NPV) of $481 million, using gold at US$3700 (A$5410) an ounce and silver at US$55 (A$80) an ounce. However, an upside case based on February spot prices of US$5055 (A$7390) gold and US$82 (A$120) silver sent the potential economics into the stratosphere, delivering a pre-tax NPV of a whopping $1.088 billion and a 40 per cent internal rate of return.



Adding to the project’s credentials, recent drilling at its Spicer’s Lode appears to have opened up some serious exploration upside after the final hole of a recent four-hole resource development campaign intersected a thick 28.1-metre zone of visual sulphide mineralisation, including sections with up to 34 per cent semi-massive sulphides. While visual estimates are no substitute for assays, the core showed a polymetallic sulphide assemblage of pyrite, sphalerite, galena, chalcopyrite and pyrrhotite. Assays from the lab are pending. The company has also defined a new discovery at Cousin Jack, roughly 350m southeast of the main Lewis Ponds resource, with initial drilling hitting encouraging base metal grades, including a 1.7-metre section containing 11.35% zinc, 0.34% copper and 18.05g/t silver from 585m. Rounding out Orbit’s portfolio is the Narraburra rare earths project, 250km southwest of its flagship Lewis Ponds. The ionic-clay rare earths deposit hosts a maiden JORC-compliant resource of 94.9 million tonnes (Mt) grading 739 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides, including a higher-grade core of 20Mt at 1079ppm. With its JV partner footing the bill to chase a promising porphyry discovery at Goodrich and a suite of potentially company-making assets in its own right, Orbit appears to have engineered multiple streams of news flow. While the Goodrich work unfolds, all eyes will be on the pending assays from Lewis Ponds to see if the visual sulphide hits can deliver the grades needed to edge the potential billion-dollar project closer to reality. World.title: Cricket Australia must get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Editorial Cricket Australia must get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa The Herald's View Editorial November 11, 2026 — 3:59pm

November 11, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The smell that has wafted around Cricket Australia’s brusque response to cheating by the Australian team in South Africa eight years ago has redeveloped into a strong stench blanketing officialdom’s claim that the matter is closed. Cricket Australian offered up three sacrificial lambs after Cameron Bancroft was filmed shoving sandpaper into his pants. Bancroft was banned for nine months. Skipper Steve Smith and batsman Dave Warner received 12-month suspensions. Smith was banned also from the captaincy for at least two years, while Warner was told he would never lead Australia. Usman Khawaja has written about the sandpaper scandal in his new autobiography. Dan Peled One of Australia’s players in that Cape Town Test, Usman Khawaja, who retired last January, has written an autobiography, Sabr, in which he claims the entire team knew of tampering with the ball in the previous Port Elizabeth Test. “It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” Khawaja told the Herald. Warner has come out and said Kawaaja’s recollection was 100 per cent accurate.“Now everyone knows the truth. It’s out there. People wanted to know it. You’ve come out and said it.”



Related Article Australian cricket Sandpaper feuds erupt: Warner takes on ex-coach Lehmann in stunning twist Mitchell Starc is the first current player to deny the allegations, saying his recollection hadn’t changed over time and his fellow bowlers knew nothing about the sandpaper use. In 2021, when the controversy re-erupted, four of the Australian bowlers in Cape Town Test, Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and Nathan Lyon, released a statement re-affirming that they did not know a “foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball” until they saw images of the sandpaper in Bancroft’s possession on the big screen at the ground. The sport personifies ethics and fair play; the official rulebook includes a preamble called the “Spirit of Cricket”. However, there has long been tension between the romanticised ideal and the pressure of professionalism. The 1932-33 “Bodyline” series shocked Australia when England bowled lethal bouncers, and a 1981 one-day international turned into national shame after Australian captain Greg Chappell instructed his younger brother, Trevor, to roll the final delivery underarm to prevent New Zealand from hitting a six to win the match. The same infamy haunts Sandpapergate.



Related Article Australian cricket Khawaja cancels book interviews after refusing to answer key question about Cummins Simon Longstaff, who led a review into the culture of Cricket Australia in 2018, said he had heard whispers that the public record of the cheating scandal was inaccurate and a cover-up was possible. “All I can say is that if what Khawaja alleges turns out to be true, then I was also lied to,” Longstaff wrote in the Australian Financial Review. Khawaja has pulled out of promotional media interviews after being challenged to comment on other players’ reactions to his claims. Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening an investigation into Sandpapergate. It is a predictable self-protection ignoring the uncomfortable reality that five players who played in South Africa are expected to feature in the Test squad to play New Zealand this summer and the likelihood the scandal will fester for years as others release their own biographies.



Cricket Australia needs to recognise that their sport personifies ethics and fair play, both on the field and the boardroom. It needs to get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa once and for all, for the good of the game. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Netanyahu’s policies face the chop as new parliament sworn in
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsrael Netanyahu’s policies face the chop as new parliament sworn in Melanie Lidman November 11, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tel Aviv, Israel – Gadi Eisenkot, the politician tasked with forming a new Israeli government, pledged on Tuesday to reverse many of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s policies as the new parliament was sworn in. The pledge sets the stage for a consequential month of legislative action and coalition negotiations. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. Gadi Eisenkot speaks to media in Jerusalem on November 10. Getty Images While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Netanyahu’s opponents now control a solid majority in parliament. Eisenkot’s bloc introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Netanyahu and his policies.



They include launching an official government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister, and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. Related Article World elections Israeli president asks Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government It was not immediately clear how quickly or far those bills would advance in the weeks ahead. Eisenkot, a former general, who campaigned as a no-nonsense straight shooter, reiterated that his goal was a government that all Israelis could trust, not one that represents only certain factions. “We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment,” Eisenkot said ahead of the Knesset swearing-in ceremony.



Netanyahu has sought to undermine the certified election results after his bloc fell short of a majority. He has repeated unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties “stole” the elections. In a speech following Tuesday’s ceremony, Netanyahu reiterated his claim that Arab politicians, who represent a minority comprising 20 per cent of Israel’s population, cannot be trusted. Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressing lawmakers at the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg He attacked Jewish opposition leaders who have signalled a willingness to partner with Arab parties to form a government. Eisenkot has left that possibility open if the parties meet several conditions, including accepting Israel’s identity as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist group. “I ask you: Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?” Netanyahu said.



Push for a new speaker Eisenkot said Netanyahu’s speech was “divisive” and “hate-filled,” adding: “I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute.” He later said he had cancelled a meeting with Netanyahu’s Likud party planned for Wednesday because of the speech. Eisenkot’s bloc triggered a process on Tuesday to install a new parliamentary speaker as they kicked off work on their legislative agenda. The majority of members submitted signatures calling for the ousting of the current Netanyahu-backed speaker, Amir Ohana, in the first step towards a vote on his replacement. The vote can take place even before a coalition government is in place. The Israeli parliament during the inaugural session following Israel’s legislative elections on October 27. Getty Images



The Knesset speaker is a powerful position. The speaker determines what bills the Knesset will take up, meaning one picked from among the Eisenkot-led opposition parties could propel their legislative agenda forward. The opposition nominated Matan Kahana, a senior member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, for the job. A vote to appoint him speaker could come as early as this week. Netanyahu as caretaker The swearing-in of the new Knesset ushered in an unusual transitional period in Israeli politics – Netanyahu and his cabinet remain in power, while the new lawmakers can introduce legislation. Meanwhile, Eisenkot will meet with party leaders as he works to build a coalition that would be likely to make him prime minister. If he fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to give Netanyahu the next opportunity to form a government.



As caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu faces court-imposed limits on his powers. But he can still pursue appointments and could try to block new legislation. He retains full authority over national security, including the military. Related Article World elections ‘We need Bibi’: How Netanyahu defied the polls Netanyahu has argued that Jewish-led parties should form a unity government to counter the threat of an Iranian attack. He renewed that call Tuesday, urging them to “set aside all other considerations,” and said Israel should work to topple the Iranian government. A governing coalition without Netanyahu could leave him politically vulnerable as he faces an ongoing corruption trial and possible findings of security failures in the lead-up to the October 7 attacks. World.content:
PoliticsFederalNegative gearing Record plunge in investor loans as tax overhaul hits property market Shane Wright Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:53pm ,first published 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The federal government’s budget overhaul of negative gearing and capital gains tax has been blamed for the biggest fall in home loans taken out by investors on record, with warnings the property market will struggle well into next year. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics released this morning showed loans to investors dropped by 30.6 per cent in the three months to September. Over the past 12 months, investor loans are down by 38.6 per cent. The number of investor loans for existing homes in NSW has tumbled by up to 50 per cent over the past three months. Jessica Shapiro The drop, however, is concentrated among investors who purchase existing homes. In NSW, investor loans for new builds fell by 18.4 per cent through the September quarter but for existing dwellings they collapsed by almost 50 per cent. It was a similar story across the rest of the country. Loans by investors for existing homes fell by 27 per cent in Victoria, by 40 per cent in Queensland and by 38.1 per cent in Western Australia.



Nationally, the ratio of investors buying existing homes to building new properties fell to its lowest level on record. The sharp falls occurred after the May budget in which Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed plans to limit negative gearing - the ability to offset losses on a rental property against a person’s total income - to new builds from July 1 next year. The 50 per cent capital gains tax concession, blamed by critics for the step-up in property prices and investor activity after it was introduced by the Howard government, will return to an inflation-adjusted basis on July 1 next year. The changes were announced after the Reserve Bank began lifting interest rates and the start of a fall in national property prices now in its seventh consecutive month.



Overall new home loans fell by 15.5 per cent through the quarter to be 21.4 per cent down over the past year. This included first home buyers with loans to new entrants to the property market falling 8.6 per cent in the quarter and 12.3 per cent over the year. Housing Minister Clare O’Neil said the figures showed a clear shift away from investors towards people wanting to buy their own home and that investors had moved towards constructing new houses. Related Article Property prices Air is coming out of the housing bubble. Is now the time for first home buyers? “We’ve had a housing market geared towards investors for a generation, and where did it get us? Plummeting home ownership, out-of-control house price increases, and a generation losing hope,” she told this masthead. “These numbers show the balance is shifting back towards Australians who are buying a home to live in, and especially to our first home buyers.”



Liberal housing spokesman Andrew Bragg said the figures showed the government’s tax policies were hurting the property market and homeowners. “No one wins from the new taxes, not first homeowners, not owners, not renters and not investors. Time for them to be repealed,” he said. JP Morgan economist Tom Ryan noted that the drop in lending to owner-occupiers was in line with other falls during periods when the Reserve Bank was tightening monetary policy. But the drop in investor lending was being exacerbated by the tax changes in this year’s budget, with Ryan warning that they are “likely to remain a structural drag” for some time.



HIA senior economist Maurice Tapang said the lift in business construction may mean that builders are constructing spec housing to protect their sub-contractors. He said the property sector had yet to feel the full brunt of the RBA’s five rate hikes and the blow to confidence dealt by the government’s tax changes. “Investors are crucial to addressing the housing under-supply and moderating downward cycles in the market. They add to rental supply and net dwelling stock, while adding nothing to housing demand,” Tapang said. “Policies that increase the cost or risk of investing in housing do not resolve that shortage but rather make it worse.” But the numbers also showed businesses are borrowing record amounts to construct apartment blocks and data centres. Building loans by businesses soared in value by 27.6 per cent in the quarter to be 51.8 per cent up over the past 12 months.



Loans for dwellings, predominantly units and apartment blocks, climbed 56 per cent over the year to a record $8.4 billion while loans for other buildings, including data centres, soared 84 per cent on an annual basis to more than $5 billion. The nation’s biggest home lender, the Commonwealth Bank, noted in its quarterly market update released on Wednesday that cost-of-living pressures and the impact of higher interest rates are starting to affect its borrowers. Bank CEO Matt Comyn said that while the economic growth was slowing, the overall economy remained resilient due to low unemployment and strong public and private infrastructure spending. “Higher inflation and interest rates continue to place uneven pressure on household incomes and business activity,” he said. Parents need to take greater responsibility for their children’s dangerous e-bike use, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon declared, as he faces a revolt over pursuits. The Police Association of NSW has directed officers to no longer pursue dangerous riders on e-bikes and motorbikes after two officers were charged after allegedly hitting a woman in a marked police car and knocking her from her bike. It is alleged the officers left the scene without rendering aid. The NSW government is seizing and crushing overpowered e-bikes. Dominic Lorrimer Lanyon and NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley on Wednesday voiced their disagreement with the powerful Police Association and reminded officers of their oath. “The NSW Police Force obviously work for their commissioner. The police have an oath of office, and they’ll continue to do that,” Lanyon said.



Association president Kevin Morton argued police were not afforded enough protections to pursue e-bikes without fearing criminal prosecution. Related Article Exclusive

Cycling Doctors urge parents to stop buying illegal e-bikes as children’s injuries double “There comes a point where enough is enough. That point has now been reached,” he said. The NSW government faces pressure to follow through on its promised e-bike safety reforms to establish an age limit for their use. Transport Minister John Graham commissioned an expert report into potential age limits which was handed to him in June, however, the minister will not make a decision on the ban until next year.



The government has also refused to release the findings of the report, meaning parents buying e-bikes as gifts for their children this Christmas have no way of knowing whether it will be legal for their children to ride them next year. Lanyon said it was the responsibility of parents to ensure a bike is age-appropriate for their child. “When e-bikes are used safely and appropriately, they are a great form of conveyance, they are not dissimilar to a push-bike when they’re ridden appropriately, but most children aren’t given a push-bike by their parents without being shown how to use them properly,” he said. “We ask the same for e-bikes. They are inherently dangerous if ridden incorrectly.” A number of children and teenagers have been hospitalised after e-bike crashes in NSW, including an 11-year-old and a 13-year-old who were thrown from a bike during a crash with a Corolla in Albion Park on Tuesday night.



Related Article City life Revealed: The plan to strip 5000 e-bikes from Sydney’s streets The 11-year-old, who was riding on the back of the bike as a passenger, was flown to Sydney Children’s Hospital at Randwick with serious injuries. A 14-year-old boy was injured on Tuesday when he crashed his e-bike into a stationary car in Teralba. Last week, a five-year-old boy was hospitalised with serious injuries including a brain bleed, a fractured skull and a broken leg when he was hit by an e-bike while walking along the footpath outside Tahmoor Public School, in the Wollondilly Shire. The rider of the e-bike was identified as a 16-year-old boy, who is assisting police with their investigation. World.title: Children’s author and Little Britain star David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct
World.content:
WorldEuropeCourts Children’s author and Little Britain star David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct Sylvia Hui and Brian Melley Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:36pm ,first published November 11, 2026 — 1:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. British comedian and children’s author David Walliams allegedly used his fame to groom girls and young women for sex, two British news outlets reported on Tuesday (UK time). ITV News and The Guardian newspaper said their joint investigation featured interviews with multiple women who gave first-hand accounts of Walliams’ conduct. One woman alleged the former Little Britain star sexually assaulted her at his house when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them when they were teens. Loading Walliams, 55, denied the allegations. He had sought a court injunction to bar ITV News and The Guardian from identifying him in their reporting. His lawyers claimed that publication of sexual misconduct allegations would lead him to take his own life.



A judge rejected his injunction request last week, but protected his identity until late Monday. “I am not a sexual predator,” Walliams said, according to ITV. “I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” “Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely, and it is something that I never did,” he added. David Walliams, pictured in London in 2025. Scott A Garfitt/Invision/AP Walliams is best known for comedy sketches on Little Britain, a hugely popular British TV show in the 2000s, but he’s also a celebrated children’s book author with some 40 published titles that sold more than 60 million copies worldwide, according to his website.



His lawyer, Sara Mansoori, earlier told the High Court that he had made a suicide attempt when he received letters from ITN and Guardian News and Media seeking his response to the allegations. He later made another attempt, she said, and he was recently admitted to the hospital for psychiatric care. The case drew widespread attention in Britain because it highlighted questions over public figures’ right to privacy and what media can report on the basis of public interest. Gavin Millar, representing the media companies, has said that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a strong public interest in publishing them. He told the court that the investigation involved speaking to more than 100 people, and alleged that over a period of years Walliams “used his status and influence as a well-known public figure to establish contact with young women, some considerably younger than him, and that he engaged or sought to engage in seriously inappropriate conduct,” according to a summary of the court judgment. Some of the alleged conduct could amount to criminal offences if proven, it said.



Walliams was dropped last year by publisher HarperCollins after allegations were made of inappropriate behaviour. Few details were published at the time, but The Guardian reported on Tuesday that there were concerns about his behaviour for years, including an allegation that he had an inappropriate sexual relationship with a junior female employee. Several of his books, including Gangsta Granny, have been adapted into BBC comedy dramas and stage productions. Walliams (far left) left his role as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent in 2022 after apologising for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants. Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images Walliams was also a judge for years on Britain’s Got Talent, though in 2022 he stepped down after apologising for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants. The BBC said on Tuesday it was removing some programs, including Little Britain, while it carried out a review of “all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms”.



In Australia, the ABC confirmed on Wednesday that it had “removed some content” from ABC iview, believed to be two movies, Ratburger and Grandpa’s Great Escape, both of which are adapted from Walliams’ novels and include Walliams in the cast. Stan* also confirmed it had removed the film Fing!, which was adapted from Walliams’ 2019 book of the same name, from its content slate. The film was shot in Queensland and was due to be released this year. Variety also reported Walliams, who co-wrote the script, had a cameo in the fantasy film axed. “We take the allegations reported regarding David Walliams seriously,” the film’s producers said in a statement to Variety. “Our thoughts are with anyone who has been affected. We have removed his cameo appearance from Fing!, and he will have no involvement in the film’s release or promotion.” The literary agency Independent Talent Group also said it was dropping Walliams following the new allegations. In dismissing the injunction bid by Walliams, Justice Matthew Nicklin said such a legal measure would mean “an exceptionally serious interference” with the rights of the media companies. He noted that Walliams had a “serious and longstanding psychiatric vulnerability” which must be taken seriously, and said a decision allowing the allegations to be published will substantially increase his risk of suicide. However, he added that the evidence did not “establish that suicide is inevitable”.

World.title: Trump’s triumphal arch has new enemies – the Kennedys
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s triumphal arch has new enemies – the Kennedys Luke Broadwater November 11, 2026 — 3:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Washington: President Donald Trump’s planned 76-metre triumphal arch has come under legal fire on multiple fronts: from veterans, a historian and the governments of the District of Columbia, Virginia and Arlington County. Now comes another legal challenge, from the storied Kennedy family. Visitors at John F. Kennedy’s grave site at Arlington National Cemetery, with the Lincoln Memorial in the distance. The New York Times Arguing that the arch, with its golden angels and flame on top, would cast a shadow on their relatives’ graves in Arlington National Cemetery, nine members of the Kennedy family moved to join existing litigation in Washington on Tuesday seeking to block the project. They also say the arch would obstruct the intended sight line from the eternal flame at president John F. Kennedy’s gravesite, “destroying an essential element of the gravesite’s design.”



A judge in another case has temporarily paused construction of the arch – one of Trump’s favourite projects. If allowed to proceed, it would rise between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The filing claims that the placement would obstruct “a line of sight that was designed to represent the unification of the nation following the Civil War and that has existed for nearly a century”. A model of President Donald Trump’s proposed arch to commemorate the country’s 250th anniversary. Getty The arch “will permanently cast a shadow over plaintiffs’ parents’ graves and the graves of servicemen and -women who made the ultimate sacrifice for this country,” the filing added. The plaintiffs are children or grandchildren of senators Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, the former president’s brothers, who are buried near him.



“A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come,” two of the plaintiffs, Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy, who are children of Robert Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy, said in a statement. Related Article US midterms Facing midterm reckoning, Trump unveils plan for luxury DC golf course Trump’s project has received mixed news recently. On Thursday, the National Capital Planning Commission, led by the president’s allies, gave the project final approval, clearing the way for Trump to break ground. But immediately afterwards, a federal judge blocked construction. The ruling by Judge Tanya Chutkan of the District Court for the District of Columbia halted construction for 14 days while legal challenges make their way through the court system. In a 33-page opinion, Chutkan said the arch required congressional approval and that its construction could prove costly to both Virginia and the District of Columbia while disrupting traffic at the cemetery, one of the region’s most-visited sites.



The Kennedys’ lawsuit includes some of those same arguments but expands on the arch’s personal impact on the family. John F. Kennedy (left) with brothers, Robert Kennedy (centre), and Ted Kennedy in 1960. AP Wirephoto “The gigantic proposed arch is an illegal interference with Arlington National Cemetery and the heroes remembered there, including at the gravesites and memorials of the Kennedy brothers and Ethel Kennedy,” the plaintiffs’ lawyers, Norman Eisen and Steve Jonas of the Democracy Defenders Fund, said in a statement. “Only Congress has the constitutional power to authorise an intrusion of this magnitude. Today, members of the Kennedy family are joining with the other litigants in this case to protect this historic site – and to defend the rule of law and separation of powers.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

World.title: Trump’s Fed nightmare: Rates won’t be slashed. They could surge now
World.content:
BusinessThe economyInflation Opinion Trump’s Fed nightmare: Rates won’t be slashed. They could surge now Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:34pm , first published 11:59am

Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:34pm ,first published 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If Donald Trump expects Kevin Warsh, his hand-picked chair of the US Federal Reserve Board, to deliver the interest rate cuts that he has continuously clamoured for, he is about to be disappointed. Again. It now appears inevitable that the Fed will deliver its second rate rise in this cycle – the first was in September – after the US inflation rate came in above expectations for the third successive month. He won’t like it, but Donald Trump’s demands for lower interest rates will most likely be ignored by the Fed. Alex Brandon The only question – and just raising it will upset Trump – is whether the US central bank hikes its policy rate by 25 basis points or 50 basis points when it meets again next month. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Tuesday that consumer prices rose 0.4 per cent in October. While calculations are muddied by the fact that a government shutdown meant there was no data collected in October last year, most calculations put the annual inflation rate at 4 per cent.



Even if energy and food costs are excluded to remove the direct effects of the war in the Middle East on oil and fuel costs, “core” inflation in October was 0.3 per cent and the annual core inflation rate 2.8 per cent – well above the Fed’s target of 2 per cent. Moreover, inflation is spreading across the US economy, thanks to Trump’s tariffs and the indirect effects of the higher oil and refined product prices on transport costs that are now feeding into goods and services prices. The only question – and just raising it will upset Trump – is whether the US central bank hikes its policy rate by 25 basis points or 50 basis points when it meets again next month. Fed officials are already preparing the ground for more than one rate hike. Fed governor Christopher Waller (a Trump appointee) told an audience in London on Tuesday that, should the inflation rate for the month come in above 0.3 per cent, a half-percentage point (50 basis point) rate rise might be needed. A conventional 25 basis point rise, he argued, would do little to win confidence that the Fed was serious about tackling inflation.





The inflation rate rose even though oil prices were mostly flat throughout the month. It would appear to be the delayed impacts of higher gasoline and, in particular diesel prices, that are now flowing through the economy and bleeding into consumer prices. The oil price has fallen back this month to trade at around $US92 a barrel and gasoline prices are sliding, albeit they are, at $US3.98 a gallon, still about 30 per cent higher than they were a year ago. Diesel prices are still 65 per cent higher than a year ago. Following the Democrats’ success in the midterms, Fed governors are less likely to feel intimidated by potential administration retaliations if they back rate rises. AP The oil price has been falling because oil flows from the Middle East have been restored to close to pre-war levels (albeit with far higher transport and insurance costs) and because Trump keeps saying that a negotiated end to the war is within reach, although he has said similar things throughout this year, but the conflict has yet to be resolved. With the US midterm elections out of the way, the administration may, however, find it easier to accede to some of Iran’s demands.



Even if the oil price continues to retreat, however, refined product prices – of which diesel is the key product – are unlikely to subside as quickly, as the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine have significantly damaged refinery capacity. The result of the midterms will help the Fed if it starts more aggressively raising US interest rates. That might infuriate the president, but there is little he can do about it. If the wars were to end soon, it would still take well into next year for volumes to recover. In the meantime, the higher cost of transporting goods and food will continue to push up goods and grocery prices. Tariffs remain another contributor to the inflation rate with their stop-start history, thanks to the courts consistently ruling them illegal and the Trump administration’s continuing efforts to reimpose them using new legislative headings. Toy prices, for instance, were 9 per cent higher than a year ago. Auto parts and repairs prices were up 0.6 per cent in October. Then there’s the impact of the boom in artificial intelligence, which is pushing up the prices of semiconductors and impacting the prices of computers, smartphones and other devices as well as electricity prices.



The inflation data underscores why US voters gave the Republicans such a thrashing at the midterm elections. For ordinary US households, the cost-of-living pressures are real and intensifying. Related Article Analysis

US midterms Donald Trump’s humiliation is an opportunity for America The result of the midterms – a Democrat majority in both chambers of Congress – will help the Fed if it, as expected, starts more aggressively raising US interest rates. That might infuriate a president who wanted Warsh to deliver greatly lower rates, but there is little he can do about it. Trump has tried, unsuccessfully, to remove former Fed chair Jerome Powell from the board, threatening to prosecute him for cost overruns in the renovations of the Fed’s Washington headquarters. He’s still trying to unseat another governor, Lisa Cook, with flimsy accusations of mortgage fraud. Even if he were able to sack Cook (there is a handpicked administration panel “investigating” her), or Powell decided to retire before his term ends in January 2028, the Democrats are most unlikely to approve a new Trump nomination to the board. And other Fed governors are now less likely to feel intimidated by potential administration responses to votes in favour of rate rises.



It’s not been a good week for Trump and his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. On Monday, the Congressional Budget Office released its summary of the outcomes from the 2026 fiscal year which, in the US, ends on September 30. The Trump administration presided over a deficit of $US2 trillion ($2.9 trillion), or 6.2 per cent of GDP, a significant increase from the $US1.8 trillion (5.8 per cent of GDP) deficit in fiscal 2025. The administration is spending more (outlays were up 6 per cent) while, thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s tax cuts for companies and the wealthy, generating only 3 per cent revenue growth. Corporate tax revenue fell 16 per cent. Customs revenue fell 11 per cent because the administration had to refund $US126 billion after the US Supreme Court deemed Trump’s original global tariffs illegal. Loading America’s finances aren’t improving. In October, the CBO estimates, there was a deficit of $US409 billion, 30 per cent more than the same month last year, with revenues shrinking and spending growing.



With government debt of more than $US40 trillion and the net interest cost of that debt climbing 11 per cent in the year to September, to $US1.14 trillion, a rising rate environment would only increase the threat to America’s financial stability and its ability to sustain even its modest – by comparison with other developed economies – social security net. Bessent, who promised to lower the deficit-to-GDP ratio to 3 per cent, says economic growth will fix America’s public finances. It won’t, and Trump’s second term will, just like his first term, leave a legacy of unfulfilled promises and unsustainable debt and deficits. Ordinary Americans will be much poorer for the experience. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Orbit kicks off partner-funded NSW copper-gold drilling
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Orbit kicks off partner-funded NSW copper-gold drilling Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 11, 2026 — 4:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Orbit Resources has fired up the drill rig for a second stage of partner-funded diamond campaign at its Goodrich Porphyry prospect, 70 kilometres south-west of Orange, within the highly prospective Lachlan Fold Belt in New South Wales. The four-hole, 1000-metre program follows July’s stage-one discovery of the aptly named “Pencil Porphyry” - a narrow, vertically extensive mineralised structure - which delivered a solid hit of 136.55m grading 0.32 per cent copper, 0.16 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 43g/t molybdenum from 81.45m. That intercept also contained a richer 3.55-metre core running at an impressive 2.8 per cent copper. Orbit Resources has begun a new diamond drilling program at its Goodrich copper-gold project in New South Wales. Geologically, the company’s initial discovery was a textbook hit, intersecting a chalcopyrite-bearing monzonite porphyry. The intrusion also exhibited mineralised “unidirectional solidification textures”, key pathfinders for large ore systems, suggesting the ground may hold further treasures lurking below. The new drilling will test the lateral and down-dip extent of the interpreted porphyry system and investigate its continuity with historical copper-gold intercepts associated with the project’s nearby Goodrich open pit.



‘Stage two drilling is now underway and is designed to test how far the existing porphyry extends.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens Orbit’s joint venture partner, Canadian-listed Great Plains Metals Corp, is fully funding the program and is now providing an additional $1 million of work, including a minimum of 500m of drilling under the joint venture agreement as it works towards earning a 70 per cent stake. The deal will leave Orbit holding a 30 per cent interest, giving it cost-effective exposure to further exploration success without having to foot the bill during the earn-in period. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “Stage-one drilling at Goodrich returned a broad interval of copper-gold-molybdenum mineralisation from relatively shallow depth. Stage-two drilling is now underway and is designed to test how far the existing porphyry extends, and whether it connects with the shallower historical copper-gold intercepts around the Goodrich open pit.” While the JV drilling at Goodrich provides a free kick at goal, Orbit’s main game remains its flagship Lewis Ponds gold-silver-zinc project, also in the Lachlan Fold Belt. The project already hosts a hefty mineral resource of 17.52 million tonnes (Mt) containing 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent. A scoping study on Lewis Ponds outlined a robust base-case pre-tax net present value (NPV) of $481 million, using gold at US$3700 (A$5410) an ounce and silver at US$55 (A$80) an ounce. However, an upside case based on February spot prices of US$5055 (A$7390) gold and US$82 (A$120) silver sent the potential economics into the stratosphere, delivering a pre-tax NPV of a whopping $1.088 billion and a 40 per cent internal rate of return.



Adding to the project’s credentials, recent drilling at its Spicer’s Lode appears to have opened up some serious exploration upside after the final hole of a recent four-hole resource development campaign intersected a thick 28.1-metre zone of visual sulphide mineralisation, including sections with up to 34 per cent semi-massive sulphides. While visual estimates are no substitute for assays, the core showed a polymetallic sulphide assemblage of pyrite, sphalerite, galena, chalcopyrite and pyrrhotite. Assays from the lab are pending. The company has also defined a new discovery at Cousin Jack, roughly 350m southeast of the main Lewis Ponds resource, with initial drilling hitting encouraging base metal grades, including a 1.7-metre section containing 11.35% zinc, 0.34% copper and 18.05g/t silver from 585m. Rounding out Orbit’s portfolio is the Narraburra rare earths project, 250km southwest of its flagship Lewis Ponds. The ionic-clay rare earths deposit hosts a maiden JORC-compliant resource of 94.9 million tonnes (Mt) grading 739 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides, including a higher-grade core of 20Mt at 1079ppm. With its JV partner footing the bill to chase a promising porphyry discovery at Goodrich and a suite of potentially company-making assets in its own right, Orbit appears to have engineered multiple streams of news flow. While the Goodrich work unfolds, all eyes will be on the pending assays from Lewis Ponds to see if the visual sulphide hits can deliver the grades needed to edge the potential billion-dollar project closer to reality. World.title: Cricket Australia must get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Editorial Cricket Australia must get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa The Herald's View Editorial November 11, 2026 — 3:59pm

November 11, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The smell that has wafted around Cricket Australia’s brusque response to cheating by the Australian team in South Africa eight years ago has redeveloped into a strong stench blanketing officialdom’s claim that the matter is closed. Cricket Australian offered up three sacrificial lambs after Cameron Bancroft was filmed shoving sandpaper into his pants. Bancroft was banned for nine months. Skipper Steve Smith and batsman Dave Warner received 12-month suspensions. Smith was banned also from the captaincy for at least two years, while Warner was told he would never lead Australia. Usman Khawaja has written about the sandpaper scandal in his new autobiography. Dan Peled One of Australia’s players in that Cape Town Test, Usman Khawaja, who retired last January, has written an autobiography, Sabr, in which he claims the entire team knew of tampering with the ball in the previous Port Elizabeth Test. “It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” Khawaja told the Herald. Warner has come out and said Kawaaja’s recollection was 100 per cent accurate.“Now everyone knows the truth. It’s out there. People wanted to know it. You’ve come out and said it.”



Related Article Australian cricket Sandpaper feuds erupt: Warner takes on ex-coach Lehmann in stunning twist Mitchell Starc is the first current player to deny the allegations, saying his recollection hadn’t changed over time and his fellow bowlers knew nothing about the sandpaper use. In 2021, when the controversy re-erupted, four of the Australian bowlers in Cape Town Test, Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and Nathan Lyon, released a statement re-affirming that they did not know a “foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball” until they saw images of the sandpaper in Bancroft’s possession on the big screen at the ground. The sport personifies ethics and fair play; the official rulebook includes a preamble called the “Spirit of Cricket”. However, there has long been tension between the romanticised ideal and the pressure of professionalism. The 1932-33 “Bodyline” series shocked Australia when England bowled lethal bouncers, and a 1981 one-day international turned into national shame after Australian captain Greg Chappell instructed his younger brother, Trevor, to roll the final delivery underarm to prevent New Zealand from hitting a six to win the match. The same infamy haunts Sandpapergate.



Related Article Australian cricket Khawaja cancels book interviews after refusing to answer key question about Cummins Simon Longstaff, who led a review into the culture of Cricket Australia in 2018, said he had heard whispers that the public record of the cheating scandal was inaccurate and a cover-up was possible. “All I can say is that if what Khawaja alleges turns out to be true, then I was also lied to,” Longstaff wrote in the Australian Financial Review. Khawaja has pulled out of promotional media interviews after being challenged to comment on other players’ reactions to his claims. Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening an investigation into Sandpapergate. It is a predictable self-protection ignoring the uncomfortable reality that five players who played in South Africa are expected to feature in the Test squad to play New Zealand this summer and the likelihood the scandal will fester for years as others release their own biographies.



Cricket Australia needs to recognise that their sport personifies ethics and fair play, both on the field and the boardroom. It needs to get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa once and for all, for the good of the game. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Netanyahu’s policies face the chop as new parliament sworn in
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsrael Netanyahu’s policies face the chop as new parliament sworn in Melanie Lidman November 11, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Tel Aviv, Israel – Gadi Eisenkot, the politician tasked with forming a new Israeli government, pledged on Tuesday to reverse many of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s policies as the new parliament was sworn in. The pledge sets the stage for a consequential month of legislative action and coalition negotiations. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. Gadi Eisenkot speaks to media in Jerusalem on November 10. Getty Images While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Netanyahu’s opponents now control a solid majority in parliament. Eisenkot’s bloc introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Netanyahu and his policies.



They include launching an official government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister, and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. Related Article World elections Israeli president asks Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government It was not immediately clear how quickly or far those bills would advance in the weeks ahead. Eisenkot, a former general, who campaigned as a no-nonsense straight shooter, reiterated that his goal was a government that all Israelis could trust, not one that represents only certain factions. “We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment,” Eisenkot said ahead of the Knesset swearing-in ceremony.



Netanyahu has sought to undermine the certified election results after his bloc fell short of a majority. He has repeated unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties “stole” the elections. In a speech following Tuesday’s ceremony, Netanyahu reiterated his claim that Arab politicians, who represent a minority comprising 20 per cent of Israel’s population, cannot be trusted. Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressing lawmakers at the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg He attacked Jewish opposition leaders who have signalled a willingness to partner with Arab parties to form a government. Eisenkot has left that possibility open if the parties meet several conditions, including accepting Israel’s identity as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist group. “I ask you: Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?” Netanyahu said.



Push for a new speaker Eisenkot said Netanyahu’s speech was “divisive” and “hate-filled,” adding: “I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute.” He later said he had cancelled a meeting with Netanyahu’s Likud party planned for Wednesday because of the speech. Eisenkot’s bloc triggered a process on Tuesday to install a new parliamentary speaker as they kicked off work on their legislative agenda. The majority of members submitted signatures calling for the ousting of the current Netanyahu-backed speaker, Amir Ohana, in the first step towards a vote on his replacement. The vote can take place even before a coalition government is in place. The Israeli parliament during the inaugural session following Israel’s legislative elections on October 27. Getty Images



The Knesset speaker is a powerful position. The speaker determines what bills the Knesset will take up, meaning one picked from among the Eisenkot-led opposition parties could propel their legislative agenda forward. The opposition nominated Matan Kahana, a senior member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, for the job. A vote to appoint him speaker could come as early as this week. Netanyahu as caretaker The swearing-in of the new Knesset ushered in an unusual transitional period in Israeli politics – Netanyahu and his cabinet remain in power, while the new lawmakers can introduce legislation. Meanwhile, Eisenkot will meet with party leaders as he works to build a coalition that would be likely to make him prime minister. If he fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to give Netanyahu the next opportunity to form a government.



As caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu faces court-imposed limits on his powers. But he can still pursue appointments and could try to block new legislation. He retains full authority over national security, including the military. Related Article World elections ‘We need Bibi’: How Netanyahu defied the polls Netanyahu has argued that Jewish-led parties should form a unity government to counter the threat of an Iranian attack. He renewed that call Tuesday, urging them to “set aside all other considerations,” and said Israel should work to topple the Iranian government. A governing coalition without Netanyahu could leave him politically vulnerable as he faces an ongoing corruption trial and possible findings of security failures in the lead-up to the October 7 attacks. World.title: Record plunge in investor loans as tax overhaul hits property market
World.content:
PoliticsFederalNegative gearing Record plunge in investor loans as tax overhaul hits property market Shane Wright Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:53pm ,first published 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
