World.title: Trump’s Fed nightmare: Rates won’t be slashed. They could surge now
World.content:
BusinessThe economyInflation Opinion Trump’s Fed nightmare: Rates won’t be slashed. They could surge now Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:34pm , first published 11:59am

Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:34pm ,first published 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If Donald Trump expects Kevin Warsh, his hand-picked chair of the US Federal Reserve Board, to deliver the interest rate cuts that he has continuously clamoured for, he is about to be disappointed. Again. It now appears inevitable that the Fed will deliver its second rate rise in this cycle – the first was in September – after the US inflation rate came in above expectations for the third successive month. He won’t like it, but Donald Trump’s demands for lower interest rates will most likely be ignored by the Fed. Alex Brandon The only question – and just raising it will upset Trump – is whether the US central bank hikes its policy rate by 25 basis points or 50 basis points when it meets again next month. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Tuesday that consumer prices rose 0.4 per cent in October. While calculations are muddied by the fact that a government shutdown meant there was no data collected in October last year, most calculations put the annual inflation rate at 4 per cent.



Even if energy and food costs are excluded to remove the direct effects of the war in the Middle East on oil and fuel costs, “core” inflation in October was 0.3 per cent and the annual core inflation rate 2.8 per cent – well above the Fed’s target of 2 per cent. Moreover, inflation is spreading across the US economy, thanks to Trump’s tariffs and the indirect effects of the higher oil and refined product prices on transport costs that are now feeding into goods and services prices. The only question – and just raising it will upset Trump – is whether the US central bank hikes its policy rate by 25 basis points or 50 basis points when it meets again next month. Fed officials are already preparing the ground for more than one rate hike. Fed governor Christopher Waller (a Trump appointee) told an audience in London on Tuesday that, should the inflation rate for the month come in above 0.3 per cent, a half-percentage point (50 basis point) rate rise might be needed. A conventional 25 basis point rise, he argued, would do little to win confidence that the Fed was serious about tackling inflation.





The inflation rate rose even though oil prices were mostly flat throughout the month. It would appear to be the delayed impacts of higher gasoline and, in particular diesel prices, that are now flowing through the economy and bleeding into consumer prices. The oil price has fallen back this month to trade at around $US92 a barrel and gasoline prices are sliding, albeit they are, at $US3.98 a gallon, still about 30 per cent higher than they were a year ago. Diesel prices are still 65 per cent higher than a year ago. Following the Democrats’ success in the midterms, Fed governors are less likely to feel intimidated by potential administration retaliations if they back rate rises. AP The oil price has been falling because oil flows from the Middle East have been restored to close to pre-war levels (albeit with far higher transport and insurance costs) and because Trump keeps saying that a negotiated end to the war is within reach, although he has said similar things throughout this year, but the conflict has yet to be resolved. With the US midterm elections out of the way, the administration may, however, find it easier to accede to some of Iran’s demands.



Even if the oil price continues to retreat, however, refined product prices – of which diesel is the key product – are unlikely to subside as quickly, as the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine have significantly damaged refinery capacity. The result of the midterms will help the Fed if it starts more aggressively raising US interest rates. That might infuriate the president, but there is little he can do about it. If the wars were to end soon, it would still take well into next year for volumes to recover. In the meantime, the higher cost of transporting goods and food will continue to push up goods and grocery prices. Tariffs remain another contributor to the inflation rate with their stop-start history, thanks to the courts consistently ruling them illegal and the Trump administration’s continuing efforts to reimpose them using new legislative headings. Toy prices, for instance, were 9 per cent higher than a year ago. Auto parts and repairs prices were up 0.6 per cent in October. Then there’s the impact of the boom in artificial intelligence, which is pushing up the prices of semiconductors and impacting the prices of computers, smartphones and other devices as well as electricity prices.



The inflation data underscores why US voters gave the Republicans such a thrashing at the midterm elections. For ordinary US households, the cost-of-living pressures are real and intensifying. Related Article Analysis

US midterms Donald Trump’s humiliation is an opportunity for America The result of the midterms – a Democrat majority in both chambers of Congress – will help the Fed if it, as expected, starts more aggressively raising US interest rates. That might infuriate a president who wanted Warsh to deliver greatly lower rates, but there is little he can do about it. Trump has tried, unsuccessfully, to remove former Fed chair Jerome Powell from the board, threatening to prosecute him for cost overruns in the renovations of the Fed’s Washington headquarters. He’s still trying to unseat another governor, Lisa Cook, with flimsy accusations of mortgage fraud. Even if he were able to sack Cook (there is a handpicked administration panel “investigating” her), or Powell decided to retire before his term ends in January 2028, the Democrats are most unlikely to approve a new Trump nomination to the board. And other Fed governors are now less likely to feel intimidated by potential administration responses to votes in favour of rate rises.



It’s not been a good week for Trump and his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. On Monday, the Congressional Budget Office released its summary of the outcomes from the 2026 fiscal year which, in the US, ends on September 30. The Trump administration presided over a deficit of $US2 trillion ($2.9 trillion), or 6.2 per cent of GDP, a significant increase from the $US1.8 trillion (5.8 per cent of GDP) deficit in fiscal 2025. The administration is spending more (outlays were up 6 per cent) while, thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s tax cuts for companies and the wealthy, generating only 3 per cent revenue growth. Corporate tax revenue fell 16 per cent. Customs revenue fell 11 per cent because the administration had to refund $US126 billion after the US Supreme Court deemed Trump’s original global tariffs illegal. Loading America’s finances aren’t improving. In October, the CBO estimates, there was a deficit of $US409 billion, 30 per cent more than the same month last year, with revenues shrinking and spending growing.



With government debt of more than $US40 trillion and the net interest cost of that debt climbing 11 per cent in the year to September, to $US1.14 trillion, a rising rate environment would only increase the threat to America’s financial stability and its ability to sustain even its modest – by comparison with other developed economies – social security net. Bessent, who promised to lower the deficit-to-GDP ratio to 3 per cent, says economic growth will fix America’s public finances. It won’t, and Trump’s second term will, just like his first term, leave a legacy of unfulfilled promises and unsustainable debt and deficits. Ordinary Americans will be much poorer for the experience. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Past, present and future health champions honour MAPAS pioneer Professor Colin Mantell
World.content:
Generations of Māori and Pacific health professionals have gathered at Waipapa Marae to honour the legacy of the man who helped shape the future of Māori and Pacific medical education.

Emeritus Professor Colin Mantell (Ngāi Tahu) died peacefully on 3 October 2026, leaving behind a remarkable legacy in medicine, medical education, and Māori and Pacific health.

Over a career spanning more than six decades, Mantell helped transform the pathways available to Māori and Pacific students entering medicine. An internationally recognised researcher and specialist in obstetrics and gynaecology, he went on to become the University of Auckland's inaugural Professor of Māori and Pacific Health.

Among his many contributions to the health sector was his role as the founding chair of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS), which sought to grow a health workforce that better reflected and served Māori and Pacific communities.

"He leaves behind generations of doctors he inspired, a grateful community, and a family who loved him fiercely," Mantell's obituary states.

Over a career spanning more than six decades, Professor Colin Mantell (Ngāi Tahu) helped transform the pathways available to Māori and Pacific students entering medicine. Supplied / Wanaka App

Throughout the kawe mate, held on Wednesday at Waipapa Taumata Rau, Auckland University, generations of colleagues and health leaders reflected on Mantell's commitment to creating a fairer health system.

In the late 1990s, Mantell became a driving force behind Vision 20:20, a kaupapa aimed at growing the number of Māori and Pacific people working across Aotearoa's health system.

As part of that vision, the university established a foundation programme for Māori and Pacific students preparing for health professional study, which later became Hikitia Te Ora, the Certificate in Health Sciences.

RNZ/ Layla Bailey-McDowell

Reflecting on the programme, Mantell said at the time, it was important that students did not feel they were "always on the outer, always at risk of failure", and instead received support that recognised their individual needs and potential.

Professor Papaarangi Reid, Tumuaki of Te Kupenga Hauora Māori, said Mantell recognised early that meaningful change in health required a different approach to medical education.

"Generations of students have walked through doors that Colin helped open. His legacy lives in us, in the communities we serve and in the continuing work of MAPAS. We owe him an enormous debt of gratitude."

RNZ / Coco Lance

Among those paying tribute at the kawe mate was Professor David Tipene-Leach, who was involved in the programme's early development.

"Colin Mantell was a visionary," Tipene-Leach told RNZ.

An obstetrician by training, Mantell became concerned by the differences in health outcomes between Māori and Pacific babies and those of non-Māori and non-Pacific backgrounds.

Tipene-Leach (Pōrangahau, Ngāti Kere and Ngāti Manuhiri) said Mantell recognised the need to address those inequities and used his position within the medical school to help grow a pathway for Māori and Pacific students into health professions.

"He grew the MAPAS scheme from two, three entries a year up to the huge number of entries that they have now."

That legacy was echoed throughout the kawe mate, as speakers reflected on Mantell's lifelong commitment to addressing inequities in Māori and Pacific health.

Professor David Tipene-Leach (Pōrangahau, Ngāti Kere and Ngāti Manuhiri). RNZ / Coco Lance

Tipene-Leach said Mantell took responsibility for nurturing MAPA's vision and expanding its reach.

At the time Tipene-Leach began medical school in 1974, there were just three Māori students in his year, and one in the year before.

Today, MAPAS has produced more than 1,000 graduates from the University of Auckland, with dozens of students entering the programme each year.

The tribute comes as MAPAS faces renewed political scrutiny, with debate over the future of targeted admission schemes for Māori and Pacific students.

Tipene-Leach said the programme's value could be demonstrated through the outcomes of its graduates.

A kawe mate was held at Waipapa Taumata Rau, honouring the legacy of Emeritus Professor Colin Mantell (Ngāi Tahu). RNZ/ Layla Bailey-McDowell

"We've heard from the present controversy that's going on around whether we should or shouldn't have a MAPAS scheme," he said.

"We've found that these MAPAS graduates, they pass at the same rates, they stay in New Zealand, they don't go overseas, they are more likely to become general practitioners. And we know there's a shortage of that. They're more likely to go into the regions, into rural medicine, and we know there's a shortage there.

"These are exactly the doctors that we should be training in New Zealand."

After five decades in medical practice, Tipene-Leach said his vision was for a Māori health workforce equipped to serve its own communities.

A Tino Rangatiratanga Flag flies at Waipapa Marae. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

"I've been in practice for 50 years now, and it's always been that we have a Māori workforce that is able to service our community and be the front line of service in our community. But the truth is that what we need is we need allies who are there with us in the battle for good health for Māori people, for Pacific people, in fact, for everybody in Aotearoa New Zealand who at the moment don't get a fair deal."

World.title: Kaitāia mill could close in months with 157 jobs at risk
World.content:
Efforts to save almost 160 jobs at Kaitāia's remaining timber mill appear to have failed.

The Far North town's Triboard Mill, which is owned by Japanese forestry company Juken New Zealand, has been on the market since March.

However, the company said on Wednesday it had been unable to find a buyer willing to take on the current workers.

The news comes just a week after new labour force data showed Northland's unemployment rate was the highest in the country at 8.3 percent.

The two Kaitāia mills were next to each other on the northern outskirts of town.

The Northland Mill produced veneer while the Triboard Mill makes a manufactured wood product used in the construction industry.

According to Workers First Union, the Kaitāia mills are the seventh and eighth wood-processing plants to close around the country in the past two years.

Other mills to have closed include the paper production line at Kinleith Mill in Tokoroa (with the loss of 230 jobs), Eves Valley Sawmill in Tasman (140 jobs), and Karioi Pulpmill and Tangiwai Sawmill in Ruapehu (200 jobs).

Juken NZ executive director Yasufumi Tsuchiya said negotiations to sell the land, buildings and machinery were continuing with a potential buyer, who could restart the mill in future with a new workforce.

If the sale fell through the mill would be closed down and efforts to sell the land and assets would continue.

Either way, the company would stop operating the mill by March next year at the latest.

Tsuchiya said consultation with workers about those two options had started.

Juken's other Kaitāia operation, the Northland Mill, closed in August with the loss of about 60 jobs.

The Triboard Mill had 140 employees but another 17 jobs had been transferred from the closed Northland Mill.

Between then the two mills were the town's biggest employer after Te Whatu Ora/Health New Zealand.

Juken's Northland Mill was shut down in August. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Tsuchiya said the company had made "considerable efforts" to find a buyer willing to keep the mill open with its current staff.

Juken's decision to exit Kaitāia reflected weaker demand in key markets, rising costs - including power - and not enough work to sustain current operations.

The company had another Triboard mill in Wairarapa.

If the sale was successful, the timing of any restart and any future employment opportunities would be matters for the prospective buyer.

"No decisions have been made, and we will carefully consider the feedback we receive from employees during consultation before the Board determines the way forward," Tsuchiya said.

The company looked forward to working constructively with local and central government, and other stakeholders, throughout the process, he said.

Consultation with employees runs until 25 November.

The closure of the town's last mill is expected to have significant downstream effects, with many other companies - including trucking and construction firms - relying on Juken NZ contracts and products.

A sense of shock

Workers First Union organiser Marcus Coverdale said there was a sense of shock among the workers when he visited the mill this morning.

"We were hoping that the offer wasn't going to be an asset sale only, and it was going to include the workforce," he said.

"A lot of people have been there for 30-plus years and they could see the writing on the wall - but you still don't want to hear that you're not going to have employment, whether it's on this side of Christmas or the other side."

Coverdale said there was still hope a sale would go ahead.

"The word around the campfire is the buyer wants a bit of time to get to know the mill operation processes or to have a bit of a clean-out and then consider re-employing people. So they intend to reopen it and employ the local workforce in Kaitāia," he said.

"The problem with that is, and we've seen it in places like Gisborne, if you let the grass grow under people's feet, they go where the grass is greener. So they closed that mill, a buyer purchased it and re-opened it a year later, but by then they couldn't find the experienced staff to run the shifts. And that's the risk you run."

Coverdale said Juken New Zealand would announce its decision on 1 December.

If the land and assets were sold, the company would have four weeks from that date to start the redundancy process. If the sale process was unsuccessful, the company planned to close down the mill entirely in mid-March.

He said the effects would reach well beyond the workers and their families.

"It's all the subcontractors, the logging truck drivers, the delivery companies, all the people that wash the uniforms and clean the buildings … So the wider employment options are going to become more and more limited. And ultimately where the workers spend their wages are going to take a hit," he said.

"Will people be able to afford to go to the pub on a Friday night? Or can they still afford to buy their smoko? If they don't have a job, probably not. So all of those kinds of things are going to affect Kaitāia."

'Calamitous for Kāitaia'

Former Northland Age editor and long-time Kaitāia resident Peter Jackson said the closure would be "a calamity".

He had reported on the challenges facing the mill for decades but was still taken by surprise by this morning's announcement.

"A lot of people, a lot of little businesses around Kaitāia really depend on the wages that mill produces. Without them, it's going to be tough for a lot of people. And the people who were working there of course, it's going to be bloody hard for them. It'll be calamitous for Kaitāia, it really will."

Jackson said the mill had always seemed tenuous, and at the mercy of the market for Triboard going up and down, but had always survived in the past.

It would be hard to replace that number of jobs, he said.

"Jobs up here tend not to be advertised. It's word of mouth, who you know, that sort of thing. There'll be some but not that sort of number. I imagine a lot of these people will have to go on the benefit or leave. Losing the Northland mill was bad enough," Jackson said.

Northland MP Grant McCallum told Midday Report he was still hopeful a buyer would be found for the land and buildings, who would then restart the mill.

Permanent closure would be "a disaster" for the town, he said.

McCallum said he was still working with potential buyers and colleagues in government to help pull a deal together.

"There are some options on the table which we've got to work through. Obviously, we're between governments now, so that will hold things up for a bit, but I haven't given up hope of helping put a deal together that will end up with the mill in some form or another continuing to process logs in Kaitāia."

McCallum said closure of the mill could also have a detrimental effect on Northland already over-burdened roads.

"Unlike the central North Island, where the forests are surrounded by plenty of options in terms of processing or ports and so forth, in the Far North there's 50,000 hectares of forestry north of Kaitāia, and it's a long way from there to a port, which is Northport, and all the roading implications that that brings. So we have to do our best to keep processing of timber of some description in Kaitāia."

World.title: New Zealand's only David Jones store to close
World.content:
The sole David Jones store in New Zealand is to close.

The shop at Newmarket in Auckland is one of 19 stores of the iconic Australian department store that will shut.

The receivers say the stores will remain open for now as consultation with staff is done, but they are expected to shut by the end of the year.

The closures were regrettable but unavoidable if David Jones was to survive as a viable business with a future, they said.

World.title: Private school apologises after 'computer systems issue' halts NCEA English exam
World.content:
A Christchurch private school has apologised after a "computer systems issue" prevented Year 13 English students from completing their NCEA exam on Wednesday morning.

In a letter to parents, St Andrew's College rector Mark Wilson said there had been a significant disruption to the Level 3 English exam.

"The examination commenced as scheduled at 9.30am but was stopped part-way through following a computer systems issue," he said.

"This was very distressing and disappointing for the approximately 120 students affected, particularly given the preparation they had undertaken for this important examination."

The college would not explain what the issue was or answer further questions from RNZ.

Students would receive the grade from their internal examination results instead, Wilson said.

"For external examinations, where a student is unable to complete an examination because of circumstances outside their control, the established process is for a derived grade to be used. As a college, we recognise that some students have been significantly impacted by today's disruption and we are committed to supporting them through this process."

NZQA did not provide schools with sufficient paper-based copies for all students when exams were to be completed digitally, meaning there was not a paper-based exam available for all affected students to move to, Wilson said.

"Having spoken with NZQA today, we understand that digital examination incidents are not unusual and that NZQA receives multiple reports of issues during each examination season," he said.

"St Andrew's College has a robust digital environment with students well supported by devices and network infrastructure. However, as we have experienced today, no digital system is completely immune from disruption."

The problem was addressed and remaining exams would continue as planned, Wilson said.

The college would have sufficient paper copies on hand for future exams in case of any further issues.

World.title: Sports club loses $40,000 of gear in suspected fireworks related blaze
World.content:
A sports club says it has taken years of fundraising to afford gear that has now been burnt in a fire they believe was caused by fireworks.

Police are investigating after a fire at a Hamilton park destroyed thousands of dollars of football gear for junior players.

Witnesess says people were aiming firecrackers at each other at Discovery Park shortly before the blaze. Police ask anyone who saw this to come forward.

Mark Oliphant from Northern United Sports Club said the park was a second home for hundreds of kids during the football season.

"When we all learnt about it (the fire) on the Friday morning, we were despondent really," he told Checkpoint.

He said it would cost the club $40,000 to replace the gear.

Burnt gear included football goals, uniforms, balls, first aid kits, and a pitch line marker.

Oliphant said some of the gear was insured, but not all.

He said the response from the community, as well as neighbouring sports clubs, had been incredible.

"It's been quite heartwarming."

World.title: Victims come forward after late minister named a child sex offender
World.content:
A dozen victims have now come forward saying they have been abused by a Presbyterian minister.

The Presbyterian Church says nine further victims have now contacted the church about abuse at the hands of former minister David Wentworth Pimm after he was named as a child sex offender.

Pimm, who died in 2014, worked as a minister at various churches around the country from 1955 until his retirement in Feilding in 2003.

On 2 November the church said it was working with three of Pimm's victims and believed there were more, so it was naming him to encourage others to come forward for redress.

Executive secretary Reverend Erin Pendreigh said the church had now been contacted by 12 victims in total.

In a church newsletter, Pendreigh said the church's wellbeing coordinator had had a number of emails and phone calls from survivors, most of them indicating they knew others who were harmed.

"It has been interesting to hear from many that they were unaware of our redress system, or of our public apology last year. It took us naming David Pimm for them to realise we wanted to hear from them. For all our previous best efforts last year, the ripple of our intent hadn't reached some of those who had been harmed by us," she said.

"I received one message from a person who had drafted a letter a year ago - after our public apology. They shared of their experience, trying to raise the alarm regarding the behaviour of the minster, and how they felt the system had closed ranks on them and shut their efforts out."

Pendreigh earlier said the Presbyterian parish in Ōpōtiki received complaints about the abuse of a child in 2001 and 2002, followed by a 2010 complaint a victim had been abused in Karamea several decades earlier.

The 2001-2002 complaints resulted in Presbyterian Church disciplinary commission hearings in 2002 and in 2003.

"In 2003, before the end of the hearing, David Pimm resigned from the [Presbyterian Church]. I would speculate that he did so to escape the consequences of the potential findings of that commission, consequences could have included censure and the publication of his name," Pendreigh said.

No further action was taken when he resigned because of the church's rules at the time, which were changed at its 2006 general assembly, she said.

The church deeply regretted Pimm's actions and the harm he had caused and victims were let down, Pendreigh said.

"If you spoke up and were not believed or silenced, or asked to forgive, that was terribly wrong and we are truly sorry.

"We know that one of the Ōpōtiki victims spoke up and was not believed. We believe, sadly, that this is likely to have been the experience of other victims."

The church's culture had changed in responding to historic abuse as a result of the work of survivors and the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, Pendreigh said.

"As our moderator said in our public apology to all our survivors last year, we failed to provide protection and we didn't act when alarms were raised. We did not uphold our own values and commitments to vulnerable children. This breach of trust is unjustifiable and we have such profound remorse that this heart-breaking abuse was allowed to happen."

Pimm was originally from Mataura Presbyterian in Southland and studied to be a Home Missionary, or unordained minister, in Mataura in 1955.

His first position was in Granity-Karamea on the West Coast, where he remained until 1958.

Pimm was known to be involved with children and youth activities on the coast.

He trained as a minister in Dunedin from 1959 to 1961.

Pimm's first parish was in Fortrose in Southland, where he was based from 1961 to 1965, and might have been involved in children's activities in neighbouring parishes in the region.

He was based in Ōpōtiki from 1966 to 1971 and Hawke's Bay from 1972 to 1978.

Pimm was an itinerant minister from 1978 to 1981, the church did not have precise dates for his bases during that time.

He is believed to have been in Titoki in 1979, Southern Urewera in 1979 and in Lauder in Central Otago from late 1979 to 1980.

In 1980 he was in Kelso in West Otago, Riversdale in Southland and Akaroa on Banks Peninsula.

He was then based at St John's in Palmerston North from February 1981 to January 1986, when he retired.

The church said Pimm might have continued to assist in other parishes.

He retired to Knox Presbyterian Church in Feilding in 2003 and remained there for some years.

The church said anyone who wanted to report historic abuse by Pimm, or historic abuse by anyone connected with the Presbyterian Church, was encouraged to contact the church to discuss options or make a claim for redress.

World.title: Armistice Day: 'Remembering the sobering realities of going to war'
World.content:
Today marks 108 years since the guns fell silent after four years of brutal conflict in the First World War.

Armed forces, veteran's groups and civilians have marked the moment across the world with ceremonies and two minutes of silence at 11am.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

Outside Wellington's Pukeahu War Memorial, people were heading to school and work while others paused at the foot of the stairs leading up to the Hall of Memories where today's ceremony was held.

RNZ asked several students what Armistice Day meant to them.

"It's the day the war stopped on the 11th month at the 11th hour and the 11th minute," said one Awakeri School student who was attending the commemoration as a part of the of the school group's camp visit to Wellington.

"I knew what it was, but I didn't know it was happening today," said 17 year-old student Ollie.

Student Malachai Smith-Cakebread says it's important for younger people to learn about the people that fought and died in World War One. RNZ / Bill Hickman

"When we take our history classes we don't really learn about that stuff. We only learn about the American wars and World War Two. I think it's really important that learn about all those people that died for our country," 13 year-old Malachi Smith-Cakebread said

Closer to the memorial, a small crowd braved the Wellington wind at the foot of the memorial.

Mark Varley has the most recent of four generations of his family who served in the military. Michelle Varley says the younger generation need to learn about what happened during World War One and that it can happen again. RNZ / Bill Hickman

"It's always a sad day really, but always good to remember and respect," said Michelle Varley.

"My father did national service and then my grandfather was a career soldier and my great-grandfather and my great-great-grandfather," Mark Varley said.

"Everybody needs to learn from what happened and what may happen again. The younger generation especially needs to understand it 'cause the old ones are gone," Claire Rozendaal said.

Grant Crowley attended today's commemoration wearing medal's from his own 30 years of service as well as his fathers. RNZ / Bill Hickman

Grant Crowley arrived wearing medals from his own 30 years in the armed forces, as well as several of his father's, including his Distinguished Conduct Medal from his service in World War Two.

"It's important to reflect and remember on the end of World War One and also the current people serving overseas. In the UK of course they celebrate Remembrance Day [on the on the second Sunday of November]. It's important that people reflect on this day as they can," Crowley said.

Armistice Day celebrations in 1918 in Dunedin.

Ministry of Culture and Heritage chief historian Neill Atkinson said almost every family and community in the country was affected by the war, with the loss of more than 18,000 lives and thousands more coming home wounded or bearing significant psychological scars.

He said the 1918 celebrations of the signing of the Armistice were muted by the international influenza pandemic, which in two months caused the deaths of up to 9000 New Zealanders, as well as families' concerns for the more than 50,000 soldiers still far from home.

"There was this spontaneous outpouring of jubilation, but it was tinged with a sense of loss and sadness. There were scenes of joy and a lot of imperial fervour perhaps.

"People did gather and that probably helped spread the flu as well so that put a bit of a dampener on the celebrations," Atkinson said.

Armistice Day in Auckland in 1918.

Archival photographs showed thousands of people flooding the streets in the main centres as well as parades of bands and fancy dress in the provinces.

Atkinson said Anzac Day was made a public holiday ahead of Armistice Day in 1916 and typically held more attention in New Zealand and Australia.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

But he said the observance of Armistice and Remembrance Day commemorations was where the country stood alongside Britain, Canada, France, Belgium, the United States, other allied nations and former adversaries, such as Türkiye, in acknowledgement of the sacrifice of war and the vision of a peaceful future.

"The reality is that these are memorials to the shared tragedy, whatever side we're on, and the loss of brave, bright people who were the future of those countries. These are really focussed on 'remember the cost' that the war places on countries and, in particular, places on families," Atkinson said.

Former chief of the Armed Forces retired Lieutenant General Rhys Jones said WWI shocked the world with a scale of trauma and losses previously unseen.

"It's not a victory celebration. It's remembering the sobering realities of going to war and therefore the responsibilities of governments [who] make any decisions about armed conflict to take those decisions very seriously and recognise the impact that they will have on their people," Jones said.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

Jones said the massive conflict that would spring from the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria in 1914 served to underline lessons that remained relevant today.

"Just because the Archduke was killed millions of soldiers then lost their lives. So war should be fought in the manner of which you are trying to achieve the objective.

"And the most important of the lessons out of the First World War is, when you've actually fought the war, and won, then make the world a better place," Jones said.

RSA national president Tony Hill. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Royal New Zealand Returned and Services Association national president Tony Hill said the day had broadened to include the remembrance of the sacrifices of all wars and the more recent military and peace keeping efforts of the country's armed forces.

"This is Kiwis standing up to do the right thing. It gives us another opportunity to reflect on what our veterans are doing even today.

"We've just had elections over the weekend. How cool is that, that we're in a democracy where we can have free and fair elections, because of our people that have gone overseas and continue to do so?" Hill said.

World.title: St Bede's abuse inquiry to cover 50 years of school's history
World.content:
An independent inquiry into historical sexual abuse at St Bede's College will examine whether there were attempts to conceal or suppress any complaints of abuse.

The terms of reference - released six months after the school announced an inquiry - cover nearly 50 years of the school's history and will examine whether it knew, or ought to have known, about complaints of sexual abuse and what action was taken in response.

RNZ earlier revealed that former priest Rowan Donoghue had admitted sexually abusing four boys at the school between 1996 and 2000.

It was then revealed Donoghue admitted sexual abuse to leaders of his religious order, the Society of Mary, in 2007. The order immediately removed Donoghue from public ministry. Donoghue was unable to identify the anonymous complainant and instead of notifying police, the order sent him to Australia for a six-month programme that provided "professional risk assessment and therapy" for people accused of sexual abuse.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

It was also revealed the school was also notified nearly 20 years ago of allegations involving him.

Another priest, former rector Fr Brian Cummings, was also accused of abuse by three different complainants in 1996, 2014 and 2023. Cummings, who died in 2022, "strenuously denied" the allegations.

Following RNZ's reporting, the school said it was investigating what was known historically about Donoghue and how the matters were addressed. That work was being led by the current board and rector Jon McDowall.

Then, after Donoghue was jailed for seven years and eight months, the school announced it had decided to commission an independent investigation.

Former priest Rowan Donoghue has admitted sexually abusing four boys at the school between 1996 and 2000. Nathan McKinnon / RNZ

On Wednesday, RNZ asked McDowall for an update on the investigation, including what the terms of reference are, who the investigator is and when it's expected to be released.

McDowall then sent the school community an update on the inquiry which he said had been scheduled for release on Wednesday.

In the letter, McDowall said: "Abuse happened in our College's history, and it caused deep and lasting harm. I am truly sorry that this happened, and that victims and survivors continue to live with the impact of that harm.

"As I have shared previously, the Board of Proprietors and the Board of Trustees together commissioned an external inquiry. We have taken the time to get the terms of reference right, so that the inquiry can be thorough, fair and independent."

The terms of reference includes investigating the rules, policies, procedures and systems in place at the school to prevent or respond to sexual abuse from 1977 to the present day.

The inquiry would also look at the acts and omissions of St Bede's, its trustees, officers and staff in responding to, or addressing, complaints of sexual abuse.

This includes whether those people were aware, or ought to have been aware, of a complaint of sexual abuse at St Bede's, and what if anything those people did in response to any complaints of sexual abuse. It would also look at whether there were any attempts to conceal or suppress knowledge or reporting of any complaints of sexual abuse.

"For the purposes of the inquiry, a complaint of sexual abuse means any complaint, report, disclosure, allegation or expression of concern made to, or otherwise coming to the attention of, St Bede's, its trustees, officers and staff to the effect that sexual abuse may have occurred, whether or not that complaint, report, disclosure, allegation or concern is later found to be made out."

The inquiry also includes investigating the adequacy of the systems, policies and procedures in place at the school today to prevent any future sexual abuse.

"The inquiry will not investigate or determine criminal or civil liability of any entity or any person or whether any act or omission by that entity or person complied with the law. Nor will the inquiry determine, as a question of fact, whether any particular instance of sexual abuse occurred."

The terms of reference also said the school had received complaints from former students that they were sexually abused by clergy, staff and/or students while at the school.

McDowall said the inquiry is being led by Janna McGuigan, a senior barrister in Christchurch with "experience in conducting sensitive inquiries".

"She will be assisted by an inquiry team, including Bridie McKinnon from the law firm Buddle Findlay. The inquiry is independent of St Bede's, the Board of Proprietors, the Board of Trustees and the Society of Mary."

He said the school was "committed to understanding what it knew, and what it did, about complaints of sexual abuse".

"We do this first and foremost for the survivors, who deserve to have these matters examined honestly and independently, and also for our wider community. Our boys today, and those who come after them, deserve a College that learns from its past.

"As a Catholic Marist school, care for each person is at the heart of who we are, and facing these matters openly is part of living that out."

McDowall said the inquiry would keep the identities of participants confidential as well as all interview notes and any written material they receive from participants.

"Ms McGuigan's report will not identify participants, except on an anonymised basis, without the participant's consent."

The school would not be making any further comment while the inquiry is underway.

The inquiry begins on Wednesday, with the aim of providing a report by May 2027.

A summary of the inquiry's findings and recommendations will be publicly released subject to any privacy and legal limitations.

McDowall said the school today operated with "clear safeguarding expectations, strong oversight, and a culture where student wellbeing comes first".

World.title: ACL battles haven't halted these AFL draft hopefuls
World.content:
In just the second game of this year's footy season, Gus White did not realise he had suffered an ACL injury when he hurt his knee.

"I landed a bit funny and hyperextended my knee … it didn't hurt that bad," he said.

" I went and got scans a couple of days later, the result came back with the ACL, which was really devastating. "

The 18-year-old is one of many teenage footballers vying for a chance in the AFL draft later this month — and is hopeful he will be in contention, despite only playing one full game of football this year.

"I'm obviously really nervous, not having much control over my playing this year," he said.

For months, White has been firmly focused on recovery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

White said he initially sat in the emotions of the injury but quickly shifted his focus.

"I just gave myself 24 to 48 hours to sit in my thoughts and really feel it and from then move on and accept that it's happened," he said.

" 'Control the controllables' was the main goal — and [to] just stay as positive as I could. "

The South Adelaide product just hit the six-month milestone of recovery, a significant halfway mark of an injury that sidelines most players for about a year.

'Every journey's different'

When the injury first happened, White spoke to someone who had trodden the same path a year earlier.

North Adelaide's Memphis Webb injured his ACL last year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

It was round 2 of the 2025 SANFL season when North Adelaide's Memphis Webb injured his ACL.

"The 12 months was long, but I made strategies and figured out ways to get through it," he said.

Webb decided to step away from football for the year as he recovered.

"I learnt a lot about myself, because before that my life had pretty much just been football," he said.

" Obviously it wasn't great not playing footy for a year, but it was almost a blessing as well. "

Webb stepped away from football for a year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The 18-year-old said the recovery process had given him a lot of time to reflect, and had reignited his love for football when finally returned to playing in round 4 this year.

"I was like a little kid again, playing footy for the first time," Webb said.

The midfielder said he was at the match, but not yet back playing, when White did his ACL against North Adelaide in round 2.

"We had a good chat about things to expect for him — I just said, 'Every journey's different, don't try and compare to other people'," he said.

Webb returned to the field earlier this year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

White said Webb was one of the first people he went to about his injury.

"I asked him how he dealt with things and what worked for him, what didn't," White said.

White, who is also a midfielder, said seeing someone else experience the same injury and return to the field after such a hard time was motivating.

"It sort of opens that light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

White says discussion with Webb helped boost confidence in recovery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

'Dream to play AFL footy'

White was invited to the AFL Draft Combine, where top junior prospects undergo physical testing and interviews, but was unable to be involved.

He was hopeful his junior years of footy had been enough to show prospective AFL clubs what he could achieve.

"Ever since I was four years old, it's been the dream to play AFL footy, so if my name were to be called out on draft night, I'll be over the moon," he said.

Webb is prepared for all eventualities. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Webb was also invited to the national combine but instead featured at the state event due to sickness.

While feeling nervous ahead of the draft, he was grateful for the experience so far.

"Not many people my age get to experience this journey that I've been on," he said.

" I'm just looking forward to it, whatever happens will happen. "

The AFL draft will be held over two nights on November 19 and 20.

World.title: Minjee Lee set to end horror 2026 season with Tour Championship absence
World.content:
Minjee Lee will miss the LPGA's rich and prestigious Tour Championship for the first time in more than a decade after calling an end to her deflating 2026 season.

Australia's triple major champion has opted out of The ANNIKA, the all-important penultimate event of the year starting on Thursday, rendering Lee no chance of scraping into next week's $US11 million ($16 million) showpiece in Florida.

Lee hasn't missed the season-ending championship since 2014.

But after slumping from third in the world rankings last October to 24th, her equal-lowest standing in 11 years, the WA superstar has opted for a reset following her last-place finish at the Japan Classic on Sunday.

Battling swing issues, the 30-year-old has slumped to 79th in the season-long point standings, with only the top 60 to qualify for the Tour Championship in Naples from November 19-22.

The 11-times LPGA Tour winner tied for 13th last year, with her best result in the event being a share of seventh on debut as a teenager in 2015.

While Lee will be absent this week, four Australians will be striving to punch their tickets to the Tour Championship at Pelican Golf Club in Belleair.

Perched safely in 11th place in the points race, Hannah Green is also sitting out The ANNIKA tournament.

But Cassie Porter (47th), Grace Kim (51st), Karis Davidson (54th) and Robyn Choi (61st) are all teeing it up.

Currently one spot outside the qualification zone, Choi likely needs a top-30 finish to clinch a maiden berth at the Tour Championship after enjoying a fruitful Asian swing.

Having become the first woman ever to clinch player-of-the-year honours before the Tour Championship, world No.1 Nelly Korda is chasing more history this week.

The American can become the first LPGA professional to win the same event for the fourth time since The ANNIKA tournament namesake Annika Sorenstam in 2005.

Korda also has a chance to become the fifth player in LPGA Tour history to win the same tournament at least four times and the first since Se Ri Pak at the Jamie Farr Kroger Classic in 2003.

AAP

World.title: Warner jabs former Australian coach Lehmann over Sandpapergate sanctions
World.content:
David Warner has fired an indirect jab at Darren Lehmann, suggesting the ex-Australian coach knew of the use of sandpaper in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Warner agreed with former International Cricket Council match referee Chris Broad, who said that Lehmann must have known of Australia's use of sandpaper on the ball, and if he did not, then he should not have been coach.

"Darren Lehmann surely knew all about it," Broad told Track Radio.

"And if he didn't, he shouldn't have been the coach at the time.

"He has got away lightly because he, OK, he left his job a few months later, but he didn't get any sanctions."

Warner replied to Track Radio's social media post of Broad's comments, writing on X: "I couldn't agree more and that's hard for me to say!"

Lehmann, who stepped down as Australia's coach in the aftermath of the 2018 scandal in South Africa, has denied personal knowledge of the Test team using sandpaper on the ball.

"I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann, who will co-host the ABC's cricket podcast this season, told Summer Grandstand on the weekend.

"It's just how it's being done, and how you would know to that extent? That's an individual case-by-case, to be fair.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

Loading...

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Lehmann's comments are at odds with Usman Khawaja's claims the whole team knew of the sandpaper plans, and the illegal tactic was also used in the match prior to being uncovered by television cameras at the infamous 2018 Test in Cape Town.

Cricket Australia (CA) has ruled out reopening its investigation into the scandal.

Warner on Monday night backed Khawaja's claims, labelling CA's investigation as "rushed and botched" after it found only he, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith knew of the plan.

CA banned Smith and Warner from playing any cricket for one year and also suspended Bancroft for nine months. Smith and Warner were also stripped of their respective captain and vice-captain roles.

Paceman Mitchell Starc repeated his denial of the sandpaper plot when he became the first player from the match to front media, citing a statement he and his fellow bowlers made in 2021.

Usman Khawaja's (left) claims that everyone knew about the use of sandpaper has been backed by David Warner (second from left), denied by Darren Lehmann (right), while Steve Smith (second from right) is yet to comment. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"We [bowlers] weren't aware anything was taken on to the field to be tampered with," Starc said on Tuesday.

"We saw [the sandpaper] on the big screen in Cape Town."

Asked why he and Khawaja had differing views, Starc responded: "That's a question for him."

"I'll stick to what I said … at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people."

Australian Cricketers Association chief executive Paul Marsh said on Tuesday it was understandable players' versions of events could differ.

Loading...

"Players and staff at the heart of the issue are entitled to share their experiences, just as others are entitled to put such a challenging period in their life behind them," Marsh said in a statement.

"There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened.

"But we must recognise that there are humans in the centre of this and we are calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

Marsh's statement attracted the ire of former Test batsman Damien Martyn, who posted on X: "This statement from our players union does not reflect all ex players' opinions."

Meanwhile, the author of a review into Australia's cricket culture said he may have been lied to by players.

Simon Longstaff led an Ethics Centre team tasked with examining the sport's culture, but not the sandpaper scandal itself.

"Those matters had been investigated by Cricket Australia, and the findings were concluded," Longstaff wrote in the Australian Financial Review on Wednesday.

"Even so, we picked up whispers — few and very faint — that, perhaps, the public record did not tell the full story.

"All I can say is that if what Khawaja alleges turns out to be true, then I was also lied to.

"It is easy enough to understand how a group of players might perpetuate — either by act or omission — what could turn out to be a lie."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Usman Khawaja makes changes to book tour after tense TV interview
World.content:
Usman Khawaja's publisher Penguin has confirmed that "adjustments" have been made to his book tour following a tense TV interview.

Khawaja's book, Sabr, released on Tuesday, contains an entire chapter titled "Sandpaper" dedicated to Australia's infamous 2018 tour of South Africa, which resulted in Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft being suspended for ball-tampering.

The 37-year-old appeared uncomfortable during an appearance on the ABC's 7.30 on Tuesday night, when he dodged questions from host Sarah Ferguson about the aforementioned chapter.

Khawaja denies starting 'witch-hunt' over Sandpapergate claims Usman Khawaja rejects claims he has reopened some of Australian crickets biggest wounds just to sell copies of his new book as he admits concerns it may have damaged friendships.

In a written statement to ABC Sport, Penguin pushed back on reports suggesting Khawaja's book tour had been cancelled altogether.

The publisher would not confirm what specific interviews had been cancelled, but that "adjustments" had been made.

"The book tour is 100 [per cent] still going ahead, we've just had to make some adjustments this week but no major cancellation of the tour at all," the statement read.

Penguin also confirmed Khawaja will be doing further interviews regarding his new book.

In the 7.30 interview, Khawaja was adamant that he did not want a "witch-hunt" to take place as a result of his claim that the entire Australian team was aware of the plan to tamper with the ball against South Africa.

Khawaja's account has been backed by Warner, who described it as being "100 per cent accurate" in his own statement on Monday night.

Bancroft refused to speak in depth on Khawaja's claims in a short interview with reporters as he arrived at Melbourne Airport prior to a Sheffield Shield clash between Western Australia and Victoria at the MCG this week, while Smith is yet to speak publicly regarding the new book.

Australian paceman Mitchell Starc denied suggestions the bowlers were in on the sandpaper ploy in a media appearance on Tuesday afternoon.

World.title: 'Discrimination' claim as AFLW player delisted weeks out from giving birth
World.content:
The AFLW pregnancy policy has been called into question as Gold Coast Suns player Georgia Clayden was delisted this week, just weeks before she is due to give birth.

Clayden spent this season on the inactive list with "injury (pregnancy)". The club announced on Tuesday that Clayden and fellow player Sienna McMullen were informed they would not be offered contracts for the 2027 season.

Former AFLW All-Australian-turned-commentator Kate McCarthy said more needed to be done to protect and support AFLW players and female athletes who choose to become mothers during their playing careers.

"A player should be able to make the incredible life decision to start a family without fearing it could come at the expense of their football career," McCarthy wrote on Instagram

Loading Instagram content

"There needs to be greater security and a genuine opportunity for players to return to the game after giving birth."

North Melbourne premiership player Eilish Sheerin responded publicly to McCarthy's post: "So well said. In other industries this would be viewed as discrimination."

Last December, former Carlton captain Kerryn Peterson was told by Carlton that she would not be offered a contract for 2026, just months after she gave birth to her first child.

Peterson was placed on the inactive list for this season after welcoming her newborn son, Max, in August, and had planned to return to the Blues the following season.

Essendon welcomed Bess Keaney back onto its list after she had a baby last season. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Alternatively, Essendon's Bess Keaney rejoined her club's primary list this season after having a baby last year. She was placed on the club's inactive list with "injury" (pregnancy).

Rules within the Collective Bargaining Agreement allow for players returning from pregnancy to come off the inactive list at any point.

Replacement players signed in the meantime are then able to see out the entirety of their one-season contract, with the team in question allowed to have a squad of 31 for the remainder of that season.

In order for a player to return from the inactive list after pregnancy, they must be assessed as medically fit by the club doctor or an AFL medical officer.

McCarthy said it was not simply on clubs to offer this, as they needed greater support in this area too and called for policy change.

"With such limited spots in the AFLW, clubs are already forced to make incredibly difficult list management decisions. The current systems put both players and clubs in an unfair position," McCarthy said.

"Clubs should have the ability to retain a player returning from maternity leave without that player occupying one of their limited list spots. This would give the athlete the time and security to work towards returning to the level required, while allowing clubs the flexibility to manage their lists if that player isn't ready to return.

"Becoming a mother should not mean putting your football career at risk. And clubs shouldn't be forced into a position where supporting a player's return comes at the expense of another list spot. We should be creating a system that supports both. Right now, we're not."

World.title: Legends urge Australia to 'move on' from Sandpapergate amid opposing claims
World.content:
Adam Gilchrist has warned Australian cricket must move on from the Sandpapergate saga, with the drama overshadowing the start of the men's summer.

The renewed fallout from the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to dominate headlines just two days out from the first ODI against England, with all focus on Usman Khawaja's book, Sabr.

Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening the investigation into Cape Town 2018, with CEO Todd Greenberg warning a consensus between players will likely never be reached.

Khawaja denies starting 'witch-hunt' over Sandpapergate claims Usman Khawaja rejects claims he has reopened some of Australian crickets biggest wounds just to sell copies of his new book as he admits concerns it may have damaged friendships.

In the past week, Khawaja has claimed that the whole team knew of plans to use sandpaper on the ball, and that it was also implemented in the Test prior at St George's Park, Gqeberha.

David Warner has backed those claims, labelling CA's initial investigation as "rushed and botched" after it found only he, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith knew of the plan.

Mitchell Starc then denied any knowledge of the sandpaper plot when he became the first player from the match to front the media on Tuesday, citing a statement he and his fellow bowlers made in 2021.

Gilchrist said he was unsure what it could do to the Test team, ahead of a nine-month stint in which Australia hosts New Zealand then tours India and England.

But he was insistent the time had come to draw a line under the drama.

Adam Gilchrist (pictured) played 96 Tests and won three one day World Cups for Australia between 1999 and 2008. (Getty Images: PA Images/EMPICS Sport)

Asked what impact the flare-up could have, Gilchrist said: "I don't know, we will have to wait and see.

"I would suspect there are some frustrated guys because there are some differing stories floating around.

"But it's up to them to work out. It's probably best to work it out privately rather than in the public space.

"That's up to them. There are some people who have been deeply affected in a tough way, so they will want to move on from it."

Asked if it could hurt the Test team ahead of a home series against New Zealand in less than a month, Gilchrist insisted it was time to move on.

David Warner (left) has labelled Khawaja's recollection of the events as "100 per cent accurate". (Getty Image: Alex Davidson, ICC)

"If we keep getting daily Instagram updates, it will keep bubbling away," the former vice-captain said at Kayo Cricket's summer launch event.

"Guys have had their say. We've just got to deal with it and move on."

Gilchrist's comments came as former teammate Mark Waugh backed CA's stance of not reopening the investigation.

"We're going in circles with someone saying this and someone saying the opposite. Are we ever going to get to the middle ground?" Waugh said.

"I don't think we will. Because opinions are different. With someone saying this and someone saying that, you can only believe what they're saying.

Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg (right) has suggested the investigation into the incident will not be reopened. (Getty Images: Philip Brown)

"Unless there's other evidence, I don't know where you go with it, so I think you've just got to move on."

Australian Cricketers' Association chief executive Paul Marsh also suggested on Tuesday it was understandable that each player's version of events could be different.

"Eight years on, it is understandable that those involved may have different recollections and perspectives of what took place," he said in a statement.

"Players and staff at the heart of the issue are entitled to share their experiences, just as others are entitled to put such a challenging period in their life behind them.

"There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened.

"But we must recognise that there are humans in the centre of this and we are calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

AAP

World.title: Sinner targeting Australian Open return after earlier 'impossible goal'
World.content:
Two-time Australian Open winner Jannik Sinner says he is targeting the Melbourne major for his big-time comeback as he embarks on the road to regaining his world number one status.

Sinner has lost his primacy in the global rankings after 95 weeks at the summit to Alexander Zverev, having not played since winning Wimbledon in July due to a right knee injury.

"The aim is to go to Australia. The aim is also maybe to do a couple of tournaments first," Sinner told a press conference in Milan on Tuesday.

Alcaraz downs Shelton in final to claim maiden Paris Masters title Carlos Alcaraz wins the elusive Paris Masters for the first time in his career, claiming his fifth title win of the calendar year.

"Right now, I have to respect the protocols because if we rush things we could have more serious problems. I have a ‌lot of faith ‌in the process, ⁠and I'm working toward that objective.

"Initially, we had an impossible goal for my ​return in mind, so we took a different path. I'm a tennis player, not a doctor, so my only option is to trust them.

"I miss playing tennis. Right now, however, it is crucial that I take care of my body, because I want to keep playing for another 10 to 15 years."

Sinner indicated he would probably return to the court in the Six Kings Slam exhibition in Saudi Arabia in late December. The Riyadh event was postponed because of the conflict in the Middle East.

"That [is the target] but we all know the situation what's there at the moment, which is not the best, so this is not our decision as players, this is a more general decision," Sinner said.

Sinner has not played since winning his second-career Wimbledon title in July. (Getty Images/Frey)

"But I think if we want to prepare for Australia [and] I'm not playing since Wimbledon, some matches before might be very helpful."

Wimbledon was the 25-year-old Italian's fifth grand slam title in less than three years, the first being his 2024 Australian Open victory.

His rise to the top was masterminded by Australian coach Darren Cahill, ⁠who stepped down last week after four ‌years at Sinner's side.

Sweden's ​Magnus Norman has joined Sinner's coaching set-up and Cahill backed the pick.

"There's a tweet I wrote ​back in 2013 about how Norman has the ability to improve every player he coaches," he said.

"I wasn't involved in the selection process, but I believe it's an excellent ​choice."

Australia's Darren Cahill (left) is no longer a part of Sinner's coaching set-up. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Sinner said Cahill was like a "second dad" and that ​the ​two would remain close friends, adding that former ​world number two Norman shared many similarities with the South Australian.

"[Norman] ‌worked with [Stan] Wawrinka for many years and has been through a lot," Sinner said.

"He accepts the way we are already working, which is important to me so that I don't have to change everything all over again.

"I need to add 1 per cent each year to improve as a player."

"You have to ask yourself a lot of questions to get inside the mind ​of the ‌player you're coaching — that's how you earn his trust," Cahill added.

"We've built and shaped an incredible team, but 99 per cent ​of what's been achieved is down to him.

"He's the one who goes out onto the court. Everyone else contributes the final 1 per cent, and that's what makes the difference."

AAP

World.title: Khawaja denies starting 'witch-hunt' over Sandpapergate claims
World.content:
Usman Khawaja has defended his version of events about the Australian Test team's 2018 ball-tampering saga in South Africa, after former teammate Mitchell Starc maintained the bowling group had no idea about Sandpapergate.

During a wideranging interview on 7.30, Khawaja stuck to his guns on the issue once again splitting Australian cricket eight years after the infamous Test match in Cape Town when batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball.

Khawaja also denied he intended to start a "witch-hunt" or use the saga to sell copies of his newly released book, while conceding he was unsure if his claims would damage friendships he made throughout his career, especially with current Australian captain Pat Cummins.

"I'm not here to inflame the situation anymore," Khawaja said.

"I'm not here to go on a witch-hunt.

"All I've ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team, and I don't think that's a lot to say.

"I'm not asking a lot from people and I say, 'We were a part of it. That was us.' Let's just take accountability.

"I was here to tell my truth, what I saw, what I felt, and to stick with those three guys that were made out to be the only people who have taken it [accountability]."

The three players Khawaja referred to were his childhood friend David Warner, then-Australian Test captain Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft.

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith speak with umpires during the Test match. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

Smith and Warner, who was the vice-captain, were banned from cricket for 12 months and Bancroft received a nine-month ban.

Warner has since backed Khawaja's version of events "100 per cent", but on Tuesday afternoon Starc told Fox Cricket's season launch that he did not know a substance was taken onto the field to tamper with the ball.

In 2021, Starc joined fellow bowlers Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon in releasing a statement disputing any suggestion they had prior knowledge of ball-tampering plans.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021."

Cummins has not spoken publicly since the release of Khawaja's book titled Sabr: Finding my way in cricket and life.

Khawaja echoed comments made by former coach Darren Lehmann that ball tampering had been around a long time.

"If you read my book … the whole team was the architect," he said.

"Whether one person ball tampers or another.

"And when I say we were all the architects, I mean, we all need to take accountability as a team.

"I've been very clear not naming names."

He also denied his book was forcing anyone else to admit fault.

"I'm not forcing anyone to do anything," he said.

"Pat Cummins is a good friend of mine. Mitchell Starc, other players in the team, Shaun Marsh, Mitch Marsh; they're all very good friends of mine."

Khawaja 'not sure' friendship will survive this

Khawaja spoke to 7.30 about the special bond between him and Cummins, who he said had a "special place" in his heart.

Usman Khawaja and Pat Cummins were longtime teammates. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"I always used to go off the field when they used to spray alcohol, and then Pat Cummins called me back. [That was] the first time in my life I felt really part of the Australian cricket team.

"That's why I've always had so much love for Patty.

" Even when I talk about it now, it's a very emotional time, a very emotional feeling for me. "

Asked if his book might damage that friendship, Khawaja said he didn't know.

"I'm not sure," Khawaja admitted.

"I've been friends with Pat a long time.

"I've given my reasons at the end of the day … I've always stood for my values and what I think is right … but I can't speak for Pat."

Not about selling books, Khawaja says

While Khawaja was also critical of Cricket Australia's investigation of the incident, describing it as being "rushed", he was asked about the timing of the revelations made in his book.

"A lot of people have put up a narrative that I'm somehow gaining from this, but at no stage was sandpaper ever discussed in 2023 when I signed my book deal," Khawaja said.

"My manager didn't even know about it until six months ago. Neither did anyone really at Penguin.

"All they said to me was, 'Write your story.' Whether I wrote about sandpaper or not would not have made one bit of difference.

"When I gave it to them six months ago, they were shocked because I don't really talk about this to anyone.

"I could have taken it out and they couldn't say a word, but I chose to put it in there."

Khawaja, the first Muslim to play cricket for Australia, wrote in the book about his role as a trailblazer for South Asian Australian cricketers.

At times during his career, the issue of racism was raised. Khawaja himself, in his book, says he felt that after Smith was banned, he was not made captain because of the colour of his skin.

Tim Paine became Test captain after Steve Smith was stood down. (AAP: Scott Barbour)

Rather than say being overlooked was racism, Khawaja said it was simply how he felt at the time.

"There's no concrete evidence of that in terms of what I heard," Khawaja said.

"Whenever I talk about racism or anything along those lines, it's how I feel at the time, but yes that's how I felt.

"I caveat that at the same time with a year later, when Tim Paine was captain, I look back on it and I think, actually … Tim Paine was a great captain.

"At the time, I felt a bit aggrieved, but when I look back on it, I actually don't think it was the wrong decision."
